candidates.canonical_topic: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury During Thyroidectomy
candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury During Thyroidectomy. After thyroid/parathyroid surgery, unilateral recurrent-laryngeal-nerve injury usually causes breathy dysphonia, weak cough and sometimes aspiration; bilateral injury can cause stridor/airway obstruction with a surprisingly preserved voice. Not every postoperative immobile fold is a transected nerve—traction neuropraxia, edema, arytenoid injury and preexisting paresis are alternatives. Baseline voice/vocal-fold status matters because a preoperative paralysis changes both oncologic staging and contralateral operative risk. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Many unilateral neuropraxic injuries recover over months; early voice therapy and temporary injection augmentation can improve voice/swallow while recovery is awaited. Persistent unilateral paralysis can be treated with durable medialization/arytenoid procedures or selected reinnervation according to age, glottic gap and prognosis. Bilateral immobility with respiratory compromise is an airway problem first and may require reintubation/tracheostomy or later glottic-widening procedures.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury During Thyroidectomy. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Boards/chief framework: the dangerous thyroidectomy nerve problem is not merely hoarseness—it is bilateral airway obstruction. Know the Berry-ligament/laryngeal-entry danger zone, distinguish RLN from EBSLN deficits, and treat intraoperative loss of signal as information that can change whether you proceed to the second side.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Unilateral injury**: after thyroid/parathyroid surgery, unilateral recurrent-laryngeal-nerve injury usually causes breathy dysphonia, weak cough, and sometimes aspiration. **Bilateral injury**: can cause stridor/airway obstruction with a surprisingly preserved voice. **Key trap**: not every postoperative immobile fold is a transected nerve -- traction neuropraxia, edema, arytenoid injury, and preexisting paresis are alternatives. **Why baseline matters**: preoperative paralysis changes both oncologic staging and contralateral operative risk.
canonical_layers.localize: **Course**: the RLN has variable relation to the inferior thyroid artery but becomes predictably vulnerable near the ligament of Berry and laryngeal entry point. The right nerve has a more oblique course; the left ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. **Anomaly**: nonrecurrent nerve is uncommon but important, especially on the right with vascular anomaly. **Separate risk**: the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve affects pitch projection rather than fold mobility.
canonical_layers.workup: **Preoperative**: document preoperative laryngeal function when voice symptoms, prior neck surgery, invasive/posterior tumor, or other risk factors are present. Many practices obtain broader baseline exams. **Postoperative**: new postoperative dysphonia, aspiration, or breathing difficulty warrants flexible laryngoscopy. **Intraoperative monitoring**: helps identify/assess function but does not replace visual identification. **Loss of signal**: a true loss-of-signal event should prompt troubleshooting of tube/equipment, stimulation proximal/distal to localize injury, and reconsideration of staged bilateral surgery when contralateral nerve risk remains. **Neuromonitoring thresholds**: A good starting EMG amplitude is 500 microvolts or more. Loss of signal means an amplitude under 100 microvolts. If the amplitude does not recover to at least 50% of baseline (about 250 microvolts) within 20 minutes, the risk of fold paralysis is about 80%. Recovery takes about 27 days for type II (global) injuries and 62 days for type I (segmental) injuries. If the first side reads under 250 microvolts, consider staging the contralateral side. Delaying completion thyroidectomy for differentiated cancer by up to about 25 weeks is considered oncologically safe. Most injuries recover in 2-6 months. (H&N Surgery Atlas 2024, Ch 46, pp 481-483)
canonical_layers.manage: **Unilateral, acute**: many unilateral neuropraxic injuries recover over months. Early voice therapy and temporary injection augmentation can improve voice/swallow while recovery is awaited. **Unilateral, persistent**: can be treated with durable medialization/arytenoid procedures or selected reinnervation, according to age, glottic gap, and prognosis. **Bilateral**: immobility with respiratory compromise is an airway problem first and may require reintubation/tracheostomy or later glottic-widening procedures. **Nerve invaded by thyroid cancer**: The RLN is involved in about 33-61% of locally invasive differentiated thyroid cancers, and about 45% of these patients still have normal fold motion before surgery. Type A invasion (epineurium only) can usually be shaved off, with over 80% functional recovery. Type B (deeper) invasion rarely allows clearance without leaving gross tumor. INMSG guidance is to try to preserve a nerve that still works before surgery. (H&N Surgery Atlas 2024, Ch 46, p 479)
canonical_layers.operate: **Technique**: identify the RLN deliberately, minimize traction/thermal injury, and preserve its blood supply. **If transected**: consider primary repair or cable graft/reinnervation when feasible -- it may restore tone/bulk even if normal motion does not return. **If sacrifice required**: when invasive cancer requires nerve sacrifice, plan voice/airway rehabilitation at the same operation. **Staged bilateral surgery**: after loss of signal on the first side of a planned bilateral thyroidectomy, staging the contralateral side can prevent catastrophic bilateral paralysis in selected circumstances.
canonical_layers.teach: Boards/chief framework: the dangerous thyroidectomy nerve problem is not merely hoarseness—it is bilateral airway obstruction. Know the Berry-ligament/laryngeal-entry danger zone, distinguish RLN from EBSLN deficits, and treat intraoperative loss of signal as information that can change whether you proceed to the second side.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Epiglottitis. Recognize epiglottitis/supraglottitis as an AIRWAY EMERGENCY caused by rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic tissues. In children, high-risk findings are fever, severe throat pain/odynophagia, dysphagia, drooling, muffled or 'hot-potato' voice, tripod/sniffing posture, anxiety, stridor, and refusal to lie flat. The post-Hib-vaccine era changes epidemiology but not the emergency: H. influenzae type b is far less common in immunized populations, while non-type-b H. influenzae, streptococci, S. aureus and other pathogens can cause disease. Vaccination status modifies probability; it does not rule out epiglottitis. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Management has three priorities: CONTROL THE AIRWAY, TREAT INVASIVE INFECTION, THEN DE-ESCALATE SAFELY. Keep the child calm, upright, and with minimal unnecessary manipulation; summon pediatric anesthesia, ENT, PICU, respiratory therapy, and operating-room support early. Once the airway is secured, give IV third-generation cephalosporin therapy such as ceftriaxone/cefotaxime for invasive H. influenzae coverage, with additional anti-staphylococcal/MRSA coverage when severity, local epidemiology, culture data, or clinical context warrants it; tailor to cultures and susceptibilities.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Epiglottitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Chief/boards framework: EPIGLOTTITIS = DON'T AGITATE, DON'T FORCE THE THROAT EXAM, DON'T SEND AN UNSTABLE CHILD TO RADIOLOGY. Bring the airway team to the patient, maintain position of comfort/spontaneous ventilation, and secure the airway under controlled conditions before completing diagnostic workup. Then culture and treat as invasive bacterial disease.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Recognize epiglottitis/supraglottitis as an AIRWAY EMERGENCY** caused by rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic tissues. **High-risk findings in children**: fever, severe throat pain/odynophagia, dysphagia, drooling, muffled or 'hot-potato' voice, tripod/sniffing posture, anxiety, stridor, and refusal to lie flat. **Epidemiology**: the post-Hib-vaccine era changes epidemiology but not the emergency. H. influenzae type b is far less common in immunized populations, while non-type-b H. influenzae, streptococci, S. aureus, and other pathogens can cause disease. **Key trap**: vaccination status modifies probability -- it does not rule out epiglottitis.
canonical_layers.localize: **Localize obstruction to the SUPRAGLOTTIS** and distinguish airway severity from diagnostic certainty. The epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, and adjacent tissues may become markedly edematous, creating a small dynamic airway that can deteriorate with crying, instrumentation, sedation, or supine positioning. **Flexible nasolaryngoscopy**: can confirm supraglottic edema in an appropriately monitored, stable patient with immediate rescue capability. It is not a mandatory bedside test in a distressed child. **Differential**: distinguish bacterial tracheitis (toxic child with thick tracheal secretions/crusting), deep-neck infection, croup, foreign body, and anaphylaxis, because their airway and source-control strategies differ.
canonical_layers.workup: **AIRWAY STABILITY DETERMINES THE WORKUP.** In a distressed child, diagnosis is clinical enough to mobilize the airway team. Do not delay for lateral neck film, CT, labs, or throat examination. **If stable**: lateral neck imaging may show an enlarged epiglottis ('thumbprint'), but a negative film cannot safely exclude disease when the phenotype is concerning. After controlled airway establishment, obtain blood cultures and culture of supraglottic material if safely available. Check CBC/chemistry as clinically useful, but no laboratory value replaces repeated airway assessment. Review Hib immunization and immune risk, and consider public-health/infectious-disease implications when invasive H. influenzae is confirmed.
canonical_layers.manage: **Three management priorities**: CONTROL THE AIRWAY, TREAT INVASIVE INFECTION, THEN DE-ESCALATE SAFELY. Keep the child calm, upright, and with minimal unnecessary manipulation. Summon pediatric anesthesia, ENT, PICU, respiratory therapy, and operating-room support early. **Antibiotics**: once the airway is secured, give IV third-generation cephalosporin therapy such as ceftriaxone/cefotaxime for invasive H. influenzae coverage, with additional anti-staphylococcal/MRSA coverage when severity, local epidemiology, culture data, or clinical context warrants it. Tailor to cultures and susceptibilities. Provide ICU care, hydration/analgesia, and monitor for bacteremia or other invasive infection. **Key trap**: steroids are not the defining treatment and should never delay airway/antibiotic management. **Adult supraglottitis**: adult cases are often less fulminant. In one series only 3 of 23 adults needed airway intervention; the rest were managed with humidification, IV antibiotics, close monitoring and, sometimes, steroids. Decide on the airway from the patient's overall appearance, the flexible laryngoscopic view, and airway factors (habitus, mouth opening, neck extension). If intervention is needed, intubate in a controlled setting or perform an awake tracheotomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 61, p 900)
canonical_layers.operate: **Plan a CONTROLLED intubation** in the operating room or similarly resourced environment, with the most experienced pediatric airway operator, ENT present for rescue, difficult-airway equipment ready, and tracheotomy/cricothyrotomy capability appropriate to the child's age. Preserve spontaneous ventilation until the airway is secured when feasible. **Key trap**: profound paralysis/sedation before the team can ventilate the patient can convert partial obstruction to complete obstruction. Expect edema to require a smaller-than-age-predicted endotracheal tube, and secure it carefully. **Extubation**: reassess supraglottic edema after treatment and extubate only when the airway is clearly improved and the team is prepared for reintubation. An audible cuff leak can support but does not independently determine readiness.
canonical_layers.teach: **Chief/boards framework**: EPIGLOTTITIS = DON'T AGITATE, DON'T FORCE THE THROAT EXAM, DON'T SEND AN UNSTABLE CHILD TO RADIOLOGY. Bring the airway team to the patient, maintain position of comfort/spontaneous ventilation, and secure the airway under controlled conditions before completing diagnostic workup. Then culture and treat as invasive bacterial disease. **Board pearl**: know why the classic epidemiology changed -- Hib conjugate vaccination -- but also why the diagnosis still matters. Other organisms remain, under-immunized patients remain at risk, and the consequence of missing progressive supraglottic obstruction is catastrophic. Keep this card distinct from 'Croup vs Epiglottitis': the comparison card asks WHICH BRANCH; this card teaches HOW TO MANAGE THE EPIGLOTTITIS BRANCH.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Empty Nose Syndrome. Consider ENS after turbinate surgery when paradoxical obstruction, suffocation sensation, dryness, or crusting occurs despite a visibly open airway; anxiety and sleep disturbance are common comorbid burdens. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Begin humidification, saline, emollients when appropriate, and coordinated treatment of sleep and mental-health comorbidity while validating symptoms and setting realistic expectations. Use operative history, endoscopy, ENS6Q, mucosal assessment, and a carefully interpreted cotton test. Exclude inflammatory, structural, neurologic, sleep, and psychiatric contributors; no single test is definitive.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with First-Bite Syndrome. Recognize first-bite syndrome by its characteristic timing: sudden, severe cramping or electric pain in the parotid/preauricular region with the first bite of a meal, often maximal with sour or highly salivatory foods, followed by rapid diminution over subsequent bites. The history is often more diagnostic than the physical examination. It classically appears after surgery involving the deep parotid lobe, parapharyngeal space, upper cervical sympathetic chain, or external carotid artery region, but a similar pattern can occasionally herald an untreated parapharyngeal/deep-lobe lesion. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Start with expectation-setting: postoperative first-bite syndrome may diminish spontaneously, and the evidence base for medication is limited. Neuropathic-pain medications or other conservative measures can be tried when symptoms warrant, but persistent meal-limiting pain should prompt consideration of ultrasound-guided INTRAPAROTID botulinum toxin A. Inject the affected gland rather than the overlying skin; benefit can be incomplete or temporary and repeat treatment may be needed.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of First-Bite Syndrome. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl:
BOARDS/CHIEF SPLIT: first-bite syndrome = PAIN on the first bite, sympathetic denervation physiology, and intraparotid botulinum toxin when treatment is needed. Spontaneous first-bite syndrome can be a presenting sign of deep parotid/parapharyngeal or skull-base disease and deserves an anatomic explanation.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Presentation**: recognize first-bite syndrome by its characteristic timing -- sudden, severe cramping or electric pain in the parotid/preauricular region with the first bite of a meal, often maximal with sour or highly salivatory foods, followed by rapid diminution over subsequent bites. The history is often more diagnostic than the physical examination. **Context**: it classically appears after surgery involving the deep parotid lobe, parapharyngeal space, upper cervical sympathetic chain, or external carotid artery region. But a similar pattern can occasionally herald an untreated parapharyngeal/deep-lobe lesion.
canonical_layers.localize: **Localization**: localize the problem to autonomic innervation of the parotid, rather than the TMJ, teeth, trigeminal neuralgia, or recurrent suppurative sialadenitis. **Mechanism**: the leading mechanism is loss or disruption of sympathetic input to parotid myoepithelial cells, with relatively unopposed parasympathetic stimulation when salivation begins. That physiology explains why pain peaks with the first salivary stimulus and then fades during the meal. **Risk factors**: prior deep-lobe parotidectomy, parapharyngeal tumor resection, carotid-space surgery, or sympathetic chain injury makes the diagnosis especially likely.
canonical_layers.workup: **Approach**: diagnosis is usually clinical. Reconstruct the operative history and map the pain precisely -- first-bite onset, parotid distribution, meal trigger, rapid within-meal adaptation, and absence of purulence or inflammatory gland swelling. **Exam**: examine the parotid, oral cavity, dentition, TMJ, and cranial nerves to exclude mimics. **When to image**: imaging is not routinely required in a classic postoperative presentation. But new first-bite symptoms without a clear surgical cause, a palpable mass, cranial neuropathy, persistent pain between meals, or progressive asymmetry should prompt imaging of the parotid/parapharyngeal and upper neck spaces to exclude occult tumor or another structural process.
canonical_layers.manage: **Expectation-setting**: postoperative first-bite syndrome may diminish spontaneously, and the evidence base for medication is limited. **Medical therapy**: neuropathic-pain medications or other conservative measures can be tried when symptoms warrant. Persistent meal-limiting pain should prompt consideration of ultrasound-guided INTRAPAROTID botulinum toxin A. Inject the affected gland rather than the overlying skin -- benefit can be incomplete or temporary, and repeat treatment may be needed. **Key trap**: do not let symptom treatment substitute for tumor evaluation when first-bite syndrome arises without an explanatory operation.
canonical_layers.operate: **Key trap**: do not reflexively reoperate on the gland for first-bite syndrome. **Decision-making**: the advanced decision is whether symptoms are severe enough to justify image-guided or anatomically targeted botulinum toxin treatment, and whether the presentation is atypical enough to demand renewed tumor evaluation. Historical surgical denervation procedures and gland excision carry meaningful morbidity and inconsistent efficacy, so they are rarely preferred solely for this syndrome. **Prevention**: centers on understanding the sympathetic structures at risk during deep parotid/parapharyngeal and carotid-space surgery, while recognizing that oncologic clearance takes priority over preserving a nerve pathway when the two conflict.
canonical_layers.teach:
**Boards/chief split**: first-bite syndrome = PAIN on the first bite, sympathetic denervation physiology, and intraparotid botulinum toxin when treatment is needed. Spontaneous first-bite syndrome can be a presenting sign of deep parotid/parapharyngeal or skull-base disease and deserves an anatomic explanation.

**Trauma context**: **Trauma pearl**: operative injury is the classic traumatic insult. Nonoperative upper-neck or direct parotid trauma may be considered when the depth and location map to the sympathetic pathway. Deep-lobe/retromandibular injury is most intuitive but is not an absolute requirement. The published evidence is sparse, so treat trauma as an uncommon secondary context and investigate unexplained cases structurally.

v41.0 evidence note — Direct evidence for nonoperative blunt or penetrating trauma as a cause of first-bite syndrome is sparse; do not present external trauma as a common or equally established etiology. A causal attribution is anatomically plausible only when the injury could disrupt the upper cervical sympathetic chain, the peri-carotid/external-carotid sympathetic plexus, or postganglionic sympathetic fibers entering the parotid.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Penetrating and Blunt Neck Trauma. For penetrating injury determine platysma violation; for blunt injury consider occult carotid/vertebral dissection, laryngotracheal disruption, and pharyngoesophageal injury. Hard signs include active arterial bleeding, expanding hematoma, shock from neck injury, bruit/thrill, major airway compromise, air bubbling from the wound, or evolving focal neurologic deficit. Soft signs include a nonexpanding hematoma, dysphonia, dysphagia, minor hemoptysis, or subcutaneous emphysema. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Control hemorrhage with direct pressure and resuscitation; do not blindly clamp or probe a neck wound. Use a controlled airway plan with expert surgical backup when laryngotracheal disruption is suspected. Stable patients without operative indications receive selective CTA-based observation and serial examinations rather than mandatory Zone-II exploration. Suspected perforation requires prompt multidisciplinary evaluation, infection prevention, and timely repair or carefully selected nonoperative care. Perform the primary trauma survey with cervical-spine precautions.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Penetrating and Blunt Neck Trauma. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Resuscitation plus hard-versus-soft signs first. Stable patients receive selective CTA/no-zone assessment; unstable hemorrhage demands control. A negative CTA alone cannot clear a concerning esophageal trajectory. Blunt injury needs mechanism-based cerebrovascular screening.

canonical_layers.recognize: For penetrating injury, determine platysma violation. For blunt injury, consider occult carotid/vertebral dissection, laryngotracheal disruption, and pharyngoesophageal injury. **Hard signs**: active arterial bleeding, expanding hematoma, shock from neck injury, bruit/thrill, major airway compromise, air bubbling from the wound, or evolving focal neurologic deficit. **Soft signs**: a nonexpanding hematoma, dysphonia, dysphagia, minor hemoptysis, or subcutaneous emphysema. **Mechanism clues**: Neck stab wounds injure the subclavian vessels more often than gunshots, because the knife slides downward over the clavicle. Transcervical (midline-crossing) gunshots carry very high vascular/aerodigestive injury rates. In children, stabbings predominate and aerodigestive injuries are more common than vascular ones. A hypoglossal deficit or Horner syndrome implies carotid sheath injury. About 30% of carotid injuries present with a neurologic deficit. Mandatory exploration is negative in 50-70%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1842) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1844) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1845)
canonical_layers.localize: **Zones**: classic zones describe exposure -- Zone I clavicle-to-cricoid, Zone II cricoid-to-mandibular angle, Zone III angle-to-skull base -- but stable penetrating trauma is commonly evaluated with a selective no-zone pathway. Map trajectory to carotid/vertebral vessels, jugular veins, larynx/trachea, pharynx/esophagus, cervical spine, and cranial nerves. Blunt cerebrovascular screening is mechanism/risk based.
canonical_layers.workup: Perform the primary trauma survey with cervical-spine precautions. Unstable patients or hard signs requiring immediate control proceed to operative/endovascular management without routine imaging delay. Stable, selected patients undergo CTA based on mechanism and findings. **Key trap**: CTA alone cannot exclude all esophageal injuries when trajectory, symptoms, air, or CT changes remain suspicious -- add contrast evaluation and/or esophagoscopy. Use flexible laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy for suspected airway injury. **Cord injury without fracture**: because the pediatric spine is flexible, significant spinal cord injury can occur with a normal bony CT (SCIWORA), so a complete neurologic exam and MRI—not CT alone—clear the cord. MRI also clears the neck for positioning in children who cannot cooperate. Concomitant cord injury accompanies about 25% of severe cervical spine injuries, and nerve root injury another 25%. Confusion or combativeness may be hypoxia rather than brain injury, so check oximetry before sedating. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Neck", p 1853, 1858) **Guideline nuances**: ACR 2017 recommends CTA first for stable patients without life-threatening injury. Internal injury does not match the external zone in about 27% of cases, which supports the no-zone approach. The Western Trauma Association still advises exploration and/or endoscopy for symptomatic zone II wounds. If CTA is normal but aerodigestive injury is still suspected, obtain an esophagram: water-soluble contrast first, then barium if negative and suspicion persists. Flexible esophagoscopy misses injuries near the cricopharyngeus, and combining flexible with rigid endoscopy missed none in reported series. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1845) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1849)
canonical_layers.manage: Control hemorrhage with direct pressure and resuscitation. **Key trap**: do not blindly clamp or probe a neck wound. Use a controlled airway plan with expert surgical backup when laryngotracheal disruption is suspected. Stable patients without operative indications receive selective CTA-based observation and serial examinations rather than mandatory Zone-II exploration. Suspected perforation requires prompt multidisciplinary evaluation, infection prevention, and timely repair or carefully selected nonoperative care. **Pediatric ATLS points**: jaw thrust (never chin tilt) and orotracheal intubation with in-line stabilization. Needle rather than surgical cricothyroidotomy below about age 11–12 because the cricothyroid membrane is tiny, and tracheotomy in an unintubated child is hard because soft cartilage is difficult to palpate. Hypoventilation is the leading cause of pediatric cardiac arrest (infants breathe 40–60/min). Blood pressure stays normal until 25–30% of blood volume is lost, so tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and weak pulses are the early shock signs. Use two large-bore IVs or intraosseous access, warm all fluids, and grade neurologic status with the pediatric GCS or AVPU. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Neck", p 1852) **Observation and repair timing**: Observed patients need physician examination at least three times per 24 h for 48-72 h, because most vascular injuries declare within 48 h. Repair laryngeal mucosal lacerations within 24 h. Simple tracheal lacerations can be closed without tracheostomy, but gunshot wounds to the trachea get a tracheostomy for about 6 weeks. Close esophageal injuries in two layers with drainage, and place a strap muscle flap between the tracheal and esophageal repairs to prevent TE fistula. Extensive injuries may need a lateral esophagostomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1850) **Blunt cervical artery dissection**: Vertebral or carotid dissection from blunt trauma or transverse foramen fracture can cause posterior circulation or hemispheric stroke. K.J. Lee gives heparin then warfarin for about 3 months, with antiplatelet therapy when bleeding risk is high. **Current view**: trials (CADISS, TREAT-CAD) and trauma guidelines show antiplatelet therapy, usually aspirin, works as well as anticoagulation, so it is the usual first-line choice. Endovascular stenting or sacrifice is reserved for selected lesions, and most heal within about 6 weeks. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 131-132)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: ongoing major hemorrhage, expanding hematoma, threatened airway, or demonstrated vascular/aerodigestive injury needing repair. Obtain proximal/distal vascular control when possible, and select exposure by trajectory rather than enlarging a contaminated entry wound blindly. Inspect and repair/drain associated pharyngeal, esophageal, and airway injuries. **Key trap**: avoid reflexive intubation across suspected laryngotracheal separation. **Vascular exposure**: Approach zone I injuries on the right through a median sternotomy and on the left through a left anterior thoracotomy. For zone III ICA bleeding, use Foley/Fogarty balloon tamponade, or pass a No. 4 Fogarty through a shunt beyond the injury. Mandibulotomy or endovascular embolization may be needed. Ligate ECA branches and veins freely, but if both IJVs are injured, repair one. Ligate the CCA/ICA only for irreparable injury or a comatose patient with fixed pupils. In a hematoma, find the carotid by tracing the facial or superior thyroid artery retrograde. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1843) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1848)
canonical_layers.teach: Resuscitation plus hard-versus-soft signs first. Stable patients receive selective CTA/no-zone assessment; unstable hemorrhage demands control. A negative CTA alone cannot clear a concerning esophageal trajectory. Blunt injury needs mechanism-based cerebrovascular screening. **Textbook numbers behind selective management**: about 5-15% of aerodigestive injuries are asymptomatic at first, and pharyngoesophageal injury is the most commonly missed neck injury. Repair pharyngoesophageal tears primarily if found within about 24 hours. Later ones generally need drainage or diversion. Contrast studies should start with water-soluble contrast. Carotid injuries carry about 10-20% mortality. Repair is preferred over ligation, especially in a patient without an established stroke. Vertebral artery injuries are usually embolized. Historically, 50-70% of mandatory zone II explorations were negative, which drove the move to selective and CTA-based care. Pasha measures zone I from the sternal notch (clavicles) to the cricoid. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 664-666, 668)

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Frey Syndrome. Recognize Frey syndrome as gustatory sweating, warmth, flushing, or tingling over the preauricular/temporal skin during eating after parotid-region surgery or trauma. Symptoms often emerge months after parotidectomy rather than immediately postoperatively. Ask specifically about sweating or erythema triggered by chewing or salivatory foods; mild disease is commonly underreported unless the history is elicited. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the patient, not a positive starch test. Mild/nonbothersome symptoms can be observed; topical antiperspirant or anticholinergic therapy may help selected patients. For bothersome disease, map the symptomatic field and inject botulinum toxin A INTRADERMALLY in a grid over the involved skin. Response is typically strong but recurrence can require repeat injections.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Presentation**: recognize Frey syndrome as gustatory sweating, warmth, flushing, or tingling over the preauricular/temporal skin during eating, after parotid-region surgery or trauma. **Timing**: symptoms often emerge months after parotidectomy rather than immediately postoperatively. **History**: ask specifically about sweating or erythema triggered by chewing or salivatory foods. Mild disease is commonly underreported unless the history is elicited.
canonical_layers.localize: **Mechanism**: localize the problem to aberrant autonomic reinnervation across the parotid bed. Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers that previously traveled with the auriculotemporal nerve toward the parotid can regenerate into denervated cutaneous sweat glands and superficial vessels. Salivatory stimulation is therefore misdirected into sweating and vasodilation of the overlying skin. **Key contrast**: this is fundamentally different from first-bite syndrome, which is a pain syndrome linked to altered sympathetic-parasympathetic balance rather than aberrant reinnervation of sweat glands.
canonical_layers.workup: **Workup**: a characteristic history is usually sufficient for clinically significant Frey syndrome. Document the surface area and severity of gustatory sweating/flushing and how much it affects quality of life. **Minor starch-iodine test**: can objectively map the involved skin. Iodine is applied and allowed to dry, starch is added, and gustatory stimulation produces a dark color change where sweating occurs. **Imaging**: routine imaging is unnecessary unless the examination or history raises a separate concern for recurrent disease or another structural problem.
canonical_layers.manage: **Key concept**: treat the patient, not a positive starch test. **Mild/nonbothersome symptoms**: can be observed; topical antiperspirant or anticholinergic therapy may help selected patients. **Bothersome disease**: map the symptomatic field and inject botulinum toxin A INTRADERMALLY in a grid over the involved skin. Response is typically strong, but recurrence can require repeat injections. **Prevention at the index operation**: an interposition barrier such as SMAS/temporoparietal fascia, SCM, or acellular dermal material may reduce Frey syndrome in selected reconstructions, but prevention must remain subordinate to oncologic margins, facial-nerve safety, and reconstructive needs.
canonical_layers.operate: **Prevention** is more relevant surgically than late reoperation. During parotidectomy, interposition of tissue between the skin flap and parotid bed -- such as a SMAS flap, temporoparietal fascia flap, sternocleidomastoid flap, dermal-fat graft, or other barrier in selected cases -- can reduce aberrant parasympathetic reinnervation and may also improve contour. Choice depends on defect size, oncologic constraints, prior treatment, surgeon preference, and donor-site tradeoffs. **Established disease**: once symptomatic Frey syndrome is established, botulinum toxin is generally favored over surgical attempts at denervation because it is effective and far less morbid.
canonical_layers.teach: BOARDS/CHIEF SPLIT: Frey = gustatory SWEATING/FLUSHING, aberrant parasympathetic reinnervation, Minor test for mapping, and intradermal botulinum toxin. First-bite syndrome = gustatory PAIN that is maximal on the first bite, a sympathetic-denervation phenotype, and botulinum toxin delivered into the parotid gland rather than the skin.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Anaphylaxis. Suspect anaphylaxis with acute onset (minutes to a couple of hours) of illness involving skin/mucosa (urticaria, flushing, angioedema) PLUS respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxia) and/or hypotension/end-organ dysfunction, or hypotension alone after exposure to a likely allergen (a known allergen just before a skin test, the build-up/maintenance phase of SCIT, a new medication, food, or insect sting), or two or more organ systems (skin/mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, persistent GI symptoms) involved after any allergen exposure. Skin/mucosal findings are present in the large majority of cases but are absent often enough that their absence must never be used to rule anaphylaxis out, especially when hypotension or airway symptoms follow a clear allergen trigger. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Epinephrine is first-line and should be given immediately, intramuscularly in the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis), at a standard weight-based dose of 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) concentration, to a maximum single dose of 0.3 mg in children and 0.5 mg in adults; auto-injectors deliver fixed doses (commonly 0.1 mg, 0.15 mg, or 0.3 mg tiers by weight).
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Anaphylaxis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: BOARD PEARL: epinephrine is never contraindicated in true anaphylaxis, and the most common preventable error is delaying it while reaching for diphenhydramine or waiting to "see if it gets worse." Learn the vasovagal-versus-anaphylaxis discriminator cold: bradycardia + pallor + diaphoresis + rapid resolution with recumbency = vasovagal; tachycardia + urticaria/angioedema/wheeze + persistent hypotension despite positioning = anaphylaxis, treat with epinephrine.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Diagnostic criteria** -- suspect anaphylaxis with acute onset (minutes to a couple of hours) of: illness involving skin/mucosa (urticaria, flushing, angioedema) PLUS respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxia) and/or hypotension/end-organ dysfunction; OR hypotension alone after exposure to a likely allergen (a known allergen just before a skin test, the build-up/maintenance phase of SCIT, a new medication, food, or insect sting); OR two or more organ systems (skin/mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, persistent GI symptoms) involved after any allergen exposure. **Key trap**: skin/mucosal findings are present in the large majority of cases but are absent often enough that their absence must never be used to rule anaphylaxis out, especially when hypotension or airway symptoms follow a clear allergen trigger.
canonical_layers.localize: **Mechanism**: a systemic type I (IgE-mediated) or, less commonly, non-IgE mast-cell/basophil degranulation process. **Mediators**: preformed and newly synthesized mediators (histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, platelet-activating factor) cause vasodilation and increased vascular permeability (hypotension, flushing, angioedema), bronchoconstriction (wheeze, dyspnea), and increased mucus/GI smooth-muscle activity (cramping, vomiting, diarrhea) essentially simultaneously across organ systems. **Key distinction**: this is distinct from a single-organ allergic reaction (isolated urticaria, isolated bronchospasm) and distinct from a **vasovagal (neurocardiogenic)** reflex, which is a transient, self-limited autonomic response to pain, fear, or the sight of a needle rather than mediator release.
canonical_layers.workup: **Diagnosis**: anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis made in real time from the history and exam. **Key trap**: do not delay epinephrine to obtain a tryptase level or wait for laboratory confirmation. **Serum tryptase**: drawn acutely (roughly **15 minutes to 3 hours** after symptom onset) and compared with a baseline level can support the diagnosis retrospectively, particularly when the presentation was atypical or hypotension was the dominant feature. A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis (especially food-triggered reactions). **Bedside discriminator from vasovagal syncope**: anaphylaxis typically produces tachycardia, urticaria/flushing/angioedema, bronchospasm, or persistent hypotension that does NOT resolve simply by lying the patient flat. Vasovagal syncope classically produces bradycardia, pallor, diaphoresis, and transient hypotension that resolves promptly with recumbency/leg elevation, and has no urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, or persistent cardiovascular compromise.
canonical_layers.manage: **First-line treatment**: **epinephrine**, given immediately, intramuscularly in the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis), at a standard weight-based dose of **0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (1 mg/mL)** concentration, to a maximum single dose of **0.3 mg in children** and **0.5 mg in adults**. Auto-injectors deliver fixed doses (commonly **0.1 mg, 0.15 mg, or 0.3 mg** tiers by weight). **If symptoms do not improve**: epinephrine is commonly repeated every **5-15 minutes** as needed. A patient who does not respond after two doses, or who has refractory hypotension/bronchospasm, needs emergency-level care (IV fluids, oxygen, positioning supine with legs elevated if tolerated, and consideration of an epinephrine infusion) rather than escalating doses of second-line agents. **Adjuncts**: antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts for cutaneous/itch symptoms and (unproven) theoretical biphasic-reaction prevention, respectively. **Key trap**: they do NOT treat the airway/hemodynamic emergency and must never be substituted for or given before epinephrine. **Observation**: after stabilization, observe the patient (commonly on the order of several hours, longer for severe reactions, reactions requiring more than one epinephrine dose, or patients with asthma or poor access to care), because a **biphasic reaction** -- recurrence of symptoms without re-exposure, typically within **8-10 hours** but reported up to about **72 hours** later -- occurs in a meaningful minority of cases. **Discharge**: every patient treated for anaphylaxis should be prescribed and taught to use an epinephrine auto-injector and referred for allergy evaluation before discharge. **Epinephrine route (book vs current)**: Older allergy texts, including this chapter's SCIT reaction protocol, give epinephrine 0.3 mL subcutaneously, along with lying the patient flat, oxygen, IV fluids, a proximal tourniquet, IV diphenhydramine and a steroid. Current guidelines instead give 1 mg/mL epinephrine intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh, 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg in adults, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed. Intramuscular dosing reaches peak levels faster and is the board answer. Late reactions can follow apparent recovery, so observe the patient. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, p 1146)
canonical_layers.operate: **Key point**: there is no operative treatment for anaphylaxis itself. **Otolaryngologist's operative-adjacent role**: airway management when laryngeal edema/angioedema threatens obstruction. Have a low threshold for early, controlled airway intervention (including surgical airway readiness) if stridor, voice change, or rapidly progressive oropharyngeal/laryngeal swelling is present, since airway anatomy can become unsalvageable by direct laryngoscopy or intubation if intervention is delayed. **Office competency**: anyone who performs allergy skin testing or administers SCIT (a required otolaryngology-office competency) must have epinephrine, appropriate resuscitation equipment, and a rehearsed anaphylaxis protocol immediately available, and must observe patients through the standard post-injection window -- precisely because office-based immunotherapy is a recognized cause of anaphylaxis.
canonical_layers.teach: **Board pearl**: epinephrine is never contraindicated in true anaphylaxis. The most common preventable error is delaying it while reaching for diphenhydramine or waiting to 'see if it gets worse.' **Discriminator to know cold**: bradycardia + pallor + diaphoresis + rapid resolution with recumbency = **vasovagal**. Tachycardia + urticaria/angioedema/wheeze + persistent hypotension despite positioning = **anaphylaxis**, treat with epinephrine. **Dose to know by heart**: **0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 IM** in the anterolateral thigh, max **0.3 mg (child) / 0.5 mg (adult)**, repeat roughly every **5-15 minutes** as needed. **Key point**: a reaction can recur hours later (biphasic reaction), which is why observation and auto-injector prescription at discharge are part of the standard of care, not optional extras.

candidates.prompt: A patient with sleep-disordered breathing is reviewed in sleep clinic. Central Sleep Apnea / Treatment-Emergent CSA is being considered. Central apnea is cessation/reduction of airflow with absent or reduced respiratory effort; it occurs in several phenotypes including heart failure/Cheyne-Stokes, opioid-related, medical-condition, high-altitude, primary and treatment-emergent CSA. When is Central Sleep Apnea / Treatment-Emergent CSA indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
candidates.answer_text: This is usually medical sleep management, not upper-airway surgery. The procedural advanced decision is recognizing when implantable phrenic-nerve stimulation is appropriate after phenotype-specific noninvasive therapy.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the operate layer of Central Sleep Apnea / Treatment-Emergent CSA. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Do not send central apnea to airway surgery. First ask whether respiratory effort is absent, why ventilatory control is unstable, and whether hypercapnia suggests a different hypoventilation disorder.

canonical_layers.recognize: Central apnea is cessation/reduction of airflow with absent or reduced respiratory effort; it occurs in several phenotypes including heart failure/Cheyne-Stokes, opioid-related, medical-condition, high-altitude, primary and treatment-emergent CSA.
canonical_layers.localize: Most CSA reflects unstable ventilatory control around the CO2 apneic threshold rather than upper-airway collapse. Hypoventilation disorders are mechanistically distinct and should not be mislabeled CSA.
canonical_layers.workup: Use PSG pattern, medication/opioid history, cardiac/neurologic context and gas-exchange data to classify the cause. Persistent hypercapnia points toward hypoventilation rather than classic post-hyperventilation CSA.
canonical_layers.manage: Treat the underlying condition and choose PAP/oxygen/acetazolamide/ASV or other therapy according to CSA phenotype and comorbidity. Current AASM guidance also includes transvenous phrenic-nerve stimulation as an option for selected persistent CSA.
canonical_layers.operate: This is usually medical sleep management, not upper-airway surgery. The procedural advanced decision is recognizing when implantable phrenic-nerve stimulation is appropriate after phenotype-specific noninvasive therapy.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Unilateral obstruction, bleeding, unilateral polyposis, facial numbness, orbital symptoms or unilateral sinus opacification deserves a different differential than routine bilateral inflammatory CRS. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the cause: odontogenic/inflammatory disease, fungal disease, benign neoplasm or malignancy each requires a different pathway. Red flags should accelerate tissue diagnosis and multidisciplinary planning.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Unilateral Sinonasal Disease. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Unilateral disease is a diagnostic category, not a diagnosis. The board pearl is to resist labeling unilateral polyps/opacification as ordinary CRS until neoplasm, odontogenic disease and skull-base pathology are considered.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Red flags**: unilateral obstruction, bleeding, unilateral polyposis, facial numbness, orbital symptoms, or unilateral sinus opacification deserve a different differential than routine bilateral inflammatory CRS. **Foundation**: unilateral disease is a diagnostic phenotype, not a diagnosis. **Differential**: keep odontogenic disease, fungal ball/invasive fungal disease, benign tumor (including papilloma), malignancy, foreign body/local obstruction, and -- when anatomy or history suggests it -- skull-base/CSF or vascular pathology in the differential, rather than defaulting to routine bilateral inflammatory CRS logic. **Antrochoanal polyp and pediatric foreign body**: An antrochoanal polyp is a solitary polyp from the maxillary antrum that passes through the ostium into the choana and nasopharynx, typically in a child or young adult with unilateral obstruction. Histology lacks the eosinophilia of polyposis. Cure requires endoscopic removal of the intrasinus pedicle (antral portion), not just the nasal part. A nasal foreign body or rhinolith is the most common cause of unilateral purulent rhinorrhea in children. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 17-18) **Antrochoanal polyp**: a solitary, unilateral polyp that arises in the maxillary antrum and passes, usually through the posterior fontanelle or an accessory ostium, back to the choana, causing one-sided obstruction (classically in adolescents and young adults). Image or biopsy it to exclude neoplasm before 'polypectomy.' Recurrence is unlikely only if the antral attachment is fully removed (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 687).
canonical_layers.localize: Localize to nasal cavity versus specific sinus, then assess orbit, skull base, pterygopalatine/infratemporal spaces and dental origin based on symptoms and imaging.
canonical_layers.workup: **Initial workup**: perform endoscopy and review dedicated CT; add contrast MRI when tumor, skull-base/orbital extension, perineural spread, or indeterminate soft tissue is a concern. **Biopsy**: suspicious accessible lesions when safe, avoiding blind biopsy of potentially vascular or skull-base lesions. **Application -- history**: deliberately ask about epistaxis, foul smell, dental disease/procedures, immunocompromise, facial numbness, vision change, proptosis, cranial neuropathy, severe focal pain, prior surgery/trauma, and clear positional rhinorrhea. **Imaging**: perform nasal endoscopy and obtain CT to define sinus of origin, dentition, calcification/hyperdensity, remodeling versus destructive bone change, and skull-base/orbital relationships. **MRI**: for a suspected sinonasal mass or concern for skull-base, orbital, intracranial, or perineural extension, add contrast-enhanced MRI for soft-tissue mapping rather than relying on CT alone.
canonical_layers.manage: **Principle**: treat the cause -- odontogenic/inflammatory disease, fungal disease, benign neoplasm, or malignancy each requires a different pathway. **Red flags**: should accelerate tissue diagnosis and multidisciplinary planning. **Senior decision**: route management to the cause instead of treating 'unilateral disease' as one entity. Odontogenic disease needs dual ENT/dental confirmation and source control. Fungal disease follows noninvasive versus invasive pathways. A persistent unilateral mass/polyp needs tumor-level evaluation. CSF or vascular concern requires skull-base/vascular-safe planning. **Key trap**: do not repeatedly prescribe empiric CRS therapy when unilateral red flags or objective focal pathology demand tissue diagnosis or disease-specific treatment.
canonical_layers.operate: **Before surgery**: know whether the lesion could be vascular, encephalocele/CSF-related, or malignant. **Key decision**: often choosing biopsy versus definitive resection and defining the safe surgical corridor. **Safe-tissue/bailout rule**: before reflexively biopsying a unilateral lesion, review imaging and anatomy for features suggesting vascular pathology or intracranial/skull-base continuity, where an office biopsy could be dangerous. **When tissue is appropriate**: plan it so pathology can answer the actual differential. **Escalate urgently for**: necrosis in an at-risk host, orbital findings, cranial neuropathy, major epistaxis, or intracranial signs -- these findings override routine elective sinus sequencing. **Antrochoanal polyp technique**: removing the intra-antral portion is the key to avoiding failure. Use angled endoscopes and curved powered instruments through a middle meatal antrostomy, and add a small temporary inferior meatal window, a canine fossa/sublabial puncture, or a mega-antrostomy (resecting the mid-inferior turbinate down to the floor) when needed. Caldwell-Luc mucosal stripping is unnecessary (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 687).
canonical_layers.teach: **Concept**: unilateral disease is a diagnostic category, not a diagnosis. **Board pearl**: resist labeling unilateral polyps/opacification as ordinary CRS until neoplasm, odontogenic disease, and skull-base pathology are considered. **Senior unilateral rule**: asymmetry should widen the differential before it narrows it. **Workup**: endoscopy + CT localize the process; dental assessment confirms suspected dental causality; MRI adds soft-tissue/skull-base/orbital/perineural definition when a mass or extension is suspected. **Bailout**: stop before unsafe biopsy or routine CRS treatment when vascular, intracranial, invasive-fungal, orbital, or malignant disease remains plausible.

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Children with cleft palate/craniofacial syndromes commonly have chronic OME/hearing loss, velopharyngeal dysfunction, nasal obstruction and sleep-disordered breathing that evolve with growth and reconstruction. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat hearing loss proactively, use tubes when indicated, and coordinate VPI/airway treatment with speech outcomes. Avoid fixing one problem in a way that predictably worsens another.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Cleft / Craniofacial Otologic-Airway Care. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Cleft care is longitudinal systems care: ears, speech and sleep share the same altered anatomy.

canonical_layers.recognize: Children with cleft palate/craniofacial syndromes commonly have chronic **OME**/hearing loss, velopharyngeal dysfunction, nasal obstruction, and sleep-disordered breathing that evolve with growth and reconstruction. Children with cleft palate are prone to persistent otitis media with effusion (OME), conductive hearing loss, and sometimes recurrent acute otitis media (AOM). **Key distinction**: distinguish the highly prevalent effusion from recurrent acute infection, which is NOT inevitable. **Treacher Collins airway threshold**: Treacher Collins syndrome (autosomal dominant, TCOF1 on 5q32) is a bilateral expression of Tessier clefts 6, 7 and 8, with malar and zygomatic hypoplasia, a hypoplastic mandible, microtia, ossicular malformation with conductive loss, and sometimes absent parotid glands. An oropharyngeal airway diameter under 1 cm is linked to sudden death and is an indication for tracheotomy. Mandibular distraction often allows later decannulation; bone-anchored hearing devices address the conductive loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1172) **Down syndrome oral and airway features**: Children with trisomy 21 develop progressive lip enlargement, true or relative macroglossia with a fissured tongue by about age 5, a high narrow palate, a narrow nasopharynx (platybasia), pharyngeal hypotonia, delayed and missing teeth, and periodontal disease. Their chronic rhinorrhea and otitis respond poorly to adenoidectomy unless true adenotonsillar obstruction is present. Tongue reduction helps oral hygiene but has no proven speech benefit. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1171)
canonical_layers.localize: Palatal muscle dysfunction impairs Eustachian-tube opening. Craniofacial skeletal relationships affect the nasal and pharyngeal airway. Prior repairs alter surgical anatomy. **Tensor veli palatini (TVP) mechanism**: the TVP is the primary active dilator of the cartilaginous Eustachian tube. Its tendon passes around the pterygoid hamulus into the palatal aponeurosis. Coordinated contraction during swallowing pulls the tubal wall open to ventilate the middle ear. Cleft-associated variation in TVP attachment and orientation, together with altered tubal cartilage and compliance, can impair opening and promote negative middle-ear pressure and effusion. The **levator veli palatini** chiefly raises the palate for velopharyngeal closure and speech, although its movement may assist the earlier phase of tubal opening. The mechanism is multifactorial rather than a proven single cleft-margin insertion defect in every patient.
canonical_layers.workup: Use serial audiology/otoscopy, speech/resonance assessment and sleep evaluation when symptoms warrant. Coordinate with cleft/craniofacial teams because ear, speech and airway decisions interact.
canonical_layers.manage: Treat hearing loss proactively, use tubes when indicated, and coordinate VPI/airway treatment with speech outcomes. Avoid fixing one problem in a way that predictably worsens another.
canonical_layers.operate: Adenoid surgery, pharyngeal flap/sphincter procedures and airway interventions require special attention to velopharyngeal competence and OSA risk. Ear surgery should anticipate chronic ET dysfunction.
canonical_layers.teach: Cleft care is longitudinal systems care: ears, speech, and sleep share the same altered anatomy. **Board pearl**: tensor veli palatini is the primary active Eustachian-tube dilator; levator veli palatini is central to the speech-related velopharyngeal sling. **Key trap**: palate repair does NOT reliably resolve middle-ear disease. Continue age-appropriate audiology and middle-ear surveillance after repair. Consider tympanostomy tubes when persistent OME with hearing difficulty, or recurrent AOM with effusion, meets criteria -- including when assessment at palate repair supports placement. **Cleft ear numbers**: In cleft palate, effusion is present in about 97% of ears by 4 months of age, and about 96% of children need tubes (nearly half need repeat sets). Long-term sequelae are chronic perforation in about 13%, CSOM in 6% and cholesteatoma in 1-3%, and coordinated team follow-up cut cholesteatoma from 9% to 3% in one program. Eustachian tube dysfunction persists 2 years after palatoplasty in about 80%. The mean age at normal hearing and tympanometry is about 7 years, and about 70% of ears normalize with at least 6 years of follow-up. Tympanoplasty results in cleft children (including submucous cleft) match those in noncleft children. Tubes placed before palatoplasty have high otorrhea rates, and speech at age 5 was the same whether tubes went in before or at palate repair. (Cummings 7e, Ch 188, pp 2848-2849)

candidates.prompt: In the clinical or operative context of Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons, Radiation is a spatial dose treatment with acute and late toxicity; definitive, adjuvant and palliative intent answer different oncologic questions. For Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons, what structures, relationships, or physiologic mechanisms must you be able to map, and why do they matter clinically?
candidates.answer_text: Localize target volumes and organs at risk conceptually: primary bed, nodal basins, spinal cord/brainstem, salivary glands, mandible, larynx/pharyngeal constrictors and carotid/skin in salvage contexts.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the localize layer of Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.

canonical_layers.recognize: Radiation is a spatial dose treatment with acute and late toxicity; definitive, adjuvant and palliative intent answer different oncologic questions.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize target volumes and organs at risk conceptually: primary bed, nodal basins, spinal cord/brainstem, salivary glands, mandible, larynx/pharyngeal constrictors and carotid/skin in salvage contexts. **IMRT by site**: in nasopharynx, randomized trials showed IMRT equals conventional control and better preserves salivary flow. In sinus cancer IMRT lowers optic nerve dose and severe dry-eye syndrome. In oropharynx, nearly all failures after careful IMRT are in-field in high-dose volumes (marginal misses occur mainly at the match line with an anterior low-neck field). IMRT increases skin dose because of multiple beams unless skin is contoured as an avoidance structure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1063–1065, 1067)
canonical_layers.workup: For surgical decision-making, know prior dose/fields, interval, response and late effects. Post-treatment imaging must be interpreted in the context of edema/fibrosis and expected tissue change.
canonical_layers.manage: Use multidisciplinary stage/risk-based indications. Modern management balances control with swallowing, salivary, mandibular, endocrine and vascular late effects. **Dose levels and modality choices**: gross disease gets about 70 Gy and the elective (N0) neck or adjuvant bed about 50-55 Gy ('shrinking fields'). On the RTOG pre- vs postoperative trial, survival did not differ but locoregional control was better postoperatively. Postop RT needs larger fields and higher dose because the surgical bed is hypoxic. Neutron therapy is used for unresectable salivary cancers such as adenoid cystic carcinoma. Proton therapy offers tighter dose distribution. HDR brachytherapy (e.g., iridium-192) delivers a localized dose through temporary catheters. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 268-269) **Altered fractionation**: hyperfractionation (about 1.1–1.2 Gy twice daily to 74–80 Gy over the usual duration) and accelerated schedules (6–7 fractions/week or concomitant boost) improve 2-year locoregional control by about 8–20% over standard RT alone at the cost of more acute (and often late) toxicity. The original MARCH meta-analysis (2006, 15 trials, 6515 patients) showed about 6.4% absolute locoregional benefit and 3.4% 5-year survival benefit, mainly with hyperfractionation. Accelerated regimens with dose reduction gave no survival gain. Concurrent chemoradiation, not altered fractionation alone, is the modern standard. A 5-day prolongation costs about 3.5–8% local control in laryngeal cancer. SBRT (1–5 large fractions to gross tumor only) is used mainly for reirradiation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1060–1062, 1067) **Altered fractionation**: hyperfractionation = smaller fractions twice daily to a higher total dose. Accelerated = similar dose in shorter overall time (e.g., concomitant boost, DAHANCA six fractions/week). RTOG 90-03 showed better locoregional control with hyperfractionation and concomitant boost (no chemotherapy). The updated MARCH meta-analysis (2017, 33 trials) showed a 3.1% 5-year survival gain overall, driven by hyperfractionation (8.1%), but altered fractionation alone is worse than standard-fraction CRT, and adding concomitant boost to CRT (RTOG 0129) gave no benefit—reserve it for patients who cannot receive chemotherapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 102, p 1522) **Neck dose logic**: An elective dose of about 50 Gy in 2-Gy fractions controls the N0 neck in more than 90%, and gross nodal disease needs about 70 Gy over 7 weeks. Electively treat the neck when the risk of occult nodes is roughly 20% or more. In practice the threshold is often 5-10%. END and elective neck RT are equally effective, so choose the modality that matches treatment of the primary and avoids trimodality therapy. After RT for node-positive disease, reserve neck dissection for incomplete response. (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1786) (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1795)
canonical_layers.operate: Prior radiation changes wound healing, vessel quality and reconstructive risk; salvage surgery requires tissue/reconstruction planning beyond the resection itself.
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: 'the patient had radiation' is incomplete—ask where, how much, when, and what tissue consequence remains. **Radiosensitizer and hypoxia trials**: chemotherapy adds about 4% absolute 5-year survival overall in the classic MACH-NC meta-analysis, with the benefit confined to concurrent delivery (about 6.5% absolute, hazard ratio about 0.81, in the update). Hyperbaric oxygen raised response rates but not survival. Hypoxic sensitizers (nimorazole, tirapazamine) and ARCON (carbogen + nicotinamide) have no proven survival benefit outside selected trials. Correcting anemia with erythropoietin actually worsened locoregional control and/or survival. Bonner trial: RT plus cetuximab (400 mg/m² load, then 250 mg/m² weekly) improved median survival 49 vs 29 months and 3-year survival 55% vs 45% over RT alone, but cisplatin-RT remains the standard because cetuximab-RT was inferior in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer (RTOG 1016, De-ESCALaTE). EORTC/RTOG pooled analysis: only extranodal extension and positive margins clearly benefit from adding cisplatin to postoperative RT. Two or more positive nodes without ENE did not. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1062–1066) **Normal-tissue tolerance numbers**: chronic myelopathy risk is under 0.5% at 50 Gy and about 5% at 5 years (TD 5/5) near 60 Gy in 1.8–2-Gy fractions, rising steeply above that (about 50% at 68–73 Gy). Lhermitte sign (electric shocks down the spine on neck flexion) 2–6 months after RT reflects transient posterior-column demyelination and does not predict progressive myelitis, which presents 6–12 months out with paresis, sensory loss, sphincter dysfunction or Brown-Séquard syndrome. Parotid permanent loss of function occurs above a mean dose of about 26 Gy (sparing one parotid preserves flow). Temporary loss occurs after about 10 Gy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1065, 1067–1069) **Dose tiers to memorize**: about 50 Gy in 25 fractions sterilizes subclinical disease (eg, the elective N0 neck). 60 Gy/30 fx treats the postoperative bed and intermediate-risk nodal levels. 66 Gy/33 fx is used for close or positive margins. 70 Gy/35 fx treats gross disease with curative intent. Standard fractions are 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week over 6-7 weeks. 1 Gy = 1 joule absorbed per kg. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 47, p 842)

Adolescents with Down syndrome may have severe persistent OSA after adenotonsillar treatment and poor PAP tolerance because of multilevel hypotonia/anatomic collapse. When is Down Syndrome Pediatric HNS indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
candidates.answer_text: Technical principles mirror HNS implantation but require pediatric/anatomic consideration and careful branch selection, cuff placement and respiratory-sensing lead placement. Counsel regarding tongue weakness, discomfort, infection and revision.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the operate layer of Down Syndrome Pediatric HNS. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Pediatric Down-syndrome HNS is a narrow FDA-labeled rescue pathway for persistent severe OSA—not a replacement for adenotonsillectomy or PAP in routine pediatric OSA.

canonical_layers.recognize: Adolescents with Down syndrome may have severe persistent OSA after adenotonsillar treatment and poor PAP tolerance because of multilevel hypotonia/anatomic collapse.
canonical_layers.localize: HNS targets tongue-base neuromuscular collapse; DISE is required to exclude complete concentric palatal collapse and identify whether the phenotype is appropriate.
canonical_layers.workup: Current FDA labeling includes selected patients age 13–18 years with Down syndrome and severe OSA with AHI 10–50 who are not effectively treated by/are not candidates for adenotonsillectomy, cannot tolerate/effectively use PAP despite attempts, lack complete concentric palatal collapse, and have considered standard alternatives.
canonical_layers.manage: Selection must occur in an experienced multidisciplinary pediatric sleep/airway program. Implantation is followed by healing, activation, titration and objective outcome assessment rather than immediate therapeutic effect. **Anesthetic hazards in trisomy 21**: Expect marked bradycardia during sevoflurane induction, difficult mask ventilation and intubation (midface hypoplasia, relative macroglossia, short neck), postintubation stridor and bronchospasm. About half have congenital heart disease (mostly AV canal defects), and pulmonary hypertension is more common. Craniocervical instability is found on imaging in 8–63% but causes symptoms in only 1–2%. Routine preoperative cervical films are not advised and a negative film does not exclude instability, so keep the neck neutral and avoid hyperextension in every patient. (Cummings 7e, Ch 184, p 2778)
canonical_layers.operate: Technical principles mirror HNS implantation but require pediatric/anatomic consideration and careful branch selection, cuff placement and respiratory-sensing lead placement. Counsel regarding tongue weakness, discomfort, infection and revision.
canonical_layers.teach: Pediatric Down-syndrome HNS is a narrow FDA-labeled rescue pathway for persistent severe OSA—not a replacement for adenotonsillectomy or PAP in routine pediatric OSA. **General ENT care in Down syndrome**: Pasha cites atlantoaxial instability in about 25% and subluxation in about 2%, while most sources quote 10-20% with symptoms in only 1-2%. Screening radiographs do not reliably predict risk, so protect the neck in every patient during positioning and intubation. Expect subglottic narrowing and choose a tube about 2 sizes (about 1 mm) smaller. Do an ABR by 3 months and behavioral audiograms every 6 months until ear-specific testing is reliable (about age 4), then yearly. See the child every 3 months if the canals are stenotic. Get a baseline PSG by age 4 (AAP 2011). Adenotonsillectomy leaves residual OSA in more than half, so DISE-directed lingual tonsillectomy or posterior midline glossectomy may follow. The risk of Grisel syndrome after T&A is higher. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 597–598) **Cervical spine in Down syndrome**: about 15% of children with Down syndrome have atlantoaxial instability. No universal preoperative imaging rule exists, but symptomatic children (gait change, incontinence, neck pain) need flexion–extension films and neurologic evaluation before airway surgery. When instability is found, plan neutral-position intubation and positioning (with somatosensory monitoring if needed), which matters for adenotonsillectomy and DISE. Mucopolysaccharidoses carry a similar odontoid risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Anesthesiology", p 117)

candidates.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Persistent dysphonia, odynophagia, dysphagia, hemoptysis, otalgia or airway symptoms require laryngeal visualization; glottic cancers often present earlier with voice change than supraglottic disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Early disease can often be treated with single-modality transoral surgery or radiation; advanced disease requires larynx-preservation CRT versus total laryngectomy/surgery based on resectability, cartilage/function and patient factors.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Laryngeal SCC. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Organ preservation is not the same as functional preservation. A tumor-free but chronically aspirating obstructed larynx may be an unsuccessful organ outcome.

canonical_layers.recognize: Persistent dysphonia, odynophagia, dysphagia, hemoptysis, otalgia or airway symptoms require laryngeal visualization; glottic cancers often present earlier with voice change than supraglottic disease. **SCC variants and behavior**: verrucous carcinoma—exophytic, pushing margins, no cytologic atypia, superficial biopsies often nondiagnostic, pure form does not metastasize (treat by conservative excision, no neck dissection; 5-year survival about 90%; reactive nodes from inflammation). Basaloid SCC—supraglottis/piriform sinus, aggressive with nodal and distant spread. Spindle cell (sarcomatoid) carcinoma—polypoid glottic mass, biphasic, can be mistaken for sarcoma; surgery preferred, RT alone ineffective. Adenosquamous—very aggressive, up to 75% nodal metastases, 5-year survival 15–37%. Papillary SCC—exophytic with severe atypia, better prognosis. NUT carcinoma—supraglottic, fatal within a year. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1589–1591) **Verrucous carcinoma**: 1-2% of laryngeal cancers; exophytic, well-differentiated keratinizing tumor with pushing rather than infiltrative margins. It does not metastasize unless foci of conventional SCC are present, so treatment is surgical excision without neck dissection, and radiation is generally unnecessary. Superficial biopsies are often read as benign, so a deep, generous biopsy is needed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, p 790)
canonical_layers.localize: Stage by subsite, vocal-fold mobility, paraglottic/pre-epiglottic space, cartilage invasion and extralaryngeal extension; nodal risk differs greatly by glottic versus supraglottic lymphatics. **Subsite boundaries and frequency**: the supraglottis (30-35% of laryngeal cancer) runs from the epiglottic tip to the junction of the ventricle and true fold, and is lined by respiratory epithelium. The glottis (60-65%) runs from the true fold's upper surface to 1 cm below it. The subglottis (about 5%) runs from there to the lower border of the cricoid. The supraglottis comes from the 3rd-4th arches and the glottis/subglottis from the 6th, and the fusion plane between them separates lymphatic and blood supply. The paraglottic space allows transglottic spread. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 291-295) **Nodal metastasis rates by subsite and T**: supraglottic pathologic nodes about 10% T1, 29% T2, 38% T3, 57% T4, with occult rates rising from 0–14% (T1) to 40–75% (T4); usually levels II–IV, I and V only with other levels involved. Glottic: about 0.1% T1, 5% T2, 18% T3, 32% T4 (overall 5.9%), drains to II–IV and VI, bilateral rare. Subglottic: paratracheal/level VI first (often bilateral), mediastinal nodes in up to 46% (counted as distant). Distant metastasis: glottic 3–9%, supraglottic 4–15%, lung most common. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1575)
canonical_layers.workup: Flexible exam plus direct laryngoscopy/biopsy and contrast imaging define primary extent; chest staging, nutrition and swallow/airway assessment are added according to stage. **CT/MRI thresholds that change surgery**: anterior commissure soft tissue >1 mm implies tumor; any measurable soft tissue between the cricoid and airway is abnormal (subglottic spread); subglottic extension >1 cm anteriorly or >6 mm posteriorly, contralateral cord involvement >30%, or thyroid cartilage invasion generally excludes vertical partial laryngectomy. The true cord level is where thyroid, arytenoid and cricoid cartilages appear on one axial slice. Image before biopsy or wait at least 48 hours to avoid post-biopsy edema. (Cummings 7e, Ch 104, pp 1550, 1554–1557) **Cartilage invasion on imaging**: the most reliable signs are frank cartilage destruction by adjacent tumor and tumor in the medullary space (loss of T1 fat signal on MRI) or extralaryngeal extension; sclerosis alone has low specificity (about 40% in the thyroid cartilage) and often reflects perichondritis. Irregular normal ossification mimics invasion; MRI is more sensitive but less specific than CT; dual-energy CT iodine maps help. Cartilage invasion upstages to T3/T4a, predicts poorer RT response and chondroradionecrosis, and precludes most partial procedures. (Cummings 7e, Ch 104, p 1556; Ch 105, p 1576) **Distant spread and chest findings**: hematogenous metastases go most often to lung, then liver, then bone; lymphatic distant spread is to the mediastinum. Risk is higher with supraglottic or subglottic than glottic primaries, advanced stage, and neck disease. An isolated pulmonary nodule on staging CT is more likely a second primary lung cancer than a laryngeal metastasis. Pretreatment PET/CT changes management in 20-30% of advanced cases; MRI is more sensitive for cartilage invasion. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 787, 791)
canonical_layers.manage: Early disease can often be treated with single-modality transoral surgery or radiation; advanced disease requires larynx-preservation CRT versus total laryngectomy/surgery based on resectability, cartilage/function and patient factors. **Obstructing laryngeal tumor**: prefer transoral debulking (cup forceps, microdebrider or CO2 laser) to secure the airway and allow staging before definitive therapy; if a tracheostomy is unavoidable, place it high so the later resection preserves trachea. Emergency laryngectomy offers no survival advantage over tracheostomy with planned laryngectomy, and tracheostomy itself does not increase stomal recurrence (subglottic extension does). (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1576–1577) **Subglottic SCC**: rare (about 1%), usually poorly differentiated and advanced at presentation with stridor or dyspnea. It spreads to level VI (pretracheal/paratracheal) nodes and the superior mediastinum, so treatment must include level VI dissection plus hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy (and corresponding radiation fields) to reduce peristomal/stomal recurrence. Staging: T1 subglottis only, T2 extends to cords with normal/impaired mobility, T3 cord fixation, T4a through cricoid or thyroid cartilage. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 791, 794)
canonical_layers.operate: Surgical choices range from transoral laser/partial laryngeal procedures to total laryngectomy with neck treatment and reconstruction. Oncologic control must be balanced against a realistic functional larynx.
canonical_layers.teach: **Key trap**: organ preservation is not the same as functional preservation. A tumor-free but chronically aspirating, obstructed larynx can be an unsuccessful organ outcome. **Current evidence**: use this as a decision hub. Define glottic/supraglottic/subglottic subsite, T extent, vocal-fold mobility, cartilage/extralaryngeal spread, nodes, airway, and swallowing. Compare selected early endoscopic/radiation treatment, suitable organ preservation, and primary total laryngectomy for selected extensive cartilage-invasive T4a or nonfunctional larynges. Use subsite cards for exact staging and operative detail. **Survivorship numbers**: 5-year relative survival for laryngeal SCC is about 64%; N stage predicts survival more than T stage, ENE further lowers survival, and distant metastasis gives under 10% 5-year survival. Hypothyroidism risk is about 20% after RT, 50% after laryngectomy with ipsilateral lobectomy, and >65% with both—check TSH every 6–12 months. Low-dose chest CT screening is recommended for patients ≥50–55 with ≥20 pack-years (NCCN). (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1587–1588; Ch 106, p 1614)
