candidates.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Unilateral obstruction, epistaxis, facial numbness, orbital symptoms, cranial neuropathy or destructive unilateral imaging should raise malignancy rather than routine CRS. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Most resectable epithelial sinonasal cancers require multidisciplinary surgery and radiation consideration; some histologies favor different systemic/radiation strategies. Orbital preservation depends on true soft-tissue/apical invasion rather than proximity alone.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Sinonasal Malignancies. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Sinonasal cancer is a histology-plus-anatomy problem. Unilateral 'sinus disease' with red flags should trigger tissue diagnosis before routine FESS.

canonical_layers.recognize: Unilateral obstruction, epistaxis, facial numbness, orbital symptoms, cranial neuropathy or destructive unilateral imaging should raise malignancy rather than routine CRS. **Epidemiology and prognostic line**: the maxillary sinus is the most common site, then the nasal cavity among sites overall and the ethmoid among sinuses. About 90% have eroded more than one wall at presentation. Tumors posterosuperior to Ohngren's line (medial canthus to mandibular angle) do worse because of skull-base and perineural spread. Occult nodal risk is under 10%, so the N0 neck is usually not treated electively unless the nasopharynx or soft palate is involved. Exposures include nickel, chromium, mustard gas, hydrocarbons, radium and wood or leather dust (adenocarcinoma, ethmoid predominant). (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 306-309)
canonical_layers.localize: Define the epicenter—nasal cavity, maxillary, ethmoid, frontal or sphenoid—and extension to orbit, skull base, dura, pterygopalatine/infratemporal spaces and cranial nerves.
canonical_layers.workup: Perform endoscopy, contrast CT/MRI and safe biopsy. Pathology is heterogeneous, so treatment cannot be planned from location alone; histology and skull-base/orbital involvement drive staging and modality selection. **AJCC maxillary sinus T staging**: T1 is confined to the mucosa with no bone involvement. T2 erodes bone, including the hard palate or middle meatus, but not the posterior wall or pterygoid plates. T3 involves the posterior wall, orbital floor or medial wall, subcutaneous tissue, pterygoid fossa or ethmoids. T4a involves the anterior orbit, cheek skin, pterygoid plates, infratemporal fossa, cribriform plate, or sphenoid or frontal sinus. T4b involves the orbital apex, dura, brain, middle cranial fossa, cranial nerves other than V2, nasopharynx or clivus. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 32, pp 567-568)
canonical_layers.manage: Most resectable epithelial sinonasal cancers require multidisciplinary surgery and radiation consideration; some histologies favor different systemic/radiation strategies. Orbital preservation depends on true soft-tissue/apical invasion rather than proximity alone. **Reconstruction and complications**: palatal and inferior maxillary defects can be obturated: a surgical obturator is placed at the operation and later replaced with a definitive prosthesis. Dural defects need watertight pericranial/galeal, temporalis or free-flap closure. Complications to know: meningitis with CSF leak. Tension pneumocephalus, which can come from over-draining a lumbar drain and needs emergent decompression. Frontal lobe syndrome. Epiphora from nasolacrimal injury (DCR if persistent). And cavernous sinus versus orbital apex syndromes. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 311-312) **ENB staging and outcomes**: modified Kadish staging: A = nasal cavity. B = paranasal sinuses. C = beyond the sinuses. D = nodal or distant metastases. The Dulguerov TNM grades T2 by cribriform erosion, T3 by orbit or anterior cranial fossa without dura, and T4 by dura or brain. ENB is about 5% of sinonasal cancers. Neck metastases are present in about 5% at diagnosis and occur in up to 20% over a lifetime. Treat with resection (endoscopic when no major orbital, brain or skin involvement) plus 55-65 Gy adjuvant RT. Two-year survival is about 75% for Kadish A/B and 25% for C in this text. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 32, pp 566-567) **ENB and SNUC outcomes**: For esthesioneuroblastoma, combined surgery and RT beats either alone (SEER 5-year OS about 73% vs 68% surgery vs 35% RT). Late recurrences more than 10 years out require long follow-up. Regional failure (high level II, retropharyngeal) is common, so elective neck RT is favored (0/11 regional failures with elective RT vs 44% without). SNUC behaves far worse. Single-modality therapy carries about 3-fold higher mortality than combined therapy, and about 27% fail regionally by 2 years, which again supports elective neck treatment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1802) (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1803) **Elective neck by histology**: About 25% of sinonasal cancers have neck metastases overall, but the rate varies widely. Nearly 30% of SCCs have nodes at presentation, compared with under 10% of adenocarcinomas (about 7% for ITAC, so no elective neck is needed). Esthesioneuroblastoma makes the strongest case for elective neck treatment. This atlas cites 20-25% nodal disease at presentation, but most series report about 5-10% at presentation and 15-25% over time, mostly delayed. T3-T4 SCC and SNUC carry at least a 15% nodal risk and should have elective treatment. BAHNO's threshold is a nodal risk over 10-15%. (H&N Surgery Atlas 2024, Ch 41, pp 416, 421, 427)
canonical_layers.operate: Choose endoscopic, open or combined approach based on oncologic access, margins and reconstruction—not on a minimally invasive preference. Plan skull-base reconstruction, orbital management and vascular control before resection. **Open approaches and maxillectomy types**: lateral rhinotomy is the standard route for medial maxillectomy. Weber-Fergusson (lateral rhinotomy plus lip split, sublabial and subciliary/transconjunctival limbs) gives access for total maxillectomy. Midfacial degloving avoids facial scars but exposes mainly the inferomedial maxilla. Inferior (infrastructure) maxillectomy treats alveolar and limited palatal tumors. Radical maxillectomy is total maxillectomy plus orbital exenteration. Exenterate for orbital apex involvement or invasion through the periorbita. Add craniofacial resection when tumor reaches above the cribriform plate or ethmoid roof. Cavernous sinus, optic chiasm, bilateral orbit, carotid or significant brain involvement generally contraindicates resection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 309-311) **Histology-driven surgical rules**: For intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, remove the whole ethmoid complex even when disease looks one-sided, because of field change. RT can be omitted for low-grade T1-T2 ITAC. Esthesioneuroblastoma resection should include at least the anterior skull base dura and the ipsilateral olfactory bulb, followed by postoperative RT. The endoscopic route is the gold standard when not contraindicated. After craniofacial resection, 40% or more of margins are R1, which reflects efforts to preserve the orbit and brain. (H&N Surgery Atlas 2024, Ch 41, p 421, Ch 43, p 454)

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with External Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve Injury. After thyroid or neck surgery, loss of high pitch, projection, and vocal endurance with preserved gross vocal-fold motion suggests EBSLN injury, especially in a professional voice user. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use observation and voice therapy for compensation, projection, and safe vocal loading; recovery and functional impact vary. Document pitch range and task-specific symptoms. Stroboscopy may show subtle asymmetry but is not diagnostic; cricothyroid laryngeal EMG is the most specific confirmatory test when the result will change counseling or treatment.

canonical_layers.recognize: After thyroid or neck surgery, loss of high pitch, projection, and vocal endurance with preserved gross vocal-fold motion suggests EBSLN injury, especially in a professional voice user.
canonical_layers.localize: The EBSLN powers cricothyroid tension and courses variably near the superior thyroid pedicle; injury changes pitch control without classic recurrent-laryngeal-nerve paralysis.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Diagnosis**: document pitch range and task-specific symptoms. Stroboscopy may show subtle asymmetry but is not diagnostic. Cricothyroid laryngeal EMG is the most specific confirmatory test when the result will change counseling or treatment.

**Grading scale**: **Cernea classification**: describes the EBSLN's course relative to the superior thyroid pole/vessels and predicts injury risk during thyroidectomy. Type 1 crosses the vessels more than 1 cm above the superior pole (lowest risk). Type 2a crosses less than 1 cm above the pole (moderate risk). Type 2b crosses at or below the upper edge of the superior pole, often within the ligation field of the superior pedicle (highest injury risk, and more common in large glands/goiters). **Board pearl**: knowing the likely Cernea type before ligating the superior pedicle is part of deliberate nerve preservation, not just careful dissection in general. **Gutman sign**: Normally, lateral compression of the thyroid cartilage raises vocal pitch and anterior pressure lowers it. With superior laryngeal nerve (cricothyroid) paralysis the response reverses, which is the Gutman sign. It is a bedside clue to add to stroboscopy (posterior glottic rotation toward the weak side) and laryngeal EMG. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 60, p 1197)
canonical_layers.manage: Use observation and voice therapy for compensation, projection, and safe vocal loading; recovery and functional impact vary.
canonical_layers.operate: No standard restorative operation exists for isolated injury. Prevention requires capsular upper-pole dissection, individual vessel control, and visual/monitoring-assisted nerve preservation when feasible.
canonical_layers.teach: Normal vocal-fold motion does not exclude laryngeal nerve injury. Ask about high notes, projection, fatigue, and occupational voice demands.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Croup vs Epiglottitis. Use this card as an AIRWAY-TRIAGE comparison, not as a second epiglottitis chapter. Croup is usually a viral subglottic illness in a young child with barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, and symptoms that often evolve over hours after an upper-respiratory prodrome. Epiglottitis/supraglottitis is an invasive inflammatory process above the glottis: the dangerous phenotype is abrupt toxic appearance, high fever, severe odynophagia/dysphagia, drooling, muffled voice, tripod/sniffing posture, and reluctance to lie flat; cough is usually absent or not the dominant feature. Stridor in either disease signals narrowing, but quietness, fatigue, cyanosis, altered mental status, poor air movement, or decreasing stridor despite worsening effort are pre-arrest findings rather than improvement. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Branch early. CROUP: give dexamethasone to essentially all clinically diagnosed cases; add nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe disease or significant stridor at rest, then observe long enough to ensure recurrent obstruction does not emerge as epinephrine effect wanes. Humidified mist, antibiotics, and sedatives do not treat routine viral croup.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Croup vs Epiglottitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Chief/boards discriminator: BARKING COUGH + HOARSENESS + SUBGLOTTIC STRIDOR = think croup; DROOLING + DYSPHAGIA/ODYNOPHAGIA + MUFFLED VOICE + TOXIC/TRIPOD CHILD = think epiglottitis until proven otherwise. Croup management is steroid-based, with nebulized epinephrine when more severe. Epiglottitis management is airway-first and agitation-averse.

canonical_layers.recognize: Use this card as an **airway-triage comparison**, not as a second epiglottitis chapter. **Croup**: usually a viral subglottic illness in a young child with barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, and symptoms that often evolve over hours after an upper-respiratory prodrome. **Epiglottitis/supraglottitis**: an invasive inflammatory process above the glottis. The dangerous phenotype is abrupt toxic appearance, high fever, severe odynophagia/dysphagia, drooling, muffled voice, tripod/sniffing posture, and reluctance to lie flat; cough is usually absent or not the dominant feature. **Key trap**: stridor in either disease signals narrowing, but quietness, fatigue, cyanosis, altered mental status, poor air movement, or decreasing stridor despite worsening effort are pre-arrest findings rather than improvement. **Bacterial tracheitis and diphtheria**: bacterial tracheitis follows a viral prodrome. The child develops high fever, a toxic appearance and a tender trachea, and does not respond to standard croup therapy. S. aureus (including MRSA) is the main cause, followed by group A strep, pneumococcus, H. influenzae and Moraxella. Lateral films may show irregular tracheal membranes. Treatment is IV antibiotics plus bronchoscopy to remove membranes and send cultures, and intubation is often needed. Diphtheria forms a friable gray membrane over the tonsils, pharynx and larynx that bleeds when removed; treat with isolation, antitoxin and penicillin or erythromycin. In croup, heliox is an adjunct, and if intubation is needed use a smaller-than-usual uncuffed tube. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 570–572) **Pertussis in the differential**: Pertussis (Bordetella pertussis, with milder disease with B. parapertussis and others) is the least well-controlled vaccine-preventable disease in the US, and it is rising with waning immunity and vaccine refusal. A 7-10 day catarrhal phase resembling a cold is followed by paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop, and the cough can last up to 10 weeks. Infants under 1 year carry the highest morbidity. Unvaccinated young infants may show only mild congestion before gasping, apnea, cyanosis or pneumonia (death in about 1%), often without a whoop. Macrolides do not shorten symptoms after the catarrhal phase but do limit spread, and patients can be contagious for about 6 weeks. Boosters are now recommended for older children and adults, and CDC recommends Tdap during every pregnancy to protect young infants. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, p 2988)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize by **clinical compartment**. **Croup**: primarily narrows the subglottis; the classic radiographic **steeple sign** is neither required nor sufficiently sensitive/specific to make the diagnosis. **Epiglottitis**: primarily involves the epiglottis and adjacent supraglottic tissues, so swallowing pain, drooling, muffled voice, and positional distress carry more weight than a barking cough. **Other must-not-miss causes** of pediatric stridor include bacterial tracheitis, retropharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar infection, foreign body, anaphylaxis/angioedema, and deep-neck infection. **Bedside goal**: not to obtain a perfect label before acting, but to recognize which child can tolerate routine examination and which child may lose the airway if agitated or placed supine.
canonical_layers.workup: **Typical croup**: diagnosis is clinical, and routine neck radiographs, viral testing, and laboratory studies are unnecessary. Grade severity from stridor at rest, retractions, air entry, agitation/lethargy, and oxygenation rather than from the bark alone. **Suspected epiglottitis with respiratory distress**: do NOT force an oral/pharyngeal examination, tongue-depressor exam, IV placement, CT scan, or supine radiograph before an airway plan is ready. Keep the child calm in the position of comfort and mobilize pediatric anesthesia/ENT/critical care. Imaging or flexible visualization is appropriate only in a stable patient when it will change the differential and can be performed without destabilizing the airway. **After the airway is secured**, obtain blood culture and, when safely obtainable, epiglottic/supraglottic culture to refine therapy. **Croup epidemiology, scoring and recurrent croup**: Croup peaks at 1-2 years (range 6 months-3 years), is most often caused by parainfluenza type 1, and about half of affected children have a normal neck radiograph; intubation is needed in only about 2% of hospitalized children. The Westley score (consciousness, cyanosis, stridor, air entry, retractions; 0-17) is used mainly for research. For recurrent croup, endoscopy is ideally done 3-4 weeks after an episode once edema subsides; in one series about 47% had reflux and 25% an anatomic lesion (SGS or laryngomalacia), and reflux-associated cases presented younger with shorter intervals between episodes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1547) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1548)
canonical_layers.manage: Branch early. **Croup**: give dexamethasone to essentially all clinically diagnosed cases. Add nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe disease or significant stridor at rest, then observe long enough to ensure recurrent obstruction does not emerge as epinephrine effect wanes. Humidified mist, antibiotics, and sedatives do NOT treat routine viral croup. **Epiglottitis**: minimize agitation, provide oxygen only if tolerated without provoking distress, keep the child with a caregiver when possible, and move toward controlled airway management with ENT/anesthesia rather than repeated bedside procedures. After airway control, start IV therapy active against invasive **H. influenzae** and other likely bacterial pathogens, then narrow to cultures/local susceptibility and infectious-disease guidance. **Croup treatment kinetics and intubation rules**: Nebulized racemic epinephrine works within 10-30 minutes but wears off within about 2 hours, so children can be discharged after a 2-3 hour observation; corticosteroids take up to 3 hours for peak effect and oral dosing is as effective as nebulized. Heliox (usually 80% helium/20% oxygen) lowers turbulent flow but cannot be used if more than 40% oxygen is needed. If intubation is required, use a tube smaller than age-predicted, extubate when an air leak develops (usually 2-3 days), and perform endoscopy if no leak appears by about 5 days. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Upper Airway Infections", p 1548) **Bacterial tracheitis numbers**: No clinical, radiographic or laboratory finding reliably predicts bacterial tracheitis, so endoscopy (direct laryngoscopy and rigid bronchoscopy with suctioning of pseudomembranes) is the diagnostic gold standard and is also therapeutic. Between 53% and 91% need intubation. Use a tube half to one size smaller than the age-predicted size, and tracheotomy is rarely needed. Extubate once the child is afebrile, has a leak around the tube and secretions have fallen, typically after about 3 days (up to 7). Pneumonia, in about half, is the most common complication. In croup, the steeple sign is absent in about 50%, and it is not pathognomonic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, pp 2983, 2987-2988)
canonical_layers.operate: The operative decision in this comparison card is **when to escalate**, not the full technique of epiglottitis intubation. **Croup**: rarely requires intubation; escalating epinephrine requirement, exhaustion, hypercarbia, altered mental status, cyanosis, or poor air entry should trigger ICU/anesthesia involvement and controlled airway planning. **Suspected epiglottitis with progressive obstruction** is different: do NOT wait for complete obstruction or attempt a casual bedside intubation. Transfer with personnel/equipment capable of controlled airway rescue, while maintaining spontaneous ventilation and a backup surgical airway plan. The disease-specific epiglottitis card owns the detailed intubation/extubation choreography.
canonical_layers.teach: **Chief/boards discriminator**: barking cough + hoarseness + subglottic stridor = think croup; drooling + dysphagia/odynophagia + muffled voice + toxic/tripod child = think epiglottitis until proven otherwise. **Croup management** is steroid-based, with nebulized epinephrine when more severe. **Epiglottitis management** is airway-first and agitation-averse. **Key trap**: do NOT use a normal-looking throat, absence of a thumbprint sign, or current Hib vaccination as permission to dismiss a dangerous supraglottic phenotype. Hib vaccination has made classic pediatric Hib epiglottitis uncommon, not impossible, and non-Hib organisms also cause epiglottitis.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Laryngeal Fracture / External Laryngeal Trauma. After anterior-neck impact (dashboard, sports collision, clothesline, assault/strangulation), or penetrating trauma, suspect an occult laryngotracheal injury with new dysphonia, odynophagia/dysphagia, hemoptysis, dyspnea, neck tenderness/crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, a flattened thyroid prominence or palpable step-off. Hoarseness is common but symptom severity does NOT reliably grade structural injury; a patient speaking calmly may develop edema and obstruction over hours. Stridor, progressive dyspnea, expanding hematoma, inability to handle secretions, major emphysema or distortion mandates an immediately coordinated airway plan, not a trip to CT first. Assess cervical spine, possible carotid/jugular trauma and pharyngoesophageal perforation as part of multidisciplinary trauma care. Children have a higher, more flexible and less ossified larynx, which lowers obvious fracture frequency but does not exclude serious mucosal injury. A normal-appearing external neck is not a rule-out test. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?

canonical_layers.recognize: **Mechanism**: anterior-neck impact (dashboard, sports collision, clothesline, assault/strangulation) or penetrating trauma. **Red flags**: new dysphonia, odynophagia/dysphagia, hemoptysis, dyspnea, neck tenderness/crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, a flattened thyroid prominence, or a palpable step-off. **Key trap**: symptom severity does NOT reliably grade structural injury -- a patient speaking calmly can still develop airway-threatening edema over hours. **Act now if**: stridor, progressive dyspnea, expanding hematoma, inability to handle secretions, major emphysema, or gross distortion -- this mandates an immediately coordinated airway plan, not a trip to CT first. Assess for cervical spine injury, carotid/jugular trauma, and pharyngoesophageal perforation as part of multidisciplinary trauma care. **Pediatric note**: children have a higher, more flexible, less ossified larynx -- this lowers obvious fracture frequency but does NOT exclude serious mucosal injury. A normal-appearing external neck is not a rule-out test. **Pediatric tracheobronchial injury clues**: In children, blunt laryngotracheal injury most often follows bicycle handlebar falls (mean age about 10; penetrating injuries about 12), and pliable cartilage means soft-tissue injury exceeds fractures. Rib fractures accompany tracheobronchial rupture in about 24% of children (vs about 90% of adults), so their absence does not exclude injury; a continued air leak despite a chest tube is the key clue, about 80% of ruptures involve a mainstem bronchus, 15% the trachea and 5% distal bronchi, and mortality reaches 30% (half within the first hour). Esophageal injury is the most commonly missed associated injury (15-50% of penetrating cases); contrast swallow alone is only 50-90% sensitive, so combine with esophagoscopy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1627) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1628) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1630) **Clothesline injury and laryngotracheal separation**: classically a motorcycle or snowmobile rider at dusk or dawn strikes a rope or wire; the neck may look nearly normal while edema builds over hours, with only soft tissue holding the airway open. Intubation can complete the separation, so tracheotomy is the safest airway, and bilateral RLN injury is common. Airway takes precedence over voice, and later cordotomy or arytenoidectomy may be needed to decannulate. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 455-456) **Numbers**: external laryngeal trauma is rare (about 1 in 137,000 adults); hoarseness is the most common presenting feature (about 85%), then dysphagia, pain, dyspnea and hemoptysis. Concomitant cervical spine fracture occurs in roughly 10–13%, so any but the most trivial laryngeal injury counts as a distracting injury requiring CT clearance of the spine (plain films insufficient). About 40% can be managed without surgery, and roughly a quarter have long-term morbidity. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 939–941)
canonical_layers.localize: Map the injury by level: **supraglottic** (epiglottis, aryepiglottic structures), **glottic** (thyroid laminae, true folds, anterior commissure, arytenoids, cricoarytenoid joints), and **subglottic/cricoid-tracheal**. **Key anatomy**: the cricoid is a complete ring, so a fracture or hematoma there can critically narrow the only airway. **Schaefer-Fuhrman grading**: **I** = minor mucosal edema/hematoma/laceration without significant structural disruption. **II** = greater edema/hematoma or minor mucosal injury, possibly a stable nondisplaced fracture, no exposed cartilage. **III** = massive edema, exposed cartilage, substantial laceration, displaced fracture, or fold immobility. **IV** = severe unstable framework, multiple displaced fractures, major mucosal disruption, or anterior-commissure avulsion. **V** = complete laryngotracheal separation. Grade using BOTH endoscopy and CT findings -- not radiology alone. Differentiate vocal fold immobility from arytenoid dislocation/cricoarytenoid fixation versus RLN injury. Document the anterior commissure and mucosal coverage -- malrepair here causes web/stenosis or dysphonia.
canonical_layers.workup: **Airway first**: assess airway, breathing, and circulation with cervical-spine precautions and senior ENT/anesthesia/trauma support. An unstable or rapidly deteriorating airway should be secured by the team using the safest method BEFORE imaging -- a controlled awake tracheostomy below the injury is often favored for clear major framework disruption. **If stable and cooperative**: flexible nasolaryngoscopy assesses edema, blood, airway caliber, exposed cartilage, mucosal tears, and bilateral vocal fold motion; a seemingly mild scope exam can still miss a framework fracture. **Imaging**: CT neck with thin cuts and multiplanar laryngeal reconstruction defines displaced/nondisplaced thyroid/cricoid fractures once safe to image -- do not impose a 24-hour wait or image a threatened airway. Add **CTA neck** when mechanism or findings suggest vascular injury, and evaluate the cervical spine. **Suspect esophageal injury** if there is a deep laceration, air near the esophagus, swallowing symptoms, or a penetrating trajectory -- arrange esophagoscopy and/or contrast swallow. After airway control, direct laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy with arytenoid palpation (and esophagoscopy as appropriate) delineates the full extent for repair. **Monitor**: serial bedside airway and flexible-endoscopic checks in monitored care are essential even in conservatively treated injury -- typically at least 24 hours.
canonical_layers.manage: **Airway first.** Do not attempt routine blind rapid-sequence intubation across a suspected severe disruption -- it can create a false passage or complete separation. Choice among controlled fiberoptic intubation with immediate surgical backup, versus awake/local tracheostomy, depends on anatomy, stability, expertise, and associated injuries. With a clearly unstable framework or major separation, secure a surgical airway below the injury when feasible. **Group I and selected stable II** (intact mucosa, no significant displacement or airway compromise) generally receive monitored admission, head elevation, humidification, voice rest, analgesia, a swallowing assessment, and serial endoscopy. Steroids/antireflux therapy are adjuncts with variable evidence -- not substitutes for airway vigilance. A group II patient with concerning mucosal/fracture findings can still require direct endoscopy or exploration. **Operate on**: displaced fractures, exposed cartilage, large mucosal lacerations, anterior-commissure disruption, cricoarytenoid injury, persistent immobility, unstable airway, or progressive emphysema -- all require prompt operative assessment/repair. **Timing correction (common teaching error)**: expeditious repair is preferred when clinically feasible. Operative Otolaryngology recommends exploration within **24-48 hours**, and Pasha describes repair ideally within **2-3 days** after stabilization. A published mean of **5.6 days (range 3-10)** must NOT be misread as a required delay. Address immediately life-threatening injuries first, and individualize timing. **Pediatric airway and tracheal repair choices**: Awake tracheotomy under local anesthesia is not feasible in most children, so the airway is secured in the OR after inhalational induction, usually by rigid bronchoscopy with tracheotomy over the scope (or skilled intubation over a flexible scope with a surgical backup). Tracheal tears involving less than one-third of the circumference, especially posterior ones with opposed edges and a lung that re-expands, may be managed nonoperatively; larger tears are closed with interrupted absorbable sutures preserving lateral blood supply, and a tracheotomy tube should not be placed through a simple anterior laceration. Esophageal tears are closed in two layers with a vascularized flap between trachea and esophagus to prevent fistula, and surgery for vocal fold paralysis is delayed about a year. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1631) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1632) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diagnosis and Management of Pediatric Laryngotracheal Trauma", p 1633) **Hyoid fractures**: seen in about 17% of strangulation victims and most often from strangulation; nearly all (about 89%) are managed nonoperatively because plating disrupts the muscular sling and can cause dysphagia. Operate only for fragment extrusion into the airway or significant supraglottic distortion; follow with early videofluoroscopy for aspiration. Homicidal strangulation is more likely than suicidal to cause laryngotracheal separation and neurovascular injury, and airway edema can progress hours after a benign first exam. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 940, 945) **Who does not need open repair, and who needs observation**: no exploration for a nondisplaced thyroid fracture, an isolated hyoid fracture, a thyroid fracture limited to the posterior third of the lamina, or a nondisplaced cricoid fracture that does not narrow the subglottis. Also defer it in unstable patients (sepsis, head injury) or with cervical spine injury. Observe in hospital for 12-24 hours for laryngeal hematoma, generalized edema, or a strangulation or attempted hanging injury, which can swell late. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 456)
canonical_layers.operate: After a secure airway below any major disruption and associated trauma/cervical-spine planning, perform direct laryngoscopy plus bronchoscopy (and esophagoscopy if indicated) to map mucosal breaks, exposed cartilage, fold mobility, arytenoid joint integrity, anterior commissure, and cricotracheal continuity. **For displaced thyroid/cricoid fracture or major soft-tissue disruption**: expose through a suitable cervical incision; preserve perichondrium and blood supply; gently reduce cartilage to anatomic contour; fix with miniplates/sutures or tailored mesh where necessary; repair mucosal lacerations to cover cartilage; restore anterior-commissure attachment; address arytenoid dislocation or vocal-fold avulsion. **Stenting/keel is SELECTIVE** -- for unstable comminution, extensive mucosal loss, or commissure disruption -- not automatic for every fracture; weigh the risk of granulation and later removal. **Complete laryngotracheal separation is an airway catastrophe**: identify the distal trachea for secure ventilation first, then reconstruct continuity once stabilized; coordinate with trauma/thoracic teams and assess for RLN and esophageal injury. **Exit checklist**: patent secure airway/trach, intact mucosal cover, restored framework and commissure, no unrecognized esophageal or vascular injury, a feeding/aspiration plan, and staged repeat-endoscopy/stent follow-up. **Early complications**: airway edema, infection, hematoma, mucosal breakdown. **Late complications**: glottic/subglottic stenosis, web, dysphonia, dysphagia/aspiration, vocal fold immobility, decannulation failure. **Avulsed arytenoid and stents**: A completely avulsed and displaced arytenoid is better removed than repositioned. Fix cartilage fractures with miniplates. Reserve stents for severe comminution, because they provoke granulation. Acute repair gives better results than delayed reconstruction. About half of patients with laryngeal fractures asphyxiate at the scene, and survivors may have a deceptively quiet interval before sudden obstruction. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 50, p 906-907) **Fixation specifics**: place miniplates perpendicular to a vertical thyroid fracture with two screws on each side, one plate superiorly and one inferiorly, using the calcified inferior border for purchase. In young, poorly calcified cartilage use larger 'emergency' screws or absorbable plates; Prolene suture reduction is more likely to loosen and malunite, and titanium mesh can bridge comminution. Keep any nonabsorbable suture outside the lumen to prevent granulation and stenosis. On closure, resuspend the anterior fold ends to the commissure. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 458-461) **Stents after fracture repair**: stent only when the repaired framework is unstable or endolaryngeal lacerations are extensive. Options in order of preference are the Montgomery laryngeal stent, Aboulker stent, rolled Silastic sheet, a glove finger packed with foam, or a T-tube (best for cricotracheal injury, with the upper limb trimmed to sit at or just below the folds, or the patient aspirates). Secure it with transcervical sutures tied over buttons. The authors leave stents about 2-4 weeks; the commentator limits them to 7-14 days and considers mitomycin unproven. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 457-461) **Repair details**: mucosal tears closed with 5-0/6-0 absorbable suture; posterior commissure defects resurfaced with piriform, supraglottic or postcricoid advancement flaps to prevent stenosis; the anterior vocal fold ends are resuspended to the thyroid cartilage/outer perichondrium at the correct height; thyroid fractures plated (the cricoid arch never fully calcifies and is sutured). Stents (soft Silastic, fixed with a transcartilage suture) mainly for comminution or bilateral fold epithelial loss, removed at 10–14 days. After cricotracheal separation repair, keep the neck flexed for about 7 days; RLN exploration is rarely needed because at least one fold usually recovers. Voice rest 48–72 hours, NG tube until swallowing is safe, antireflux therapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 944–946)
canonical_layers.teach: **Board algorithm**: suspect after anterior neck trauma plus a voice, breathing, or swallowing change. Do airway/C-spine evaluation BEFORE CT. If stable: flexible scope and CT framework mapping. If the airway is threatened or separation is suspected: expert controlled airway, usually surgical, below the disruption. Then classify with **Schaefer-Fuhrman I-V**. **Minor stable I / selected II**: observe with serial scope for at least 24 hours. **Major mucosal/cartilage instability or group III-V**: early operative evaluation -- reconstruct cartilage, restore mucosa and anterior commissure, consider a stent only when needed. **Common teaching error to correct**: early reconstruction when safe (often within 24-48 hours) is favored -- never teach waiting 3-10 days as the optimal standard. **The most important discriminator** is exposed cartilage, displacement, commissure injury, or airway instability -- not isolated hoarseness. **Attendings may ask**: why a normal CT does not rule out mucosal injury; how to recognize arytenoid dislocation versus nerve paralysis; why cricoid injury threatens circumferential airway caliber; what short- and long-term evaluations are needed to preserve breathing, swallowing, and voice. **Arytenoid dislocation**: posterior dislocation usually follows extubation and leaves the fold higher; anterior dislocation usually results from the laryngoscope tip at intubation and leaves the fold lower. CT shows a reduced or absent cricoarytenoid joint space and EMG helps if paralysis is in question. Reduce under anesthesia — lift a posterior dislocation anterosuperiorly with a straight-blade laryngoscope (with external cricoid counterpressure), and push an anterior one back with the laryngoscope tip or a balloon. After trauma, wait about 6 months before permanent medialization for unilateral paralysis, and keep a tracheotomy rather than doing early arytenoidectomy for bilateral immobility. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 944–946)

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. You are considering Pediatric OSA / Adenotonsillar Disease. Pediatric OSA is repetitive upper-airway obstruction during sleep and is not diagnosed simply by tonsil size or snoring. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is common, but obesity, craniofacial restriction, neuromuscular disease, Down syndrome, mucopolysaccharidosis, nasal obstruction, laryngomalacia and multilevel collapse change severity and treatment response. When is Pediatric OSA / Adenotonsillar Disease the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
candidates.answer_text: Polysomnography is the gold standard when diagnostic/severity uncertainty matters and is particularly important in high-risk children or when symptoms/exam disagree. Interpret AHI with oxygen nadir, CO2/hypoventilation, arousal burden and comorbidity rather than using one number in isolation. Preoperative assessment should identify age, obesity, severe PSG findings, craniofacial/neuromuscular syndromes and cardiopulmonary disease that increase postoperative respiratory risk.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the workup layer of Pediatric OSA / Adenotonsillar Disease. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Boards/chief framework: snoring is a symptom, PSG defines physiology, and anatomy/comorbidity explain why treatment succeeds or fails. Know why intracapsular and extracapsular tonsillectomy are different tradeoffs rather than 'better versus worse.' The most important postoperative decision may be who needs monitored admission, especially when severe OSA, young age or syndromic disease makes a routine recovery pathway unsafe.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Definition**: pediatric OSA is repetitive upper-airway obstruction during sleep. **Key trap**: it is NOT diagnosed simply by tonsil size or snoring. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is common, but obesity, craniofacial restriction, neuromuscular disease, Down syndrome, mucopolysaccharidosis, nasal obstruction, laryngomalacia, and multilevel collapse change severity and treatment response. **Red flags**: witnessed apneas, gasping, growth/behavioral problems, enuresis, cardiopulmonary consequences, and discordance between symptoms and routine exam. **Adenoidectomy-specific complications**: neck pain and stiffness after adenoidectomy reflect prevertebral inflammation. Pain lasting more than 2 weeks should raise concern for C1-C2 (atlantoaxial) subluxation (Grisel syndrome). Postobstructive pulmonary edema after relief of chronic obstruction is treated with oxygen, PEEP support, fluid restriction and diuretics. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2805)
canonical_layers.localize: **Levels of obstruction**: adenoid/velopharyngeal, tonsillar/oropharyngeal, tongue-base, supraglottic, and skeletal. Tonsils that look modest while awake can still contribute meaningfully during sleep. A child with very large tonsils can also have additional multilevel disease. **Key trap**: residual OSA after adenotonsillectomy should prompt phenotype/localization thinking rather than assuming recurrent tonsil tissue. **Macroglossia causes**: True anterior macroglossia includes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15 imprinting, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, omphalocele, ear pits or creases, about 10% embryonal tumors such as Wilms and hepatoblastoma), treated with anterior wedge glossectomy. Other causes are mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler, Hunter) and congenital hypothyroidism. Down syndrome causes relative macroglossia with a large tongue base. Lymphatic or venous malformations are also in the differential. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 989-990)
canonical_layers.workup: **Gold standard**: polysomnography, when diagnostic/severity uncertainty matters. It is particularly important in high-risk children or when symptoms/exam disagree. **Interpretation**: read AHI together with oxygen nadir, CO2/hypoventilation, arousal burden, and comorbidity rather than using one number in isolation. **Preop assessment**: should identify age, obesity, severe PSG findings, craniofacial/neuromuscular syndromes, and cardiopulmonary disease that increase postoperative respiratory risk. **Adenoid grading and red flags**: grade the adenoid by the percentage of choanal obstruction on nasopharyngoscopy (1+ under 25%, 2+ 25–50%, 3+ 50–75%, 4+ over 75%), and note whether it abuts the torus tubarius. Unilateral tonsillar enlargement calls for exclusion of lymphoma, leukemia or atypical infection. With severe obstruction, consider screening for cor pulmonale (ECG, echocardiogram, CXR, capillary blood gas). Adenoidectomy is contraindicated in overt cleft palate or VPI. A superior partial adenoidectomy is the option when such a child has OSA. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 534, 540–541) **Tonsil and adenoid grading**: Tonsil size is graded 1-4 with the tongue relaxed, by how much of the oropharyngeal width is filled: 1 is 0-25%, 2 is 25-50%, 3 is 50-75%, and 4 is 75-100%. The grade correlates poorly with PSG severity. On endoscopy (Parikh), adenoid grade 1 touches nothing, grade 2 touches the torus tubarius, grade 3 adds the vomer, and grade 4 touches the soft palate at rest. On a lateral neck film, an adenoid-nasopharynx ratio above 0.73 suggests significant hypertrophy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1197) **Syndromic PSG and hematologic prep**: the AAP recommends PSG for all children with Down syndrome by age 4 (OSA in about 57%, most parents report no symptoms). Screen with PSG when starting growth hormone in Prader-Willi syndrome. Sickle cell patients get hydration and transfusion to hemoglobin about 10 g/dL before surgery, and type 1 von Willebrand disease is managed with desmopressin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2801-2806)
canonical_layers.manage: **First-line**: adenotonsillectomy for many children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy and clinically meaningful OSA. **Intracapsular tonsil surgery**: reduces pain/bleeding and speeds recovery but leaves a small risk of regrowth/revision. **Extracapsular/total tonsillectomy**: provides complete tonsillar removal and may be preferred when recurrent infection, substantial tonsillar pathology, or concern about regrowth changes the balance. **Persistent OSA**: requires reassessment for obesity, residual adenoid/tonsil tissue, tongue-base or supraglottic collapse, craniofacial restriction, and PAP/medical or additional surgical options. **Medical therapy and analgesia**: for adenoid hypertrophy, a trial of intranasal steroid or montelukast is reasonable (warn families about behavioral and mood side effects of montelukast). For acute obstruction, use a nasal trumpet with a short steroid course. After tonsillectomy, give scheduled acetaminophen plus ibuprofen. Codeine and tramadol are contraindicated after tonsillectomy in anyone under 18 (FDA), because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers can make enough morphine to cause fatal respiratory depression. A single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose reduces postoperative nausea and vomiting (AAO-HNS 2019). (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 534, 539) **Tonsil asymmetry and lymphoma**: Most apparent tonsil asymmetry in children is benign (pillar effacement or true benign asymmetry). Tonsil lymphoma usually comes with rapid enlargement over weeks, nodes larger than 3 cm, dysphagia, night sweats or fever. An asymptomatic child with asymmetry can be watched for several months. Excise when the tonsil grows, when there are B symptoms or mucosal change, or in transplant patients, where PTLD is a risk. Routine histology of normal tonsils finds occult malignancy in only about 0.01% of specimens. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1195) **Cure rates and residual-disease predictors**: meta-analysis cure after adenotonsillectomy is about 60-66% (about 60% when cure = AHI <1). One multicenter series had only 27% with AHI <1. Predictors of residual OSA are age over 7, obesity, severe OSA and asthma. Persistence is 33-76% in obese vs 15-37% in nonobese children, and up to 80% of children with Down syndrome have persistent abnormalities. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2804) **Medical and orthodontic options**: intranasal steroids (fluticasone, budesonide) and montelukast reduce AHI in mild OSA. Supplemental oxygen requires CO2 monitoring and is not a sole long-term therapy. Rapid maxillary expansion (expand over 3-4 weeks, then stabilize 6-12 months) helps children with a narrow maxilla, especially after adenotonsillectomy or with small tonsils. CPAP/BiPAP normalizes PSG in 86-100%, with 60-80% long-term adherence. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2804) **Postoperative analgesia and fluids**: codeine and tramadol are contraindicated after tonsillectomy in anyone under 18 (FDA 2017), because CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers build up toxic morphine. NSAIDs (ibuprofen) do not raise bleeding risk in Cochrane data, but ketorolac should be avoided (bleeding 4.4-18%). A single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose is recommended. Rehydrate with isotonic fluid because hypotonic fluid plus high ADH causes potentially lethal hyponatremia. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2805-2806) **Perioperative opioid and antiemetic pearls**: Children with OSA had about a 10-fold higher rate of apnea after fentanyl. Children whose oxygen saturation nadir is below 85% need about half the opioid for the same pain relief. Snoring alone has been linked to critical respiratory events under anesthesia, and the 5-item STBUR questionnaire helps predict risk. Codeine and tramadol are contraindicated after tonsillectomy in anyone under 18 because CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolism has caused deaths. A single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose reduces PONV and pain and speeds return to diet. (Cummings 7e, Ch 184, pp 2786, 2789)
canonical_layers.operate: **Key trap**: the operation is not finished when the tonsils are out -- disposition is part of surgical planning. **Admit if**: young age, severe OSA/hypoxemia, major comorbidity, syndromic/neuromuscular disease, or significant postoperative respiratory events; these support monitored admission rather than routine discharge. Intraoperative airway difficulty, opioid sensitivity, and postoperative obstruction should be anticipated. **Residual disease**: DISE or targeted airway evaluation can guide lingual tonsillectomy, supraglottoplasty, or other site-specific treatment instead of empiric repeat surgery. **Non-hemorrhagic T&A complications**: (1) Postobstructive (negative-pressure) pulmonary edema can follow sudden relief of long-standing obstruction. Treat with PEEP and gentle diuresis. (2) Grisel syndrome is atlantoaxial subluxation from inflammatory laxity of the C1–C2 ligaments, with higher risk in Down syndrome. It presents as torticollis and neck pain and needs orthopedic or spine input and a collar. (3) Nasopharyngeal stenosis comes from circumferential scarring, recurs often, and may need flaps or stents. (4) VPI is more likely with submucous cleft or preoperative hypernasality. Most cases resolve with speech therapy, and persistent cases warrant 22q11 testing. Avoid cautery or curettage at the torus tubarius to prevent eustachian tube stenosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 541–542) **Down syndrome perioperative checklist**: About 10-20% of children with trisomy 21 have atlantoaxial instability. Neck pain, hyperreflexia or clonus calls for neurosurgical or orthopedic evaluation, and an atlas-dens interval above 4 mm on flexion-extension films warrants further assessment. Plan an endotracheal tube about one size smaller than predicted (small subglottis), keep neck extension gentle, admit overnight after tonsillectomy, and limit opioids. Respiratory complications are about 5 times more common than in controls. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1204) **Sickle cell and outpatient selection**: For sickle cell disease, transfuse to a hemoglobin of about 10 g/dL, give generous IV hydration, keep the patient warm and treat pain well to avoid a crisis. Outpatient tonsillectomy is reasonable for healthy children over about 3 years old. Admit children much younger than 3, those with severe OSA, those who live far away, and those with Down syndrome, craniofacial anomalies, bleeding disorders or obesity. The chapter used AHI >15 as its severe threshold, but the current AAO-HNS trigger for overnight monitoring is AHI >=10 or nadir <80%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1205) **Grisel syndrome**: Grisel syndrome is nontraumatic atlantoaxial subluxation from inflammatory laxity of the transverse ligament after adenoidectomy, pharyngeal infection, or anesthetic injected into the prevertebral space. It is more likely after a recent URI. It presents about a week after surgery with neck pain and torticollis, and an atlas-dens interval above 4 mm in a child confirms it. Treat with immobilization and an urgent neurosurgical consult. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1211) **Delayed complications of adenotonsillectomy**: Velopharyngeal insufficiency after adenotonsillectomy is usually temporary (6 weeks to 6 months) and becomes clinically significant in about 1 in 1,500-3,000 cases. Persistent cases often involve an unrecognized submucous cleft or a 22q11 deletion. Give speech therapy after 6 months and consider pharyngoplasty after 6-12 months. Nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal stenosis comes from removing too much mucosa, especially at several levels at once. Tonsil tags are found in 9-28%, and regrowth after intracapsular surgery in about 0.5-6%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1211) **Intraoperative hazards**: After intubating a severely obstructed child, falling saturation with pink frothy secretions means postobstructive (negative-pressure) pulmonary edema: give PEEP, reintubate if needed, and diurese gently. In children aged 5-7, loose incisors can be knocked out by the mouth gag. If a tooth is missing, get a chest film. Burns of the oral commissure are the tonsillectomy complication most often litigated. Prevent them with insulated cautery tips and a moist barrier between metal retractors and the lips. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1210) **Admission thresholds differ by guideline**: AAO-HNS recommends inpatient monitoring for AHI 10 or more and/or SpO2 nadir below 80%. AAP uses AHI 24 or more, nadir below 80%, or peak end-tidal CO2 of 60 mm Hg or more. Other risk factors: age under 3, pulmonary hypertension/cardiac disease, craniofacial syndromes, failure to thrive, hypotonia and morbid obesity. Respiratory complications occur in 16-27% of children with OSA vs up to 1.3% overall. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2805)
canonical_layers.teach: **Boards/chief framework**: snoring is a symptom, PSG defines physiology, and anatomy/comorbidity explain why treatment succeeds or fails. Know why intracapsular and extracapsular tonsillectomy are different tradeoffs rather than 'better versus worse.' **Board pearl**: the most important postoperative decision may be who needs monitored admission, especially when severe OSA, young age, or syndromic disease makes a routine recovery pathway unsafe. **CHAT trial**: 464 children aged 5-9 with OSA were randomized to adenotonsillectomy or watchful waiting. At 7 months, 79% of the surgery group vs 46% of the waiting group normalized (AHI <2). Surgery improved symptoms, behavior and quality of life, but not the primary attention/executive-function (NEPSY) endpoint. Normalization was less likely in Black children, obese children and those with higher baseline AHI. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2804-2805) **Epidemiology and screening numbers**: OSA affects 1-4% of children (snoring about 7.5%), peaking at 2-6 years. Boys are affected 50-100% more often and Black children about 3.5 times more. Only 20-30% of snoring children have a positive PSG. Clinical assessment alone is 30-81% accurate. The 22-item Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire has about 78% sensitivity and 72% specificity. Untreated primary snoring progresses to OSA in only 8-10% over 1-3 years. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2799-2804)

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Pierre Robin Sequence. Micrognathia, glossoptosis, and upper-airway obstruction—often with a U-shaped cleft palate—define Pierre Robin sequence; severity ranges from feeding difficulty to life-threatening obstruction. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use a multidisciplinary pathway: specialist-directed monitored positioning, feeding support, and nasopharyngeal airway or noninvasive support when appropriate. Home sleep plans must follow infant safe-sleep and specialty guidance rather than casual prone-position advice. Assess breathing across sleep and feeding, growth, gas exchange/polysomnography when needed, swallowing, and airway level by endoscopy. Evaluate for associated syndromes such as Stickler based on phenotype and genetics.

canonical_layers.recognize: Micrognathia, glossoptosis, and upper-airway obstruction—often with a U-shaped cleft palate—define Pierre Robin sequence; severity ranges from feeding difficulty to life-threatening obstruction.
canonical_layers.localize: Mandibular hypoplasia displaces the tongue posteriorly and may impede palatal fusion, producing tongue-base rather than primary laryngeal obstruction; isolated and syndromic forms differ in prognosis. **Sher endoscopic obstruction types**: Endoscopy in Robin sequence shows four obstruction patterns: type 1, the tongue falls back to the posterior pharyngeal wall (true glossoptosis). Type 2, the tongue pushes the velum against the posterior wall. Type 3, the lateral pharyngeal walls move medially. Type 4, sphincteric circumferential collapse. Types 3-4 respond poorly to tongue-based procedures. Incidence is about 1 in 8,500-14,000. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1169)
canonical_layers.workup: Assess breathing across sleep and feeding, growth, gas exchange/polysomnography when needed, swallowing, and airway level by endoscopy. Evaluate for associated syndromes such as Stickler based on phenotype and genetics. **Stickler syndrome needs eye surveillance**: Stickler syndrome (autosomal dominant, COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2) is a leading syndromic cause of Robin sequence. It brings high myopia, cataract, and risk of retinal detachment, plus mixed hearing loss, midface flattening, and early arthropathy. Refer to ophthalmology and genetics early. A missed diagnosis leaves parents falsely counseled about low multifactorial recurrence risk when the true risk may be 50%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 45, 55)
canonical_layers.manage: Use a multidisciplinary pathway: specialist-directed monitored positioning, feeding support, and nasopharyngeal airway or noninvasive support when appropriate. Home sleep plans must follow infant safe-sleep and specialty guidance rather than casual prone-position advice. **Airway escalation numbers**: About half of infants with Robin sequence are managed with prone or side positioning alone. Of those who need more, about half do well with a nasopharyngeal airway alone, for an average of about 44 days (range 16-104), with inpatient oximetry. Tongue-lip adhesion works best in nonsyndromic infants. Mandibular distraction is favored in syndromic infants. Tracheotomy is reserved for multilevel obstruction (e.g., subglottic stenosis, sphincteric pharyngeal collapse) or major neurologic or pulmonary comorbidity. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1169) **Stepwise airway algorithm**: prone positioning, then high-flow nasal cannula or nasal CPAP (to 'break the seal' of the tongue on the posterior pharyngeal wall), then a correctly sized and secured nasopharyngeal tube (the infant larynx is high, so length matters), then intubation and surgery—tongue-lip adhesion, subperiosteal floor-of-mouth release, glossopexy, mandibular distraction, or tracheotomy. Watch for columellar/alar pressure necrosis from nasal interfaces and humidify gases. Isolated PRS 'catches up' with mandibular growth and neuromotor maturation, whereas Treacher Collins or craniofacial microsomia often needs long-term tracheotomy. Obtain polysomnography and echocardiography because chronic partial obstruction causes cor pulmonale. Mortality is mostly from OSA and failure to thrive. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Primary Care of Infants and Children With Cleft Palate", p 1879–1881) **Airway ladder**: Escalate from side or prone positioning to a nasopharyngeal airway and a McGovern nipple, then tongue-lip adhesion (benefit debated), subperiosteal release of the floor-of-mouth muscles (about 84% effective in one series), mandibular distraction, and tracheostomy. Mandibular catch-up growth over 4-6 months often relieves mild obstruction. Screen for Stickler, which is associated with myopia, retinal detachment, and mixed hearing loss. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 990)
canonical_layers.operate: Persistent significant obstruction may require mandibular distraction, tongue-lip adhesion, or tracheostomy selected by obstruction level, comorbidity, and institutional expertise; palate repair follows airway and growth stabilization. **Mandibular distraction specifics**: MDO uses bilateral osteotomies and proceeds in phases: latency of 1–5 days (shorter in infants, too short risks fibrous union, too long risks premature consolidation), active distraction at 1–2 mm/day until the tongue-base obstruction is relieved, consolidation for 4–12 weeks, then device removal. Complications include injury to the marginal mandibular and inferior alveolar nerves, tooth bud loss or dentigerous cyst, anterior open bite, relapse or nonunion, device failure and TMJ ankylosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 543)
canonical_layers.teach: Treat airway and nutrition first. Quantify obstruction and identify multilevel/syndromic disease before choosing a tongue, mandible, or tracheostomy solution. **Syndromic associations by frequency**: Stickler is the most common associated syndrome (about 18%), then 22q11 deletion (about 7%), Treacher Collins (about 5%) and Goldenhar (about 3%). PRS does not require a cleft, but the classic cleft is U-shaped. Delay polysomnography until the infant is past term, because preterm studies have a high false-negative rate. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 601)

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Salivary Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma and Perineural Spread. A salivary gland malignancy with disproportionate pain, numbness, weakness, or a long infiltrative course should raise concern for a histology notorious for perineural invasion and spread along cranial nerves, sometimes recurring locally years after apparently complete resection. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Primary treatment is surgical resection when feasible, commonly followed by postoperative radiation for adverse features including perineural invasion. Long-term surveillance matters because recurrence and distant metastasis can occur late. Map cranial nerve deficits on exam and obtain contrast MRI with attention to the involved nerve pathway and skull base when perineural spread is suspected; stage the primary, neck and chest according to disease extent.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Ear and Nasal Foreign Body Removal. A witnessed insertion, unilateral foul rhinorrhea, canal pain, hearing loss, or a visible object suggests a nasal or aural foreign body. Button batteries and paired high-powered magnets are tissue-destructive emergencies. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Choose the tool by shape: forceps for graspable objects, hook/curette or balloon behind smooth objects, suction when suitable, and positive pressure for selected nasal cases. Immobilize an aural insect with an appropriate agent only when tympanic-membrane integrity and material safety permit it. Use excellent illumination, otoscopy/rhinoscopy or endoscopy, and assess object, depth, tympanic membrane, trauma, and cooperation. Imaging is selective and must not delay battery removal.

canonical_layers.recognize: A witnessed insertion, unilateral foul rhinorrhea, canal pain, hearing loss, or a visible object suggests a nasal or aural foreign body. Button batteries and paired high-powered magnets are tissue-destructive emergencies. **Nasal foreign body numbers**: peak age is 2-4 years; most children are asymptomatic and insertion is unwitnessed. Unilateral foul mucopurulent discharge is the hallmark but may take time to develop; epistaxis occurs in up to ~7%. About 60% of objects are inorganic (toys, beads), and organic material swells and inflames faster. Button batteries can perforate the septum within as little as 7 hours (12% of nasal foreign bodies in one series). Radiographs help find metallic objects or batteries in uncooperative children with thick secretions. **Rhinolith**: a long-retained object encrusted with mineral salts that can erode into the sinus or palate; it is fractured and removed, rarely through the nasopharynx or by lateral rhinotomy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1089) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1090) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1092)
canonical_layers.localize: Risk depends on site and material: batteries generate alkaline electrical injury, paired magnets compress tissue, organic material swells, and live insects abrade the canal.
canonical_layers.workup: Use excellent illumination, otoscopy/rhinoscopy or endoscopy, and assess object, depth, tympanic membrane, trauma, and cooperation. Imaging is selective and must not delay battery removal.
canonical_layers.manage: Choose the tool by shape: forceps for graspable objects, hook/curette or balloon behind smooth objects, suction when suitable, and positive pressure for selected nasal cases. Immobilize an aural insect with an appropriate agent only when tympanic-membrane integrity and material safety permit it. **Removal set-up and aftercare**: restrain the child upright on a parent's lap, with topical lidocaine/oxymetazoline. Have a right-angle hook, 5-7 Fr Frazier suction, alligator forceps, a balloon catheter and an endoscope or microscope ready, and always get behind the object and pull forward. Positive pressure through the mouth with the other nostril occluded can expel unilateral objects. ED removal succeeds in 92-96%, but each failed attempt worsens edema and cooperation. Large nasopharyngeal or small anterior objects carry the highest aspiration risk, and routine antibiotics are not needed after uncomplicated removal. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1091) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Foreign Bodies of the Nose", p 1093)
canonical_layers.operate: Proceed to controlled microscopic/endoscopic removal with sedation or anesthesia for batteries, deep/impacted objects, poor cooperation, adjacent critical structures, or failed attempts. Avoid irrigation for batteries, swelling organic material, or suspected tympanic perforation, and limit traumatic retries.
canonical_layers.teach: The safest first attempt is the best attempt. Remove batteries and dangerous magnets immediately, match technique to object geometry, and re-examine afterward for injury or retained fragments.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Inverted papilloma is a benign but locally aggressive Schneiderian epithelial tumor, classically presenting as a unilateral nasal mass with obstruction, epistaxis, or recurrent unilateral sinus disease. It matters because recurrence can be substantial if the attachment is not cleared and because synchronous or metachronous squamous cell carcinoma can occur. Unilateral polyposis in an adult should therefore not be presumed inflammatory until neoplasm is excluded. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Definitive therapy is complete surgical excision with treatment of the attachment site rather than simple debulking. Endoscopic resection is preferred for most accessible disease, with open or combined approaches reserved for anatomy/extension that cannot be safely controlled endonasally. Long-term endoscopic surveillance is required because recurrence may be delayed. If SCC is present, treatment follows sinonasal cancer principles and may require wider resection and adjuvant therapy rather than the benign-tumor pathway.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Inverted papilloma** is a benign but locally aggressive Schneiderian epithelial tumor, classically presenting as a unilateral nasal mass with obstruction, epistaxis, or recurrent unilateral sinus disease. **Why it matters**: recurrence can be substantial if the attachment is not cleared, and synchronous or metachronous squamous cell carcinoma can occur. **Key trap**: unilateral polyposis in an adult should not be presumed inflammatory until neoplasm is excluded. **Pediatric papilloma spectrum**: vestibular squamous papillomas are common in children. They are 1-3 mm cauliflower-like growths on the septum or vestibular skin that often recur and need close follow-up (HPV-related spread to the ear canal has been reported). Inverted papilloma is rare in children. With older open techniques recurrence was 25-75%, and 10-15% have associated SCC (true malignant transformation under 2%), mainly in adults. A choanal polyp arising anywhere other than the maxillary sinus should raise suspicion for inverted papilloma. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1111)
canonical_layers.localize: These tumors commonly arise from the lateral nasal wall or sinus mucosa and grow by endophytic epithelial inversion. **Key concept**: the operative problem is the site of attachment, not the visible bulk of the mass. **Maxillary sinus attachment** may require angled endoscopic access or medial maxillectomy-type exposure. **Frontal, sphenoid, skull-base, or orbital-adjacent attachment** changes both access and morbidity. **Imaging clue**: bone hyperostosis on CT can point toward the attachment site.
canonical_layers.workup: **Workup**: perform nasal endoscopy and obtain tissue diagnosis before definitive treatment when feasible. **CT** defines bony anatomy, hyperostosis, sinus remodeling, and surgical corridors. **MRI** can distinguish tumor from retained secretions/inflammation and is particularly useful with skull-base/orbital extension or concern for malignancy. **Red flags** for carcinoma: focal bone destruction, cranial neuropathy, severe pain, or rapid change. **Key point**: preoperative imaging should be read specifically to predict the attachment site so surgery can be planned around it. **Krouse staging** (document for operative communication): **T1** nasal-cavity disease; **T2** disease involving the ostiomeatal complex/ethmoid and/or medial maxillary sinus; **T3** disease involving other maxillary walls or frontal/sphenoid sinus; **T4** disease extending beyond the sinonasal tract or associated with malignancy. Use staging as an extent descriptor, not a substitute for attachment-directed imaging and surgical planning. **MRI 'convoluted cerebriform' pattern**: contrast T1 MRI shows alternating parallel folds of cellular epithelium and less cellular stroma, which is highly predictive of IP and separates tumor from retained secretions. Loss of this pattern with infiltrative growth suggests carcinoma ex-IP. The attachment is predicted by focal hyperostosis or a bony strut on CT. Orbital symptoms (epiphora, proptosis, diplopia) should raise suspicion of malignancy (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, p 775).
canonical_layers.manage: **Definitive therapy**: complete surgical excision with treatment of the attachment site, rather than simple debulking. **Endoscopic resection** is preferred for most accessible disease, with open or combined approaches reserved for anatomy/extension that cannot be safely controlled endonasally. **Follow-up**: long-term endoscopic surveillance is required because recurrence may be delayed. **If SCC is present**: treatment follows sinonasal cancer principles and may require wider resection and adjuvant therapy rather than the benign-tumor pathway.
canonical_layers.operate: **Technique**: debulk only enough to expose the true attachment, then remove involved mucosa/periosteum and drill or otherwise treat underlying hyperostotic bone when appropriate. Choose the corridor that provides direct visualization of the attachment, rather than forcing a narrow approach that leaves hidden disease. **Preserve**: orbit, lacrimal system, skull base, infraorbital nerve, and major vascular structures when oncologically safe. **Endpoint**: confidence that the attachment -- not merely the exophytic tumor -- has been eradicated. **Frontal IP**: the frontal sinus is involved in about 1.6–15% of IP. CT focal hyperostosis predicts the attachment site in about 95%, and T2 MRI separates tumor from retained secretions. Most frontal-recess IP can be removed via Draf IIa, but attachment within the recess or sinus needs Draf IIb/III drilling of the pedicle bone. Lateral orbital-roof attachment may need an added transpalpebral approach, and topical 5-FU is an adjunct when margins are uncertain (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 729–730). **Pedicle-oriented resection and maxillary corridors**: debulk to find the insertion, then limit subperiosteal stripping and bone drilling to the attachment. This gives the same recurrence as full demucosalization with shorter surgery and fewer complications. A modular endoscopic medial maxillectomy runs from type A (middle antrostomy) to type D (endoscopic Sturmann–Canfield, removing the medial anterior maxillary wall). Canfield morbidity: epiphora 12%, premaxillary paresthesia 24%, incisor/canine hypoesthesia 29%. The prelacrimal approach, which preserves the turbinate and nasolacrimal duct ('TuNa-saving'), avoids epiphora but is harder to survey endoscopically. Plan an external or combined approach for an anterior-wall or lateral-recess frontal attachment, extensive supraorbital cell disease, or orbital involvement (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 776–777).
canonical_layers.teach: **Board framework**: unilateral mass + inverted papilloma means think attachment, recurrence, and SCC risk. **CT hyperostosis** can localize the attachment; **MRI** helps separate tumor from obstructed secretions. **Key trap**: surgery fails when the bulk is removed but the attachment is left behind -- approach selection is driven by the ability to expose and clear the attachment completely. **Site-specific malignancy and recurrence**: Malignant transformation (about 10%) arises mainly from lateral-wall lesions and is rare from the septum. Calcification may be seen on CT. Radiation is not part of treatment for benign IP. Most recurrences appear within the first 2 years, and late recurrence after that is uncommon. Polyps differ from IP by being translucent, bilateral and less vascular. An association with HPV 6/11 and EBV has been reported, but a causal role is unproven. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 19) **Recurrence and surveillance numbers**: in a meta-analysis recurrence was 13.8% after endoscopic, 18.7% after external and 12.9% after combined approaches (under 10% in large expert series). Endoscopic resection cuts recurrence risk by one-third to one-half. Risk factors are incomplete resection, higher stage (Krouse T3 about 51% higher risk than T2), recurrent tumor, smoking and dysplasia (3- to 10-fold). Most attachments are on the medial maxillary wall/fontanelle region, with multisite involvement in about 30%. A suggested schedule is endoscopy every 4 months for 2 years, every 6 months to year 5, then yearly to year 10. Image only for inaccessible cavities, symptoms or proven recurrence (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 774, 777).

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with External Auditory Canal Cholesteatoma. External auditory canal cholesteatoma (EACC) is focal accumulation of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the bony EAC with underlying osteitis, focal bony erosion, and sometimes sequestration. Patients commonly have chronic otorrhea, dull otalgia, conductive hearing loss, or an incidentally seen focal keratin pocket. The tympanic membrane and middle ear may initially be normal. EACC may be spontaneous or secondary to canal trauma, surgery, radiation, stenosis, or chronic obstruction. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Small accessible EACC without deep extension can sometimes be managed with meticulous microscopic debridement, dry-ear care, treatment of secondary infection, and serial surveillance. Persistent focal disease, progressive erosion, pain/drainage despite office care, canal stenosis, or disease that cannot be safely cleaned favors operative eradication. Unlike keratosis obturans, the management problem is not merely removing a circumferential plug; it is controlling a focal erosive epithelial process and restoring a self-cleaning canal.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of External Auditory Canal Cholesteatoma. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: EACC is focal and erosive: keratin plus localized bony erosion/sequestration in the canal. That separates it from keratosis obturans, which classically produces a dense circumferential keratin plug with generalized smooth canal widening rather than focal osteitic destruction. A destructive canal lesion also demands a malignancy/NOE differential when the host, pain, or soft tissue is atypical.
