canonical_layers.recognize: **Definition**: external auditory canal cholesteatoma (EACC) is focal accumulation of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the bony EAC with underlying osteitis, focal bony erosion, and sometimes sequestration. **Presentation**: chronic otorrhea, dull otalgia, conductive hearing loss, or an incidentally seen focal keratin pocket. **Exam**: the tympanic membrane and middle ear may initially be normal. **Etiology**: EACC may be spontaneous or secondary to canal trauma, surgery, radiation, stenosis, or chronic obstruction.
canonical_layers.localize: **Location**: the defining process is in the external auditory canal rather than the tympanic membrane retraction pocket or middle ear. **Pattern**: disease often begins along one wall of the bony canal and erodes focally -- inferior and posterior canal walls are common locations. **Advanced extension**: can extend into mastoid air cells, temporomandibular joint region, facial nerve canal, or middle ear depending on location and extent.
canonical_layers.workup: **Exam**: microscopic otoscopy after careful debridement should define whether there is a focal keratin pocket, exposed bone, granulation, or sequestrum, and whether the tympanic membrane is intact. **Imaging**: high-resolution temporal-bone CT is useful when the full extent cannot be seen, symptoms are substantial, recurrent debris is difficult to clear, or there is concern for focal bony erosion, mastoid/middle-ear extension, facial canal involvement, or an alternative destructive process. **Biopsy**: appropriate when irregular soft tissue, disproportionate pain, or atypical erosion raises concern for squamous cell carcinoma or another mimic.
canonical_layers.manage: **Conservative management**: small accessible EACC without deep extension can sometimes be managed with meticulous microscopic debridement, dry-ear care, treatment of secondary infection, and serial surveillance. **Surgical threshold**: persistent focal disease, progressive erosion, pain/drainage despite office care, canal stenosis, or disease that cannot be safely cleaned favors operative eradication. **Key trap**: unlike keratosis obturans, the management problem is not merely removing a circumferential plug -- it is controlling a focal erosive epithelial process and restoring a self-cleaning canal.
canonical_layers.operate: **Approach**: surgery is tailored to extent. **Limited disease**: may require transcanal removal with canalplasty and coverage of exposed bone using local skin, fascia, or grafting as appropriate. **Extensive disease**: more extensive posterior disease may require a postauricular approach and mastoidectomy if mastoid air cells or middle ear are involved. **Danger structures**: preserve facial nerve, temporomandibular joint capsule, tympanic membrane, ossicles, and healthy canal skin whenever possible. Reconstruct the canal to reduce recurrent trapping.
canonical_layers.teach: **Key concept**: EACC is focal and erosive -- keratin plus localized bony erosion/sequestration in the canal. **Contrast**: this separates it from keratosis obturans, which classically produces a dense circumferential keratin plug with generalized smooth canal widening rather than focal osteitic destruction. **Key trap**: a destructive canal lesion also demands a malignancy/NOE differential when the host, pain, or soft tissue is atypical.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Red flags**: unilateral mass, recurrent epistaxis, remodeling/erosion, cranial neuropathy, or atypical 'polyps' should trigger a tumor framework rather than routine CRS assumptions. **Foundation**: benign sinonasal tumors are not one biologic entity. **Inverted papilloma**: a benign but locally aggressive Schneiderian tumor with meaningful residual/recurrence risk and potential synchronous or subsequent squamous malignancy -- a unilateral polypoid mass therefore needs tumor-level evaluation rather than routine CRSwNP assumptions. **JNA (juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma)**: the classic hypervascular tumor of an adolescent male with progressive unilateral obstruction and recurrent epistaxis. **Osteoma**: a slow-growing bone-density lesion, often incidental in the frontal/ethmoid sinuses, whose mere presence on CT is not itself an indication for surgery. **Osteoma epidemiology and Gardner syndrome**: Osteoma is the most common benign sinonasal tumor (frontal more often than ethmoid). Multiple osteomas should prompt evaluation for Gardner syndrome (familial adenomatous polyposis with osteomas and soft-tissue tumors), because the colonic polyps carry a very high risk of turning malignant, so colonoscopy/GI referral is required. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 20) **Vascular benign lesions**: Septal hemangioma usually arises at Little's area or the inferior turbinate. Excise it with a cuff of mucoperichondrium, with embolization first if it is large. Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is a friable septal polyp linked to trauma or pregnancy ('pregnancy tumor') and often regresses after delivery. Glomangiopericytoma (sinonasal hemangiopericytoma) is a pericyte-derived tumor of low malignant potential, and a better prognosis goes with an actin-positive, CD34-negative immunophenotype. Treat it by excision; about 10% recur. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 20-21) **Tornwaldt cyst**: A Tornwaldt cyst is a midline cyst on the posterior nasopharyngeal wall, derived from a notochord remnant. It is usually incidental (T1/T2 hyperintense on MRI) and is observed, or marsupialized if infected or symptomatic. Tell it apart from nasopharyngeal carcinoma (which usually starts off-midline in the fossa of Rosenmuller) and from adenoid retention cysts. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 21) **Aggressive pediatric fibro-osseous/giant cell lesions**: psammomatoid (juvenile active) ossifying fibroma occurs in the first two decades, is locally aggressive in the ethmoid and frontal regions (proptosis, facial swelling), may show fluid levels on MRI, and needs complete excision. Ossifying fibroma is well circumscribed with a thick bony rim, unlike the ground-glass, poorly marginated fibrous dysplasia. Central giant cell lesions, about one-third of benign pediatric jaw tumors in one series, are slow and bone-destructive and recur after curettage. Sinonasal desmoid fibromatosis does not metastasize but invades locally, and complete resection is preferred. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1115) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1116) **Other sinonasal papillomas**: exophytic (fungiform) papilloma is the second most common type. It has a 10:1 male predominance, occurs in the 3rd–5th decades, arises from the anterior-inferior septum without sinus involvement, is driven by low-risk HPV 6/11 and almost never becomes malignant; excise it with the underlying septal perichondrium. Separate it from keratinizing vestibular skin lesions. Oncocytic papilloma is the rarest type. It occurs in the 5th–6th decades in the lateral wall/maxillary sinus, is HPV-negative, KRAS-mutated, and shows intraepithelial mucin/neutrophil microcysts, with 4–17% malignant transformation (usually SCC); manage it like IP (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, p 777). **Gardner syndrome**: Autosomal dominant (APC) syndrome of multiple osteomas of the skull, mandible and paranasal sinuses with soft-tissue fibromas, epidermoid cysts and colonic polyps that almost inevitably become malignant; multiple craniofacial osteomas should prompt GI evaluation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 14) **Lobular capillary hemangioma ('pyogenic granuloma')**: only about 10% of mucosal head and neck cases are nasal. It typically arises on the anterior septum (Little area) or turbinate heads, with peaks in male adolescents and pregnancy (about 30% of affected women were pregnant). It presents with epistaxis (75%) as a red-purple mass usually under 1 cm, with T2 hyperintensity and vivid enhancement. Excise it at the submucosal attachment plane, since debulking or cautery leads to recurrence (0 to over 40% across series). Pregnancy lesions may regress after delivery, and there is no malignant potential (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 783–785). **Sinonasal schwannoma**: only about 4% of head and neck schwannomas are sinonasal. Most arise from V1/V2 (also sympathetic or pterygopalatine ganglion fibers), most often in the ethmoid, with intracranial extension in up to 8.5%. Histology shows Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies, Antoni B myxoid areas and diffuse S-100. MRI shows a well-circumscribed, intensely enhancing mass with intralesional cysts, and T2 brightness tracks the Antoni B content. Endoscopic resection gives about 3% (or lower) recurrence, and observation is possible for small lesions in unfit patients (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 786–787).
canonical_layers.localize: **Localize**: the epicenter and spread through nasal cavity, sinuses, orbit, skull base, pterygopalatine/infratemporal fossae. Infer vascular, neural, or epithelial origin from pattern. **Application**: make localization change the operation. **IP**: use CT for bony anatomy and attachment clues, and MRI when tumor extent, skull-base/orbital relationship, or distinction from retained secretions is important -- the surgical target is the **attachment**, not simple debulking. **Suspected JNA**: recognize the vascular phenotype and map extent/feeding vessels before tissue manipulation. **Osteoma**: define sinus of origin, frontal-recess/outflow relationship, orbital or skull-base proximity, and whether the lesion is actually causing obstruction or symptoms, before attributing nonspecific headache to it.
canonical_layers.workup: **Imaging**: endoscopy plus contrast CT/MRI as indicated defines attachment, vascularity, and critical extension. **Key trap**: do not biopsy a potentially hypervascular lesion until safety is understood. **Named staging systems**: stage inverted papilloma with the **Krouse system** -- T1 confined to the nasal cavity, T2 involving the ostiomeatal complex/ethmoid/medial maxillary wall, T3 extending to the lateral/inferior/posterior/superior maxillary sinus or sphenoid/frontal sinus, T4 with extrasinus extension (orbit, intracranial, pterygopalatine/infratemporal fossa) or associated malignancy. Stage JNA with the **Fisch/Radkowski system** -- Fisch I limited to the nose/nasopharynx, II into the pterygomaxillary fossa or maxillary/ethmoid/sphenoid sinus, III extending into the infratemporal fossa/orbit with or without intracranial extradural extension, IV with intradural extension or cavernous-sinus/optic-chiasm/pituitary-fossa involvement. **Senior workup decision**: a convincing JNA phenotype is a do-not-casually-biopsy problem -- obtain contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging and vascular planning rather than provoking major hemorrhage with routine office tissue sampling. **IP**: generally requires histologic confirmation when safe, but preoperative imaging should first exclude vascular or intracranial continuity and help map attachment/extension. **Osteoma**: serial observation is appropriate for many incidental, asymptomatic lesions. Intervene when growth, sinus-outflow obstruction, recurrent secondary disease, deformity, orbital effects, neurologic/skull-base consequences, or another clearly attributable problem changes the risk-benefit balance. **Fibrous dysplasia vs ossifying fibroma**: FD is a developmental anomaly (monostotic, or polyostotic with café-au-lait spots and endocrinopathy in McCune-Albright; polyostotic is 6–10 times rarer), found in the first two decades. On CT it ranges from lytic to ground-glass/sclerotic with no capsule. Ossifying fibroma is a true neoplasm (juvenile psammomatoid type in the fronto-orbital and ethmoid bones), more common in Black women in the 2nd–3rd decades, and appears well-defined and multiloculated with an eggshell rim. OF needs complete resection (high, aggressive recurrence, especially ethmoid). FD surgery is for symptoms (optic compression, deformity) and is delayed until skeletal maturity; prophylactic optic canal decompression is not indicated, radiation is contraindicated, and bisphosphonates (pamidronate) help pain and extensive disease (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 785–786).
canonical_layers.manage: **Range**: management ranges from surveillance to endoscopic/open resection based on histology, growth, attachment, symptoms, and skull-base/orbital involvement. **Staging sets expectations**: higher **Krouse stage** IP and higher **Fisch stage** JNA both carry higher recurrence/incomplete-resection risk and more often need a combined or open approach and closer surveillance, even though the operative principles (attachment-oriented resection for IP; vascular control and embolization planning for JNA) stay the same across stages. **Senior management -- IP**: treat with complete attachment-oriented resection rather than piecemeal debulking alone. Remove involved mucosa/periosteum at the attachment and address underlying bone when required by the attachment pattern, then maintain endoscopic and/or imaging surveillance, because recurrence can be delayed and malignant transformation/coexistent SCC matters. **JNA**: management is stage- and anatomy-dependent, usually centered on definitive resection in appropriate candidates with multidisciplinary vascular planning and selective preoperative embolization when its expected blood-loss benefit outweighs embolization risk. **Osteoma**: management is observation versus anatomy-directed resection, not automatic surgery for an incidental radiographic diagnosis. **Osteoma specifics**: the most common benign sinonasal tumor, seen in 1% of sinus radiographs and 3% of sinus CTs. Classically 80% are frontal, but a large CT series found ethmoid 55% vs frontal 37.5%. Histologic types are ivory/eburnated, mature (spongiosum) and mixed. Multiple osteomas suggest Gardner syndrome (APC; colon polyposis), so screen with colonoscopy. Observe with imaging if asymptomatic and away from skull base, optic nerve and orbit. Endoscopic resection uses cavitation: drill the core and fracture the thin shell, being ready for a CSF leak when it abuts dura. Recurrence is rare, so one CT at 1 year is enough (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 780–782). **Fibrous dysplasia treatment thresholds**: Fibrous dysplasia is diagnosed by imaging without biopsy: CT shows an expansile ground-glass lesion that respects cortex and foramina. On MRI it is low on T1 and T2 and can look alarming, so a CT should follow an incidental MRI finding. Malignant change (osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma) is about 0.4% and more likely after radiation, so radiation is avoided. Treat only symptomatic disease (deformity, cranial neuropathy, pain). Headache seldom resolves with surgery. Chen-Noordhoff zones guide extent: zone 1 (fronto-orbital, zygoma, upper maxilla) gets total resection, while zones 2-4 (hair-bearing cranium, central skull base, tooth-bearing jaws) get conservative or partial contouring. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1934-1935)
canonical_layers.operate: **Principle**: plan the route around attachment and danger structures, with vascular control and reconstruction strategy when needed. **Operative danger/bailout**: if a presumed benign unilateral lesion bleeds unexpectedly, has imaging features of marked vascularity, or appears continuous with skull base/intracranial structures, stop routine biopsy/debulking and re-establish vascular/skull-base-safe planning. **IP**: failure to identify and treat the attachment is a recurrence setup -- choose an endoscopic, open, or combined corridor based on access to the attachment and critical boundaries rather than on a dogmatic approach label. **Osteoma**: do not trade an asymptomatic benign lesion for unnecessary frontal-recess, orbital, skull-base, or cosmetic morbidity when observation remains safer. **Frontal osteoma (Chiu grading)**: grade I attaches posteroinferiorly in the recess, lies medial to a sagittal plane through the lamina papyracea, and is less than 75% of the recess AP diameter. Grade II is the same but more than 75%. Grade III attaches anteriorly or superiorly in the sinus and/or extends lateral to the lamina plane. Grade IV fills the sinus. Grades I–II were the classic endoscopic limit, but many grade III lesions can now be drilled out, often with a Draf III; the frontal floor lateral to the mid-orbit stays hardest to reach. Osteomas occur in about 3–4% of people, and most are incidental and wrongly blamed for headache (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 728–729).
canonical_layers.teach: **Concept**: unilateral disease is a diagnostic category. Ask 'what is this?' before treating it as inflammation. **Chief rule**: benign does not mean one management pathway. **IP** = find/treat the attachment + surveil. **JNA** = hypervascular, image/plan before tissue, control blood-loss risk. **Osteoma** = observe most incidental lesions, operate for a real anatomic/clinical indication. **Fibrous dysplasia and the optic canal**: The optic canal is involved in up to 90% of sphenoid fibrous dysplasia. Asymptomatic patients are observed with serial vision checks, because about 97% keep stable vision without surgery. Prophylactic decompression left only 87% stable, so it can cause the loss it aims to prevent. Give steroids for acute visual decline while arranging decompression, which can be done endonasally; partial decompression is often enough. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1935)

candidates.answer_text: Use when bedside repeatability, secretion assessment or real-food trials are valuable; know the white-out limitation.

candidates.board_pearl: State the physiologic impairment, not merely the PAS score.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Technique**: fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) directly visualizes the pharynx and larynx during swallowing trials. **What it assesses**: secretion management, pooling/residue after the swallow, and penetration or aspiration both before and after the moment of laryngeal closure ('white-out'), as well as real-time response to compensatory strategies (postures, bolus modifications).
canonical_layers.localize: **Strength**: FEES localizes pharyngeal- and laryngeal-level swallowing physiology directly -- what happens to secretions and boluses at the pharynx/larynx. **Limitation**: it cannot directly visualize the oral phase or the moment of laryngeal closure itself, since the view is obscured during the actual swallow (hence 'white-out'). **Key trap**: this is a structural limitation compared to fluoroscopic (MBS) assessment of the same event.
canonical_layers.workup: Use when bedside repeatability, secretion assessment or real-food trials are valuable; know the white-out limitation. **Pediatric FEES and FEESST details**: In children, apply anesthetic in the nose only (oxymetazoline and lidocaine 1:1, or lidocaine gel on the scope tip for infants and fragile children) so that hypopharyngeal sensation is preserved. In infants, premature spillage to the vallecula can be a normal developmental pattern. Blue dye No. 1 has been linked to methemoglobinemia in infants with a leaky gut, so use green food coloring or a colored vitamin instead. On FEESST, a laryngeal adductor reflex threshold above about 4.5 mmHg correlates with a history of aspiration pneumonia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Dysphagia", p 1319) **FEESST thresholds**: an air pulse from the scope port tests the laryngeal adductor reflex. A response at about 3 mm Hg is normal, 6 mm Hg means mild sensory loss, 9 mm Hg means moderate loss, and no response at 9 mm Hg means severe loss. Test each side, because asymmetry points to the side of the lesion. FEES needs no anesthetic and can be done at the bedside, but MBS is better for the oral and upper esophageal phases. (Cummings 7e, Ch 56, p 831)
canonical_layers.manage: Findings guide diet, therapy and procedural targets; it is complementary to MBS.
canonical_layers.operate: **Role**: FEES is a diagnostic procedure, not a treatment, but its findings should drive a specific physiologic conclusion, not just a numeric score. **Key steps**: correlate findings across multiple bolus types/consistencies and volumes, test compensatory strategies in real time (chin tuck, effortful swallow, bolus modification) to see what actually improves safety for that patient, and directly visualize secretion management, since silent aspiration of secretions is itself clinically important information. **Failure mode**: reporting only a penetration-aspiration scale (PAS) score without stating the underlying physiologic impairment driving it -- for example, delayed pharyngeal swallow trigger vs. reduced laryngeal closure vs. impaired pharyngeal clearance. The PAS score is a severity marker, not a mechanism, and treatment planning requires the mechanism. **Ongoing plan**: repeat FEES to assess response to therapy or disease progression, and pair with MBS when oral-phase or precise timing information is needed that FEES cannot provide.
canonical_layers.teach: State the physiologic impairment, not merely the PAS score.

candidates.prompt: In the clinical or operative context of Nasal Anatomy for Endoscopy, Use inferior turbinate/floor, middle turbinate, uncinate, bulla, basal lamella, sphenoethmoidal recess and choana as sequential orientation landmarks. For Nasal Anatomy for Endoscopy, what structures, relationships, or physiologic mechanisms must you be able to map, and why do they matter clinically?
candidates.answer_text: Use inferior turbinate/floor, middle turbinate, uncinate, bulla, basal lamella, sphenoethmoidal recess and choana as sequential orientation landmarks.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the localize layer of Nasal Anatomy for Endoscopy. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Never advance an instrument into a space you cannot localize relative to orbit/skull base.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Sequence**: endoscopic orientation proceeds from the nasal floor/inferior turbinate anteriorly, along the middle turbinate and its axilla, to the uncinate process and ethmoid bulla. It continues through the **basal lamella** (the true boundary between anterior and posterior ethmoid), and back to the sphenoethmoidal recess and choana. **Key principle**: each landmark confirms position before advancing to the next.
canonical_layers.localize: **Lateral limit**: the **lamina papyracea** marks the lateral limit toward the orbit throughout the anterior and posterior ethmoid. **Superior limit**: the skull base/fovea ethmoidalis marks the superior limit. **Key internal landmark**: the **basal lamella** of the middle turbinate is the single most reliable internal landmark, separating anterior ethmoid cells (draining to the middle meatus) from posterior ethmoid cells (draining to the superior meatus). **Ethmoid lamellae and recessus terminalis**: From front to back, the ethmoid lamellae are the uncinate (1st), the bulla (2nd), the basal lamella of the middle turbinate (3rd) and the superior turbinate lamella (4th). The basal lamella runs vertically to the cribriform plate in front, obliquely to the lamina papyracea in the middle, and horizontally to the lateral wall at the back. In about 80% of people the uncinate inserts on the lamina papyracea. This forms a blind recessus terminalis, and the frontal sinus then drains medial to the uncinate. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 3-7) **Keros depths**: Keros classified olfactory fossa depth as type I 1-3 mm, type II 4-7 mm, and type III 8-16 mm (the book prints 3-7 and 7-16 mm). Type III leaves a long, thin lateral lamella unbacked by frontal bone and is the most hazardous for skull-base injury. Also note a low posterior ethmoid height on CT. When it is present, keep posterior dissection inferior and medial. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of the Paranasal Sinuses in Pediatric Patients With Special Considerations for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery", p 958) **Anterior ethmoid artery position**: The AEA runs between the bulla lamella and the middle turbinate basal lamella, usually one cell behind the frontal ostium, slanting from posterolateral to anteromedial in the ethmoid roof. It lies anterior to the bulla face only when a suprabullar recess exists. It hangs on a mesentery below the skull base in about 36% and is both suspended and dehiscent in about 16%. On coronal CT look for the notch in the lamina papyracea between the superior oblique and medial rectus on the first cut posterior to the globe. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 4, p 25–26)
canonical_layers.workup: Endoscopy and multiplanar CT should agree; reconstruct drainage pathways before operating.
canonical_layers.manage: Management depends on pathology; anatomy is the safety framework for office and OR procedures.
canonical_layers.operate: **Context**: this module is anatomic orientation underlying every endoscopic sinus procedure rather than a standalone operation. **Key steps**: identify each landmark in sequence before any instrumentation, and use image guidance/navigation when anatomy is distorted by prior surgery, extensive polyposis, or tumor. **Danger structures**: orbit (lamina papyracea) and skull base (fovea ethmoidalis/cribriform plate) -- both thin and can be asymmetric or dehiscent, especially after prior surgery. **Failure mode**: advancing an instrument into any space, a cell or a recess, without first confirming its position relative to the orbit and skull base. **Key trap**: disorientation, not technical difficulty, is the leading cause of orbital and skull-base injury in sinus surgery. **Postoperative relevance**: accurate anatomic documentation at the index procedure -- which cells were opened, where the skull base was identified -- materially changes the safety of any future revision surgery.
canonical_layers.teach: Never advance an instrument into a space you cannot localize relative to orbit/skull base.

candidates.board_pearl: The ear is cartilage sculpture covered by thin skin. If you reconstruct skin without framework, the contour will fail.

canonical_layers.recognize: Auricular defects vary from skin-only loss to exposed cartilage, rim loss or composite framework injury; the ear's thin skin and three-dimensional cartilage contour limit simple closure.
canonical_layers.localize: Identify helical rim, antihelix, concha, tragus and lobule involvement and whether cartilage support is missing. Posterior auricular skin provides useful local tissue.
canonical_layers.workup: For trauma, assess avulsion viability and canal injury; for oncologic defects, establish margin control. Defect size, cartilage loss and subunit determine reconstruction.
canonical_layers.manage: Options include secondary healing for selected concavities, full-thickness graft, local advancement/rotation flaps, Antia-Buch-type rim advancement and staged cartilage/framework reconstruction. **Acute auricular trauma**: drain an auricular hematoma promptly by incision and drainage, then close the dead space with a through-and-through bolster or quilting sutures to prevent reaccumulation, perichondritis, and cauliflower ear; lacerations are closed by approximating the perichondrium; exposed cartilage must be covered. Helical rim defects under about 2 cm can be closed primarily; larger ones use chondrocutaneous (Antia-Buch) advancement. A partial avulsion often survives on a skin pedicle as small as 1-2 mm. Complete avulsion warrants microvascular replantation when feasible; otherwise bury the cartilage in a postauricular or abdominal pocket for later reconstruction. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 674) **Defect-by-region rules**: conchal bowl defects heal by second intention or FTSG if perichondrium is intact (cartilage loss here causes no deformity). Helical rim is the site of about half of auricular skin cancers; wedge excision is acceptable for defects under ~15% of height (~2 cm), using a star-shaped wedge to avoid cupping, and up to 15% height asymmetry is not noticed. Lobule defects should never get STSG alone (contracture) and an auriculomastoid flap should be designed ~30% larger. Larger rim loss can use a tubed postauricular flap (3 stages), Antia-Buch advancement, or a contralateral composite graft. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 467–469) **Perichondritis vs auricular hematoma**: Perichondritis follows high (helical or scaphal) piercing, acupuncture, surgery, burns or frostbite. It is usually caused by *P. aeruginosa* or *S. aureus*, spares the lobule (which has no cartilage), and in children needs IV antipseudomonal therapy. Drain any collection, because suppuration destroys cartilage and leaves a cauliflower ear. A traumatic hematoma or seroma (wrestling, boxing) is incised and drained under sterile conditions, followed by a contoured through-and-through bolster or quilting sutures and frequent rechecks for reaccumulation. Relapsing polychondritis also spares the lobule, but it is recurrent and bilateral, involves the nose, larynx or trachea and joints, and is treated with steroids. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 628-629)
canonical_layers.operate:
**Principle**: restore the cartilage framework before skin coverage when structural support is lost, and avoid flattening the sulcus or narrowing the EAC.

**Grading scale**: named staged costal-cartilage techniques differ mainly in stage count and timing. **Brent's technique**: 4 stages roughly 3 months apart (framework carving/placement; lobule transposition; elevation with sulcus creation and skin grafting; tragus construction/conchal excavation). **Nagata's technique**: compresses this into 2 stages spaced further apart (a single framework incorporating tragus and lobule at once, followed by elevation with a cartilage wedge, flap, and skin graft), and is typically performed later, when more costal cartilage is available. **Tanzer's original technique**: historically described as a multi-stage approach (lobule transposition, framework construction/placement, elevation, tragus construction, conchal definition), and was the predecessor that Brent's method refined. Its exact original stage count is reported inconsistently across secondary sources and is not restated here as a specific number. **Acute auricular trauma**: Irrigate lacerations and avulsions copiously. Cover exposed cartilage with local flaps or skin grafts, reconstruct the canal and meatus first, and align the helical rim and tragus precisely. Partial avulsions usually survive because the blood supply is rich. A complete avulsion can be reattached immediately (microvascular when feasible; leeches or anticoagulation help venous congestion; avoid pressure dressings and cool the part). If reattachment is impossible, the cartilage can be de-skinned and banked in a postauricular pocket. Treat a hematoma by incision and drainage with a through-and-through bolster, quilting sutures or a stent. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 879-880)
canonical_layers.teach: The ear is cartilage sculpture covered by thin skin. If you reconstruct skin without framework, the contour will fail.

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Recurrent aspiration, cough/choking, pneumonia or feeding-related respiratory symptoms with otherwise unexplained findings should raise concern for a posterior laryngeal/tracheal cleft. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Conservative feeding/aspiration strategies may suit selected minor defects; injection augmentation or endoscopic/open repair is selected by cleft depth, symptoms and comorbidity.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Laryngotracheal Cleft. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: swallowing tests show the consequence; endoscopy defines the cleft anatomy.

canonical_layers.recognize: Recurrent aspiration, cough/choking, pneumonia or feeding-related respiratory symptoms with otherwise unexplained findings should raise concern for a posterior laryngeal/tracheal cleft. **Associated anomalies and syndromes**: Clefts have associated anomalies in about 56%, most often tracheoesophageal fistula (20-27%) and tracheomalacia (about 80%); over 6% of children with TEF have a cleft, which is missed in about three-quarters until aspiration persists after TEF repair, so a cleft should be excluded in every TEF patient. Syndromic associations include Pallister-Hall (autosomal dominant: hypothalamic hamartoblastoma, hypopituitarism, imperforate anus, polydactyly) and Opitz G/BBB (hypertelorism, hypospadias, cleft lip/palate, dysphagia). Redundant mucosa between the arytenoids at endoscopy should raise suspicion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1526) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1604)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the defect along the posterior interarytenoid/cricoid/tracheal wall and distinguish shallow interarytenoid deficiency from deeper cleft extension.
canonical_layers.workup:
Instrumental swallow evaluation defines functional aspiration, but **definitive anatomic diagnosis** usually requires careful operative palpation/inspection under anesthesia.

Suspect a cleft with persistent aspiration, recurrent pneumonia, cyanotic feeding events, chronic cough, or failure to thrive despite an unrevealing flexible examination. Swallow testing defines functional aspiration, but definitive diagnosis requires rigid endoscopy with palpation of the interarytenoid/posterior laryngeal region, because a shallow cleft can be visually subtle. **Associated findings**: tracheobronchomalacia is found in about a third of cleft patients, and TEF in 12%–56%; other midline defects should prompt evaluation for VACTERL, Pallister-Hall, or Opitz-Frias (Opitz G/BBB) syndromes. Avoid strong downward pressure when palpating the interarytenoid notch, which can create a false cleft. Refer to neurology when aspiration exceeds what the anatomy explains. (Cummings 7e, Ch 214, p 3148)
canonical_layers.manage:
**Conservative approach**: feeding/aspiration strategies may suit selected minor defects. Injection augmentation or endoscopic/open repair is selected by cleft depth, symptoms, and comorbidity.

Use feeding modification, thickening when safe, reflux/nutrition support, and multidisciplinary aspiration management for suitable low-grade disease. Persistent pulmonary morbidity, failure of conservative therapy, or a deeper cleft supports endoscopic repair. Extensive clefts may require open reconstruction and coordinated airway/esophageal planning. **Staged management for type I–II**: give a 4–6 month trial of thickened feeds, positioning, and reflux/pulmonary optimization; about half of type I (91%–100% in some series) succeed without surgery. Interarytenoid injection augmentation (0.2–0.6 mL) helps more than 70% at least temporarily (about 3 months average) and predicts success of formal repair. Endoscopic repair is the gold standard for definitive closure (success 75%–100%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 214, pp 3148–3151)
canonical_layers.operate: Endoscopic repair requires precise posterior exposure, mucosal preparation/closure and avoidance of injury to adjacent laryngeal structures; deeper defects may require open approaches. **Repair approach, results and failure**: Most type I-II clefts are repaired endoscopically (success over 80%), for example with a single-layer mass closure using mattress sutures, the top one through both cuneiform cartilages; clefts below the folds generally need an open (anterior laryngofissure or transtracheal) offset two-layer closure, with an interposition graft such as tibial or sternal periosteum when failure risk is high (revision, prior TEF repair, Opitz). Preliminary tracheotomy, gastrostomy and fundoplication each improve the odds of success, and uncontrolled reflux lowers it. Breakdown occurs distally as a fistula or proximally as recurrence, usually within weeks; mortality ranges 11-46% and reaches 93% for clefts extending into the thoracic trachea. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1527) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1604) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Airway Surgery: Open Approach", p 1605) **Open repair for deep clefts**: most type III and all type IV clefts need open repair, usually anteriorly via midline thyrotomy, cricoidotomy, and tracheofissure (good exposure, low RLN risk), with two- or three-layer closure and an interposed graft. Consider tracheostomy to avoid prolonged positive pressure, and ECMO/bypass for distal extension. About half of type IV repairs have complications (dehiscence most common), and mortality for large type IV clefts is 44%–76%. The Sandu–Monnier modification splits types III and IV into a/b subtypes; limited type IIIa clefts can be repaired endoscopically. (Cummings 7e, Ch 214, pp 3151–3152)
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: swallowing tests show the consequence; endoscopy defines the cleft anatomy.

A normal-looking flexible larynx does not exclude a cleft. Palpation during rigid endoscopy is the diagnostic commitment point.
source_basis: Cummings 7e: Laryngotracheal Clefts

candidates.prompt: A patient with sleep-disordered breathing is reviewed in sleep clinic. HNS Troubleshooting / Nonresponse is being considered. Persistent symptoms, high residual AHI, discomfort, tongue deviation, poor nightly use or loss of benefit after HNS implantation requires troubleshooting before labeling the device a failure. When is HNS Troubleshooting / Nonresponse indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
candidates.answer_text: Before lead revision or repositioning, prove that programming and phenotype optimization cannot solve the problem. Revision carries hypoglossal, pleural, scar and device risks.

candidates.board_pearl: HNS nonresponse is a systems problem: patient use + programming + anatomy + device integrity. Do not jump directly to revision.

canonical_layers.recognize: Persistent symptoms, high residual AHI, discomfort, tongue deviation, poor nightly use or loss of benefit after HNS implantation requires troubleshooting before labeling the device a failure.
canonical_layers.localize: Failure can reflect adherence/activation, programming, stimulation pattern, cuff/lead position, residual palatal/lateral-wall collapse, weight change or nonobstructive sleep events.
canonical_layers.workup: Review objective device usage/settings and postoperative sleep testing, examine tongue motion and reassess airway phenotype; DISE with stimulation or imaging is selective for unexplained nonresponse.
canonical_layers.manage: Optimize amplitude, electrode configuration, timing and comfort, address weight/nasal/PAP-combination needs and treat residual anatomic collapse. Revision is reserved for a defined hardware/anatomic problem.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Chronic congestion/rhinorrhea without a convincing IgE-mediated pattern suggests nonallergic rhinitis; escalating topical decongestant use with rebound obstruction suggests rhinitis medicamentosa. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Remove triggers, use saline and phenotype-directed intranasal therapy; stop the offending topical decongestant in rhinitis medicamentosa and support withdrawal with anti-inflammatory therapy as appropriate.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Nonallergic Rhinitis / Rhinitis Medicamentosa. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Not every chronically congested patient has allergy or sinusitis. Ask what triggers symptoms and exactly what sprays the patient is using before ordering more tests or scheduling surgery.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Recognize** NONALLERGIC RHINITIS (NAR) as a phenotype-driven chronic rhinitis syndrome in which symptoms such as congestion and rhinorrhea are not explained by clinically relevant systemic IgE-mediated allergy. **Key trap**: do not use 'vasomotor rhinitis' as a wastebasket diagnosis. **Subphenotypes**: irritant/odor exposure, temperature or weather change, gustatory rhinorrhea, medication effects, hormonal states, rhinitis medicamentosa, and eosinophilic NARES. Local allergic rhinitis is a separate possibility when systemic testing is negative but the history remains strongly allergen-linked. **NARES specifics**: NARES presents with perennial allergic-type symptoms (paroxysmal sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, itch) but negative skin and serum testing. A nasal smear shows eosinophilia (about 10-20%). It can be a forerunner of AERD and nasal polyposis. It responds best to intranasal corticosteroids. By contrast, a nasal smear with more than about 25% eosinophils in an atopic patient supports allergic rhinitis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 38, 46-47) **NARES specifics**: defined by nasal cytology eosinophils above 10% with negative skin/serum IgE testing. Symptoms are more severe than in AR or other NAR subtypes, and NARES is associated with olfactory loss, obstructive sleep apnea, later nasal polyposis and aspirin sensitivity (it may precede the AERD triad). Intranasal steroids are the mainstay (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 637, 641). **Pregnancy rhinitis**: nasal congestion that affects about 20% of pregnant women, usually in the later trimesters, and resolves within about 2 weeks of delivery. Smoking is the only known risk factor. It is associated with asthma and reduced quality of life. Hypothyroidism and acromegaly are other hormonal causes (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 637). **Atrophic rhinitis, primary vs secondary**: primary disease occurs mainly in developing, subtropical/temperate regions and is associated with Klebsiella ozaenae (also Staphylococcus, Proteus mirabilis, E. coli). Secondary disease follows surgical overresection (empty nose syndrome), granulomatous disease or radiation. Rhinitis medicamentosa can also be grouped here. Symptoms are paradoxical obstruction, dryness and crusting (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 639). **Occupational rhinitis**: classified as primary occupational rhinitis (new symptoms after starting a job) or work-exacerbated rhinitis (preexisting rhinitis made worse at work). High-molecular-weight agents (>10 kDa, plant, animal, microbial) tend to cause IgE-mediated disease, while low-molecular-weight agents (<10 kDa, diisocyanates, anhydrides, metals) act through less defined, often nonallergic, mechanisms and can be triggered by a single high-dose exposure. Its severity predicts the severity of occupational asthma. Reviewing the safety data sheet for workplace chemicals helps (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 639–640).
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the dominant problem by symptom physiology rather than by label alone. Predominant watery rhinorrhea points toward excessive parasympathetic/glandular secretion; congestion may reflect neurovascular mucosal swelling or coexisting inflammatory/structural disease. NARES has eosinophilic inflammation without conventional systemic sensitization, while local allergic rhinitis requires evidence of local allergen-driven disease. **Key trap**: septal deviation, valve compromise, turbinate hypertrophy, CRS, medication overuse and CSF rhinorrhea are not interchangeable with NAR.
canonical_layers.workup: Start with trigger chronology, medication review, laterality, prior surgery/trauma, allergy pattern and focused nasal examination/endoscopy. Use skin-prick or serum-specific IgE testing selectively when the history leaves allergic rhinitis plausible. **Key trap**: a negative systemic test does not automatically prove NAR or exclude local allergic rhinitis. **Danger presentations**: unilateral persistent clear watery drainage after trauma/skull-base surgery, salty/metallic postnasal taste, recurrent meningitis or positional leakage should trigger CSF-leak evaluation rather than empiric rhinitis treatment. Unilateral bleeding, mass effect or progressive obstruction requires structural/neoplastic evaluation. **Nasal cytology phenotypes**: Nasal cytology (surface scraping, stained and read over at least 50 high-power fields) separates nonallergic rhinitis phenotypes. These are NARES (eosinophils), NARMA (mast cells), NARNE (neutrophils) and NARESMA (eosinophils plus mast cells). In allergic rhinitis the infiltrate is eosinophils > mast cells > basophils. The test is rarely used and nonspecific, but these acronyms are tested. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1134-1135) **Diagnostic aids**: a validated questionnaire found that onset after age 35, no family history of allergy, no outdoor or cat-triggered symptoms, and symptoms with perfumes/fragrances gave a 96% likelihood of NAR. Cold dry air provocation is more specific for NAR than histamine challenge. Nasal cytology alone cannot separate NAR from AR, but eosinophils suggest NARES, mast cells suggest NARMA and neutrophils suggest NARNE (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 640–641).
canonical_layers.manage: Treat the dominant phenotype. **Board pearl**: the 2020 Rhinitis Practice Parameter supports either an **intranasal antihistamine** or **intranasal corticosteroid** as first-line monotherapy for NAR, with combination therapy when needed. For predominantly watery rhinorrhea -- especially gustatory or trigger-driven disease -- **intranasal ipratropium** is a high-yield symptom-directed option. Add saline and trigger avoidance when useful. Stop chronic topical decongestant overuse in rhinitis medicamentosa and transition to safer therapy. **Key trap**: do not prescribe allergen immunotherapy for nonspecific NAR without evidence of clinically relevant allergen-driven disease. **Rhinitis of pregnancy**: Rhinitis of pregnancy is the most common hormonal rhinitis. Congestion without sneezing typically starts near the end of the first trimester and resolves after delivery. It may relate to estrogen-driven cholinergic effects and mucosal hyaluronic acid. Manage it with saline, avoidance, and an intranasal steroid if needed (budesonide has the most reassuring pregnancy data). Avoid decongestants. Other hormonal causes are oral contraceptives, hypothyroidism and puberty. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 47) **Weaning rhinitis medicamentosa**: Topical decongestants should be limited to 3-5 days. To wean, stop the decongestant and start saline and an intranasal steroid. A short oral steroid burst works well for severe rebound. Long-term overuse can cause persistent mucosal change. Defer turbinate surgery until the patient is fully weaned. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 41, 48) **Drug details**: beclomethasone and fluticasone propionate are the only intranasal steroids FDA-approved for NAR, and weather-sensitive idiopathic rhinitis may respond poorly to them. Azelastine helps (bitter taste is the classic side effect) and olopatadine works off-label. Azelastine plus fluticasone beats fluticasone alone. Ipratropium 0.03% is approved for AR/NAR rhinorrhea (0.06% for viral colds), helps only rhinorrhea, and needs caution in glaucoma and prostatic hypertrophy (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 641). **Capsaicin and botulinum toxin**: topical capsaicin, a TRPV1 agonist, desensitizes nociceptive C fibers by Ca2+-mediated afferent atrophy and improved idiopathic rhinitis symptoms for up to 36 weeks in a Cochrane review. Mucosal burning limits tolerance. Botulinum toxin injected into the inferior/middle turbinate heads lowers rhinorrhea only, for up to about 12 weeks (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 637, 641–642).
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery does not treat the abstract diagnosis of NAR. Operate only when a separate anatomic problem -- such as meaningful septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy or nasal-valve dysfunction -- contributes to obstruction after appropriate medical assessment. In refractory chronic rhinorrhea, posterior nasal nerve-targeted procedures may be considered in appropriately selected patients after phenotype confirmation and counseling, but first exclude CSF leak and other dangerous unilateral causes. **Key trap**: unexplained unilateral clear drainage is a diagnostic problem before it is an ablation target. **Vidian neurectomy and posterior nasal nerve ablation**: The vidian nerve forms from the greater superficial petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic) in the pterygoid canal at the floor of the sphenoid. It runs to the pterygopalatine ganglion. Endoscopic division (reached through the sphenopalatine foramen, following the canal posterolaterally) reduces rhinorrhea but causes dry eye (shown on Schirmer testing), nasal and palatal dryness, and cheek or dental numbness. Posterior nasal nerve cryoablation in the posterior middle meatus is a less invasive option, with headache, dry eye, epistaxis and synechiae as possible side effects. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 43, 49) **Vidian neurectomy vs posterior nasal nerve procedures**: the vidian nerve is formed by the greater superficial petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic). Endoscopic vidian neurectomy controls rhinitis in up to about 91% but risks dry eye and palatal numbness because lacrimal and palatal fibers run in the canal. Cutting or cryoablating the postganglionic posterior nasal nerve at the sphenopalatine foramen/posterior middle meatus spares lacrimal fibers, and office nitrous-oxide cryoablation improved NAR symptoms to 1 year (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 642). **Endoscopic vidian neurectomy**: Indicated for refractory vasomotor (and selected allergic) rhinitis with troublesome watery rhinorrhea after topical therapy, including intranasal anticholinergics, fails or is not tolerated. Make a wide antrostomy to the posterior wall, raise a lateral wall flap, remove the crista ethmoidalis and posterior maxillary wall, ligate the SPA, then divide the vidian nerve where its canal opens at the junction of the medial pterygoid plate and sphenoid floor, along with the more medial pharyngeal (palatovaginal) nerve that runs nearly perpendicular to it. Push bone wax into the canal to prevent regrowth. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 23, p 191–192)
canonical_layers.teach: **Senior model**: NAR is not 'allergy tests negative, therefore vasomotor.' Ask what triggers the symptoms, which symptom dominates, and what competing diagnosis would make treatment unsafe. Match therapy to phenotype -- ipratropium for secretion-dominant rhinorrhea, intranasal antihistamine and/or steroid for broader NAR symptoms -- and reserve procedures for a defined structural or refractory-rhinorrhea indication. **The dangerous miss**: ablating or repeatedly treating a unilateral CSF leak as rhinitis. **Pearls**: NAR typically starts in adulthood without seasonal variation and with less itching and sneezing than AR (except NARES). NAR patients have more acute and chronic rhinosinusitis than AR patients and are more often diagnosed with OSA, of greater severity. Elderly ('senile') rhinitis is mainly bilateral watery rhinorrhea that responds well to ipratropium. Ulceration, heavy crusting or septal perforation points toward vasculitis, granulomatous disease or malignancy (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 640).

candidates.prompt: In the clinical or operative context of Auditory Neuroanatomy / Cochlear Physiology, Sound becomes neural code through middle-ear transmission, cochlear traveling-wave mechanics, hair-cell transduction and tonotopic auditory pathways. For Auditory Neuroanatomy / Cochlear Physiology, what structures, relationships, or physiologic mechanisms must you be able to map, and why do they matter clinically?
candidates.answer_text: Localize from outer/middle ear to cochlea, spiral ganglion/CN VIII, cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate and auditory cortex.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the localize layer of Auditory Neuroanatomy / Cochlear Physiology. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: audiology becomes easier when every test is tied to the structure that generates the response.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Neuroanatomy of the Auditory System; Physiology of the Auditory System; Cochlear Transduction

canonical_layers.recognize:
**Concept**: sound becomes neural code through middle-ear transmission, cochlear traveling-wave mechanics, hair-cell transduction, and tonotopic auditory pathways.

**Pathway**: trace sound from stapes motion through the cochlear traveling wave to inner-hair-cell transduction, spiral-ganglion activation, CN VIII, cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate, and auditory cortex. **Tonotopy**: basal cochlea encodes high frequencies and apical cochlea low frequencies; tonotopy is preserved centrally.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize from outer/middle ear to cochlea, spiral ganglion/CN VIII, cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate and auditory cortex.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Approach**: use the pattern of audiometry, speech testing, OAEs, and electrophysiology to decide whether the deficit is conductive, cochlear, neural, or central.

**Localize using the measurement**: OAEs reflect outer-hair-cell function, cochlear microphonic reflects receptor potentials, ABR reflects synchronized auditory-nerve/brainstem activity, speech discrimination stresses neural/central encoding, and behavioral thresholds integrate the entire pathway. **Key trap**: cross-check discordant tests before assigning a lesion.
canonical_layers.manage: Management follows localization: amplify or implant when peripheral access is the problem; pursue neurologic/retrocochlear evaluation when neural/central patterns are discordant.
canonical_layers.operate: Operative hearing procedures succeed only if the downstream neural pathway can use the delivered signal; counsel accordingly in malformation/neural deficiency.
canonical_layers.teach:
**Teach**: audiology becomes easier when every test is tied to the structure that generates the response.

**By lesion type**: conductive disease attenuates input before the cochlea. Cochlear loss disrupts transduction/compression. Auditory neuropathy preserves cochlear receptor activity but loses synchronized neural firing. Central lesions impair pathway processing despite a potentially normal peripheral audiogram.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. After head trauma, hemotympanum, otorrhea, hearing loss, vertigo or facial weakness should prompt temporal-bone injury assessment. Modern management is driven by functional complications rather than memorizing longitudinal versus transverse labels alone. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Most fractures are observed with treatment of specific complications. Persistent conductive loss suggests ossicular injury; CSF leak, complete facial paralysis or vascular injury require dedicated pathways.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Temporal Bone Fracture. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Ask what the fracture damaged: nerve, labyrinth, ossicles, dura or carotid. That predicts management better than the old orientation terminology.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Scope**: use this card for acute temporal-bone trauma, after life-threatening head/cervical injuries have been stabilized. **Red flags**: hemotympanum or bloody otorrhea, tympanic-membrane/EAC injury, hearing loss, vertigo, facial weakness, and CSF otorrhea/rhinorrhea. **Key step**: document facial function EARLY with the House-Brackmann grade, and whenever possible note whether weakness was immediate versus delayed and complete versus incomplete. That chronology materially changes prognosis and the facial-nerve workup. **Onset of facial palsy**: of facial nerve injuries examined before paralytics are given, 27% are immediate and 73% are delayed, appearing 1–16 days after injury. Delayed onset recovers completely in about 94%. Immediate onset in about 75% treated conservatively, and some immediate-onset cases are transections. Distinguish true delayed onset from delayed diagnosis in intubated patients, who should be managed as immediate onset (Cummings 7e, Ch 147, p 2211). **Labyrinthine concussion and blast**: injury without otic capsule violation causes short-lived vertigo and imbalance (days to weeks) and a noise-induced pattern of hearing loss with a 4-kHz notch. Nystagmus may beat toward the injured side in the first hours before reversing. Posttraumatic BPPV is common. Blasts (over 200 dB SPL) injure the inner ear more when the TM and ossicles stay intact. About 15% have dizziness. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2533) **Pediatric fracture specifics**: Temporal bone fractures occur in 18-40% of skull fractures. Only about 2.5-5.6% violate the otic capsule, and fewer than 20% of pediatric fractures leave permanent SNHL. Facial palsy occurs in 5-33% of children with temporal bone fractures (less often than in adults, possibly because the skull is less ossified). CSF fistula occurs in 10-30% of children, similar to adults. Hemotympanum is seen in 20-65% of temporal bone fractures and TM perforation in 20-50%. In one series of 115 children with traumatic facial weakness, *55% had an upper-motor-neuron (central) cause*, with lower-face predominance and preserved emotional movement. Older head CTs missed up to a third of fractures. Battle sign appears at 4-5 days. Never irrigate a traumatized ear. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 884-888, 890, 892) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 869)
canonical_layers.localize: **Classification**: classify modern fractures primarily as otic-capsule sparing versus otic-capsule violating/disrupting, because this better predicts major neurotologic sequelae than the older longitudinal/transverse labels. Otic-capsule violation raises concern for severe SNHL/vestibular injury, CSF leak, and facial-nerve injury. **Complication localization**: EAC/TM/ossicular injury -> conductive loss; cochlea/labyrinth -> SNHL/vertigo; fallopian canal -> facial palsy; tegmen/posterior-fossa plate -> CSF fistula; carotid canal involvement -> vascular injury concern. **Key trap**: a fracture line is an anatomic description, not by itself an indication for surgery.
canonical_layers.workup: After trauma stabilization, perform careful otoscopy without aggressive canal manipulation, bedside tuning forks when feasible, serial facial-nerve examination, and formal audiometry once the patient can participate. **Imaging**: standard trauma CT may identify the injury. Obtain thin-cut high-resolution temporal-bone CT when facial paralysis, suspected CSF fistula, significant hearing/vestibular injury, or operative planning requires detailed anatomy. Add vascular imaging when the fracture trajectory or associated findings raise concern for carotid injury. **CSF confirmation**: if clear otorrhea is uncertain, beta-2 transferrin can confirm CSF. **Key trap**: for complete traumatic facial paralysis, electrophysiologic testing is timed after Wallerian degeneration has evolved, rather than performed reflexively on day 0. Contemporary society guidance uses serial electrodiagnostics around the 10-14 day window in appropriate patients. **Carotid and pneumolabyrinth**: carotid injury occurred in about 18% of fractures crossing the carotid canal versus about 5% when the canal was spared. However, angiography in asymptomatic carotid-canal fractures has shown low yield. Pneumolabyrinth on CT usually means profound deafness that does not recover. It is also associated with facial palsy, though the vertigo is transient in about 90% (Cummings 7e, Ch 147, pp 2210–2211).
canonical_layers.manage: **Principle**: treat the complication, not the fracture line. **CSF leak**: most uncomplicated traumatic CSF leaks are initially managed conservatively with observation and measures that reduce intracranial-pressure strain. Persistent/recurrent leakage, meningitis, or a repairable high-risk defect warrants skull-base repair planning. **Hemotympanum**: usually resolves; persistent conductive loss after the acute period suggests ossicular disruption and merits repeat audiometry/imaging. **Vestibular symptoms**: persistent symptoms receive diagnosis-specific treatment and rehabilitation. Suspected perilymphatic fistula is a separate surgical decision. **Hearing loss**: severe/profound SNHL requires hearing-rehabilitation counseling. **Key trap**: avoid teaching routine prophylactic antibiotics for every temporal-bone fracture as a universal rule -- infection strategy depends on the specific wound/CSF scenario and local evidence-based practice. **Canal injury and late sequelae**: an EAC laceration almost always overlies a fracture. Stent the canal (a wick or packing with antibiotic-steroid drops) to prevent stenosis. Repair a complete canal stenosis, because trapped skin forms canal cholesteatoma. Epithelium trapped in the fracture line can cause delayed middle ear or mastoid cholesteatoma years later, which justifies long-term otologic follow-up. Persistent vertigo needs evaluation for perilymphatic fistula and BPPV. A complete unilateral vestibular loss is managed with a short course of suppressants and then vestibular rehabilitation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, p 663) **Traumatic CSF otorrhea**: Most traumatic CSF otorrhea stops within about 2 weeks with bed rest, head elevation of 15-25 degrees and avoiding straining. Use a lumbar drain for a persistent leak or raised ICP. Operate for a leak lasting more than 2 weeks, a large petrous defect, a late-onset leak, brain herniation or recurrent meningitis. The subtemporal (middle fossa extradural) route preserves hearing and gives direct dural access. The transmastoid route avoids a craniotomy. Diagnosis: the halo sign is suggestive only. Glucose testing is unreliable (false positives in 45-75% of nasal secretions). Beta-2 transferrin needs only a tiny sample and is highly specific. With an intact drum, CSF looks like OME and may drain from the nose when the head is lowered. High-resolution CT shows the bony defect in about 70%. Intrathecal fluorescein and MR cisternography can localize the leak. The otic capsule heals by fibrous union, so it remains a lifelong route for meningitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 888) **Hearing after head trauma in children**: The most common pattern is SNHL, reported in 13-83% after head or temporal bone trauma. Labyrinthine concussion gives a 4-8 kHz noise-like notch with good discrimination. A retrocochlear pattern (poor discrimination, tone decay) comes from eighth-nerve stretch. Low-frequency losses tend to recover. Suspect ossicular disruption, and consider exploration, when the air-bone gap is more than 50 dB initially or still more than 30 dB at 6 weeks. The usual injury is incus dislocation or incudostapedial separation. The malleus is the least often injured. Children rarely report a unilateral loss, so get an audiogram after any ear trauma and repeat it every 3-6 months until stable. Avoid cortical bone grafts in children because they tend to ankylose. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 889-891, 883) **Facial nerve decompression timing in trauma**: Most fracture-related nerve injury is in the perigeniculate region, at the distal labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion, where traction from the greater petrosal nerve concentrates force. Fisch's criterion is ENoG degeneration over 90% within 6 days of onset. Surgery can be delayed up to about 3 weeks after an immediate palsy so that edema and hematoma settle. For long-standing paralysis, where electrical testing is no longer valid, wait about 12 months unless CT shows gross canal disruption, then explore if there is no clinical or EMG recovery. Take care with middle fossa exploration: 14 of 15 patients had MRI evidence of temporal lobe contusion. For an unexpected palsy after ear surgery, loosen packing and let local anesthetic wear off, then re-explore urgently if function does not return. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2594-2595) **Pediatric fracture-related facial palsy**: In a series of 1015 children with head injury, 71 had temporal bone fractures and 21% of these had facial paralysis. Transverse fractures cause palsy in up to 50%. Children can keep good tone and eye closure despite a transected nerve, so examine carefully. With immediate complete palsy, follow with serial ENoG. Stable function above 10% for 5 days predicts a good outcome, while rapid decline is an indication to explore. Decompress from the meatal segment to the stylomastoid foramen: translabyrinthine if hearing is dead, combined transmastoid-middle fossa if hearing is intact. Be prepared for grafting (sural or great auricular nerve), TM, ossicular and CSF repair. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 862-863)
canonical_layers.operate: **Key selective-operative branch**: the facial nerve. Delayed or incomplete traumatic weakness generally has a favorable spontaneous prognosis and is not an automatic decompression indication. Immediate complete paralysis warrants neurotology evaluation, high-resolution imaging, and appropriately timed electrodiagnostics. **Decompression threshold**: marked degeneration (often taught as >90% on ENoG in a complete palsy) may support decompression in a carefully selected patient when imaging/clinical localization is concordant. The evidence is LOW QUALITY, and the threshold is not an automatic operation. Suspected transection or penetrating injury changes the problem toward exploration/repair. **Approach**: choose transmastoid, middle-fossa, or combined exposure according to the suspected injured segment and hearing status. Persistent CSF fistula and delayed ossicular disruption are separate complication-directed operations. **Immediate complete traumatic palsy**: Electrical tests are misleading for the first 48-72 hours, so obtain high-resolution CT and an audiogram and explore as soon as the patient is stable. Remove bone spicules, incise the sheath, and graft immediately if the nerve is lacerated. The nerve is usually injured in the perigeniculate/horizontal segment. Use transmastoid exposure for the perigeniculate region to the stylomastoid foramen, translabyrinthine exposure when hearing is gone, and middle fossa exposure for the labyrinthine/IAC segment when hearing and the ossicular chain are intact. For delayed or incomplete palsy, follow with serial electrical testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 892)
canonical_layers.teach: **Chief/boards sequence**: stabilize -> document face/hearing/vestibular/CSF -> classify otic capsule -> image the complication -> treat the complication. **Modern discriminator**: otic-capsule sparing versus violating predicts clinically relevant morbidity better than simply longitudinal versus transverse. Immediate complete facial palsy triggers imaging plus delayed/serial electrodiagnostics. Delayed/incomplete palsy usually does not equal decompression. **Key trap**: do not overstate ENoG or decompression evidence -- society recommendations are weak/low-quality, so integrate timing, completeness, CT localization, and trajectory. **Classic numbers still tested**: longitudinal fractures make up about 75% (temporoparietal blow, conductive loss, EAC step-off, Battle sign). Transverse fractures make up about 25% (frontal or occipital blow, SNHL and vertigo). Facial nerve injury occurs in about 30-50% of transverse or otic-capsule-violating fractures. However, most traumatic facial palsies overall come from longitudinal fractures because those are more common. Incudostapedial joint separation is the most common ossicular injury. Pasha times formal audiometry at about 2-8 weeks (sooner if a new loss is not explained by hemotympanum). Over 90% of traumatic CSF leaks stop with conservative care. Current practice classifies fractures as otic capsule-sparing or otic capsule-violating, which predicts facial palsy, SNHL and CSF leak better than the longitudinal/transverse scheme. (Pasha 6e, Ch 10, pp 661-663) **High-yield numbers**: facial paralysis occurs in 7% of fractures. Capsule-violating fractures carry 4–5 times the risk of facial palsy and 2–4 times the risk of CSF fistula. CSF fistula occurs in 17%. Meningitis risk is 1% without a fistula, 5–11% if a leak lasts under 1 week, and up to 88% if a leak persists indefinitely. In children, intracranial injury is more common (58%) and facial palsy less common (3%) (Cummings 7e, Ch 147, key points p 2207).

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the ENT service. this condition can produce severe esophageal/gastric or laryngeal injury despite limited oral burns. Drooling, dysphagia, chest/abdominal pain, stridor or respiratory distress indicate significant risk. What are your immediate priorities, what is the first definitive management step, and which finding should trigger escalation?
candidates.answer_text: NPO/supportive care, analgesia and multidisciplinary GI/surgical/ENT involvement depend on severity; perforation/mediastinitis requires urgent source control. Long-term follow-up addresses esophageal stricture and swallowing/nutrition.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Caustic Ingestion. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: A normal mouth does not clear the esophagus. The must-not-miss problems are airway injury and transmural perforation.

canonical_layers.recognize: Caustic ingestion can produce severe esophageal/gastric or laryngeal injury despite limited or absent oral burns. **Key trap**: up to **30%** of patients with significant esophageal injury show no visible oropharyngeal damage, so a clean-looking mouth does not clear the esophagus. **Red flags**: drooling, dysphagia, chest/abdominal pain, stridor or respiratory distress indicate significant risk. Acids are more likely than alkalis to cause chemical epiglottitis and airway obstruction. **Symptoms do not track injury**: in a large pediatric series 12% of asymptomatic children had severe esophageal injury while 82% of symptomatic children had none, and in another series 61% of children without oral lesions still had esophageal injury. Nonetheless, unintentional ingestion without symptoms rarely causes significant injury; endoscopy is reserved for oral lesions, marked symptoms, or intentional ingestion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, p 3129)
canonical_layers.localize: Assess airway/larynx and GI tract separately. **Acids**: cause coagulation necrosis with eschar formation that limits deeper penetration, so esophageal injury is comparatively less common than gastric injury (pooling and reflex pylorospasm increase stomach contact time). **Alkalis**: cause liquefaction necrosis that breaks down cell membranes and penetrates deeply, with injury related to concentration, amount and tissue contact time. **Anatomic narrowings** at highest risk (cricopharyngeus, aortic-arch crossing, left mainstem bronchus, diaphragmatic hiatus) have prolonged contact time.
canonical_layers.workup: **Initial steps**: stabilize airway/hemodynamics. Do not induce emesis or attempt neutralization -- both can worsen injury. Do not attempt routine dilution with oral fluids either. Consult poison control and the treating team regarding substance-specific immediate management. **Imaging trap**: barium esophagram is inadequate as a first-line study, with a high false-negative rate for mucosal injury, and should not substitute for specialist-directed evaluation. Late presentations require individualized imaging and procedural decisions, because friable tissue can increase endoscopy risk. **EGD timing**: per the **2025 update** to pediatric caustic-ingestion management, **EGD within 24 hours** is the optimal window for evaluating injury severity and prognosis in symptomatic patients. In adults, endoscopy decisions depend on exposure and risk even when symptoms are mild. Asymptomatic children warrant individualized risk assessment, poison-control input and observation, rather than routine radionuclide screening. **Endoscopy timing and the window to avoid**: CONFLICT within sources: the site gives both 24-48 hours and within 24 hours. The book recommends endoscopy at 24-72 hours in symptomatic children. Lesions may be underestimated before 24 hours, and endoscopy should be avoided between days 5 and 15, when the esophageal wall is weakest. Stop advancing the scope at the first severe (circumferential or necrotic) burn. Having two or more of drooling, vomiting and stridor predicts an esophageal burn better than any single sign. Current pediatric guidance favors endoscopy within about 24 hours (generally after 12 hours), and all sources agree on avoiding the subacute window. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Caustic Injuries and Acquired Strictures of the Esophagus", p 1372) **Endoscopic grading (Zargar) and pathophysiology**: grade 0 is normal and grade I is edema or erythema. Grade IIA shows hemorrhage, erosions, blisters or superficial ulcers, and grade IIB is circumferential. Grade IIIA shows focal deep gray-black necrosis, IIIB extensive necrosis, and IV perforation. Grades 0-IIA almost always heal, while most IIB and III lesions stricture. Endoscope within 12-48 h. Avoid the period of greatest wall weakness (about days 5-15), and the wall stays fragile for about 3 weeks. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis with deep burns, whereas acid causes coagulative necrosis but can perforate the stomach. Oropharyngeal burns do not predict esophageal injury. Long-term SCC surveillance is needed. Ingestions are bimodal: accidental at age 1-5 and intentional (more severe) in adolescents and adults. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 36, p 661) **Initial ED rules**: Give no activated charcoal (it does not bind caustics), do not induce vomiting, and place no blind NG tube (perforation risk). If dilution is used, limit it to 15 mL/kg. Household bleach (pH about 7) is usually only an irritant and can be observed. Endoscopy is best done 12-48 hours after ingestion. Later endoscopy is riskier, especially from about day 5 to day 15, when the wall is weakest. A flexible scope is preferred, the endoscopist usually stops at the first circumferential burn, and tracheoscopy is considered if esophageal injury is found. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, pp 3128–3129)
canonical_layers.manage: **Supportive care**: NPO/supportive care, analgesia and multidisciplinary GI/surgical/ENT involvement depend on injury grade (endoscopic staging, e.g., **Zargar**). Perforation or mediastinitis requires urgent source control. **Higher-grade injury** (roughly **Zargar 2b** and above): specialists may consider early nasogastric tube placement under direct endoscopic visualization to maintain enteral access. Evidence that this prevents stricture is limited, and placement must not be blind. **Key trap**: the role of corticosteroids, prophylactic antibiotics and acid-suppression remains an unresolved evidence question as of the **2025 review** -- these are not settled standard-of-care interventions, and none should be taught as a required step. **Follow-up**: long-term follow-up addresses esophageal stricture (dilation, and in refractory cases adjuncts such as intralesional steroid or mitomycin C) and swallowing/nutrition. **Stricture risk and dilation**: Stricture forms after about 77% of Zargar 2b burns and essentially 100% of grade 3 burns, and grades 0-2a rarely stricture. Start dilation at about 3-4 weeks after barium mapping; dilation that begins late (after about 6 weeks) has more perforations and recurrences. Balloon (radial) dilation tears less than bougies, which exert longitudinal shear. Retrograde dilation over a string through a gastrostomy is the safest for long strictures. Caustic strictures resist dilation more than peptic or anastomotic strictures (success about 60-80%). The book still recommended steroids for grade 2a burns, whereas current reviews treat their benefit as unproven. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Caustic Injuries and Acquired Strictures of the Esophagus", p 1373) **Steroids and late care**: a meta-analysis (10 studies, 572 patients) found steroids do not reduce stricture after grade II burns. Strictures are dilated with reassessment every 2–3 weeks; late presenters (>48 hours) are imaged with water-soluble contrast rather than scoped. Laundry detergent pods can cause CNS depression and respiratory distress that warrant ICU care and airway protection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, p 3129) **Laryngeal involvement and airway**: the larynx is involved in about 40% of caustic ingestions; alkali causes deep liquefaction necrosis that worsens over time, acid causes coagulation necrosis. Admit for at least 24 hours of airway observation; facial burns, oral soot and laryngeal edema predict need for airway intervention. Translaryngeal intubation after caustic laryngeal injury was associated with later tracheotomy for stenosis in every case in one series, so tracheotomy is preferred when an airway is needed. Endoscopy should be done within 24 hours, before edema and ulceration make instrumentation riskier. Inhalation burns affect about 30% of burn patients and increase mortality sixfold. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 948–949)
canonical_layers.operate: ENT involvement focuses on the threatened laryngeal airway (friable, edematous tissue changes intubation risk and technique); GI/thoracic/general surgery manage deeper esophagogastric perforation or necrosis, which can carry substantial mortality and demands prompt multidisciplinary source control.
canonical_layers.teach: A normal mouth does not clear the esophagus -- up to 30% of significant esophageal injuries show no visible oral burns. The must-not-miss problems are airway injury and transmural perforation. Do not teach steroids or prophylactic antibiotics as a required step; current review states the evidence for both remains unresolved. **Late carcinoma risk**: After a severe caustic burn, the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is roughly 1,000 times higher, with a latency of 13-71 years, and up to 7% of patients with esophageal carcinoma have a childhood caustic ingestion. Patients with caustic strictures need lifelong surveillance even without symptoms. For strictures that need dilation indefinitely, esophagectomy with gastric pull-up or colon interposition is an alternative. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Caustic Injuries and Acquired Strictures of the Esophagus", p 1377)
