candidates.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. TED severity and inflammatory activity are different axes; proptosis, diplopia/exposure and optic neuropathy do not all require the same treatment. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Coordinate thyroid control, smoking cessation and activity/severity-directed medical/ophthalmic therapy. Urgent vision-threatening disease is different from rehabilitative surgery after inactive disease.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Thyroid Eye Disease / Graves Ophthalmopathy. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: active inflammation determines timing; severity determines urgency and the functional problem to solve.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Management of Thyroid Eye Disease

canonical_layers.recognize:
**Framework**: TED severity and inflammatory activity are different axes. Proptosis, diplopia/exposure, and optic neuropathy do not all require the same treatment.

**Current evidence**: assess activity and severity separately. The 7-item CAS includes spontaneous and gaze-evoked pain, eyelid redness/swelling, conjunctival redness, chemosis, and caruncle/plica inflammation. At least **3/7** commonly supports active disease at initial assessment. **Urgent**: sight-threatening dysthyroid optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown requires urgent ophthalmologic management. **Phases and thyroid status**: About 5-10% of patients with Graves orbitopathy are euthyroid and about 10% are hypothyroid, so normal thyroid labs do not exclude it. The active inflammatory phase lasts roughly 1.5-3 years before the cicatricial phase. Immunosuppression works only in the active phase, while elective surgery waits for inactivity. Upgaze is usually the first motility limitation. The older NO SPECS scheme grades only severity, so it has been replaced by VISA (more used in North America) and EUGOGO, which also score activity. Smoking and radioiodine worsen the eye disease, whereas methimazole, PTU and thyroidectomy appear neutral. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 58, pp 1110-1112)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize disease to extraocular muscles and orbital fat within a fixed bony orbit; apical crowding threatens the optic nerve while inferior/medial rectus enlargement drives common motility patterns.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Assessment**: assess visual acuity/color, pupils, cornea, motility/diplopia, proptosis, and optic-nerve risk with ophthalmology. CT helps define muscle/apical anatomy when decompression is considered.

**Current evidence**: document acuity, color vision, pupils, corneal exposure, fields/disc, exophthalmometry, lids, motility/diplopia, activity, and severity over time. Image when optic neuropathy, atypical disease, or decompression planning is at issue. **Before biologic therapy**: assess smoking, thyroid control, pregnancy, metabolic risk, and hearing risk. **Imaging pitfall**: get a noncontrast CT of orbits and sinuses (also usable for navigation) before decompression. Avoid iodinated IV contrast, which has caused severe acute exacerbations of Graves disease. MRI is usually unnecessary when the diagnosis is clear. Indications for decompression are disfigurement, exposure keratopathy and compressive optic neuropathy (dyschromatopsia, RAPD, falling acuity), the last being urgent (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 765–766). **Imaging and labs**: CT or MRI shows extraocular muscle enlargement in about 70% of patients: fusiform 2-8-fold belly enlargement sparing the tendons, bilateral in 90%, inferior and medial recti most often. Patients under 40 tend toward fat expansion and those over 60 toward muscle swelling. Apical crowding without much proptosis carries the highest risk of compressive optic neuropathy. TRAb is detected in about 98% of untreated Graves patients. Grading systems are NOSPECS, EUGOGO CAS (active if ≥3/7 initially or ≥4/10 on follow-up), and VISA. (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1919) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1920)
canonical_layers.manage:
**Principle**: coordinate thyroid control, smoking cessation, and activity/severity-directed medical/ophthalmic therapy. Urgent vision-threatening disease is different from rehabilitative surgery after inactive disease.

**Current evidence**: use lubrication, smoking cessation, and thyroid optimization for suitable mild disease. **Active moderate-to-severe TED**: match therapy to phenotype -- IV glucocorticoids remain important for inflammatory disease, while teprotumumab is an important option particularly for prominent proptosis/diplopia, after individualized safety, access, and preference assessment. **Sight-threatening optic neuropathy**: treat urgently with high-dose IV glucocorticoids and decompression when response is inadequate. **Rehabilitative sequence**: decompression, then strabismus, then eyelid surgery, once sufficiently inactive/stable. **Medical specifics**: RAI worsens or triggers orbitopathy in at least 15% (38% in a Cochrane analysis), and oral prednisone for several weeks afterward reduces this. Selenium helps mild disease. Pulsed IV methylprednisolone (500 mg weekly for 6 weeks, then 250 mg weekly for 6 weeks) beats oral prednisone (80-100 mg) in efficacy and safety. Orbital RT (e.g., 20 Gy in 10 fractions) helps motility and soft tissue in early active disease, but avoid it in diabetics (retinopathy). Total and subtotal thyroidectomy do not differ in their effect on eye disease. Current EUGOGO (2021) first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe active disease is IV methylprednisolone plus mycophenolate. Teprotumumab (IGF-1R antibody, FDA-approved 2020) is an alternative that reduces proptosis but can cause hearing loss, so get a baseline audiogram. (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1920) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1921) **Decompression outcomes and diplopia**: Endoscopic decompression recesses the globe by about 3.5 mm on average (range 2–12 mm), and adding a lateral wall gives about 2 mm more. New or worse diplopia occurs in up to one-third, usually temporary. Preserving the inferomedial orbital strut lowers the risk, and persistent diplopia is treated with strabismus surgery 8–10 months later. Bilateral single-stage surgery is generally recommended. A balanced decompression helps avoid asymmetry. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 18, p 150, 155–156) **Post-decompression complications**: do not pack postoperative epistaxis at the bedside because orbital contents are exposed. Return to the OR instead. Retrobulbar hematoma can still threaten vision and may need canthotomy/cantholysis. Give intraoperative and tapered postoperative steroids against edema-related optic neuropathy. Sinusitis or mucocele from herniated orbital fat can appear decades later. SNOT-22 improves at 1 year, so sinonasal function is not harmed long term (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 767–768).
canonical_layers.operate: Orbital decompression is wall/fat-selective and anatomy-specific; balance decompression against new/worsened diplopia and protect orbit/skull base/sinuses. **Diplopia-sparing options and outcomes**: an inferomedial bony strut (first feasible in 71% of orbits, now about 100% with angled instruments), a medial periorbital 'sling' along the medial rectus borders, and balanced medial plus lateral decompression (postoperative diplopia still 10–33%). Medial plus inferior decompression reduces proptosis by about 3.2 mm, and adding the lateral wall gives about 5.6 mm total. Sling preservation in balanced decompression costs little (about 5.1 mm), but strut preservation lowers reduction (about 3.6 mm). For compressive optic neuropathy, remove the walls and periorbita completely rather than sparing them (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 766–768). **Endoscopic decompression details**: Avoid surgery in the active phase except for compressive optic neuropathy. The surgical sequence is decompression, then strabismus surgery, then eyelid surgery. Endoscopic medial wall and medial floor decompression reduces proptosis by about 3.2-5.1 mm. Preserve the inferomedial strut and a 10-mm periorbital sling over the medial rectus to limit diplopia. New diplopia occurs in 19-45% after endoscopic decompression, versus 0-15% with balanced medial-lateral decompression. The posterior limit is the annulus of Zinn thickening near the sphenoid face. Incise the periorbita posterior to anterior, and do not pack the nose. (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1921) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1922) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1923) **Endoscopic medial and inferomedial decompression**: Indications are proptosis (including cosmetic), exposure keratopathy, diplopia, and compressive optic neuropathy. Resect the middle turbinate, make a wide posterior maxillary antrostomy, complete sphenoethmoidectomy, then remove the lamina papyracea from the skull base to the orbital floor and from the maxillary line to the sphenoid face (the sphenoethmoid angle is the posterior limit), leaving a thin strip of lamina at the skull base. Downfracture the medial orbital floor medial to the infraorbital nerve, then incise the periorbita from posterior to anterior with a sickle/arachnoid knife and divide fibrous bands so fat prolapses. For severe disease, a balanced three-wall decompression adds an external lateral wall decompression. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 18, p 149–155) **Endoscopic medial/inferior decompression technique**: do a wide maxillary antrostomy (back to the posterior wall and down to the inferior turbinate) and a total ethmoidectomy, but leave the most anterior/superior frontal-recess cells alone so prolapsed fat does not obstruct the maxillary or frontal sinus. Remove the lamina from the sphenoid face to the frontal process of the maxilla, up to the frontoethmoid suture, and the floor medial to the infraorbital canal (the lateral limit). For apical compressive optic neuropathy, drill the orbital process of the palatine bone. Incise the periorbita posterior to anterior and lyse fibrous bands. Avoid packing, and tell anesthesia not to mask-ventilate at extubation (pneumo-orbita risk) (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 767–768).
canonical_layers.teach:
**Teach**: active inflammation determines timing. Severity determines urgency and the functional problem to solve.

**Current evidence**: CAS measures activity -- it is not a stand-alone treatment switch. Separate activity, severity, sight threat, and the dominant inflammation-versus-proptosis/diplopia phenotype. **Key trap**: teprotumumab is not automatically first-line for every patient.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Large conductive air-bone gap after trauma, chronic ear disease or surgery with relatively normal TM/pressure suggests this condition; hypercompliant tympanometry can support but does not prove it. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Observe or amplify if functional burden is acceptable; reconstruct when hearing benefit is expected and the middle ear is safe/aerated enough for durable mechanics.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Ossicular Discontinuity. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Ossiculoplasty succeeds when mechanics and middle-ear environment are favorable. A technically perfect prosthesis in a poorly ventilated scarred ear may fail.

canonical_layers.recognize: Large conductive air-bone gap after trauma, chronic ear disease or surgery with relatively normal TM/pressure suggests ossicular discontinuity; hypercompliant tympanometry can support but does not prove it. **Patterns of inflammatory ossicular damage**: The incus long process is eroded most often, from poor blood supply and adherence of a posterosuperior pocket. The stapes crura come second (from pockets or cholesteatoma). Manubrium erosion goes with perforation but adds little loss. Incudostapedial discontinuity behind an intact drum gives a maximal 50-60 dB loss, which is less when a perforation coexists. A conductive loss of about 30 dB with a perforation implies ossicular involvement. High compliance suggests discontinuity and low compliance fixation, though the distinction is unreliable. In children, fixation is usually from adhesive otitis media and rarely from tympanosclerosis. CT detects only large defects. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 820-821)
canonical_layers.localize: Common disruptions involve incudostapedial joint, long process of incus, malleus/incus fixation or erosion around cholesteatoma. Stapes superstructure and footplate status determine reconstruction options.
canonical_layers.workup: Use otoscopy and complete audiometry; temporal-bone CT may show gross discontinuity but small joint defects can be missed. Definitive diagnosis is sometimes operative.
canonical_layers.manage: Observe or amplify if functional burden is acceptable; reconstruct when hearing benefit is expected and the middle ear is safe/aerated enough for durable mechanics. **Pediatric ossiculoplasty decisions**: Operate only when neither ear has had effusion or atelectasis for at least 1 year (risk is higher the younger the child). Bilateral maximal conductive loss favors surgery. For unilateral mild to moderate loss, fit a hearing aid and defer surgery to adolescence, when local anesthesia is possible. In cholesteatoma surgery, stage the ossiculoplasty to the second look. Prefer the child's own incus (interposition) over prostheses. Never do a stapedectomy with a perforation, and rarely if ever in a child with recent otitis, because of the risk of suppurative labyrinthitis. Freed fixed ossicles often refix, and footplate status predicts TORP results. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 821-822)
canonical_layers.operate: Reconstruction depends on malleus, stapes superstructure, footplate mobility, TM position and middle-ear space. PORP/TORP, cartilage and autologous ossicle techniques should create stable coupling without excessive pressure on the stapes. **Reconstruction options and targets**: The incus lenticular/long process is the most common erosion site because of its tenuous blood supply. Options: incudostapedial joint prosthesis or hydroxyapatite bone cement for a small gap, sculpted autologous incus, PORP to an intact stapes capitulum (target air-bone gap ≤20 dB), and TORP to the footplate (target ≤30 dB), with cartilage between prosthesis and drum to prevent extrusion. Cadaveric homograft ossicles have largely been abandoned in the US because of disease-transmission concerns. Always check for lateral chain fixation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 378) **Reconstruction outcomes and transformer numbers**: in most series, at least two-thirds of PORPs and at least half of TORPs reach an air-bone gap of 20 dB or less. Incus interposition brings about 66% within 20 dB, and results are stable over time. A cartilage disc under the prosthesis head reduces extrusion, and a footplate shoe stabilizes a TORP. The ideal transformer predicts about 28 dB of gain (about 26 dB from the roughly 20:1 TM/oval-window area ratio plus about 2 dB from the 1.3:1 lever). Measured gain is about 23 dB, peaking near 1 kHz. Mastoid cavities have a shallow middle ear, so short prostheses are needed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 19, p 369-373)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Persistent symptoms after prior sinus surgery may reflect residual inflammatory disease, scarring/stenosis, missed cells/ostia, recirculation, odontogenic disease, migraine or a wrong original diagnosis. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Optimize inflammatory phenotype and topical delivery; revise only anatomy that contributes to persistent disease. Biologics may be preferable to repeated surgery in selected severe type-2 CRSwNP.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Revision FESS. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Revision surgery is diagnostic humility plus anatomy. First ask why the first treatment failed; otherwise you may repeat the same failure with fewer landmarks.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Differential**: persistent symptoms after prior sinus surgery may reflect residual inflammatory disease, scarring/stenosis, missed cells/ostia, recirculation, odontogenic disease, migraine, or a wrong original diagnosis. **Foundation**: persistent symptoms after ESS do NOT automatically mean 'failed surgery.' **Approach**: revision evaluation starts by naming the failure mechanism -- persistent/residual disease from unopened or incompletely opened anatomy; recurrent inflammatory disease such as polyposis/AERD; scar, synechiae, or ostial stenosis; maxillary recirculation from an antrostomy that does not incorporate the natural ostium; retained uncinate or ethmoid/frontal partitions; middle-turbinate lateralization; osteitis; untreated sphenoid/frontal disease; odontogenic, fungal, neoplastic, or host-factor disease; inadequate topical delivery/adherence; or a nonrhinogenic symptom generator such as migraine/neuralgia. **Key trap**: a technically patent cavity plus discordant symptoms is a reason to reconsider the diagnosis, not an automatic indication for more surgery.
canonical_layers.localize: Reconstruct anatomy from CT and endoscopy before entering the nose. Prior surgery may remove familiar landmarks while leaving dangerous skull-base/orbital relationships unchanged.
canonical_layers.workup: **Confirm**: active CRS objectively, and review prior operative notes, pathology/cultures, and treatment adherence. **CT**: should be read as a surgical map for residual partitions, frontal recess, sphenoid, orbit, skull base, and neo-ostial stenosis. **Application**: reconstruct what happened before planning what to revise. Review the original operative note, pathology/cultures, prior CT, postoperative endoscopy, complications, disease phenotype, treatment adherence, and the duration/quality of any postoperative improvement. **Current workup**: perform current nasal endoscopy and obtain a **fine-cut sinus CT** for revision planning. **On imaging/endoscopy, trace**: the natural maxillary ostium and prior antrostomy for recirculation, residual uncinate, retained anterior/posterior ethmoid or frontal-recess cells, middle-turbinate position, synechiae/stenosis, osteitic partitions, persistent sphenoid/frontal disease, and altered orbit/skull-base boundaries. **Reconsider**: dental source, fungal disease, unilateral tumor, immune/CF/PCD, AERD/type-2 inflammation, and nonrhinogenic facial-pain/headache pathways when the pattern demands them. **Skull base trajectory and carotid risk**: If the maxillary sinus height is more than twice the posterior ethmoid height (ratio above 2:1), a trajectory guided by the maxillary sinus tends to lead into the skull base rather than the sphenoid. Carotid dehiscence in the sphenoid appears in about 5–25% of radiographic/cadaveric studies, and with asymmetric sphenoids the intersinus septum usually inserts on one carotid canal. Use CT of 2–3 mm or thinner with reformats, and note lateral lamella depth, AEA course, Onodi cells, and a lateralized turbinate remnant. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 14, p 115–116) **Host factors to screen before revising**: AERD (polyp recurrence 36–96%, aspirin desensitization about 1 month after surgery, once polyps and eosinophilia are controlled). GPA, sarcoidosis and EGPA (surgery can worsen GPA and sarcoid, get rheumatology/immunology input first). CF or PCD. Immunodeficiency (CRS prevalence rises when CD4 falls below 50 cells/mm3). Continued smoking. And poor adherence. Think of atypical adult CF with poorly pneumatized sinuses, Pseudomonas colonization, neo-osteogenesis, GI or non-asthma lung disease, or a family history. Endoscopic medial maxillectomy may suit these patients (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 713–714).
canonical_layers.manage: **Principle**: optimize inflammatory phenotype and topical delivery, and revise only anatomy that contributes to persistent disease. **Biologics**: may be preferable to repeated surgery in selected severe type-2 CRSwNP. **Management decision**: correct the demonstrated driver before committing the patient to another operation. Optimize topical anti-inflammatory delivery and phenotype-specific therapy; coordinate dental source control, host-factor treatment, AERD/CRSwNP strategy, or other disease-specific care when those mechanisms dominate. **Key trap**: if prior sinus openings are patent and the remaining symptoms are not explained by objective sinonasal disease, do not revise normal/patent anatomy simply because the patient has had ESS before. **Indication for revision**: a defined surgically correctable target remains and the expected benefit outweighs the added risk of scarred anatomy.
canonical_layers.operate: **Principle**: re-establish constant landmarks before crossing scar. Work from known to unknown, preserve viable mucosa, and create durable access for postoperative care rather than chasing every radiographic opacity. **Senior operative decision**: make revision surgery hypothesis-driven and anatomy-specific. Preserve working prior openings and remove only the residual/scarred partitions or diseased tissue needed to restore the intended drainage pathway, topical access, and disease control. **Maxillary recirculation**: connect the accessory/prior opening to the **true natural ostium** rather than enlarging the wrong window. **Frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid revision**: use the preoperative CT as an active surgical map, because normal landmarks may be absent or distorted -- re-establish reliable landmarks before advancing through scar. **Lower the threshold for image guidance** when altered lamina, skull base, optic/carotid relationships, prior turbinate loss, osteitis, or dehiscence are present. **Danger-zone/bailout rule**: if orientation becomes uncertain near orbit, skull base, carotid, optic nerve, or a suspected dehiscence, stop dissection, control bleeding, re-localize using fixed landmarks plus imaging/navigation and angled visualization, and defer unsafe tissue removal rather than converting uncertainty into a CSF, orbital, or vascular injury. **Frontal sinus rescue procedure**: For frontal obstruction from a lateralized, partially resected middle turbinate, raise a medially based mucosal flap from the turbinate stump, remove the bony remnant (a Draf IIb), and advance the flap over the bare bone: in effect, a IIb with an advancement flap. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 10, p 91) **Revision technique rules**: in revision frontal surgery, first remove every residual bony partition. Dilation or drilling only complements this. Avoid balloon-only revision when partitions remain, since retained mucosa can be trapped against the lamina or skull base. For neo-osteogenesis or circumferential scarring, use nonanatomic procedures: Draf III/modified Lothrop, maxillary mega-antrostomy, or transseptal sphenoidotomy (posterosuperior septectomy, full removal of the sphenoid face and drilling of the intersinus septum into one common opening, with optional floor 'nasalization'). Cover exposed bone with mucosal grafts when possible (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 715–716).
canonical_layers.teach: **Concept**: revision surgery is diagnostic humility plus anatomy. First ask why the first treatment failed, or you may repeat the same failure with fewer landmarks. **Chief rule**: a good revision operation starts with a new hypothesis. Ask whether the problem is residual anatomy, scar/stenosis/recirculation, recurrent inflammatory biology, an untreated focal/host source, poor topical access/adherence, or a non-sinus diagnosis. **Workup**: endoscopy plus fine-cut CT define the correctable target; prior records explain how the anatomy got there. **Principle**: preserve what works, fix only what is causally wrong, and treat loss of orientation in scarred danger zones as a reason to stop and re-map -- not as a reason to dissect harder. **Postoperative plan**: after revision, longitudinal topical therapy and **3-12 month** symptom/QOL plus endoscopic outcome assessment remain part of the operation's success. **Unexpected neoplasia and iatrogenic leak**: unsuspected neoplasm turns up in about 0.46% of bilateral inflammatory CRS specimens. Never perform a major oncologic resection on the basis of a frozen section. Refer with a detailed description of attachment sites if needed. An intraoperatively recognized skull base breach should be repaired at once unless intracranial injury needs imaging first. Postoperative clear rhinorrhea calls for β2-transferrin or β-trace testing and early repair because of meningitis risk. The SPA territory can be embolized, but ethmoidal arteries (ophthalmic branches) cannot, and medical lowering of orbital pressure alone is inadequate for orbital hematoma (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 716–717).

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Sudden or fluctuating hearing loss, vertigo or disequilibrium after barotrauma, penetrating trauma, surgery or major pressure event can suggest a perilymph leak, but symptoms are nonspecific. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Activity/pressure precautions and observation are reasonable in selected stable cases; urgent surgical exploration is considered for compelling traumatic leaks, progressive SNHL or severe persistent symptoms.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Perilymph Fistula / Inner-Ear Window Leak. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Perilymph fistula is a clinical diagnosis with imperfect testing. The strongest cases have a credible pressure/trauma mechanism plus cochleovestibular change.

canonical_layers.recognize: Sudden or fluctuating hearing loss, vertigo or disequilibrium after barotrauma, penetrating trauma, surgery or major pressure event can suggest a perilymph leak, but symptoms are nonspecific. **Diving inner-ear injuries**: alternobaric vertigo occurs on ascent (decreasing ambient pressure) in up to 26% of divers and lasts about 10-15 minutes. Inner ear barotrauma (usually on descent) gives hearing loss and tinnitus with vertigo in about 35%, managed like a fistula (bed rest, head elevation). Inner ear decompression sickness (especially deep mixed-gas diving) presents mainly with vertigo and needs urgent hyperbaric oxygen. Outcomes are best when it is started early (one study cites within 68 minutes). (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2534)
canonical_layers.localize: Leak is usually conceptualized at the oval or round window, creating abnormal communication between perilymphatic space and middle ear. Third-window disorders can mimic pressure/sound-induced symptoms.
canonical_layers.workup: Use audiometry and vestibular assessment; CT is useful for trauma/third-window anatomy. There is no single highly reliable bedside test for idiopathic fistula, so diagnosis depends on context and exclusion of better explanations. **Diagnosis remains clinical**: suspect PLF with sudden/fluctuating SNHL or vertigo after strain, barotrauma, violent sneeze or nose-blowing. Mondini dysplasia is strongly associated with PLF in children. No preoperative test is reliable (fistula test, ECoG SP/AP, beta-2 transferrin of middle-ear fluid all have limited sensitivity), and absence of visible leak at exploration does not exclude it. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 488) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Balance Disorders", p 454-455) **Ambiguity of diagnosis**: no audiometric profile distinguishes proven fistulas, inter-observer agreement at exploration is low, and beta-2 transferrin is insensitive for the tiny volumes involved. Natural fissures (fissula ante fenestram, round window niche to posterior ampulla) are common and of unclear significance. Many patients once labeled fistula actually have superior canal dehiscence. CT pneumolabyrinth supports a traumatic fistula, and definite traumatic cases can still resolve with conservative care. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2533)
canonical_layers.manage: Activity/pressure precautions and observation are reasonable in selected stable cases; urgent surgical exploration is considered for compelling traumatic leaks, progressive SNHL or severe persistent symptoms. **Conservative regimen and fistula test sensitivity**: Initial care is bed rest with head elevation and strain avoidance (open-mouth sneezing, stool softeners) for about 5–10 days, with exploration and window grafting reserved for persistent symptoms or progressive hearing loss. The Hennebert fistula test is only about 10–40% sensitive, and there is no definitive preoperative test. Labyrinthine concussion (posttraumatic vertigo and SNHL without fracture) is a self-limited mimic that may leave BPPV. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 419–420) **Outcome after pediatric exploration**: In a Pittsburgh series of 160 explored ears, hearing stabilized in 83.5% with a confirmed PLF and in 93% with no PLF found, and improved in only 8.7% vs 1.8%. This suggests that much of the apparent 'stabilization' is the natural history (as with EVA). Repair packs the window with fascia, muscle or areolar tissue. Beta-2 transferrin on the leaked fluid is neither fast enough nor reliable enough to use during surgery. Explore only after the etiologic workup is complete and the family has been counseled about the controversy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 540-541)
canonical_layers.operate: Middle-ear exploration evaluates oval/round-window regions and allows sealing with soft tissue/fascia when a leak is suspected. Avoid excessive manipulation of the stapes/vestibule. **Exploration technique**: When possible, explore under local anesthesia with sedation so that the patient can do a Valsalva maneuver. Remove posterosuperior canal bone until the oval window is fully seen, and take down the round window overhang and mucosal folds. Clear fluid that reaccumulates in a niche is often transudate or pooled local anesthetic, not perilymph, so it does not confirm a fistula. Inspect fissures in front of the oval window and below the round window. Routinely patch the round window niche even when exploration is negative, but be conservative at the oval window to avoid a conductive loss. Explore early for penetrating trauma or suspected stapes subluxation. For suspected chronic fistula with stable hearing, try vestibular rehabilitation first. Beta-2 transferrin testing of middle-ear fluid is not recommended. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, p 2554)
canonical_layers.teach: Perilymph fistula is a clinical diagnosis with imperfect testing. The strongest cases have a credible pressure/trauma mechanism plus cochleovestibular change.

candidates.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. The clinically N0 neck can still harbor occult metastasis; treatment depends on primary site, T stage, depth/biology and expected nodal drainage rather than a universal elective neck dissection. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Elective neck treatment may be surgical or radiation-based depending on the primary strategy. Therapeutic neck dissection addresses clinically involved nodal basins; postoperative RT/CRT depends on adverse pathology such as extranodal extension and margins.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Neck Management by Primary Site. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Neck management starts with the primary site. Ask: what levels are at risk, is the neck clinically positive, and is the primary being treated surgically or nonsurgically?

canonical_layers.recognize: The clinically N0 neck can still harbor occult metastasis; treatment depends on primary site, T stage, depth/biology and expected nodal drainage rather than a universal elective neck dissection.
canonical_layers.localize: Know predictable nodal drainage: oral cavity commonly levels I–III; oropharynx frequently II–IV with retropharyngeal considerations; larynx/hypopharynx patterns depend on subsite and midline involvement.
canonical_layers.workup: Use high-quality neck examination and imaging; suspicious nodes require tissue diagnosis when it changes treatment. In oral cavity SCC, depth of invasion contributes to the elective-neck decision. After definitive RT/CRT, response imaging guides whether residual nodal surgery is needed.
canonical_layers.manage: Elective neck treatment may be surgical or radiation-based depending on the primary strategy. Therapeutic neck dissection addresses clinically involved nodal basins; postoperative RT/CRT depends on adverse pathology such as extranodal extension and margins. **Bilateral (N2c) necks**: treat with bilateral neck dissection plus adjuvant radiation. Dissect the less involved side first and try to save its internal jugular vein. If both IJVs are threatened, space the two dissections about 3-4 weeks apart so collateral venous drainage can develop, which avoids facial/cerebral edema, SIADH and blindness. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 275, 277)
canonical_layers.operate: A selective dissection is oncologic only when the selected levels match the disease pattern. Preserve nonlymphatic structures when safe, but do not compromise nodal clearance to spare a structure invaded by tumor.
canonical_layers.teach: Neck management starts with the primary site. Ask: what levels are at risk, is the neck clinically positive, and is the primary being treated surgically or nonsurgically? **Soft palate cancer**: under 2% of mucosal head and neck cancers, usually on the oral surface so found early, but nodal risk exceeds 40% even for small midline lesions (clinical nodes up to 50%, bilateral 5-15%) to levels II-IV and retropharyngeal nodes. Second primary rates are high (about 13% synchronous, 26% metachronous). Larger tumors are usually treated with (chemo)radiation to avoid velopharyngeal insufficiency, with bilateral neck treatment in advanced cases. Surgical defects are best reconstructed with a thin radial forearm flap. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 824-825)

canonical_layers.recognize: Sellar and selected midline skull-base lesions may present with endocrine excess or failure, visual-field loss, cranial neuropathy, headache, or incidental imaging findings; not every lesion requires surgery. **Sellar/suprasellar differential**: pituitary adenoma accounts for about 90% of sellar tumors (10-15% of intracranial tumors); micro- is under 10 mm and macro- over 10 mm, and a dumbbell shape comes from the diaphragma sellae waist. Prolactinoma is the most common functional adenoma (about 30% of all, 50-60% of functional) and is treated first with cabergoline or bromocriptine. Rathke cleft cyst (about 15% incidentally, rarely symptomatic, F:M 2:1) is a nonenhancing midline cyst followed with yearly MRI. Craniopharyngioma is bimodal (5-15 and 45-60 years) and suprasellar. The adamantinomatous type (90%, children) is cystic, T1-bright and calcified; the papillary squamous type (adults) is solid. Parasellar meningioma shows a dural tail in 60-70%. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 34, pp 604-606) **Pediatric pituitary adenoma**: Pituitary adenomas are rare in children (about 3% of supratentorial masses) and are usually functioning: prolactinoma is most common, then ACTH- and GH-secreting tumors. Nonfunctioning, TSH and gonadotroph adenomas make up only 3-6%. Children often present with endocrine signs (growth failure, short stature, delayed puberty) rather than visual loss. Surgery is indicated for every type except prolactinoma, which is treated medically, and radiation is avoided in children. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1924, 1933) **Craniopharyngioma**: A WHO grade 1 Rathke cleft tumor of the sellar/suprasellar region with bimodal ages: children (adamantinomatous, calcified, cystic, T1 bright from protein/cholesterol) and middle-aged adults (papillary, T1 isointense). After surgery expect endocrinopathy: permanent DI in about 90%, cortisol and thyroid replacement in about 90%, GH replacement in about 50%, and hypothalamic obesity in about 50%. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 134)
canonical_layers.localize: The endonasal corridor crosses the sphenoid to the sella, bounded by carotids and cavernous sinuses laterally, optic apparatus superiorly, and clivus posteriorly; extended approaches reach planum, cribriform, and clival targets. **Sphenoid variant rates and intercarotid distances**: The optic nerve bulges into the sphenoid sinus in about 57% of specimens, its canal is dehiscent in about 6%, and about 1% have no bony canal at all. The cavernous carotid makes a prominent bulge in about 67% and is dehiscent in about 6%; V2 is prominent in about 48% (dehiscent in 5%) and the vidian nerve in 18%. The carotids are closest just below the tuberculum sellae (mean about 14 mm, range 10–17 mm), about 20 mm apart at the sellar face, and about 17 mm apart at the clivus, so the suprasellar corridor is the narrowest. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, p 2664) **Landmarks that protect the carotid in extended approaches**: In transpterygoid exposure, finding the vidian canal early leads you to the carotid at the junction of its petrous and paraclival segments. When the nasopharynx and longus muscles are taken down to reach C1 and the odontoid, stay medial to the eustachian tube, because the parapharyngeal ICA runs directly posterolateral to it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2671, 2675)
canonical_layers.workup: Obtain dedicated MRI, CT for bony and sphenoid anatomy when operative planning requires it, complete pituitary testing, formal visual assessment when indicated, and multidisciplinary endocrinology-neurosurgery-rhinology review. **Pituitary adenoma subtypes and stalk effect**: Microadenomas are under 10 mm and macroadenomas over 10 mm; about two thirds secrete hormone (prolactin about 48%, GH 10%, ACTH 6%, TSH 1%). Prolactinomas are treated first with cabergoline or bromocriptine; other functioning and symptomatic tumors go to surgery. A nonfunctioning macroadenoma compressing the stalk raises prolactin (usually under 200 ng/mL) by removing dopamine inhibition. Apoplexy (hemorrhagic infarction) causes sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and panhypopituitarism. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 134-135)
canonical_layers.manage: Observe appropriate incidental/noncompressive lesions and use disease-specific medical therapy such as dopamine agonists for most prolactinomas; optimize endocrine deficits before surgery. **Rathke cleft cyst management**: A small nonenhancing nodule inside the cyst is considered pathognomonic for Rathke cleft cyst, which otherwise can be hard to tell from a cystic adenoma or craniopharyngioma. Incidental cysts are observed. Symptomatic (headache) or enlarging cysts are fenestrated and drained into the sphenoid through an endoscopic transsellar or infrasellar route. The lining is not stripped, because removal adds CSF leak and gland injury risk without benefit. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1933) **Pediatric craniopharyngioma strategy**: Craniopharyngioma is the most common benign pediatric sellar/parasellar tumor (up to half of pediatric sellar tumors), usually adamantinomatous. Gross total resection gives the lowest recurrence (mean about 17%), and recurrences cluster 3.5-5 years after treatment. With hypothalamic invasion, subtotal resection plus radiation may be preferred, because aggressive removal risks hyperphagia and obesity, memory and behavior problems, and temperature dysregulation. Tumors are classed by position relative to the stalk (pre-, trans-, or retroinfundibular), which sets endonasal difficulty; pituitary transposition for retroinfundibular tumors risks hypopituitarism. Cystic recurrences can be aspirated or treated with intracystic bleomycin or beta-emitting isotopes, and these cases carry a high postoperative CSF leak risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1933-1934, 1939) **Postoperative diabetes insipidus criteria**: After sellar surgery, urine output above 2-3 mL/kg/h for 2 consecutive hours suggests DI. It is confirmed by serum sodium above 150 mEq/L with dilute urine (specific gravity under 1.005, osmolality 50-150 mOsm/kg). Mild DI is managed with fluid and electrolyte replacement. Desmopressin is given for persistent DI, severe dehydration or sodium disturbance, or troublesome polyuria and thirst. Postoperative DI is usually self-limited. Patients at risk of cortisol deficiency get perioperative stress steroids. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1938) **Postoperative instructions after a dural repair**: For about 30 days, no moderate or strenuous exertion, straining, nose blowing or closed-mouth sneezing, and use stool softeners and a high-fiber diet. Packing may stay 7–10 days after extended approaches. Saline irrigations and debridement every 2 weeks, with the first surveillance imaging at about 3 months once the cavity has healed. Be ready to recognize and treat acute anterior pituitary insufficiency and other transient or permanent endocrine problems from stalk manipulation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2676–2677) **Postoperative diabetes insipidus monitoring**: After transsphenoidal surgery, check urine specific gravity and sodium about every 6 hours; DI is suggested by dilute urine (SG under 1.003) with rising sodium over 145. On MRI a microadenoma is a hypointense nonenhancing focus within the brightly enhancing gland on T1. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 135)
canonical_layers.operate: The rhinologist creates the corridor and reconstruction while neurosurgery treats the lesion. Plan carotid localization and multilayer closure before dural entry; preserve or harvest a vascularized nasoseptal flap when a high-flow leak is plausible. **Intraoperative carotid injury protocol**: apply immediate pressure with a pattie and harvest crushed muscle (neck or thigh) to pack over the tear until bleeding stops. Cover it with a nasoseptal flap and gentle packing, and go directly to angiography (pseudoaneurysm, need for endovascular sacrifice or stent). Use a 'rescue' nasoseptal flap incision when a leak is possible: cut only the posterior third of the superior incision to protect the posterior septal pedicle. Postoperative CSF leak is the most common complication. Tension pneumocephalus presents with rapid neurologic decline and is less common than after open surgery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 34, pp 609-610) **Pediatric reconstruction options**: The nasoseptal flap (posterior septal artery) can reconstruct anterior, sellar and clival defects in children, but it is small relative to the skull base before about age 14. Middle turbinate and palatal flaps are usually impractical in children. Backups are the pericranial flap (supraorbital/supratrochlear) for anterior defects, the inferior turbinate flap or temporoparietal fascia flap for central defects, and temporoparietal fascia or temporalis muscle for lateral defects. Dural defects are closed with an inlay fascial graft plus a vascularized onlay flap. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1922, 1930, 1940) **Open approaches and facial growth in children**: The skull base reaches mature shape at about 12 years and the face at about 16. Extensive craniofacial osteotomies, periosteal stripping, and radiation can disturb growth centers and cause asymmetry. Permanent teeth usually erupt after age 10, so a Le Fort I down-fracture is avoided in young children. Plan any maxillotomy with a panoramic film or coronal CT to spare tooth buds; midface degloving and transmaxillary routes give wide exposure while preserving dentition. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1931, 1940) **Matching the endonasal module to the target**: Transcribriform (unilateral or bilateral, with ethmoid artery division and often a Draf III) is for olfactory-groove meningioma, esthesioneuroblastoma, CSF leak, encephalocele and sinonasal malignancy. Transtuberculum-transplanum is for planum and tuberculum meningiomas, craniopharyngioma, Rathke cleft cyst and suprasellar adenoma, and the nasoseptal flap is raised before the bony work. Transclival is for clival and retroclival lesions such as chordoma. The craniocervical (odontoid) corridor mainly treats extradural compression from basilar invagination (for example rheumatoid), plus foramen magnum meningioma and chordoma with inferior extension. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2671–2675)
canonical_layers.teach: This is a team operation whose success includes endocrine and visual outcomes, carotid safety, and durable CSF-leak prevention—not merely tumor removal. **Internal carotid injury**: Carotid injury is the most catastrophic complication of endonasal skull base surgery. Temporize with controlled hypotension, packing or a crushed muscle patch, and transfusion, then go urgently to angiography for endovascular occlusion or stenting. Do not start extended endonasal cases without neurointerventional backup. A mini-Doppler, navigation, and landmarks (paraclival carotid canal, vidian canal leading to the anterior genu, eustachian tube as the lateral limit in the lower clivus) reduce the risk. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 30, p 275, 279–280, 283) **Limits of a purely endonasal approach**: Before the vascularized nasoseptal (Hadad-Bassagasteguy) flap was introduced in 2006, CSF leak rates after expanded endonasal surgery were about 20%-30%; with the flap they fell to about 5%. A purely endonasal approach is contraindicated when tumor involves the nasal bones, the anterior table of the frontal sinus, the skin over the dorsum or frontal sinus, or the orbit to a degree that needs exenteration. Relative contraindications are superficial soft-tissue involvement, the need for vascular reconstruction and very long expected operations. Disease lateral to the mid-orbital roof, or no usable septal flap, pushes toward a combined endoscopic and craniotomy approach. (Cummings 7e, Ch 176, pp 2641, 2647-2648) **Complication benchmarks**: A 1997 US survey of transsphenoidal pituitary surgery found carotid injury in 1.1%, CNS injury in 1.3%, vision loss in 1.8%, CSF fistula in 3.9%, meningitis in 1.5% and mortality of about 0.9%. In a 700-patient expanded endonasal series, neurovascular complications occurred in about 1%. Optic injury usually happens at the superolateral sphenoid wall or posterior ethmoid. During transplanum work, vision can also be lost from injury to the superior hypophyseal artery. Blindness from orbital hematoma can reverse if it is decompressed promptly. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2676–2677)

canonical_layers.recognize: Primary hyperparathyroidism at a young age, multigland disease, recurrent disease, family history, jaw tumors, pituitary/pancreatic tumors, or unusual parathyroid pathology should prompt consideration of a hereditary syndrome; recurrent hyperparathyroidism after prior parathyroid surgery can also rarely reflect parathyromatosis. **Penetrance**: primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common and usually the first feature of MEN1, present in over 90 percent of carriers by about age 50, and it is multiglandular. In MEN2A it is less common (roughly 10 to 30 percent) and usually milder, often found when the thyroid is removed for medullary carcinoma. **Syndromic forms**: About 95% of MEN1 patients develop HPT, usually multigland and in the third or fourth decade. About 30% of MEN2A patients develop HPT. HPT-jaw tumor syndrome (CDC73/HRPT2) involves asynchronous parathyroid tumors, carcinoma in 15-20%, ossifying fibromas of the jaws, renal cysts and uterine lesions. Neonatal severe HPT is homozygous FHH, presents by 6 months, and needs urgent total parathyroidectomy. FHH itself is diagnosed by a Ca/Cr clearance ratio below 0.01 and is not operated on. (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1902) (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1903)
canonical_layers.localize: Hereditary syndromes such as MEN1, MEN2A, CDC73-related disease and familial isolated hyperparathyroidism alter the expected gland distribution and recurrence risk. Parathyromatosis refers to multiple implants/foci of hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue, sometimes after capsular disruption or seeding.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Villaret Syndrome (Retroparotid Space Syndrome). Ipsilateral CN IX, X, XI, and XII palsy PLUS Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). This is Collet-Sicard syndrome (IX-XII) with the added finding of sympathetic-chain injury, which localizes the lesion to the retroparotid space rather than the jugular foramen or skull base alone. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Management follows the same logic as other parapharyngeal space tumors: observe, irradiate, or resect based on diagnosis, growth, and symptoms, always characterizing vascularity before any needle biopsy of a suspected vascular lesion. Cross-sectional imaging characterizes the prestyloid versus poststyloid parapharyngeal compartment (see Parapharyngeal Space Tumor) together with vascular imaging when a vascular lesion is suspected; add laryngoscopy and swallow evaluation to document baseline lower-cranial-nerve function.

canonical_layers.recognize: Ipsilateral CN IX, X, XI, and XII palsy PLUS Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). This is Collet-Sicard syndrome (IX-XII) with the added finding of sympathetic-chain injury, which localizes the lesion to the retroparotid space rather than the jugular foramen or skull base alone.
canonical_layers.localize: **Anatomy**: the retroparotid (retrostyloid/poststyloid parapharyngeal) space contains the carotid sheath (ICA, IJV), cranial nerves IX-XII as they course extracranially, and the cervical sympathetic chain, all in close proximity immediately behind the parotid gland. **Key distinction**: a mass here -- a vagal or sympathetic-chain schwannoma, paraganglioma, or nodal/malignant disease extending posteriorly -- can compress all of these structures at once. This is what distinguishes Villaret from Vernet (jugular foramen only, no XII, no Horner) and from Collet-Sicard (skull base, no Horner).

canonical_layers.operate: Resection is tailored to the compartment and diagnosis; expect and counsel for potential permanent multi-nerve deficits (voice, swallow, shoulder function, and oculosympathetic findings) and plan functional rehabilitation proactively rather than reactively.

candidates.canonical_topic: Radioactive Iodine and TSH Suppression in DTC
candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Radioactive Iodine and TSH Suppression in DTC. 2025 ATA FOUR-BAND RAI/TSH DECISION: RAI remnant ablation, adjuvant treatment of suspected microscopic cancer and treatment of known iodine-avid disease are different intents. RAI is administered following total or near-total thyroidectomy, not routinely after lobectomy; completion thyroidectomy may be considered when RAI is indicated. Neither RAI nor chronic TSH suppression is automatic after a DTC diagnosis. Appropriately selected low-risk papillary microcarcinoma may undergo active surveillance or surgery alone without RAI. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: 2025 ATA RAI CANDIDACY: after total thyroidectomy, do not routinely administer RAI for low-risk DTC; consider it for low-intermediate or intermediate-high risk according to histology, disease burden, postoperative Tg/imaging, likely benefit and preference; recommend it for high-risk disease and appropriate distant metastases. Distinguish adjuvant RAI from treatment of identified iodine-avid tumor and reevaluate utility for RAI-refractory disease. Counsel about sialadenitis/xerostomia, lacrimal injury, marrow effects and possible second malignancy.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Radioactive Iodine and TSH Suppression in DTC. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: BOARDS/CHIEF DECISION: specify RAI intent (remnant ablation versus adjuvant versus known disease), operation performed, four-band ATA recurrence risk and pathology, postoperative Tg/imaging, and dynamic response before selecting RAI and TSH strategy. Post-total-thyroidectomy-plus-RAI excellent Tg is <0.2 ng/mL unstimulated or <1 stimulated with negative imaging; without RAI use treatment-specific thresholds. Excellent/indeterminate response generally means TSH in the normal range.

canonical_layers.recognize: **2025 ATA four-band RAI/TSH decision**: RAI remnant ablation, adjuvant treatment of suspected microscopic cancer, and treatment of known iodine-avid disease are different intents. RAI is administered following total or near-total thyroidectomy, not routinely after lobectomy. Completion thyroidectomy may be considered when RAI is indicated. **Key trap**: neither RAI nor chronic TSH suppression is automatic after a DTC diagnosis. Appropriately selected low-risk papillary microcarcinoma may undergo active surveillance or surgery alone without RAI.
canonical_layers.localize: **Mechanism**: RAI treats iodine-avid remnant or tumor; thyroid hormone suppresses TSH-driven stimulation. **Risk bands**: use four 2025 ATA recurrence-risk bands -- LOW <10%, LOW-INTERMEDIATE 10-15%, INTERMEDIATE-HIGH 16-30%, HIGH >30%. Assign using histologic subtype, microscopic versus gross extrathyroidal extension, vascular invasion extent, aggressive histology, positive margins/residual tumor, number/size/extranodal spread of involved nodes, distant disease, and postoperative findings. An intrathyroidal well-differentiated tumor without important adverse features commonly belongs in low risk. Gross extension, distant disease, or bulky residual/nodal disease raise risk. **Key trap**: individual findings do not all map to one universal band. Apply the histology-specific ATA table, and distinguish recurrence risk from AJCC stage.
canonical_layers.workup: **Before RAI**: decide the intent using final pathology, operative extent and residual disease, postoperative neck ultrasound, Tg with anti-Tg antibodies, imaging, and iodine-avidity when relevant. Interpret Tg in light of lobectomy versus total thyroidectomy and prior RAI. Reassess response longitudinally, rather than waiting for an arbitrary 12-month cutoff. **2025 ATA dynamic response after total thyroidectomy plus RAI**: **EXCELLENT** = negative imaging and nonstimulated Tg <0.2 ng/mL or stimulated Tg <1 ng/mL. **INDETERMINATE** = nonspecific imaging, nonstimulated Tg 0.2-1 or stimulated Tg 1-10, or stable/declining TgAb. **BIOCHEMICALLY INCOMPLETE** = nonstimulated Tg >1 or stimulated Tg >10, or rising TgAb, without structural disease. **STRUCTURALLY INCOMPLETE** = persistent/new structural disease regardless of Tg. **Without RAI**: excellent-response nonstimulated Tg threshold is <2.5 ng/mL with negative imaging. **Key trap**: after hemithyroidectomy, response classification differs, and Tg cutoffs from total thyroidectomy must not be imported.
canonical_layers.manage: **2025 ATA RAI candidacy**: after total thyroidectomy, do not routinely administer RAI for low-risk DTC. Consider it for low-intermediate or intermediate-high risk according to histology, disease burden, postoperative Tg/imaging, likely benefit, and preference. Recommend it for high-risk disease and appropriate distant metastases. Distinguish adjuvant RAI from treatment of identified iodine-avid tumor, and reevaluate utility for RAI-refractory disease. **Counseling**: counsel about sialadenitis/xerostomia, lacrimal injury, marrow effects, and possible second malignancy. Pregnancy and breastfeeding preclude treatment. Verify pregnancy status and ensure lactation has ceased for the guideline-recommended interval. Use low-iodine preparation and appropriate TSH stimulation with thyroid hormone withdrawal or recombinant human TSH based on indication. **TSH goals (2025 ATA recommendations 45-46 and Table 9)**: individualize initial suppression based on recurrence risk, persistent disease, and harms. Do not prescribe fixed legacy targets (<0.1, 0.1-0.5, or 0.5-2 mIU/L) indiscriminately. An excellent or indeterminate response generally calls for TSH within the laboratory normal reference range. Biochemically or structurally incomplete response may warrant TSH below that range, particularly with progressive disease. Long-term suppression is not suggested for low/intermediate-risk patients without biochemical or structural recurrence. Weigh atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis, and other suppression harms, especially in older patients.
canonical_layers.operate: **Choice of operation**: choose lobectomy versus total thyroidectomy from primary tumor extent, nodal/distant disease, bilateral pathology, risk, functional morbidity, and patient priorities -- not solely to make RAI possible. For selected low-risk unilateral DTC, lobectomy may be definitive and does not require RAI. **Completion thyroidectomy**: consider it for residual cancer, or when pathology and postoperative assessment establish a compelling RAI indication -- not as a reflex to any incidental cancer diagnosis.
canonical_layers.teach: **Boards/chief decision**: specify RAI intent (remnant ablation versus adjuvant versus known disease), operation performed, four-band ATA recurrence risk and pathology, postoperative Tg/imaging, and dynamic response before selecting RAI and TSH strategy. **Key numbers**: post-total-thyroidectomy-plus-RAI excellent Tg is <0.2 ng/mL unstimulated or <1 stimulated with negative imaging. Without RAI, use treatment-specific thresholds. Excellent/indeterminate response generally means TSH in the normal range. Incomplete response may justify below-normal TSH. **Key trap**: older numeric suppression targets are historical, rather than universal 2025 ATA mandates.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. White plaque is a visual descriptor spanning benign keratosis through invasive cancer; vascular/mucosal features alter concern. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Risk-factor modification and lesion-specific surveillance/excision/ablation while preserving voice.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Leukoplakia / Laryngeal Dysplasia. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Never equate 'leukoplakia' with one histologic diagnosis.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Definition**: 'leukoplakia' is a purely visual/descriptive term for a white mucosal plaque. It spans a wide histologic range -- from benign hyperkeratosis, through varying grades of dysplasia, to invasive carcinoma. **Key trap**: the term itself carries no diagnostic or prognostic information until tissue is examined, so it should never be treated as if it were itself a histologic diagnosis.
canonical_layers.localize: **Exam/stroboscopy features**: findings raise or lower concern independent of the white color itself. **Higher-risk findings**: an irregular, friable, or ulcerated surface, associated abnormal vascularity, reduced mucosal wave over the lesion, or a fixed/immobile segment -- all increase suspicion for higher-grade dysplasia or invasive disease. **Lower-risk findings**: a thin, smooth, mobile-appearing plaque is more suggestive of benign keratosis. **Key trap**: appearance alone cannot substitute for biopsy.
canonical_layers.workup: Stroboscopy and biopsy/excision when risk warrants; pathology grade drives surveillance/treatment. **Narrow-band imaging**: NBI filters white light down to blue and green bands that hemoglobin absorbs, which highlights the microvessels under leukoplakia and directs biopsy to the most suspicious area. The Ni vascular classification reached about 89% sensitivity and 93% specificity. The simpler ELS scheme separates longitudinal vessel changes (benign) from perpendicular changes such as dots and loops (papilloma, dysplasia, cancer). In one study it reached 100% sensitivity and 95% specificity. NBI also finds second primaries in the oropharynx and hypopharynx better than white light. (Cummings 7e, Ch 54, p 817)
canonical_layers.manage: Risk-factor modification and lesion-specific surveillance/excision/ablation while preserving voice. **Numbers for high-grade lesions**: severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ progresses to invasive cancer in roughly 15-25%. After excision (microflap preferred over stripping, to keep the mucosal wave), follow every 2-3 months for 5 years with a low threshold to re-biopsy. Microinvasive carcinoma can be re-excised every 3 months until two consecutive biopsies are negative. Radiation is an alternative, usually for recurrence. CO2 laser ablation gives no specimen. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 296-297) **Carcinoma in situ options**: excision preserving the lamina propria (microflap) or RT are both effective. Surgical recurrence is about 20% but repeated excision achieves control equivalent to RT, whereas RT gives about 93.5% local control. RT is favored for multiply recurrent or diffuse lesions, unreliable follow-up, or anesthesia risk. Vocal fold stripping is abandoned. In-office 532-nm pulsed KTP (or 585-nm pulsed dye) photoangiolysis targets sublesional vessels and allows bilateral anterior commissure treatment with little web risk, but only after an initial operative biopsy because no specimen is obtained. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1571–1572)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: biopsy persistent, changing, irregular, vascular, stiff, or otherwise suspicious leukoplakia to establish histology. Selected thin, smooth, low-risk lesions may first receive risk-factor treatment with a defined short-interval exam and biopsy if they persist. Appearance alone never establishes histologic grade. **Setup**: microlaryngoscopy for biopsy, or, when the lesion is amenable, complete microflap excision that serves as both diagnosis and treatment. **Key steps**: excise or biopsy with attention to obtaining adequate tissue for grading, while preserving as much normal vibratory mucosa as possible, since many lesions ultimately prove benign or low-grade. **Danger structures**: the vibratory mucosa/superficial lamina propria -- particularly relevant when repeat excisions are needed for recurrent or persistent disease. **Failure mode**: managing a lesion based on its visual appearance ('leukoplakia' as a working diagnosis) without histologic confirmation, or assuming a single benign biopsy result means no further surveillance is needed for a persistent or recurrent lesion. **Postoperative plan**: pathology-directed follow-up. Close surveillance (serial laryngoscopy) for dysplasia given recurrence and progression risk, and standard oncologic management if invasive carcinoma is found.
canonical_layers.teach: Never equate 'leukoplakia' with one histologic diagnosis.
