candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Children may present with falls, delayed motor milestones, episodic vertigo, motion intolerance or school/sports difficulty rather than a precise dizziness history. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the cause and use vestibular/balance rehabilitation when deficits affect development or safety.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Pediatric Vestibular Disorders. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: a child who 'is clumsy' may be describing vestibular dysfunction with the vocabulary available to them.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Evaluation and Management of Pediatric Vestibular Disorders

canonical_layers.recognize: Children may present with falls, delayed motor milestones, episodic vertigo, motion intolerance or school/sports difficulty rather than a precise dizziness history. **Migraine variants and mimics**: benign paroxysmal torticollis of infancy (recurrent, side-alternating head tilt with pallor/vomiting) is a migraine precursor that may evolve into benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood. Image to exclude posterior fossa disease. Basilar-type migraine (now called migraine with brainstem aura in ICHD-3, typically adolescent girls, often perimenstrual) is rarer than vestibular migraine (<10% meet criteria). Refractive errors or convergence insufficiency can cause dizziness with headache, so a cycloplegic eye exam is part of the workup. Familial episodic ataxia (autosomal dominant) may respond to acetazolamide, and 'tornado epilepsy' can mimic vertigo. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Balance Disorders", p 456-458) **Pediatric Ménière disease is rare**: Ménière disease accounted for only about 2.9% of children evaluated for vertigo. More than half of pediatric vertigo was due to otitis media, vestibular neuronitis, benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood or migraine. Still consider Ménière disease when vertigo comes with aural fullness, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. Children with vestibular symptoms plus SNHL after temporal bone trauma (especially oval window involvement) may have a perilymph fistula, and the vertigo may improve after repair even though the SNHL rarely does. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 869, 874) **Otitis media as a cause of imbalance**: Otitis media is the most common cause of vestibular disturbance in children, and parents often report clumsiness while effusion is present. Vestibular testing is abnormal with effusion and returns to normal after tube placement. Some children with past otitis but no current effusion still test abnormal, which suggests a residual labyrinthine effect. Labyrinthitis is the other otitis-related cause. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, p 769)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize peripheral vestibular, migraine, central, visual/proprioceptive and developmental contributors while considering hearing loss and congenital inner-ear disease.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Workup selection**: age-appropriate vestibular testing, audiology, and neurologic/developmental assessment are selected by phenotype. Interpret norms with age/attention limitations.

Use age-appropriate history from child and caregiver, neurologic/ocular-motor examination, hearing testing, positional testing, and selective vestibular tests. **Common branches**: vestibular migraine/recurrent vertigo of childhood, BPPV after trauma, unilateral/bilateral vestibular hypofunction, inner-ear malformation, medication effect, and central disease. School difficulty or delayed motor milestones may be the presenting functional clue. **EEG and BPVC criteria**: children with recurrent episodic vertigo should have an EEG to exclude epileptic vertigo, with prolonged video EEG if the routine study is normal and no spell was captured. Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood requires at least 5 attacks of sudden vertigo resolving within minutes to hours, with normal neurologic, audiometric, and vestibular findings and a normal EEG between attacks. It typically affects ages 1–4, about 20% go on to typical migraine, and frequent spells can be treated with cyproheptadine prophylaxis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 136) **Pediatric testing choices**: rotary chair (child on a parent's lap, physiologic stimulus, less nausea) makes infants and young children testable and helps confirm bilateral loss, since calorics can be absent when rotation is normal. Bithermal calorics use 30 and 44 C, with ice water if no response. A reduced vestibular response above about 24% (Jongkees) suggests peripheral hypofunction, while directional preponderance is nonlocalizing. Pediatric balance can be screened with the P-CTSIB (foam plus visual-conflict dome) and age-normed motor scales (Peabody, Bruininks-Oseretsky). VEMP amplitudes vary with age, so interpret cautiously. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Vestibular Evaluation", p 414-421) **Three-part bedside vestibular screen**: You can screen without a lab. (1) Ask about motor milestones (head control, sitting, walking age). (2) Time one-foot standing. Expected times are a brief stand at 30 months, 2 seconds at 36 months, 5 seconds at 4 years, and from age 5 about 10 seconds eyes open (red flag under 8) and more than 5 seconds eyes closed (red flag under 4). (3) Check horizontal canal function with a clinical head impulse test, or in infants 6 months or younger by spinning the caregiver's stool and looking for postrotary nystagmus. Infants this young cannot visually suppress the VOR. Any single abnormal component justifies formal testing. Even a 10-day static-balance exercise program improved standing balance in children with SNHL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 198, pp 2953-2954)
canonical_layers.manage:
**Management**: treat the cause and use vestibular/balance rehabilitation when deficits affect development or safety.

Treat the cause, use migraine lifestyle/preventive therapy when indicated, perform repositioning for BPPV, and prescribe pediatric vestibular/balance rehabilitation for hypofunction. Coordinate neurology, audiology, physical therapy, and school/fall-safety support. **Key trap**: chronic vestibular suppressants impede compensation and are rarely a long-term solution.
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery is reserved for specific structural disease; most pediatric vestibular care is diagnostic and rehabilitative.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: a child who 'is clumsy' may be describing vestibular dysfunction with the vocabulary available to them.

Children often report dizziness imprecisely. Translate the complaint into timing, triggers, hearing/neurologic associations, and observed balance function before assigning an adult vestibular label.
source_basis: Cummings 7e: Evaluation and Management of Pediatric Vestibular Disorders

candidates.prompt: A patient with sleep-disordered breathing is reviewed in sleep clinic. Sleep difficulty caused by misalignment of biologic timing differs from insomnia caused by inability to sleep despite appropriate timing. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Behavioral timing, light and melatonin-based strategies belong in sleep medicine; treat coexisting OSA independently.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: ask when the patient can sleep normally—not only whether they can sleep.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Sleep Apnea and Sleep Disorders

canonical_layers.recognize: Sleep difficulty caused by misalignment of biologic timing differs from insomnia caused by inability to sleep despite appropriate timing.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the issue to circadian phase and work/school/light schedule rather than pharyngeal anatomy.
canonical_layers.workup:
Use sleep logs/actigraphy and schedule history. Distinguish delayed/advanced phase, shift-work, and jet-lag patterns.

Define habitual sleep timing across work and free days with sleep diary and actigraphy. Then distinguish delayed phase, advanced phase, irregular rhythm, non-24-hour disorder, shift-work disorder, and behaviorally imposed insufficient sleep. **Key point**: PSG is reserved for suspected comorbid sleep disease, not required to prove a timing disorder.
canonical_layers.manage:
Behavioral timing, light, and melatonin-based strategies belong in sleep medicine. Treat coexisting OSA independently.

Use precisely timed light, darkness, melatonin, and schedule shifts matched to the circadian phase. **Key point**: timing determines whether the clock advances or delays. Address school/work constraints and avoid sedatives or stimulants as substitutes for realignment when possible.
canonical_layers.operate: ENT surgery does not correct circadian misalignment.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: ask when the patient can sleep normally—not only whether they can sleep.

Circadian treatment is a phase-response intervention: the right therapy at the wrong clock time can push the patient farther in the wrong direction.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Clear middle-ear fluid, recurrent meningitis or persistent unilateral effusion can reflect tegmen defect/encephalocele. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Repair symptomatic/persistent leaks using transmastoid, middle-fossa or combined strategy based on site/size/anatomy.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of CSF Otorrhea / Temporal Encephalocele. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: A 'middle-ear effusion' that is actually CSF changes every subsequent step.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Suspect** a tegmen defect with or without encephalocele when a patient has persistent unilateral "middle-ear effusion" that does not behave like typical otitis media with effusion, clear watery otorrhea, recurrent meningitis, or a previously placed tube with unremitting clear drainage. **Key trap**: any of these should prompt testing the fluid (beta-2 transferrin) rather than assuming routine effusion.
canonical_layers.localize: **Location**: the tegmen tympani/mastoideum, the thin bony roof separating the middle ear/mastoid from the middle cranial fossa. Herniated dura, with or without brain tissue (encephalocele), through that defect is what produces the CSF leak. **Imaging**: high-resolution CT (bony defect) paired with MRI (soft-tissue herniation) together define site and size before planning repair.
canonical_layers.workup: High-resolution temporal-bone CT plus MRI for soft tissue/encephalocele; assess spontaneous-leak risk factors and intracranial-pressure physiology.
canonical_layers.manage: Repair symptomatic/persistent leaks using transmastoid, middle-fossa or combined strategy based on site/size/anatomy.
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: confirmed CSF leak or symptomatic encephalocele, or recurrent meningitis traced to a tegmen defect. **Setup**: strategy (transmastoid, middle fossa, or combined) is chosen by defect size, location, and number of defects. Small, single, accessible defects often suit a transmastoid approach, while larger or multiple defects, or those far anterior/medial on the tegmen, often need a middle fossa approach for adequate exposure. **Key steps**: reduce any herniated encephalocele tissue (resect if non-functional/necrotic, reduce if viable), and repair the bony defect in a multilayer fashion (e.g., bone/cartilage graft plus soft tissue, sometimes with fascia) rather than soft tissue alone, which is prone to re-herniation. **Danger structures**: the dura and underlying temporal lobe, the ossicular chain and facial nerve in the middle ear/mastoid field, and the sigmoid sinus depending on approach. **Failure mode**: treating a leak as routine middle-ear effusion and placing a tube, which does not address the underlying dural defect and can worsen the leak or delay diagnosis of an evolving intracranial problem. Recognizing that the "effusion" is actually CSF changes every subsequent step, including the urgency of imaging and referral. **Postoperative plan**: monitor for recurrent leak or meningitis, and consider intracranial pressure physiology (e.g., obesity-associated idiopathic intracranial hypertension) as a contributor that may need separate management to prevent recurrence.
canonical_layers.teach: A 'middle-ear effusion' that is actually CSF changes every subsequent step.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Distinguish reversible mucosal congestion from fixed soft-tissue/bony enlargement and from nasal-valve/septal obstruction. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Optimize rhinitis therapy first; reduction is for persistent symptomatic hypertrophy and should preserve mucosal function.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Inferior Turbinate Hypertrophy. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Aggressive resection can trade obstruction for dryness/crusting and dysfunctional airflow.

canonical_layers.recognize: Distinguish reversible mucosal/vascular congestion (responsive to decongestion, allergy treatment, or the nasal cycle) from fixed soft-tissue or bony turbinate enlargement that will not improve medically, and from a nasal-valve or septal problem that only mimics turbinate-driven obstruction. **Technique**: decongestion testing on exam helps separate these before committing to turbinate-directed treatment.
canonical_layers.localize: Obstruction is localized to the inferior meatus/nasal floor level; because the septum, internal nasal valve, and inferior turbinate all contribute to airflow at roughly the same anterior nasal segment, an isolated turbinate reduction in a patient whose real problem is septal deviation or valve collapse will under-deliver on symptom relief.
canonical_layers.workup: Examine before/after decongestion; endoscopy when posterior disease or other pathology is possible.
canonical_layers.manage: Optimize rhinitis therapy first; reduction is for persistent symptomatic hypertrophy and should preserve mucosal function.
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: fixed turbinate hypertrophy causing nasal obstruction refractory to medical therapy (topical steroid, antihistamine/decongestant trial), confirmed not to be primarily valve or septal in origin. **Setup**: options range from submucosal reduction (radiofrequency, microdebrider-assisted submucosal resection) to partial turbinectomy for more severe/bony hypertrophy. **Key steps**: preserve the functional mucosa and as much of the turbinate's normal architecture as possible while reducing bulk, since the turbinate performs real physiologic humidification/warming function. **Danger**: excessive or overly aggressive resection risks **empty nose syndrome** -- a paradoxical sensation of obstruction despite a wide-open airway, from loss of the mucosa's airflow-sensing function -- as well as chronic crusting and dryness. **Failure mode**: treating turbinate size as the only variable and resecting aggressively rather than conservatively. More tissue removed does not reliably mean more symptom relief, and can trade one problem (obstruction) for another (dryness/crusting/dysfunctional airflow). **Postop plan**: saline irrigation and humidification during healing, with realistic counseling that conservative techniques preserve function even if initial obstruction relief feels less dramatic. **Relative durability of techniques**: Outfracture alone is easy but gives poor long-term results. Intramural cautery or radiofrequency is office-friendly but fades, especially if rhinitis goes untreated. Submucosal resection of erectile tissue (with or without bone) that spares the medial mucosa gives the most durable benefit. Total turbinectomy is avoided because of atrophic rhinitis and empty nose syndrome. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 23-24) **Procedure hierarchy and evidence**: Procedures escalate from outfracture, to submucosal soft-tissue reduction (cautery, laser, radiofrequency, microdebrider), to submucosal bone plus soft-tissue resection, to full-thickness anterior resection. In long-term comparisons submucosal resection plus outfracture performed best at 6 years; microdebrider reduction kept 93% of patients improved at 10 years and outperformed bipolar radiofrequency over time. Total turbinectomy is reserved for tumor. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 2, p 11–14)
canonical_layers.teach: Aggressive resection can trade obstruction for dryness/crusting and dysfunctional airflow.

candidates.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Persistent lymphadenopathy with systemic symptoms or atypical nodal pattern may require lymphoma-specific tissue handling. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Hematologic therapy dominates; surgery is diagnostic or for selected complications rather than routine nodal clearance.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Neck Lymphoma. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Plan the biopsy with pathology before destroying the architecture needed for diagnosis.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Red flags**: consider lymphoma when cervical lymphadenopathy is persistent, associated with systemic ("B") symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), or shows an atypical pattern for reactive or metastatic squamous disease (e.g., multiple, non-tender, rubbery nodes across multiple levels, or disease in a patient without a typical head and neck cancer risk profile). **Key point**: this clinical suspicion should change how the node is biopsied, not just what is on the differential. **Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin patterns**: HL peaks at ages 15-40. It spreads contiguously, rarely involves Waldeyer ring, preauricular or occipital nodes, and involves the mediastinum in more than 85%. Pruritus occurs in about 25%, and alcohol-induced nodal pain in under 1%. B symptoms are fever >38 C, drenching sweats, or >10% weight loss in 6 months. NHL often involves Waldeyer ring (asymmetric tonsil), preauricular nodes and extranodal sites. Indolent FL/SLL produces bilateral soft mobile 1-2 cm nodes that can wax and wane (FL regresses spontaneously in up to 20%). A dominant or necrotic node suggests transformation, so excise it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1775) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1777) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1781) **HIV-associated lymphomas**: Lymphoma is the second most common HIV malignancy (up to 19%): diffuse large B-cell most common, then Burkitt (doubling time 24-48 h, unrelated to CD4 count, rarely jaw-based outside endemic Africa). Plasmablastic lymphoma typically arises in the oral cavity of HIV patients and should trigger HIV testing. Prognosis is poor. HIV Hodgkin lymphoma presents later with mixed cellularity or lymphocyte-depleted histology. Open biopsy is preferred to define subtype. Treatment is chemotherapy (R-CHOP or R-EPOCH) with concurrent ART. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 211-213)
canonical_layers.localize: Unlike metastatic SCC, where FNA cytology is usually adequate, lymphoma diagnosis and subtyping require preserved nodal architecture (immunophenotyping, sometimes molecular/flow cytometry studies), so the 'localization' question that matters most here is which node to sample and by what method, not which anatomic level is involved.
canonical_layers.workup: Imaging and tissue diagnosis with architecture/flow cytometry planning; FNA alone may be insufficient for classification. **Staging and specimen handling**: Ann Arbor stage I is one nodal region or one extralymphatic site, II is two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm, III is both sides of the diaphragm, and IV is diffuse extralymphatic organ involvement. The suffix A or B records B symptoms. Labs include CBC, LDH, beta-2 microglobulin and LFTs. Pasha lists CT/PET of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis plus bone marrow biopsy. Under the current Lugano approach, PET/CT stages FDG-avid lymphomas and makes routine marrow biopsy unnecessary in Hodgkin lymphoma and most DLBCL. Send the excised node fresh, not in formalin, for flow cytometry, and avoid steroids before biopsy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 6, pp 325-326) **Biopsy and specimen rules**: Excisional or incisional biopsy remains the preferred initial diagnostic method. FNA plus flow gives subtype accuracy of only about 50-70%, so FNA alone is not sufficient for a first diagnosis, though it is acceptable for relapse, SLL, or lymphoblastic lymphoma. Core biopsy (12-16 gauge, multiple cores) is diagnostic in about 78-95%. Send fresh tissue in saline (never on dry gauze, never fixed overnight), with the clinical question. Steroids before biopsy rarely ruin diagnosis if tissue is obtained within 24-48 h, except in lymphoblastic lymphoma. Withhold them for SVC syndrome alone, and give them only for life-threatening airway compromise. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1776) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1777) **Staging**: HL uses Ann Arbor with Cotswolds modification: A/B symptoms, E for limited contiguous extranodal disease, and X for bulk (>10 cm, or mediastinal mass ratio >0.33 on CXR or >0.35 on CT). NHL uses Lugano, which drops the A/B suffix and counts tonsils, Waldeyer ring and spleen as nodal tissue. FDG PET/CT is the staging study of choice. It upstages 10-20% of HL and makes routine marrow biopsy unnecessary in HL. Indolent MZL/MALT and SLL may not be FDG avid. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1778) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1780) **Benign lymphoproliferative mimics of neck lymphoma**: Castleman disease (giant/angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia) has hyaline-vascular (radial capillaries into follicles) and plasma-cell histologic types and is treated by complete excision of the localized mass. Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy) is a benign self-limited histiocytic adenopathy with emperipolesis. Kimura disease is a chronic eosinophilic inflammatory mass of subcutaneous tissue, salivary glands and nodes, mostly in Asian men, with blood eosinophilia and high IgE. Distinguish from angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia. Options include steroids, radiation and excision. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 6-7, 19, 30)
canonical_layers.manage: Hematologic therapy dominates; surgery is diagnostic or for selected complications rather than routine nodal clearance. **Treatment frameworks**: Early favorable HL is treated with 2 cycles of ABVD plus 20 Gy involved-field RT (GHSG HD10), and early unfavorable HL with 4 cycles of ABVD plus 30 Gy. Cummings gives 6 cycles of ABVD for advanced HL, with a 7-factor IPS for prognosis and interim PET to guide escalation or de-escalation. Current NCCN options for advanced HL also include brentuximab vedotin plus AVD and nivolumab plus AVD. Brentuximab vedotin targets CD30. DLBCL is the most common NHL and the most common extranodal head and neck lymphoma. It is treated with R-CHOP (with or without RT for limited stage), and prognosis follows the IPI: age >60, ECOG 2 or higher, stage III-IV, more than one extranodal site, high LDH. Double-hit (MYC plus BCL2/BCL6) disease does poorly. FL prognosis uses FLIPI. Burkitt and lymphoblastic lymphoma need an emergent oncology consult, CNS-directed chemotherapy, and tumor lysis precautions. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1778) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1779) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1780) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1783) **Sinonasal lymphomas**: In Western patients these are mostly DLBCL of the maxillary sinus, which often invades the orbit and is EBV-negative. DLBCL here has a higher risk of CNS/leptomeningeal relapse, so intrathecal methotrexate or cytarabine prophylaxis is recommended. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (formerly lethal midline granuloma) is more common in Asian and South American patients. It is angiocentric and necrotic, so multiple biopsies are often needed. It is virtually always EBV-positive (EBER in situ) and CD56-positive, and plasma EBV DNA tracks disease. More than 80% present at stage I-IIE. RT alone relapses in about 50%, so concurrent or sequential RT with asparaginase-based chemotherapy (e.g., SMILE) is used. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1784) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1785)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: persistent lymphadenopathy suspicious for lymphoma, especially with systemic symptoms or an atypical nodal pattern. **Setup**: discuss the suspected diagnosis with pathology before biopsy, since the biopsy technique itself is a key decision point here. **Key steps**: obtain tissue for morphology, immunophenotyping and flow cytometry. Excisional biopsy of an accessible representative node is preferred when feasible, but an adequate image-guided core biopsy with multiple cores can establish many lymphoma diagnoses when excision is unsafe or impractical. FNA alone is generally insufficient for initial lymphoma classification. **Danger structures**: standard for whatever neck level is biopsied (spinal accessory nerve in level V, marginal mandibular nerve near the submandibular region, etc.) -- the anatomic risk is not disease-specific, but choosing the wrong biopsy technique is. **Failure mode**: performing FNA alone (yielding insufficient architecture for subtyping), or a piecemeal/core biopsy that destroys the nodal architecture needed for definitive diagnosis, leading to a delayed or repeat procedure. Plan the biopsy approach with pathology input before, not after, obtaining tissue. **Postoperative plan**: expedite pathology review and staging workup, and route the patient to hematology-oncology promptly once lymphoma is confirmed, since surgery's role here is diagnostic, not therapeutic.
canonical_layers.teach: Plan the biopsy with pathology before destroying the architecture needed for diagnosis. **HL survivorship**: After about 15-20 years, deaths from second cancers and coronary disease exceed deaths from HL. Cumulative second-cancer risk is about 25% at 30 years, including head and neck mucosal cancers (RR about 3-5), thyroid cancer, breast cancer in young women, and lung cancer in smokers. MI mortality is about 2.5-fold higher. These risks drive the move to omit or reduce RT in nonbulky early disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1779) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1780)

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Localize expansile petrous-apex disease by CT density/bone behavior and MRI signal; cholesterol granuloma, cholesteatoma and neoplasm behave differently. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Observe stable incidental lesions or drain/resect according to diagnosis, symptoms, growth and access corridor.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Petrous Apex Lesions. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: The safest route is chosen from lesion biology and available aerated/anatomic corridors.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Recognize**: an expansile petrous apex lesion is recognized on imaging, often incidentally, and must be distinguished by CT bone behavior and MRI signal characteristics. **Cholesterol granuloma**: T1 and T2 hyperintense, expansile, smoothly marginated. **Petrous apex cholesteatoma/epidermoid**: T1 hypo- to isointense, restricted diffusion. **Neoplasm**: variable, often with more aggressive bone destruction or enhancement. These behave differently and require different management.
canonical_layers.localize: **Localize**: location within the petrous apex, and its relationship to the internal carotid artery, cochlea, internal auditory canal, and Meckel's cave, determines which surgical corridor (if any) is safe. **Key trap**: an asymptomatic, non-expansile lesion in a good position for observation is managed very differently from one abutting the carotid canal or causing cranial neuropathy.
canonical_layers.workup: Use complementary CT and MRI including diffusion when appropriate; compare serial imaging when observation is plausible. **Cystic apex lesion signal table**: Mucocele: expansile, T1 low/T2 bright, nonenhancing. Apicitis: irregular non-expansile erosion, T1 low/T2 bright, enhancing. Cholesteatoma: expansile, T1 low/T2 bright, nonenhancing, restricts diffusion. Cholesterol granuloma: expansile, bright on T1 and T2, contains brown 'motor oil' fluid. Chondrosarcoma arises off midline at the petrooccipital synchondrosis, unlike midline chordoma. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, p 398) **Telling the cystic apex lesions apart**: Cholesterol granuloma is about 20 times more common than apex epidermoid but is still uncommon (about 1 for every 35 vestibular schwannomas). It is the only apex lesion bright on both T1 and T2, with smooth borders and no restricted diffusion. Epidermoid is T1 dark, T2 bright, scalloped and diffusion-restricting. Mucocele is T1 dark and T2 bright with only rim enhancement. Asymmetric marrow in a non-pneumatized apex is T1 bright but does not expand, enhance or stay bright on T2, and it darkens with fat suppression. Leave it alone. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2709–2710) **Contralateral apex and CT density clues**: With petrous apex cholesteatoma the opposite apex is often sclerotic, whereas cholesterol granuloma arises in a well-pneumatized system with an extensively aerated opposite apex. On CT, cholesterol granuloma is isodense to brain, cholesteatoma is hypodense to brain and isodense to CSF, and a mucocele is hypodense unless infected. Mucous cyst: no erosion, T1 low, T2 high. Benign slow lesions remodel bone with sclerotic margins, while neoplasms erode irregularly and enhance (unlike cholesteatoma, granuloma, mucocele and dermoid). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 42, pp 904-905)
canonical_layers.manage: Observe stable incidental lesions or drain/resect according to diagnosis, symptoms, growth and access corridor.
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: symptomatic, growing, or diagnostically uncertain lesions. A stable, asymptomatic, imaging-characteristic cholesterol granuloma or trapped fluid can often be observed with serial imaging rather than operated on. **Setup**: corridor choice (transcanal infracochlear, infralabyrinthine, middle fossa, or transsphenoidal endoscopic approach for medially positioned lesions) depends on the lesion's exact position and the available aerated or safe anatomic pathway around the cochlea, carotid, and labyrinth. **Key steps**: for a cholesterol granuloma, the goal is usually drainage and creation of a permanent aeration tract rather than complete lesion removal, since recurrence is common without ongoing drainage. A neoplasm instead requires biopsy/resection matched to its specific pathology. **Danger structures**: internal carotid artery, cochlea and labyrinth, and lower cranial nerves, depending on the chosen corridor. **Failure mode**: choosing an approach based on surgeon familiarity rather than the lesion's biology and the actual aerated/anatomic corridors available in that patient's temporal bone -- the safest route is dictated by the anatomy and diagnosis, not a default technique. **Postoperative plan**: serial imaging to confirm the drainage tract remains patent (cholesterol granuloma) or to monitor for recurrence (neoplasm), since these lesions are tracked over years, not just at a single postoperative visit. **Choosing a drainage route**: The transcanal infracochlear route between the jugular bulb and carotid gives dependent drainage into the middle ear. A blocked tube can be revised through an office myringotomy, but the route needs carotid exposure and slow canal healing. The infralabyrinthine route can be impossible with a high jugular bulb, and revision needs formal reexploration. A middle fossa catheter to the mastoid preserves hearing and stays patent long-term. An endoscopic transsphenoidal approach is the preferred hearing-sparing route when the cyst abuts the posterolateral sphenoid wall with favorable pneumatization. Keep it open with a silicone stent or a small nasoseptal flap. Translabyrinthine drainage is reserved for dead ears. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2710, 2725–2726, Ch 177, p 2671, Ch 178, p 2686) **Transcochlear approach**: The transcochlear approach reaches the skull base medial to the porus and anterior to the brainstem (petroclival lesions). Through a labyrinthectomy, the facial nerve is skeletonized from the stylomastoid foramen to the geniculate. The GSPN and chorda are cut, the nerve is rerouted posteriorly, and the cochlea is drilled out. The limits are the carotid anteriorly, the superior petrosal sinus above, the jugular bulb below, and the sigmoid sinus behind. It sacrifices hearing and almost always leaves at least temporary facial weakness. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 49, p 875)
canonical_layers.teach: The safest route is chosen from lesion biology and available aerated/anatomic corridors.

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Differentiate articulation/phonologic disorder, motor speech disorder, resonance/VPI, hearing-related language effects and voice disorder before assigning an ENT cause. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the mechanism with speech therapy, hearing access, structural surgery or neurologic/developmental support as appropriate.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Pediatric Speech Disorders. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: 'speech delay' is a symptom—first decide whether the bottleneck is hearing, language, articulation, motor control or resonance.

canonical_layers.recognize: Differentiate articulation/phonologic disorder, motor speech disorder, resonance/VPI, hearing-related language effects and voice disorder before assigning an ENT cause. **Intelligibility and sound development milestones**: By 24 months a child uses about 10 consonants, mostly at the start of words. By 36 months most vowels are correct and final consonants appear. By 48 months most consonants are present, but late sounds (r, l, s, sh, th) may still be in error. Refer if parents estimate that a stranger understands less than 50% of the child's speech at 22 months, less than 75% at 37 months, or less than 100% at 47 months. Speech delay affects about 15.6% of 3-year-olds and 3.8% of 6-year-olds, with a male predominance. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1947-1948) **Childhood apraxia of speech features**: Apraxia of speech is a motor planning disorder, while dysarthria is a disorder of motor execution. Apraxia shows many inconsistent sound errors, abnormal prosody, disrupted transitions between sounds and syllables, and difficulty with volitional nonspeech oral movements. It can occur without a confirmed neurologic lesion. It needs intensive motor-based therapy and is not an ENT surgical problem. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1948) **Intelligibility and sound milestones**: A stranger should understand about 25% of a child's speech at 18 months, 50–75% at 24 months, and 75–100% at 36 months. Early sounds (p, m, h, n, w, b, then k, g, d, t) come first, while r, l and s come much later. English has about 44 phonemes. (Cummings 7e, Ch 183, pp 2767–2768)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize communication failure to hearing input, oral articulators, palate/velopharynx, motor planning/control or language development.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Foundational workup**: audiology and speech-language evaluation. Nasendoscopy/fluoroscopy is reserved for suspected resonance/velopharyngeal physiology.

Separate speech-sound production, motor speech, resonance, fluency, and language delay. Confirm hearing, oral mechanism, palate/velopharyngeal function, development/cognition, multilingual exposure, and neurologic signs. **Key trap**: use formal speech-language evaluation rather than attributing delay to ankyloglossia or recurrent otitis by assumption. **Language referral indicators by age**: Refer for full speech-language evaluation when a child falls at or below about the 10th percentile. At 12 months, the trigger is no response to at least one familiar word in a familiar setting, or little interest in communicating with a caregiver. At 24-36 months, it is fewer than 50 words or no two-word combinations (Language Development Survey). 50-60% of these toddlers still score at or below the 10th percentile at ages 3-5. A 3-year-old speaking mainly single words, or a 4-year-old who cannot hold a simple conversation in roughly three-word utterances, should be referred. Verify hearing on the day of testing, because transient conductive loss is common. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1945-1946) **Do not stop at hearing loss: screen for autism**: Cummings cites the older CDC estimate of about 1 in 59 children with autism. The current CDC surveillance estimate is about 1 in 31 (2022 data), with boys affected roughly 3-4 times as often. Autism can be reliably diagnosed by age 2. About 4% of deaf or hard-of-hearing children also have autism, yet only about a quarter get that diagnosis by age 4. Autism-specific clues are echolalia or pronoun reversal, absent joint attention and pointing, poor imitation of gestures, no pretend play, and language regression. Children with specific language impairment (7–8% at kindergarten) want to communicate and do pretend play. Refer early to a multidisciplinary autism clinic: fewer than 10% stay nonverbal with intervention, and starting before age 5 matters. (Cummings 7e, Ch 183, pp 2769–2770)
canonical_layers.manage:
**Treat the mechanism**: speech therapy, hearing access, structural surgery, or neurologic/developmental support as appropriate.

Provide early speech-language intervention matched to the deficit, restore hearing access when impaired, and route structural resonance disease to a cleft/velopharyngeal team. **Key trap**: surgery treats a demonstrated structural mechanism -- it does not replace therapy for phonologic, language, or motor-planning disorders. **Stuttering natural history and when to treat**: Stuttering usually begins at about 2.5-5 years. Prevalence is under 1%, with a lifetime incidence of about 5%. About 75% of young children recover, usually within 6-12 months of onset (sometimes 18-24 months), but full recovery becomes much less likely after about age 7. The male to female ratio is near 1:1 to 2:1 at onset and 3-4:1 in adults, because more girls recover. About 30% also have a speech sound disorder. Refer or treat when there is a family history, stuttering for 3-6 months or more, rising frequency, physical tension or struggle, negative reactions, or a coexisting speech or language disorder. Fluent speech in the office does not rule it out, and parent reports are reliable. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1950-1953)
canonical_layers.operate: ENT surgery corrects anatomic contributors but cannot replace motor/language learning; operative decisions should be made with the speech team.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: 'speech delay' is a symptom—first decide whether the bottleneck is hearing, language, articulation, motor control or resonance.

A child can pronounce sounds poorly, plan speech poorly, resonate abnormally, or have delayed language—four different problems. Name the domain before ordering an operation. **Prevalence and prognosis of language disorders**: About 12-15% of English-speaking children have some language disorder, and 5-7% have specific language impairment (no neurologic, sensory, cognitive or emotional cause). Family history of speech, language or reading problems is a risk factor. Prognosis for complete mastery is guarded: in a longitudinal study, over 70% of children with language disorders at age 5 still had language, cognitive and academic deficits in adolescence. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1946-1947)

canonical_layers.recognize: Tip shape is the product of lower-lateral-cartilage form, support, projection, rotation and skin/soft-tissue envelope—not simply tip width.
canonical_layers.localize: Medial crura, domes and lateral crura create different vectors; lateral-crural weakness or malposition can also create external-valve dysfunction.
canonical_layers.workup: Standardized functional/aesthetic analysis and photography; define projection, rotation, symmetry, alar support and valve behavior before selecting a maneuver. **Tip recoil test and approach selection**: pressing the tip toward the lip tests how well the tip support springs back. Weak tips with thin skin and thin sidewalls need support preserved or added. Nondelivery approaches (cartilage-splitting or retrograde eversion) suit minimal refinement. Delivery approaches (bipedicle chondrocutaneous flaps) suit moderate bulbosity, with refinement using transdomal and interdomal sutures. The open approach suits revision cases, asymmetric or twisted noses, cleft-lip noses and markedly over- or underprojected tips. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, p 471, 486)
canonical_layers.manage: Use cartilage-sparing reshaping, sutures and support grafts according to the mechanical deficit; avoid destructive cephalic over-resection. **Projection and rotation maneuvers**: shield graft adds ~1–2 mm projection. A columellar strut supports but does not increase projection. Plumping grafts at the columellar base open the nasolabial angle (illusion of projection). Rotation rises with caudal septal trim, lateral crural shortening/overlay, or lateral crural steal. Decreases with caudal septal excision near the spine or dorsal augmentation (apparent). Tongue-in-groove fixes medial crura to the caudal septum to correct hanging columella or excess show. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 486–488)
canonical_layers.operate: Preserve adequate lateral-crural support and choose columellar/septal-extension, lateral-crural-strut, rim or other grafts only for a defined structural objective. **Endonasal approach options**: nondelivery (cartilage-splitting via intracartilaginous incision, or retrograde via intercartilaginous incision) allows conservative cephalic trim with no major support disruption. Delivery (intercartilaginous + marginal incisions) brings out the lower lateral cartilage as a bipedicled chondrocutaneous flap but divides the scroll, a major support. Open approach (marginal + transcolumellar) preserves major support but sacrifices the skin envelope attachment (minor). A complete transfixion incision releases medial crural–septal attachment and lowers projection. Preserve at least 6–10 mm of lateral crus to prevent alar collapse/notching. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 483–485) **Complete vs interrupted strip**: conservative cephalic trim preserving a complete, uninterrupted lateral crural strip of at least about 6 to 10 mm (often 7 to 9 mm) keeps long-term support and natural contour. Interrupted-strip (dome division) techniques, reserved for severe asymmetry or overprojection, always cost some support. They tend to rotate the tip cephalically, so use them with a columellar strut and only when rotation is wanted. Avoid a complete transfixion incision when possible, because it destroys the medial crural-caudal septal attachment, a major support. Postoperative tip ptosis from lost support is one of the most common rhinoplasty errors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, pp 483-486, 499)
canonical_layers.teach: ThePlasticsFella's useful framing is support-preserving tip modification: every maneuver should have a projection, rotation, contour or valve purpose. **Profile targets and timeline**: aim for the tip-defining point about 1 to 2 mm above the cartilaginous dorsum, which creates a supratip break. A gentle 2 to 3 mm slope is acceptable. In women, a slightly more open nasolabial angle and a subtle columellar double break are desirable. Shape columellar struts with a gentle curve and stop them short of the tip skin to avoid a tent-pole look. The final result takes about 12 to 18 months to settle. Remove the external splint at 5 to 7 days. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, p 500-502, 509)

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Not every sleepy, restless or poorly sleeping child has obstructive sleep apnea; insomnia, parasomnias, circadian disorders, restless sleep and central disorders enter the differential. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use behavioral/sleep-medicine pathways for nonobstructive disorders and avoid adenotonsillectomy when the physiology is not obstructive.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Nonobstructive Pediatric Sleep Disorders. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: snoring surgery treats obstruction, not every form of poor sleep.

canonical_layers.recognize: Not every sleepy, restless or poorly sleeping child has obstructive sleep apnea; insomnia, parasomnias, circadian disorders, restless sleep and central disorders enter the differential. **Infant sleep safety and behavioral insomnia**: daytime sleepiness in a child is never normal and needs investigation. SIDS peaks at 1–4 months, but the risk lasts to 12 months. Risk factors are male sex, prematurity, prone sleeping, multiple births, a teenage mother, maternal substance use and secondhand smoke. Prevention is back-to-sleep positioning on a firm mattress, with no bed sharing and no loose objects. Behavioral insomnia has two types: sleep-onset association (treat by gradually withdrawing parental intervention, stopping night feeds after 6 months, and using scheduled awakenings) and limit-setting (treat with consistent bedtimes, parent education and CBT). (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 536, 538–539) **Parasomnia timing rule**: NREM parasomnias (sleep terrors, sleepwalking, confusional arousals, sleep-related eating) arise from slow-wave sleep in the first two-thirds of the night with amnesia for the event. REM parasomnias (nightmares, sleep paralysis, REM behavior disorder) cluster in the last third of the night with vivid recall. Sleep terrors (ages about 3-10) carry tachycardia/tachypnea. Confusional arousals lack an autonomic surge. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, pp 2796-2797) **Kleine-Levin and idiopathic hypersomnia**: Kleine-Levin syndrome is episodic hypersomnia in adolescents (median onset 15 years, male predominance 2-3:1) with hyperphagia and hypersexuality, and symptom-free intervals. Idiopathic hypersomnia (daily sleepiness for at least 3 months by ICSD-3) differs from narcolepsy by normal hypocretin, no cataplexy and fewer than 2 sleep-onset REM periods, and responds less well to stimulants. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2796) **Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder**: affects 5-10% of adolescents. Sleep onset is delayed 2-3 hours or more (often 2-6 a.m.) with normal architecture once asleep. Treat with sleep hygiene, chronotherapy that gradually advances bedtime, and melatonin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2796)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the sleep complaint to initiation/maintenance, breathing, movement, arousal/parasomnia or excessive sleepiness.
canonical_layers.workup: History, sleep schedule and targeted PSG/labs are selected by phenotype; iron evaluation may be relevant in movement/restless-sleep syndromes. **MSLT criteria for narcolepsy**: after an overnight PSG excludes other sleep disorders, an MSLT (20-minute nap opportunities) showing mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less (normal about 15) plus sleep-onset REM in at least 2 naps (a SOREMP on the preceding PSG can count as one) supports narcolepsy. CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency defines type 1, whereas type 2 has normal hypocretin and no cataplexy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2795)
canonical_layers.manage: Use behavioral/sleep-medicine pathways for nonobstructive disorders and avoid adenotonsillectomy when the physiology is not obstructive. **Narcolepsy and RLS treatment**: narcolepsy is treated with sleep hygiene/scheduled naps, stimulants or modafinil for sleepiness, REM-suppressing tricyclics/SSRIs, and sodium oxybate (GABA-B agonist) for cataplexy. For restless legs/PLMD in children, give iron when ferritin is below 50 µg/L. Cummings also lists dopaminergic agents, gabapentin and benzodiazepines, but the current AASM (2024) RLS guideline favors iron and alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin) and advises against standard use of dopamine agonists because of augmentation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2795)
canonical_layers.operate: The surgical decision is often 'do not operate' until obstructive anatomy is demonstrated.
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: snoring surgery treats obstruction, not every form of poor sleep. **Age-based sleep needs (AASM)**: 4-12 months 12-16 h including naps. 1-2 years 11-14 h. 3-5 years 10-13 h. 6-12 years 9-12 h. 13-18 years 8-10 h. RLS affects about 2% of children, often with family history and 'growing pains'. Rhythmic movement disorder (head banging, rocking) is usually benign and treated with a safe environment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2795)
source_basis: Cummings 7e: Nonobstructive Pediatric Sleep Disorders

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. A crooked septum matters only if it contributes meaningfully to the symptomatic airflow bottleneck. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Septoplasty when symptoms persist and septal anatomy is causal; combine with other functional treatment only when indicated.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Septal Deviation. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Preserve dorsal/caudal support and avoid bilateral opposing mucosal injury.

canonical_layers.recognize: A deviated septum is a common incidental imaging/exam finding and only becomes a surgical target when it meaningfully contributes to symptomatic nasal obstruction -- correlate the side and location of deviation with the patient's actual obstructive symptoms rather than treating any visible deviation as inherently pathologic.
canonical_layers.localize: **Localize**: the deviation's level (caudal/columellar, mid-septal, or high dorsal/bony) and direction. **Why it matters**: this determines both the functional impact -- caudal deviation affects the internal/external nasal valve most directly -- and the technical approach needed to correct it, including whether cartilage support near the keystone or caudal strut must be preserved.
canonical_layers.workup: Anterior rhinoscopy/endoscopy plus valve/turbinate assessment; CT is not required for routine isolated deviation. **Exam pearls**: watch the sidewalls during quiet and forced breathing. Habitual 'sniffers' collapse their sidewalls regardless of valve competence. The Cottle maneuver has many false positives. Lifting the upper lateral cartilage with a cotton applicator or curette is more specific for internal valve narrowing. Tip ptosis can itself obstruct airflow. A previously fractured bony pyramid can hold the dorsal septum off midline, and septoplasty alone will not fix that. On acoustic rhinometry, the first notch is the valve and the second is the anterior inferior/middle turbinates. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 441, 445)
canonical_layers.manage: Septoplasty when symptoms persist and septal anatomy is causal; combine with other functional treatment only when indicated. **Pediatric septoplasty and growth**: postnatal septal cartilage does not appear to be a primary growth center. In cadaver data the cartilage completes most growth by ~age 2, while the perpendicular plate keeps growing into adulthood. Complete septal resection impairs midface growth in animals, but limited, conservative resection of only the deviated segment in children has not shown growth harm. Conservative septoplasty is therefore acceptable even in young children with significant obstruction. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Physiology", p 930) **Turbinates and postoperative care**: medical therapy is first-line for mucosal turbinate hypertrophy from rhinitis. Never perform total turbinectomy, because it predisposes to empty nose syndrome with drying and crusting. Prefer conservative submucosal or partial resection (e.g., a modified Mabry approach). After septoplasty, suction gently on days 5 to 10, allow gentle nose blowing after week 3, and avoid strenuous exercise for 6 weeks. Soft Silastic splints are optional. Many insurers require 6 weeks of failed nasal steroid therapy before approving septoplasty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 445, 455-456)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: symptomatic nasal obstruction attributable to septal deviation, refractory to medical management, or with a clearly mechanical component unlikely to respond to medical therapy. **Setup**: septoplasty via a hemitransfixion or similar incision, elevating mucoperichondrial flaps bilaterally. **Key steps**: resect or reposition the deviated cartilage/bone while preserving an adequate dorsal and caudal strut (typically at least **1-1.5 cm**) for structural support. Avoid creating opposing mucosal tears on both sides at the same location, which risks a septal perforation. **Danger structures**: the septal cartilage's blood supply (subperichondrial dissection preserves it) and the keystone area, where overly aggressive cartilage removal destabilizes the nasal dorsum. **Failure mode**: over-resecting cartilage for a cosmetically 'straighter' septum at the cost of losing structural support, producing saddle nose deformity or valve collapse later, or creating bilateral mucosal injury at the same site leading to perforation. **Postoperative plan**: splints or quilting sutures to prevent hematoma, saline care during healing, and reassessment of the functional (not just cosmetic) result. **Caudal deviation techniques**: For caudal deformities, score the concave side along the axis of the bend to release cartilage memory. In the swinging-door maneuver the quadrangular cartilage is freed from the maxillary crest groove, an inferior strip is trimmed, and the cartilage swings to midline and is fixed to the nasal spine periosteum with a figure-of-eight absorbable suture. The doorstop variant skips the strip excision and sutures the cartilage onto the opposite side of the crest. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 1, p 5–6) **Septoplasty technique specifics**: the Killian incision is about 1 to 2 cm behind the caudal margin. A hemitransfixion incision can convert to a full transfixion. Preserve at least a 1-cm dorsal and 1-cm caudal L-strut, including the nasal spine. Before removing bony septum, make a superior cut so twisting the perpendicular plate does not fracture the cribriform plate. Reset cartilage displaced off the maxillary crest into the groove and suture it to the spine periosteum. A one-sided crest spur can be shaved with a 2-mm osteotome. Use crushed cartilage as an interposition barrier, close even unilateral flap tears, and quilt with 5-0 plain to prevent hematoma. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 447-450) **Caudal and high-septal deviations**: in the tongue-in-groove maneuver (Rethi/Kridel), the caudal septum is set between the medial crura and fixed with a transcutaneous columellar-septal suture. This fixes the caudal septum in the midline and avoids aggressive caudal trimming, but it can change tip projection and rotation. Correct high dorsal bowing with spreader grafts or a Boccieri crossbar graft on the concave side, scoring, or shaving. Release the upper lateral cartilages from the septum when straightening a crooked dorsum. Trim the caudal septum only when it is too crooked to straighten or so long it pushes the columella down. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 450-451, 454)
canonical_layers.teach: Preserve dorsal/caudal support and avoid bilateral opposing mucosal injury.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Differentiate bacterial-pattern persistent/severe/double-worsening illness from viral URI; imaging is not routine in uncomplicated disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Observation or guideline-concordant antibiotic strategy depending on severity/context, plus symptom care; escalate orbital/intracranial complications urgently.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Purulent-colored drainage alone does not prove bacterial sinusitis.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Adult acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS)** is diagnosed from the TIME COURSE, not from green mucus alone. **AAO-HNSF criteria**: acute-rhinosinusitis symptoms that persist WITHOUT improvement for at least **10 days**, OR symptoms that worsen again within 10 days after an initial improvement ('**double worsening**'). Purulent drainage should occur with nasal obstruction and/or facial pain-pressure-fullness. **Key trap**: most early viral URIs improve without antibiotics -- isolated facial pain, headache, tooth pain, or discolored drainage without the appropriate syndrome and trajectory should make you reconsider the diagnosis. **Pediatric (AAP) criteria differ from the adult guideline**: diagnose ABRS in a child with (1) persistent nasal discharge and/or daytime cough for more than 10 days without improvement, (2) severe onset with fever of at least 39 C plus purulent discharge for at least 3 consecutive days, or (3) worsening around days 6-7 after initial improvement (new or recurrent fever, or more discharge or cough). About 5-10% of URIs in young children meet criteria (~6.7% with strict use). Uncomplicated colds last 5-10 days and peak by days 3-6, any fever is early and short (under 48 h), and discharge quality changes normally. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1040) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1042) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1043) **IDSA's three entry criteria (vs AAO-HNSF)**: (1) persistent symptoms for 10 or more days without improvement; (2) severe onset, meaning fever of 39°C or higher with purulent discharge or facial pain for at least 3–4 consecutive days at the start; (3) worsening ('double sickening'): new fever, headache or more discharge after a typical viral URI of 5–6 days that had been improving. The severe-onset arm is IDSA-specific and is not part of the AAO-HNSF adult definition (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, pp 645–646).
canonical_layers.localize: ABRS is an acute inflammatory/infectious process arising after impaired sinus ventilation and mucociliary clearance, commonly following viral mucosal edema and ostial obstruction. **Key question**: is disease still confined to the sinonasal compartment, or has it crossed a boundary? Orbital symptoms suggest spread through the thin lamina papyracea/ethmoid region. Frontal disease can threaten bone and intracranial spaces. **Red flag**: severe unilateral maxillary disease should raise an odontogenic source or obstructing lesion, rather than being treated as generic bilateral URI-associated ABRS.
canonical_layers.workup: Diagnose uncomplicated ABRS **CLINICALLY**. **Key trap**: do not obtain routine plain films or CT simply to prove sinusitis when the history meets criteria. **Image when**: a complication or alternative diagnosis is suspected, disease is atypical/unilateral, or the clinical course is not behaving like uncomplicated ABRS. **Endoscopy**: can identify middle-meatal purulence or another lesion, but is not required for routine diagnosis. **Culture**: not a first-visit test -- use an endoscopically directed middle-meatal culture or operative specimen when treatment fails, disease is complicated, the host is immunocompromised, or resistant/unusual microbiology is a meaningful concern. Reassess the diagnosis rather than ordering a scan reflexively for every nonresponder.
canonical_layers.manage: For uncomplicated adult ABRS, use **shared decision-making**: either watchful waiting or initial antibiotic therapy is appropriate when reliable follow-up exists. **Board pearl**: watchful waiting is no longer restricted only to 'mild' disease in the **2025 AAO-HNSF update**. Provide analgesia and consider saline irrigation and/or topical intranasal corticosteroid for symptom relief. **First line if antibiotics chosen**: **amoxicillin with or without clavulanate**, generally for **5-7 days** in the updated guideline. Select an alternative based on true beta-lactam allergy, local resistance, recent antibiotic exposure, and patient-specific risk, rather than automatically escalating everyone to a fluoroquinolone. **Pediatric antibiotic dosing**: for mild uncomplicated pediatric ABRS in a child 2 or older without daycare or recent antibiotics, use amoxicillin 45 mg/kg/day divided twice daily, or 80-90 mg/kg/day where penicillin-nonsusceptible pneumococcus is prevalent. Use high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (80-90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin component) for age under 2, daycare, antibiotics within 30 days, moderate or severe illness, or treatment failure. A single dose of ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM can bridge a vomiting child. Reassess at 72 hours if there is no improvement. TMP-SMX and macrolides are poor choices because of pneumococcal resistance, and second/third-generation cephalosporin cross-reactivity in penicillin allergy is much lower than the historical 8-18%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1048) **IDSA antibiotic rules**: empiric amoxicillin-clavulanate for adults and children. High-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate is used for (1) regions with high penicillin-nonsusceptible S. pneumoniae, (2) severe infection, (3) recent hospitalization or antibiotics within the past month, or (4) immunocompromise. Macrolides (about 30% pneumococcal resistance) and TMP-SMX (30–40% resistance) are not for empiric use, nor is second- or third-generation oral cephalosporin monotherapy. Doxycycline is the adult alternative (not for children) (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 646). **Penicillin allergy, duration and failure**: for type I allergy in adults use doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin); in children with type I allergy use levofloxacin; for non-type I allergy in children use a third-generation cephalosporin (cefixime or cefpodoxime) plus clindamycin. Routine MRSA coverage is not recommended. Treat 5–7 days in adults and 10–14 days in children. Change therapy if the patient worsens after 72 hours or fails to improve after 3–5 days; failure on high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate or a fluoroquinolone should prompt a search for another diagnosis such as CRS, allergy or a facial pain disorder (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 646). **Guideline version difference and adjuncts**: K.J. Lee (citing the AAO-HNSF guideline) offers observation for mild disease with assured follow-up and antibiotics for moderate-severe disease (persistent or worsening symptoms or temperature over 38 C), which is the older 2007 framing. Since 2015 the guideline has offered watchful waiting regardless of severity, and the 2025 update recommends watchful waiting with assured follow-up for all uncomplicated ABRS, matching the site. Both agree that amoxicillin with or without clavulanate is first line (5-7 days in adults). In penicillin allergy, doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) is the alternative. Intranasal steroids, saline irrigation and analgesics are options for symptom relief. Oral corticosteroids are not recommended, and decongestants and antihistamines lack evidence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 28, p 510) **Adjuncts**: intranasal steroids shorten symptom duration and lower symptom intensity, and saline or topical decongestants may help with symptoms. Oral decongestants are not recommended (poor efficacy, side effects), and antihistamines do not help nonallergic patients (sedating ones may thicken secretions) (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 646).
canonical_layers.operate: ABRS itself is not an operative diagnosis. **The advanced decision**: failure or complication. **When to reassess**: any patient who worsens at any time or fails to improve after the initial management interval -- confirm that the syndrome is actually ABRS, look for dental disease, migraine/neuralgia, resistant organisms, an obstructing lesion, immunocompromise, or progression beyond the sinuses, and change therapy when appropriate. **Red flags demanding urgent escalation**: orbital signs, vision change, ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, severe frontal swelling, meningismus, focal neurologic deficit, altered mental status, or toxic deterioration -- these need urgent cross-sectional imaging, IV therapy, and ENT/ophthalmology/neurosurgical escalation as indicated. **Key point**: drainage is directed at a defined abscess, threatened vision, intracranial complication, source-control problem, or other complication -- not at routine uncomplicated ABRS.
canonical_layers.teach: **Chief/boards model**: ABRS is a **trajectory** diagnosis. Viral = early and improving. ABRS = **>=10 days** without improvement, or **double worsening**. Uncomplicated adult disease does not require imaging, culture, or automatic antibiotics. **Board pearl**: the 2025 update deliberately expands watchful waiting to all uncomplicated ABRS when follow-up is assured, and uses amoxicillin with or without clavulanate first-line when antibiotics are chosen. **Key trap**: the dangerous pivot is not 'more sinus pressure' -- it is loss of compartment containment (orbital, bony, intracranial, or systemic findings), which changes the problem from outpatient symptom management to urgent complication control.

candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Symptoms can arise from septum, turbinates, internal/external valve, dynamic lateral-wall collapse or mucosal disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Medical therapy treats mucosa; septoplasty/turbinate/valve procedures target distinct structural problems and may need combination treatment.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Functional Nasal Obstruction. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: A deviated septum on exam does not prove it is the dominant cause of obstruction.

canonical_layers.recognize: Differentiate structural obstruction (septum, turbinates, static/dynamic internal or external nasal valve dysfunction) from inflammatory rhinitis and other contributors -- these may coexist. **Exam**: observe the nasal sidewall/alar rim with quiet and deep inspiration, and assess targeted support with modified Cottle or nasal dilator maneuvers. **Key trap**: improvement with a standard cheek-traction Cottle maneuver suggests a valve contribution but is nonspecific -- it does not by itself localize the level or predict the best operation.
canonical_layers.localize: **Internal nasal valve**: the angle between the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage and the septum, normally around **10-15 degrees**. It is the narrowest, highest-resistance segment of the nasal airway in most people. It is a common site of obstruction after rhinoplasty or trauma that narrows this angle. **External nasal valve**: defined by the nostril rim/alar cartilage and skin. It collapses when alar cartilage support is weak, particularly on deep inspiration.
canonical_layers.workup: Diagnosis is primarily clinical. **Exam**: anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to assess the septum, turbinates, and valve regions, along with dynamic assessment of valve collapse on inspiration and Cottle/modified Cottle maneuvers. **NOSE scale**: the NOSE (Nasal Obstruction Symptom Evaluation) scale is a validated, widely used patient-reported outcome measure that quantifies baseline severity and tracks response to treatment. **Objective testing**: acoustic rhinometry and rhinomanometry are used selectively and correlate imperfectly with patient-reported symptoms -- treatment decisions should not rest on objective testing alone.
canonical_layers.manage: Treat coexisting inflammatory or mucosal disease when present. **Key trap**: do not require an ineffective septoplasty/turbinate procedure before addressing clearly documented nasal valve dysfunction. **Match treatment to anatomy**: septoplasty for obstructing deviation, turbinate management for appropriate hypertrophy, and valve-directed support/reconstruction for static or dynamic valve problems, alone or combined when indicated. Discuss nonoperative dilator devices and shared treatment goals with the patient.
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: consider surgery when symptomatic obstruction corresponds to documented anatomical findings and conservative treatment appropriate to the cause is insufficient or unwanted. Examine septum, turbinates, and internal and external valve separately, using dynamic observation and targeted maneuvers. **Key trap**: a positive Cottle maneuver or NOSE score alone is not a surgical indication. **Technique**: correct obstructing septal deviation and turbinate hypertrophy as indicated, and provide valve-specific support (e.g., spreader, batten, or lateral-crural grafting, suture, or selected minimally invasive approaches) when the valve contributes. Valve repair may be done simultaneously with other surgery or alone -- prior septoplasty is not a prerequisite. Avoid destabilizing septal support or excessive turbinate reduction. Reassess patient-reported symptoms with the **NOSE scale** and examination, remembering the scale is subjective rather than an objective airflow measurement.
canonical_layers.teach: Separate structural from mucosal causes before operating, and identify which structural element is responsible (septum vs turbinate vs which valve) -- septoplasty does not fix a collapsing valve, and valve surgery does not fix allergic rhinitis. Track outcomes with the same validated NOSE scale used at baseline.
source_basis: Cummings Otolaryngology--Head and Neck Surgery, 7e -- internal/external nasal valve anatomy and structural nasal obstruction workup

AAO-HNS Position Statement: Nasal Valve Repair, revised July 2026 -- valve repair as distinct procedure; prior septoplasty/turbinate surgery is not required.
