candidates.canonical_topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Crusting, septal perforation, destructive lesions, refractory inflammation or multisystem symptoms can reflect vasculitis, granulomatous, autoimmune, infectious or toxic disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the systemic driver with the appropriate specialty while controlling local infection, crusting, bleeding and structural complications.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: a septal perforation is a finding, not a diagnosis.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Systemic Disease of the Nose and Sinuses

canonical_layers.recognize: **Red flags**: crusting, septal perforation, destructive lesions, refractory inflammation, or multisystem symptoms can reflect vasculitis, granulomatous, autoimmune, infectious, or toxic disease. **Systemic-inflammatory/destructive phenotype**: refractory 'CRS' with persistent crusting, bloody discharge or epistaxis, ulceration, septal perforation, progressive saddle-nose change, or disease extending beyond an ordinary mucosal pattern should trigger a systemic diagnosis rather than another empiric sinus-treatment cycle. **Differential** (searchable aliases): granulomatosis with polyangiitis (**GPA**; legacy Wegener granulomatosis), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (**EGPA**; legacy Churg-Strauss), sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, destructive sinonasal disease, septal perforation, saddle nose, and vasculitis. **GPA clues**: pulmonary, renal, otologic, orbital, and subglottic disease. **EGPA clues**: asthma plus eosinophilia with sinonasal/polyposis disease, and neuropathic, pulmonary, cutaneous, or cardiac features. **IgG4-related disease**: tumefactive orbital/lacrimal/salivary involvement can support this diagnosis. **Key trap**: granulomatous sinonasal disease requires infectious and other mimics to remain visible. **Rhinoscleroma**: Rhinoscleroma is chronic granulomatous infection with Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, endemic in Eastern Europe, North Africa, South Asia and Latin America. It passes through three stages: catarrhal (purulent rhinorrhea, crusting), granulomatous (painless nodules, epistaxis, septal destruction, possible laryngeal or subglottic spread) and fibrotic (stenosis). Histology shows Mikulicz cells (foamy macrophages full of bacilli) and Russell bodies. Treatment is long-term culture-directed antibiotics (tetracycline or ciprofloxacin) plus debridement, with airway evaluation. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 45-46) **Rhinosporidiosis**: Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous infection with Rhinosporidium seeberi, acquired from contaminated water (South Asia, Africa). It causes a friable, strawberry-like, bleeding polypoid nasal mass and can involve the conjunctiva. Histology shows large sporangia with spores and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. Treatment is excision with cautery of the base, sometimes with dapsone. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 46) **Other systemic nasal findings**: Sarcoidosis gives submucosal yellow nodules (cobblestoning), crusting and perforation. Langerhans cell histiocytosis can present as a nasal mass or perforation. Lupus causes septal ulceration and perforation, and polyarteritis nodosa can cause nasal mucosal lesions. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma ('lethal midline granuloma') destroys midline structures and needs deep, repeated biopsies. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 21-22) **Nasal clues to systemic/infectious disease in children**: sarcoid can show tiny (~1 mm) yellow submucosal nodules on boggy hyperemic mucosa. Diphtheria gives a white-yellow septal membrane with serosanguineous, highly contagious discharge that excoriates the upper lip, and characteristically little fever because the toxin is poorly absorbed from the nose. Rhinoscleroma and leprosy present first with obstruction before necrotic discharge. Granulomatous lesions (GPA, NK/T-cell lymphoma, EGPA, Sporothrix, Coccidioides) look alike and require biopsy, culture and special stains. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 970) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nasal Obstruction and Rhinorrhea", p 975) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1039) **Rhinoscleroma**: caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, it is endemic in Central America, Africa, India and the Middle East and often begins at epithelial transition zones (vestibule, subglottis). It progresses through catarrhal (honeycomb crusts), granulomatous (painless masses, septal destruction) and sclerotic (stenosis, stridor) stages. Mikulicz cells (vacuolated macrophages containing bacilli) and Russell bodies (plasma cells with inclusions) are diagnostic. Treat with long-term tetracycline or fluoroquinolone plus debridement. Rhinosporidiosis (Rhinosporidium seeberi, South Asia, stagnant water) forms friable 'strawberry' polyps studded with white sporangia, and it is treated by excision plus dapsone. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 31, pp 551-552) **Lethal midline granuloma differential**: Midline destructive lesions of the nose and palate include extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (formerly polymorphic reticulosis), granulomatosis with polyangiitis, cocaine-induced midline destructive lesion and idiopathic midline destructive disease. Localized lymphoma has historically been treated with radiation (about 50 Gy) and disseminated disease with chemotherapy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 20) **Septal perforation site clues and other infections**: Syphilis classically perforates the bony septum, whereas most other causes (cocaine, GPA, trauma) involve cartilage. Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae, grows best at 27-33 °C) favors cool tissues and causes early nasal disease and saddle nose. Treat with dapsone plus rifampin and clofazimine. Rhinosporidiosis (South India, Sri Lanka) causes friable 'strawberry' nasal polyps requiring excision. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 227, 229, 231) **Sarcoidosis and EGPA numbers**: on careful history, 61% of sarcoid patients report nasal symptoms, with obstruction the most common ENT complaint. The mucosa has a 'strawberry skin' look (submucosal granulomas on red mucosa), ACE is raised in about 80%, and biopsy of submucosal nodules has high yield. EGPA is ANCA-positive in only about 40% (p-ANCA/MPO, which goes with renal disease, pulmonary hemorrhage and mononeuritis). It runs prodromal (asthma/atopy), eosinophilic and vasculitic phases, with nasal involvement in 60–70% and polyps in 75%. The older ACR 1990 criteria (now replaced by the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria) include eosinophilia over 10%, neuropathy, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, sinus abnormality and extravascular eosinophils on biopsy (4 or more: sensitivity 85%, specificity 99.7%). EGPA is treated with steroids, rituximab and mepolizumab (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, pp 790–791).
canonical_layers.localize: Localize destructive disease to septum, turbinates, lateral wall, palate and skull-base/orbital structures, while looking for systemic sites such as lung, kidney, skin and eye.
canonical_layers.workup: **Biopsy**: viable edge tissue when needed, paired with targeted serology/culture/systemic evaluation. **Key trap**: avoid nonspecific panels without a phenotype -- workup is phenotype- and organ-directed, not an ANCA-or-serum-marker shortcut. **Imaging**: for destructive disease, document endoscopic distribution and obtain CT; use MRI when orbit, skull base, perineural, intracranial, or tumefactive soft-tissue extension is a question. **Systemic screen**: ask about pulmonary symptoms/hemoptysis, renal disease, neuropathy, asthma/eosinophilia, skin disease, and medication/exposure history; obtain urinalysis/renal function, CBC with differential/eosinophils, inflammatory markers, and chest evaluation when clinically indicated. **PR3-/MPO-ANCA**: can support AAV, but a positive result does not replace clinicopathologic synthesis, and a negative result does not exclude disease, particularly EGPA. **Biopsy technique**: use viable active tissue when tissue is needed, coordinate pathology for vasculitic/granulomatous/fibroinflammatory patterns, and exclude infection, cocaine/levamisole injury, foreign material, and malignancy before assigning a systemic inflammatory label. **Sarcoidosis** requires a compatible syndrome with granulomatous evidence when needed, and exclusion of alternative granulomatous causes. **IgG4-related disease** requires clinical, imaging, and pathologic correlation -- serum IgG4 alone is not diagnostic. **EGPA classification criteria**: Classic EGPA (Churg-Strauss) criteria require 4 of 6: asthma, peripheral eosinophilia above 10%, mono- or polyneuropathy, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, paranasal sinus abnormality, and biopsy showing extravascular eosinophils (sensitivity about 85%, specificity about 99.7%). Coronary arteritis can cause myocardial infarction, and hearing loss may occur. Treatment is corticosteroids, with cyclophosphamide for organ-threatening disease and rituximab or anti-IL-5 options. The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria now replace the 1990 set: obstructive airway disease +3, nasal polyps +3, mononeuritis multiplex +1, eosinophils at least 1×10⁹/L +5, extravascular eosinophilic inflammation on biopsy +2, cANCA/PR3 −3 and hematuria −1, with a score of 6 or more classifying EGPA. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 43-44) **GPA test performance**: c-ANCA (PR3) is positive in about 95% of active systemic GPA but only about 60% of localized disease over its course, and about 10% are p-ANCA positive instead. Nasal biopsy has low yield: only about 24% (12 of 51) showed histology suggestive of GPA in one study, so a negative biopsy does not exclude it. CT may show bony erosion with neo-osteogenesis (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 789). **Cocaine-induced midline destructive lesion vs GPA**: CIMDL mimics GPA clinically, radiographically and histologically (leukocytoclastic vasculitis, fibrinoid necrosis). About half of ANCA-positive CIMDL patients have PR3/c-ANCA, but human neutrophil elastase (HNE) ANCA is common in CIMDL and not in GPA, so it is the discriminating test, along with urine/hair toxicology. Isolated septal perforation occurs in about 4.8% of habitual users, and destruction can extend to the palate, orbit and skull base. Immunosuppression has no role. Abstinence is the treatment, and reconstruction (rib cartilage) waits for proven abstinence (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 791).
canonical_layers.manage: **Goal**: treat the systemic driver with the appropriate specialty while controlling local infection, crusting, bleeding, and structural complications. **Key point**: management follows the systemic disease and threatened organs. **Coordinate**: rheumatology and, as indicated, pulmonology, nephrology, allergy/immunology, ophthalmology, or other involved specialties, rather than treating the nose in isolation. **AAV treatment**: systemic immunosuppression selected by disease severity and organ threat -- ENT care manages local consequences and obtains diagnostic tissue without delaying systemic rescue for organ-threatening disease. **Sarcoidosis and IgG4-related disease**: likewise require systemic clinicopathologic assessment before disease-directed medical therapy. **Key trap**: keep the separate canonical CF/PCD and immunodeficiency-associated CRS pathways separate, rather than duplicating those host-factor algorithms here. **GPA course and nasal care**: untreated active GPA killed more than 80% within 3 years (mean survival under 6 months). Induction uses steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab (methotrexate for minor disease), and maintenance uses azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab. About 85–90% enter remission, but about 50% relapse within 5 years. S. aureus nasal carriage independently predicts relapse. Use topical saline/antibiotic irrigations and steroids. CT abnormalities alone are not a surgical indication, and nasal reconstruction should wait until the disease has been inactive for 6–12 months (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, pp 789–790).
canonical_layers.operate: **Key trap**: delay elective reconstruction until destructive activity is controlled when possible -- active disease can defeat an otherwise technically sound repair. **Senior operative boundary**: serial ESS is not a diagnostic or therapeutic reflex for unexplained destructive systemic disease. **Define the purpose of surgery before entering the OR**: obtain representative biopsy, drain/source-control a true infectious complication, debride nonviable tissue when disease-specific care requires it, improve topical access in selected controlled disease, or correct fixed obstruction after the systemic process is understood. **Reconstruction timing**: avoid elective reconstructive correction of septal/saddle deformity during active destructive inflammation -- reconstruct when disease control is durable enough to protect the repair. **Red flag**: escalating tissue loss, orbital/skull-base extension, airway involvement, pulmonary hemorrhage, or renal injury is a systemic rescue problem, not a reason for progressively wider routine FESS.
canonical_layers.teach: **Board pearl**: a septal perforation is a finding, not a diagnosis. **Teaching synthesis**: when the nose looks destructive rather than merely inflamed, widen from 'sinusitis' to systemic disease and dangerous mimics. The resident should be able to: name GPA, EGPA, sarcoidosis, and IgG4-related disease; identify pulmonary/renal/neurologic/orbital/airway clues; explain why ANCA or serum IgG4 is supportive rather than independently diagnostic; choose safe tissue and systemic evaluation; and state the limited, purpose-driven role of sinonasal surgery after the disease process is defined.

candidates.canonical_topic: Restless Legs / Periodic Limb Movement Disorders
candidates.prompt: A patient with sleep-disordered breathing is reviewed in sleep clinic. RLS is an urge to move the legs with uncomfortable sensations, worse at rest/evening and relieved by movement; PLMS are repetitive movements during sleep and are not the same diagnosis. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat reversible contributors and coordinate sleep/neurology management. Avoid surgical OSA pathways unless independent obstruction is present.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Restless Legs / Periodic Limb Movement Disorders. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: a restless sleeper may need iron/sleep-neurology evaluation, not a bigger airway operation.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Sleep Apnea and Sleep Disorders

canonical_layers.recognize: RLS is an urge to move the legs with uncomfortable sensations, worse at rest/evening and relieved by movement; PLMS are repetitive movements during sleep and are not the same diagnosis.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize symptoms to sensorimotor/sleep physiology rather than airway obstruction.
canonical_layers.workup:
Review medications, renal/neurologic contributors, and iron status when clinically appropriate. PSG is useful for PLMS, but RLS is primarily a clinical diagnosis.

**Diagnose RLS clinically** by an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, worse at rest and in the evening/night, relieved by movement, and not better explained by another condition. Check ferritin/iron indices and aggravating medications. Periodic limb movements on PSG are supportive but do not by themselves diagnose symptomatic RLS or PLMD.
canonical_layers.manage:
Treat reversible contributors and coordinate sleep/neurology management. Avoid surgical OSA pathways unless independent obstruction is present.

Check **morning ferritin** and transferrin saturation. **AASM good-practice thresholds**: oral or IV iron in adults when ferritin is <=75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation is <20%, IV iron when ferritin is 75-100 ng/mL, and iron supplementation in children when ferritin is <50 ng/mL. Address alcohol, caffeine, antihistaminergic, serotonergic, and antidopaminergic drugs plus untreated OSA. For adults needing medication, **gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, or pregabalin** are guideline-supported. Routine chronic dopamine-agonist use is discouraged because of augmentation and impulse-control risk.
canonical_layers.operate: No ENT operation treats RLS/PLMD; the advanced skill is recognizing the alternate source of disrupted sleep.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: a restless sleeper may need iron/sleep-neurology evaluation, not a bigger airway operation.

RLS is a waking symptom diagnosis; PLMS is a PSG observation. Treat the patient, not an isolated limb-movement index. **RLS genetics and drug pearls**: BTBD9 links to iron homeostasis and PLMs. Secondary RLS occurs with iron deficiency (ferritin), renal failure, pregnancy, and drugs (SSRIs, TCAs, antihistamines, dopamine antagonists). Rebound = worsening at end of dose. Augmentation = earlier, stronger, wider symptoms on dopaminergics. About 80% of RLS patients have PLMs, but PLMs are not required. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 174-175)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. Hoarseness/throat symptoms may be infectious, inflammatory, irritant, phonotraumatic or systemic; chronic symptoms should not be reflexively labeled reflux. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Hydration, voice conservation/therapy and cause-specific treatment are foundational. Address smoking/irritants and treat proven infection/systemic disease.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Acute / Chronic Laryngopharyngitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: inflammation is a phenotype; define the cause before prescribing a chronic label.

canonical_layers.recognize: Hoarseness/throat symptoms may be infectious, inflammatory, irritant, phonotraumatic or systemic; chronic symptoms should not be reflexively labeled reflux. **Drug-induced dysphonia**: anticoagulants, thrombolytics, and PDE-5 inhibitors predispose to vocal fold hematoma; bisphosphonates cause chemical laryngitis; inhaled steroids cause mucosal irritation and candidiasis; ACE inhibitors cause cough; androgens/danazol virilize the voice; antipsychotics can cause laryngeal dystonia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 80-81) **Granulomatous and chronic infectious laryngitis**: TB laryngitis is usually secondary to pulmonary TB and favors the posterior larynx (interarytenoid), producing ulcerated granulation that mimics carcinoma; syphilis causes painless edema (secondary) or destructive gummas (tertiary); scleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) and blastomycosis both produce pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia that can be misread as SCC; leprosy causes supraglottic ulceration (treated with dapsone). Biopsy with cultures/special stains is the key step. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 91-93) **Fungal laryngitis spectrum**: Candida (white friable plaques, inhaled steroids, immunosuppression, radiation, antibiotics), Aspergillus (allergic to invasive), blastomycosis (red ulcers/miliary nodules on the folds), histoplasmosis (anterior larynx/epiglottic ulcers), and coccidioidomycosis (nodular mass). All may mimic malignancy, so biopsy before assuming cancer; treat with systemic antifungals and secure the airway if needed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 93) **Specific laryngitides**: inhaled steroids cause dysphonia in 5–50% of users (chemical irritation or Candida plaques that mimic leukoplakia); use a spacer, reduce the dose, and give antifungals. MRSA is a common bacterial cause. Idiopathic ulcerative laryngitis follows a URI with bilateral mid-fold ulcers and severe cough; it resolves in about 3 months, and early biopsy should be avoided. Antibiotics do not help acute viral laryngitis. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 52) **Granulomatous laryngitis**: Laryngeal tuberculosis typically involves the posterior glottis/interarytenoid area with ulceration and granulation and can produce a turban-shaped epiglottis; it mimics carcinoma, so biopsy plus AFB culture and chest imaging are needed. Blastomycosis and histoplasmosis also produce ulcerative laryngeal or oral lesions with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia that can be misread as SCC. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 228, 230-231)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize by laryngeal/pharyngeal exam and distinguish diffuse inflammation from focal lesion, impaired motion or malignancy.
canonical_layers.workup: Use laryngoscopy when symptoms persist or red flags exist. Target testing to suspected infection/systemic disease; avoid indiscriminate reflux testing or antibiotics. **Laryngeal TB in modern series**: in a review of 60 cases, hoarseness was nearly universal, lesions were granulomatous or ulcerative, and the true and false vocal folds were the most common sites. 47% had active pulmonary TB, 33% inactive pulmonary TB, and 15% isolated laryngeal disease. Isolated laryngeal TB tends to be focal, unilateral and atypical, so it mimics carcinoma; biopsy with AFB stains is required. More than a third of patients with disseminated leprosy in India have laryngeal involvement. (Cummings 7e, Ch 61, p 902)
canonical_layers.manage: Hydration, voice conservation/therapy and cause-specific treatment are foundational. Address smoking/irritants and treat proven infection/systemic disease. **AAO-HNS Hoarseness CPG (2018)**: do not give antireflux medication for hoarseness without reflux signs/symptoms (option if chronic laryngitis signs), do not routinely give oral steroids before the larynx is visualized, strongly avoid routine antibiotics, examine the larynx before prescribing voice therapy, and scope when hoarseness lasts >4 weeks or sooner with red flags (tobacco/alcohol, neck mass, hemoptysis, dysphagia, otalgia, airway compromise, neurologic signs, recent intubation or neck surgery). Botulinum toxin is recommended for spasmodic dysphonia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 81, 83-84) **Candida and chronic bacterial laryngitis**: Candida laryngitis appears as diffuse white speckling of the folds or supraglottis. It belongs in the differential of laryngeal leukoplakia along with keratosis, thick mucus and cancer, even in immunocompetent patients. Treat laryngeal or refractory disease with systemic fluconazole, and switch to itraconazole for fluconazole-resistant strains. Chronic bacterial laryngitis, such as purulent chondritis after intubation injury or relapsing polychondritis (often S. aureus), can present with hoarseness and stridor lasting more than a month and needs drainage plus prolonged antibiotics. (Cummings 7e, Ch 61, p 900–901) **Laryngeal candidiasis**: Risk factors are inhaled (especially powder) corticosteroids, reflux, immunosuppression, and antibiotics. White plaques on red mucosa can mimic leukoplakia. Treat with a systemic antifungal (topical or swallowed nystatin is ineffective) and pause the inhaled steroid if possible. Biopsy plaques that persist after treatment to exclude carcinoma. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 50, p 901)
canonical_layers.operate: Operative biopsy is reserved for suspicious or persistent focal pathology rather than diffuse uncomplicated inflammation.
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: inflammation is a phenotype; define the cause before prescribing a chronic label.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, skew, impaired smooth pursuit/saccades, severe truncal ataxia or neurologic deficits push dizziness toward a central process. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the underlying neurologic disease and use vestibular rehabilitation selectively; chronic central compensation may still improve with therapy.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Central Vestibular Disorders. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: central versus peripheral is an eye-movement/localization problem, not a symptom adjective.

canonical_layers.recognize: Direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, skew, impaired smooth pursuit/saccades, severe truncal ataxia or neurologic deficits push dizziness toward a central process. **Posterior-circulation syndromes**: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome from vertebral or PICA occlusion: acute vertigo and nystagmus, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner, dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral limb ataxia, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss, with hearing spared. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency gives brief vertigo with neck extension or rotation plus the '4 Ds' (dizziness, diplopia, dysphagia, drop attacks). Subclavian steal causes vertigo with arm use, an interarm blood pressure difference, and a weak radial pulse. Multiple sclerosis presents with vertigo in about 10–15%. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 421–423) **Central nystagmus patterns and their drugs**: *downbeat*: Chiari malformation or cerebellar degeneration; treat with 4-aminopyridine. *Upbeat*: pontomedullary or pontomesencephalic junction, or fourth ventricle. *Periodic alternating* (horizontal nystagmus reversing about every 2 minutes): cerebellar nodulus; treat with baclofen. *Pendular*: MS, or oculopalatal tremor after brainstem stroke; may respond to memantine or gabapentin. *Purely torsional*: vestibular nuclei (e.g., syringobulbia). *Seesaw*: midbrain. *Convergence-retraction*: Parinaud syndrome. *Dissociated, abducting-eye nystagmus*: INO. *Rebound nystagmus*: cerebellar disease. Nystagmus outside the plane of the stimulated canal ('perverted') is central. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, p 2500) **Central positional vertigo and fourth-ventricle masses**: Positional vertigo can come from lesions of the dorsolateral fourth ventricle or dorsal vermis. Suspect it when positional nystagmus has a short or no latency, an atypical direction (for example pure downbeat), appears in several positions, does not fatigue, and fails to respond to repositioning maneuvers. Fourth-ventricle tumors (medulloblastoma in children, ependymoma, epidermoid) can cause headache, vomiting and vertigo with head-position change from intermittent CSF obstruction (Bruns syndrome). Dizziness occurs in about 81% of posterior fossa tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2544, 2547) **Chiari malformation**: Chiari I is defined by cerebellar tonsils more than 5 mm below the foramen magnum on sagittal MRI. It is an incidental finding in about 3.6% of people, and symptoms usually begin at age 25-35: occipital headache brought on by cough, sneeze, bending or lifting, arm weakness and sensory loss, ataxia (24%-49%) and, less often, vertigo (8%-18%) or downbeat nystagmus. Lower cranial nerve involvement can bring the patient to ENT with dysphagia, aspiration or hoarseness. About a third do not improve after decompression. Chiari II appears in infancy with hydrocephalus and myelomeningocele. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2548) **Multiple sclerosis**: Vertigo is the first symptom of MS in only about 5% of patients but occurs in up to 60% at some point, and MS causes about 10% of central acute vestibular syndromes. Plaques in the vestibular nuclei or the CN VIII root entry zone are the usual cause, and other signs such as internuclear ophthalmoplegia usually point to a central lesion. BPPV is still the most common cause of vertigo in people with MS, so do positional testing. MRI shows white-matter lesions in over 90% of cases, and CSF oligoclonal bands are common. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2548-2549) **Hereditary, degenerative and paraneoplastic ataxias**: Familial episodic ataxia is autosomal dominant. Stress-triggered attacks of vertigo and ataxia last minutes to hours, start between childhood and early adulthood, and respond markedly to acetazolamide. Friedreich ataxia (autosomal recessive GAA expansion in frataxin, onset usually before age 20) combines sensory neuropathy with areflexia, Babinski sign, cardiomyopathy and diabetes, with square-wave jerks and low VOR gain. Late-onset cerebellar atrophy shows rebound and vertical nystagmus. Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration progresses rapidly over months, sometimes with opsoclonus-myoclonus, from anti-Purkinje antibodies (small cell lung, breast or ovarian cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma), and it often appears before the cancer is found. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2549) **CABV and CANVAS**: cerebellar ataxia with bilateral vestibulopathy (CABV) is progressive imbalance and oscillopsia from vestibulocerebellar atrophy plus bilateral vestibular loss. Adding a non-length-dependent sensory neuropathy (ganglionopathy) makes it CANVAS, a late-onset recessive disorder. It can also occur with SCA3/SCA6, Friedreich ataxia, paraneoplastic disease, cerebellar-type MSA and Wernicke. Signs are marked DVA loss, poor pursuit and optokinetic responses, an abnormal VVOR (the single most informative bedside test), gaze-evoked or downbeat nystagmus and gait ataxia. Work up with MRI, sensory nerve action potentials and VNG/vHIT. Treatment is vestibular rehabilitation, avoiding cerebellar toxins (alcohol, solvents, some antiepileptics) and assistive devices. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 331-333) **Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome**: PICA/vertebral thrombosis infarcts the lateral medulla: vertigo, nystagmus, vomiting, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral ataxia with falling toward the lesion, and crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body pain/temperature). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 36) **Vertebrobasilar insufficiency and subclavian steal**: VBI causes vertigo with other brainstem signs (diplopia, dysarthria, visual change, hemiparesis) and drop attacks without loss of consciousness provoked by neck motion; isolated hearing loss/tinnitus is unusual. Subclavian steal (stenosis proximal to the vertebral origin) gives arm-exercise-provoked vertigo, occipital headache and visual symptoms, with an interarm blood pressure difference. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 32, 51)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize by ocular-motor pattern to brainstem/cerebellar pathways rather than relying on the patient's word 'vertigo.' **Alexander's law**: in a peripheral vestibular lesion, nystagmus is stronger when the patient looks toward the fast phase and weaker when looking away. Dandy syndrome is oscillopsia from bilateral vestibular loss, iatrogenic or idiopathic (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, p 2090). **Skew deviation and the ocular tilt reaction**: skew is a vertical misalignment not explained by an ocular muscle palsy. Detect it with the alternate cover test or a Maddox rod. With peripheral or vestibular-nucleus lesions (below the decussation), the lower eye is on the side of the lesion. Above the decussation (MLF or INO, midbrain), the higher eye is on the lesion side, and the head tilts toward the lower eye. The full ocular tilt reaction is head tilt, skew and conjugate ocular torsion. A fourth nerve palsy is worst with the eye down and in (Bielschowsky head tilt), whereas skew changes little with gaze and may lessen when supine. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, p 2490; Ch 166, pp 2500–2501) **Saccade and pursuit localization**: overshoot or undershoot dysmetria points to the dorsal vermis or fastigial nuclei. In Wallenberg syndrome, saccades overshoot toward the lesion and undershoot away from it, and vertical saccades drift toward the lesion; superior cerebellar peduncle lesions do the opposite. Slow horizontal saccades suggest pontine disease (e.g., SCA2); slow vertical saccades suggest the midbrain (PSP, Huntington, Niemann-Pick). Square-wave jerks (5 degrees or less) are prominent in PSP and cerebellar disease. Ocular flutter (horizontal) and opsoclonus (multidirectional) suggest encephalitis or paraneoplastic disease such as neuroblastoma. Flocculus lesions impair ipsilateral pursuit, and sedatives, anticonvulsants and age also degrade pursuit. Normal saccade latency is about 200 ms. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, pp 2501–2502) **ENG/VNG patterns that point central**: spontaneous or positional nystagmus with normal calorics; direction-changing nystagmus or failed fixation suppression; bilaterally reduced calorics with no history of labyrinthine disease, middle-ear disease or ototoxicity; saccadic pursuit or dysmetric saccades, especially with normal calorics; hyperactive calorics (loss of cerebellar inhibition) with an intact drum and no mastoid cavity; and perverted (wrong-direction) caloric nystagmus. Peripheral patterns are unilateral caloric weakness, direction-fixed nystagmus, fatiguing positional nystagmus and intact fixation suppression. Alexander's law grades peripheral nystagmus: first degree only when gazing toward the fast phase, second degree also in primary gaze, third degree in all gaze directions. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 321-322, 326) **Craniovertebral junction anomalies**: Chiari I is cerebellar tonsillar descent at least about 5-6 mm below the foramen magnum, obstructing CSF flow and causing downbeat nystagmus, occipital headache and lower cranial neuropathies. Platybasia (skull-base angle over about 143 degrees) and basilar invagination (odontoid migrating into the foramen magnum) occur with Down syndrome, Klippel-Feil and rheumatoid arthritis; treatment is decompression and/or fusion depending on reducibility. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 133)
canonical_layers.workup:
In acute vestibular syndrome, bedside eye movements are interpreted only in the correct clinical context. Imaging/neurologic evaluation is urgent when a central pattern is suspected.

**HINTS/HINTS-plus**: in an acute vestibular syndrome, a trained examination can identify central physiology, but it is not a screening mnemonic for intermittent dizziness or untrained use. **Red flags that lower the threshold** for stroke-pathway imaging and neurology involvement: direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, skew, severe truncal ataxia, new hearing loss, focal neurologic deficits, headache/neck pain, vascular risk, or an atypical course. **Key trap**: early MRI can be falsely negative in posterior circulation stroke. **Vertebral artery dissection**: Dissection is easy to miss because dizziness is its most frequent symptom (about 58%) and most patients have no neck pain, so no single symptom rules it out. It causes only about 2% of ischemic strokes overall but a large share of strokes under age 45 (mean onset about 46 years), and trauma, chiropractic manipulation or connective-tissue disease is present in fewer than half. Diagnose with CT or MR angiography; antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is first line, with endovascular treatment as an option. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2545) **Craniovertebral junction disorders**: Cervicomedullary compression can cause tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss, dysphagia and hoarseness, and it can lead to needless ear surgery if missed. In basilar impression (from Paget disease, rheumatoid arthritis, osteomalacia, osteogenesis imperfecta or rickets), the odontoid tip rises above Chamberlain's line (posterior hard palate to the posterior lip of the foramen magnum) or lies behind Wackenheim's clivus-canal line; platybasia alone causes no symptoms. Atlas assimilation often comes with Klippel-Feil fusion. Atlantoaxial instability is seen radiographically in 10%-30% of people with Down syndrome (atlantodens interval 4-5 mm), but only 1%-2% have symptoms. MRI is the key study. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2547-2548) **Bedside VOR tests beyond HINTS**: the head-shake test (about 2 Hz for 15 seconds) produces nystagmus whose fast phase usually beats away from the weaker ear and correlates with caloric asymmetry. Vertical or torsional nystagmus after horizontal shaking (cross-coupling) means a CNS cause must be excluded. Loss of more than 5 Snellen/LogMAR lines of dynamic visual acuity with >2 Hz head shaking suggests bilateral vestibular loss. Failure to suppress nystagmus with fixation during VOR suppression points to the vestibulocerebellum. An abnormal visually enhanced VOR (VVOR) shows combined vestibular, cerebellar and pursuit failure. The head-heave test (a quick lateral head translation) checks the utricle and helps predict recovery after vestibular neuritis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 318-320)
canonical_layers.manage:
Treat the underlying neurologic disease and use vestibular rehabilitation selectively. Chronic central compensation may still improve with therapy.

Activate urgent stroke/neurologic evaluation for suspected central acute vestibular syndrome. For established nonacute central imbalance, treat the underlying disorder and use individualized vestibular/physical rehabilitation, fall prevention, and assistive strategies rather than chronic vestibular suppressants. **Cerebellar infarction and hemorrhage**: A cerebellum-only infarct presents with severe vertigo, vomiting and ataxia but few brainstem signs, so it is mistaken for acute labyrinthitis; prominent gait ataxia and gaze-evoked nystagmus are the clues, and early MRI can be falsely negative. After a latent interval of about 24 to 96 hours, cerebellar swelling can compress the brainstem and progress to coma and death unless surgical decompression is done, so admit and observe. Cerebellar hemorrhage (mortality about 20%-74%) is shown on noncontrast CT, which should be the first study to exclude blood. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2543-2545) **Vertebrobasilar insufficiency treatment**: Vertebrobasilar ischemia is usually atherosclerotic (vertebral origin in men of European descent; intracranial disease more often in African American, Asian and female patients) and seldom causes vertigo alone without diplopia, ataxia, numbness, weakness or bulbar symptoms. Nonacute care is risk-factor control. For symptomatic 50%-99% intracranial stenosis, aspirin works as well as warfarin with less bleeding and is preferred; warfarin is reserved for cardioembolic stroke. Get CT first to exclude hemorrhage, and route acute stroke to neurology for thrombolysis decisions. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2543)
canonical_layers.operate: ENT surgery has no role for most central vestibular disease; the advanced decision is knowing when not to operate and when to escalate to stroke/neurology pathways.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: central versus peripheral is an eye-movement/localization problem, not a symptom adjective.

Peripheral-appearing vertigo does not exclude stroke. HINTS is powerful only in the correct continuous acute vestibular syndrome, performed and interpreted by a trained examiner.

candidates.answer_text: Match intervention to a defined structural objective and patient goal; avoid chasing isolated measurements without considering whole-face balance.

canonical_layers.recognize: Aesthetic analysis is structured description, not 'looks good/bad': facial thirds/fifths, symmetry, profile, skin envelope, nasal projection/rotation and chin-lip relationships.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize an aesthetic concern to skeletal framework, cartilage, soft tissue, skin or dynamic muscle and distinguish regional imbalance from an isolated nasal or eyelid problem.
canonical_layers.workup: Use standardized photography and reproducible measurements/views. Functional nasal, ocular and facial-nerve issues are assessed separately but integrated into the plan. **Dedo cervical classification**: I youthful neck; II skin laxity; III excess fat; IV platysmal banding; V microgenia/retrognathia; VI low hyoid. Turkey-gobbler neck is loss of the cervicomental angle (over 120°) from failed platysmal decussation; ptotic submandibular glands are addressed with a platysmal sling. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 480, 501) **Photography and reference lines**: Frankfort horizontal (top of tragus/EAC to infraorbital rim) orients all photos; use a 90–105 mm lens (35 mm equivalent), blue background and two lights at 45°. Rhinoplasty set: frontal, both laterals, both obliques, base and smiling lateral. The ideal chin lies on the Gonzalez-Ulloa zero meridian, a line through nasion perpendicular to Frankfort horizontal. Nasal ratios: columella:base:dorsum about 3:4:5, 2–3 mm columellar show, basal view isosceles triangle with columella 2/3 and lobule 1/3. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 480–483, 507) **More profile norms**: nasofacial angle 30-40 degrees (ideal 36); nasomental angle 120-132 degrees, with lips about 4 mm (upper) and 2 mm (lower) behind the nasomental line; Goode projection ratio 0.55-0.60; Simons tip projection about equal to upper lip length (1:1); columellar show 3-5 mm; upper-to-lower lip height 1:2; mentocervical angle 80-95 degrees. Ideal chin per Gonzalez-Ulloa is on the zero meridian (nasion perpendicular to Frankfort). The upper lid crease is about 11 mm (7-15) from the lash line, and the brow peaks above the lateral limbus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 16, p 240-244)
canonical_layers.manage: Match intervention to a defined structural objective and patient goal; avoid chasing isolated measurements without considering whole-face balance.
canonical_layers.operate: Every maneuver should have a predicted vector/volume/support effect and an anticipated tradeoff. Preoperative analysis should be traceable to the operative plan.
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: describe first, diagnose the structural imbalance second, choose a maneuver third. **Poor aesthetic candidates and premature-aging syndromes**: unrealistic expectations, many prior surgeons, psychiatric instability, and smoking (over 12-fold skin slough risk). Cutis laxa (autosomal recessive, loose skin, hernias, emphysema) benefits from rhytidectomy; progeria and Werner syndrome do not. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 480, 500–501)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Discrete bacterial-pattern episodes with symptom-free intervals are different from chronic daily symptoms. this condition is generally defined as four or more distinct episodes of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a year, each meeting criteria for acute disease with resolution of symptoms between episodes — the symptom-free interval is what separates this from chronic rhinosinusitis with exacerbations. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat individual bacterial episodes appropriately; prevention/surgery depends on documented pattern and anatomy rather than symptom count alone.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Recurrent Acute Rhinosinusitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Do not convert every recurrent viral URI into RARS.

canonical_layers.recognize: Discrete bacterial-pattern episodes with symptom-free intervals differ from chronic daily symptoms. **Definition**: recurrent acute rhinosinusitis (RARS) is generally defined as **four or more distinct episodes** of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a year, each meeting criteria for acute disease, with resolution of symptoms between episodes. The symptom-free interval is what separates this from chronic rhinosinusitis with exacerbations. **Key point**: the recurrence pattern itself is a clinical signal, not just a frequency count -- it should prompt a search for an underlying driver rather than repeated courses of antibiotics alone. **Pediatric definition and workup**: in children, recurrent acute sinusitis is defined like recurrent AOM: 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 in 12 months, with complete resolution in between (the adult definition is 4 or more per year). Daycare-driven viral URIs are the usual cause. Evaluate for allergy, cystic fibrosis (sweat test), quantitative immunoglobulins with IgG subclasses and pneumococcal polysaccharide responses, ciliary function, dental apical abscess and reflux before escalating. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1049)
canonical_layers.localize: **Predisposing factors** to evaluate for, because they are identifiable and often modifiable: allergic rhinitis and other atopic disease; anatomic variants that impair sinus drainage (significant septal deviation, concha bullosa, Onodi cell obstructing natural ostia); immunodeficiency (screen when episodes are unusually frequent or severe); and, in children, cystic fibrosis or primary ciliary dyskinesia when accompanied by other suggestive features. **Emerging concept**: biofilm-associated bacterial persistence is also increasingly recognized as a contributor to a recurrent pattern rather than true reinfection each time.
canonical_layers.workup: Confirm the pattern and consider endoscopy/CT when episodes are recurrent and intervention is contemplated; assess dental, immune or anatomic contributors selectively.
canonical_layers.manage: Treat individual bacterial episodes appropriately; prevention/surgery depends on documented pattern and anatomy rather than symptom count alone.
canonical_layers.operate: **Key trap**: do not convert every recurrent viral URI into RARS. **Also**: offer surgery only after documenting true discrete bacterial-pattern episodes with symptom-free intervals, failure of appropriate medical/preventive management, and relevant endoscopic or CT anatomy. **Technique**: tailor limited sinus opening to the repeatedly involved sinus and natural drainage pathway. Surgery is not justified by four self-diagnosed viral URIs, or by a normal inter-episode evaluation without corroborating evidence. **Balloon sinus dilation basics**: A balloon catheter passed over a guidewire widens the natural maxillary, frontal, or sphenoid ostium without removing bone. It can be used alone (office or OR, under topical/local anesthesia) or as a hybrid with standard ESS. It cannot treat the ethmoids, which have no single ostium, so balloon-only treatment suits focal outflow disease such as recurrent acute rhinosinusitis or limited nonpolypoid CRS. Polyps, heavy osteitis, and extensive ethmoid disease are poor fits. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 13, p 105, 112) **Balloon placement checks**: Confirm wire position before inflating. For the frontal sinus, a sharp spot of light that moves across the forehead means the true sinus, while a diffuse glow suggests an ethmoid or suprabullar cell. For the maxillary sinus, the wire must pass through the natural ostium. Dilating elsewhere creates an accessory ostium and recirculation. For the sphenoid (ostium about 1–1.5 cm above the choana, medial to the superior turbinate), transillumination is unreliable. Use fluoroscopy or navigation if there is doubt. Inflate to about 8–12 atmospheres. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 13, p 107–108)
canonical_layers.teach: **Key trap**: do not convert every recurrent viral URI into RARS. **Also**: RARS requires at least four distinct acute episodes per year with resolution between them. **Board pearl**: the surgical question is not the count alone -- it is whether objectively credible recurrent disease maps to an anatomic drainage target after medical contributors have been addressed.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Characterize acute vs chronic, size/site, edge, infection, hearing loss and ossicular/inner-ear clues. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Keep ear dry, treat infection when present, observe many acute perforations; tympanoplasty for persistent symptomatic/performance-limiting perforation when appropriate.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Tympanic Membrane Perforation. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: A perforation is a window into middle-ear disease, not always the primary diagnosis.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Characterize before managing**: assess any perforation along several axes. **Tempo**: acute (traumatic/infectious, often self-limited) versus chronic (present beyond ~3 months, unlikely to close spontaneously). **Size and quadrant**. **Margin appearance**: rolled/epithelialized edges suggest chronicity and reduce spontaneous closure chances. **Infection**: presence of active infection/otorrhea. **Deeper disease signs**: associated hearing loss, retraction, or keratin debris suggesting cholesteatoma. **Classification and misnomers**: Classify perforations by site (pars tensa quadrant or pars flaccida), extent (one quadrant under 25%, two or more quadrants, or total) and duration (acute, or chronic after 3 months). So-called *marginal* posterosuperior and *attic* perforations are usually deep retraction pockets or cholesteatomas, not true holes. A small perforation alone has little effect on hearing, whereas a large one gives about 20-30 dB. 'Chronic otitis media inactive' is a misnomer. The correct term is chronic perforation without otitis media. In the Pittsburgh tube trials, 14.8% had a perforation at the tube site after extrusion but only 1.4% stayed chronic and needed repair, so watchful waiting (most heal in 2-3 months) is appropriate. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 769-772)
canonical_layers.localize: **Site matters** beyond the hole itself. Marginal or attic perforations carry a higher risk of associated cholesteatoma and ossicular erosion than a central pars tensa perforation. **Key trap**: a perforation with an air-bone gap larger than expected for its size should raise concern for ossicular discontinuity, rather than assuming the perforation alone explains the hearing loss.
canonical_layers.workup: Otoscopy/microscopy and audiometry; CT only when trauma, cholesteatoma, ossicular injury or other deeper disease is suspected.
canonical_layers.manage: Keep ear dry, treat infection when present, observe many acute perforations; tympanoplasty for persistent symptomatic/performance-limiting perforation when appropriate. **Pediatric chronic perforation and tympanoplasty timing**: A dry perforation ventilates the ear but removes the protective middle-ear gas cushion, so the ear is exposed to water contamination and nasopharyngeal reflux. Pediatric myringoplasty or tympanoplasty succeeds in about 80% of children older than about 5-6 years. One series favored repair after age 6 rather than delaying further, to limit inner-ear damage. Tube-related perforations needing tympanoplasty were about 2.4% in the Pittsburgh trials, and higher with long-term tubes. Weigh contralateral ear status and ET function when timing repair. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 772-773) **Traumatic perforation details**: Common mechanisms are an open-hand slap, a blast or firecracker, water impact (diving, water-skiing), a cotton swab, and irrigation of hard cerumen. The loss is usually 20-40 dB conductive. For a fresh perforation, the inverted edges can be unfolded and supported on Gelfoam. If edges have epithelialized, mechanical freshening with a fat or paper myringoplasty healed 87% vs 67% with trichloroacetic acid cautery. A *paper patch test* helps separate the perforation's share of the loss from ossicular injury: if hearing does not improve with the patch, suspect discontinuity. CT shows incus or malleus dislocation in about 90%. Explore urgently for SNHL with vertigo (stapes subluxation or a round window tear, sealed with tissue) or for immediate facial paralysis. Defer elective tympanoplasty in children with active ET problems. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 881-883) **AOM with acute perforation and otorrhea**: Treat with antibiotics rather than observation, because a perforation marks a severe episode. Culture pus aspirated at or through the perforation, and add a topical quinolone, pumped in by pressing the tragus. Use a quinolone drop FDA-approved for a nonintact drum (ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone or ciprofloxacin-fluocinolone). Avoid aminoglycoside (neomycin-polymyxin-hydrocortisone) drops and acetic acid or Burow solution when the middle ear is open. Keep the ear dry, and expect the drum to close within about a week. If otorrhea persists 2-3 weeks despite proper oral therapy, examine under the microscope (under anesthesia if needed) to look for cholesteatoma or tumor, culture the middle ear, and give culture-directed IV therapy. If it still persists, do tympanostomy and simple mastoidectomy even when CT shows no coalescence, because mastoid osteitis is the usual cause. Do not close an uncomplicated perforation before 3 months. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 770-772)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: a persistent (generally beyond 3 months), symptomatic (hearing loss, recurrent infection, water-precaution burden) perforation, or one associated with suspected ossicular/deeper disease. **Setup**: myringoplasty (graft alone) for a simple perforation with a normal ossicular chain, or tympanoplasty with ossicular assessment/reconstruction when discontinuity is suspected. **Key steps**: freshen the perforation edges, elevate a tympanomeatal flap if using an underlay technique, place graft material (temporalis fascia, perichondrium, or fat for a small perforation) under or over the remnant drum, and support with packing. **Danger structures**: the chorda tympani (preserve when possible) and, if working near the ossicular chain, the incus and stapes superstructure. **Failure mode**: treating every perforation as the primary diagnosis rather than as a window revealing deeper middle-ear disease (cholesteatoma, ossicular erosion) that must be addressed at the same operation -- otherwise the repair will fail or mask progressive disease. **Postoperative plan**: water precautions during healing, and audiometry at follow-up to confirm both graft take and hearing improvement, not graft closure alone. **Underlay versus overlay**: Medial (underlay) grafting under the annulus and drum remnant is quicker, technically easier, and sufficient for most, especially posterior, perforations. Lateral (overlay) grafting suits large or anterior perforations but takes longer and risks anterior blunting, lateralization, entry into the glenoid fossa, and more postoperative conductive loss. Temporalis fascia is the most common graft. Cartilage, perichondrium, fat, and acellular dermis are alternatives. A perforation gives a flat tympanogram with canal volume above about 1.5 mL. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 377–378, 388) **Pediatric tympanoplasty timing**: success in children (roughly 35–94%) is lower than in adults because of URIs, ongoing eustachian tube dysfunction (especially with cleft palate, Down syndrome or craniofacial anomalies) and less reliable postoperative care. Results improve with age up to about 13. Many surgeons wait until the adenoid pad is regressing (about age 7) or regressed (about age 10), or first treat adenoid and nasal disease. The contralateral ear should be free of effusion, retraction and recurrent infection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 592)
canonical_layers.teach: A perforation is a window into middle-ear disease, not always the primary diagnosis.

candidates.prompt: A patient with sleep-disordered breathing is reviewed in sleep clinic. Excessive daytime sleepiness with cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hypnagogic phenomena points beyond obstructive snoring and toward central hypersomnolence. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Refer/manage through sleep medicine; ENT surgery does not treat narcolepsy, though coexisting OSA may still need independent treatment.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Narcolepsy / Central Hypersomnolence Recognition. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: sleepiness is not synonymous with OSA.

canonical_layers.recognize: Excessive daytime sleepiness with cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hypnagogic phenomena points beyond obstructive snoring and toward central hypersomnolence. **Narcolepsy mimics**: idiopathic hypersomnia features long (>10 h) unrefreshing sleep, naps that do not refresh, and short MSLT latency without SOREMPs. Kleine-Levin syndrome affects adolescent males with recurrent episodes of days-weeks of hypersomnia plus hyperphagia, hypersexuality, and cognitive change, normal between episodes. Chronic insufficient sleep remains the most common cause of hypersomnia. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 179-181)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the problem to sleep-wake regulation rather than upper-airway collapse.
canonical_layers.workup:
Confirm adequate sleep and exclude untreated OSA/medications before sleep-medicine testing such as PSG followed by MSLT when indicated.

Confirm chronic daily sleepiness despite adequate sleep opportunity. Obtain sleep logs/actigraphy. Exclude insufficient sleep, circadian misalignment, medication/substance effects, OSA, and depression. Then perform attended PSG followed by properly conducted MSLT when indicated. **Cataplexy** strongly supports narcolepsy type 1. CSF hypocretin testing is reserved for selected diagnostic uncertainty. **MSLT/MWT protocols**: MSLT follows an overnight PSG with >=6 hours of sleep, after 1-2 weeks of regular sleep off stimulants. 4-5 nap opportunities at 2-hour intervals. Narcolepsy if mean sleep latency <=8 min with >=2 sleep-onset REM periods. MWT (4 x 40-minute trials in a dim room) measures ability to stay awake for occupational/treatment assessment and needs no prior PSG. CSF hypocretin-1 <110 pg/mL (or <1/3 of normal) defines type 1 narcolepsy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 4, pp 161-162, 180)
canonical_layers.manage:
Refer/manage through sleep medicine. ENT surgery does not treat narcolepsy, though coexisting OSA may still need independent treatment.

Refer to sleep medicine for wake-promoting therapy and cataplexy/REM-symptom management, scheduled sleep strategies, driving/work/school safety, and treatment of coexisting OSA. **Key point**: airway surgery does not treat central hypersomnolence when obstructive disease is absent or controlled.
canonical_layers.operate: The operative decision is to avoid attributing hypersomnolence to anatomy when the physiology is central.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: sleepiness is not synonymous with OSA.

MSLT is interpretable only after adequate sleep and exclusion/treatment of confounders; sleep-onset REM periods are not meaningful when sleep deprivation or REM-modulating medications invalidate the test.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. A this condition user may be disabled by subtle change that would be acceptable to a casual voice user; occupational demand is part of disease severity. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Voice therapy, load modification, amplification, medical treatment and surgery are selected to restore function while protecting the vibratory cover.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Professional Voice. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: 'normal speaking voice' does not equal normal occupational function.

canonical_layers.recognize: A professional voice user may be disabled by subtle change that would be acceptable to a casual voice user; occupational demand is part of disease severity. **Laryngopathia premenstrualis**: premenstrual voice change with slight hoarseness, muffling, vocal fatigue and loss of the highest notes. Uncommon in untrained women but reported by up to about one-third of singers. Varices tend to enlarge before and during menses, raising hemorrhage risk. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 2, p 12) **Performer history specifics**: ask about rehearsal and performance counts, rest between shows, venue size, amplification and in-ear monitors, role difficulty and whether an understudy exists. For teachers, class and room size, amplification, subject (music, gym) and duties such as recess. AAO-HNS defines a voice professional as anyone whose voice is essential to their job. Airplane cabin air is 5% humidity or less, and oil-based stage smoke causes irritation, allergy and bronchospasm. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 2, p 13)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize limitation to mucosal vibration, glottic closure, motor control, respiratory support, resonance and compensatory muscle tension.
canonical_layers.workup: Stroboscopy, perceptual/acoustic assessment and task-specific evaluation should reproduce the professional demand when possible.
canonical_layers.manage: Voice therapy, load modification, amplification, medical treatment and surgery are selected to restore function while protecting the vibratory cover. **Systemic corticosteroids for performers**: steroids are appropriate when the risk of permanent damage is low: edema from episodic overuse, mild-to-moderate laryngitis, allergic edema, and (empirically) hemorrhage. If the performance is within 24 hours, give dexamethasone 4 mg plus methylprednisolone 60 mg IM. In subacute cases, give a 3–5 day oral burst with a rapid taper. Never use them for the first time just before a performance, because idiosyncratic voice worsening or mood effects can occur. Trial them before a studio session instead. Avoid inhaled or topically applied laryngeal steroids, which irritate the mucosa and promote Candida. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 850) **Medications singers should avoid**: avoid sedating antihistamines and antihistamine-decongestant combinations because they dry the mucosa. Treat allergy with nasal steroids, nonsedating agents or immunotherapy. Avoid aspirin because of hemorrhage risk. Avoid topical anesthetic throat sprays: they let the singer overwork an injured fold, so a singer who cannot perform without one should not perform. Menthol dries the mucosa and can become a habit. Guaifenesin may thin secretions. Beta-blockers for stage fright should be used only rarely, never routinely, because they blunt performance. Hydrate to pale urine (at least about 64 oz a day, more when flying). (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 848–850) **Vocal fold varix**: varices occur mostly in female professional singers and may enlarge before and during menses, raising the risk of hemorrhage. Assess their functional impact with serial stroboscopy across the menstrual cycle. First-line care is hydration, avoiding caffeine, and voice therapy. Hormonal manipulation is unproven. Treat with surgery or laser for recurrent hemorrhage, enlargement, or persistent dysphonia despite maximal behavioral care. In the OR, apply 1:10,000 epinephrine and coagulate the feeding and then the draining vessels with a defocused 1–2 W CO2, KTP or PDL laser, sparing the medial vibratory surface. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 849, 852)
canonical_layers.operate: Microsurgery must minimize epithelial/lamina propria trauma; return-to-performance planning is part of the procedure, not an afterthought. **Post-microflap recovery phases**: give 5–7 days of complete voice rest for limited dissection, or 10–14 days for extensive or revision surgery. Next, with SLP guidance, start at about 5 minutes of talking and double it daily, reaching full conversation by weeks 3–4. Repeat stroboscopy at 2–3 weeks. From months 2–3, singing reeducation with a pedagogue follows. Most patients return to professional activity at about 3 months, and follow-up runs to about 24 months. Intubate gently with the smallest tube, done by the surgeon or an experienced anesthesiologist. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 852–853)
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: 'normal speaking voice' does not equal normal occupational function. **When to cancel a performance**: cancel for submucosal hemorrhage, an enlarging varix, a mucosal break (tear), significant systemic illness, or severe laryngitis. Hemorrhage, an enlarging varix and a mucosal break call for absolute voice rest, and a mucosal break also calls for aggressive antireflux therapy and close follow-up for scar, granuloma or polyp. A mild URI or mild-to-moderate edema carries less risk, and the final decision belongs to the performer. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 849–850) **Other surgery in singers**: tonsillectomy, UPPP, adenoidectomy, septoplasty, sinus and turbinate surgery and maxillary expansion can all change resonance. Even mild new hypernasality can damage a singing career. Stage UPPP over months and keep nasal and adenoid surgery conservative. Get a baseline audiogram in all serious singers, and suggest in-ear monitors to prevent oversinging against stage noise (the Lombard effect). (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 853)
