candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. A persistent pediatric neck mass is more often inflammatory/congenital than malignant, but hard/fixed nodes, supraclavicular location, B symptoms, cranial neuropathy or progressive growth require oncologic evaluation. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treatment is histology-specific and often multidisciplinary. Preserve long-term growth, cranial nerve, swallowing, hearing and endocrine function whenever oncologically safe.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Pediatric Head & Neck Tumors. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: In children, the wrong biopsy can complicate the right cancer operation. Diagnose the compartment and histology before cutting.

canonical_layers.recognize: A persistent pediatric neck mass is more often inflammatory/congenital than malignant, but hard/fixed nodes, supraclavicular location, B symptoms, cranial neuropathy or progressive growth require oncologic evaluation. **Pilomatrixoma**: a benign hair-matrix tumor with a bimodal age peak (about 5-15 and 50-65 years). About 50-60% occur in the head and neck, usually as a firm, calcified, skin-tethered nodule 3 cm or smaller on the cheek, neck, or preauricular region, sometimes with bluish skin and a 'tent sign'. Ultrasound shows a calcified subcutaneous nodule. Treat with complete excision, including the attached skin, to prevent recurrence. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 233) **Other pediatric malignancies**: lymphoma is the most common pediatric head and neck malignancy. Burkitt is the most common pediatric NHL, with c-MYC translocation and a starry-sky pattern. It is EBV-positive in 90–95% of endemic and 15–20% of sporadic cases. Hodgkin lymphoma peaks in teenagers, often with a mediastinal mass. Diagnose it by excisional biopsy sent fresh, and avoid steroids before biopsy. Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood. Neck disease can cause Horner syndrome and heterochromia, and urine catecholamines help with the diagnosis. Pediatric NPC is usually undifferentiated and advanced at presentation. Excluding hemangioma, infection and malformation, more than half of solid pediatric parotid masses are malignant. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common pediatric salivary malignancy, and acinic cell carcinoma is second. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 611–614) **NF1 in the head and neck**: NF1 (17q11.2, autosomal dominant, about 50% de novo) was diagnosed by the older NIH criteria, two or more of: six or more café-au-lait macules (>5 mm before puberty, >15 mm after), two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, axillary or inguinal freckling, optic glioma, two or more Lisch nodules, a distinctive bony lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, long-bone cortical thinning), or an affected first-degree relative. **Current view**: the 2021 revised criteria are the standard. They add a heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant and choroidal abnormalities as features, and a child of an affected parent needs only one other feature. Plexiform neurofibromas can involve the parotid, carotid, retropharyngeal and masticator spaces, and cervical neurofibromas can be mistaken for lymph nodes. Resect for rapid growth (to exclude malignant change), pain or deficit, airway compression, or disfigurement. Legius syndrome (SPRED1) mimics the pigmentary findings. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 138) **Pediatric sinonasal/nasopharyngeal malignancy**: rhabdomyosarcoma (embryonal or alveolar) is the most common primary nasal/sinus malignancy in children and can be congenital. It presents as a friable mass with obstruction and epistaxis, sometimes with ipsilateral otitis media with effusion, deep facial pain or a sixth nerve palsy (parameningeal spread). Lymphoma is the most prevalent malignancy across the nose, nasopharynx and sinuses, and extranodal nasal NHL (including NK/T-cell lymphoma with angioinvasive necrosis) does worse than Waldeyer ring Hodgkin disease. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma in children presents with a posterior triangle node and unilateral otitis media with effusion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Epistaxis", p 983) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1109) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1112) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1118) **Temporal bone rhabdomyosarcoma and LCH masquerade as otitis**: RMS is the most common pediatric temporal bone malignancy, usually embryonal, with a mean age of about 4 years. It presents as an aural polyp (54%), discharge that is often bloody, a periauricular mass, or facial palsy (in up to 64% in one series, about 30% are found because of a nerve palsy). Diagnosis is delayed about 8 weeks, and up to 50% are misread on the first biopsy. As a parameningeal site it is at least IRSG stage II, and it is treated with chemoradiation (fewer than 5% are resected). *LCH* involves the temporal bone in 15-61% of cases. It typically presents in a child under 3 with otorrhea or a polyp refractory to antibiotics, postauricular swelling and a high ESR. CT shows a punched-out lytic lesion that spares the otic capsule. Diagnosis rests on S-100/CD1a and Birbeck granules. Get a skeletal survey and systemic workup. Treatment is curettage or low-dose RT (6-10 Gy) for unifocal disease, with a cure rate above 90%, or vinblastine-prednisone for multifocal disease. Biopsy any granulation tissue in a child's ear that does not respond to treatment. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 895-902) **Rhabdomyosarcoma by site**: about 35% of pediatric RMS arises in the head and neck, 70% before age 12 and 43% before age 5. Orbit (most common orbital malignancy of childhood) presents as rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. Nasopharyngeal and sinonasal tumors in preschoolers mimic otitis media with effusion, rhinorrhea, obstruction, or 'sinusitis' headache with months of delay. Aural RMS presents as unilateral bloody otorrhea with a soft polyp in the canal or middle ear mistaken for otitis, and about 50% already have neurologic deficits, most often facial palsy. Multiple cranial neuropathies imply skull-base/CNS spread. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1812) **Burkitt lymphoma**: a highly proliferative B-cell NHL with c-myc translocation and a 'starry sky' pattern. Endemic (African) BL (mean age about 9) is EBV-positive in 80–90% and presents as a jaw mass, maxilla more than mandible, with loose teeth, trismus, or proptosis. Sporadic (US) BL (mean age about 12) is EBV-associated in only 15–20%, usually abdominal (ileocecal), with about one-quarter in the head and neck as asymptomatic nodes or Waldeyer ring masses. Treatment is urgent multiagent chemotherapy. Surgery is for diagnosis. Localized head and neck disease has about 90% long-term survival. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1811–1812) **Pediatric neuroblastoma in the neck**: neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid malignancy under age 5 (40% diagnosed before age 1), but only 2–5% of primaries are cervical sympathetic. Most neck disease is metastatic from below the diaphragm (also skull, orbit, jaw). A primary cervical tumor can present with Horner syndrome or heterochromia iridis, airway or feeding compromise, or lower cranial neuropathies. Calcification is seen in about 50% on CT, urine catecholamines (VMA/HVA) are elevated in 70–90%, and MIBG, bone scan, and marrow biopsy complete staging. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1823) **Rhabdomyosarcoma staging logic**: RMS is the most common pediatric sinonasal malignancy, with the orbit the most common head and neck subsite. Embryonal type (55–65%, including botryoid) has the best prognosis, alveolar (20–30%, teens) is worse, and anaplastic/undifferentiated types are worst. Risk group combines site-based TNM stage (orbit and non-parameningeal head and neck sites are favorable stage 1, while the nasopharynx, nasal cavity, sinuses, temporal bone, and infratemporal fossa are parameningeal), clinical group by completeness of resection, and histology. Biopsy plus chemoradiation is standard. Five-year survival is about 95% for orbital and 74% for parameningeal disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 94, p 1364) **Langerhans cell histiocytosis**: Clonal Langerhans cell proliferation (CD1a and S100 positive, Birbeck 'tennis racket' granules on EM) commonly presents in the temporal bone mimicking mastoiditis or chronic otitis with granulation, lytic lesions and facial palsy. Forms: eosinophilic granuloma (localized, older children/young adults, curettage or low-dose radiation), Hand-Schüller-Christian (triad of skull lesions, exophthalmos and diabetes insipidus in about 10%), and Letterer-Siwe (infants under 3, disseminated with hepatosplenomegaly, high mortality, chemotherapy). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 223-225) **Pediatric HL vs NHL**: Hodgkin lymphoma usually stays in one axial nodal group (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic) and spreads in order to contiguous nodes. It rarely involves Waldeyer ring or mesenteric nodes and is rarely extranodal. Classic HL is about 95% of US cases, nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype, mixed cellularity favors children under 10, and nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL is 10-15%. NHL involves multiple peripheral nodes, spreads noncontiguously, often involves Waldeyer ring and the mesentery, and often presents extranodally (mediastinum 35-45%, abdomen 25-30%). Pediatric NHL subtypes are Burkitt 35-40%, and lymphoblastic, diffuse large B-cell and ALK-positive anaplastic large cell about 15-20% each. NHL is staged with the St. Jude (Murphy) system rather than Ann Arbor. Prefer abdominal MRI over CT in children. (Cummings 7e, Ch 204, pp 3022-3024) **Temporal bone LCH specifics**: Temporal bone involvement is present in about 10% of children with eosinophilic granuloma, 75% with Hand-Schüller-Christian disease and 40% with Letterer-Siwe disease, and is the first presentation in up to 25%. LCH polyps arise in the mastoid and erode the posterosuperior canal wall. They often spare the middle ear and ossicles behind a normal drum, and the otic capsule resists erosion, so SNHL, vertigo or facial palsy is rare. About 30% of unifocal cases progress, and mortality approaches 10% (worse under age 1 or with liver, lung, spleen or marrow disease). The Histiocyte Society counts the temporal bone as a *special site* (vinblastine-prednisone for 6 months). Follow monthly or every 2 months for the first year, with CT at 1 year. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 42, pp 899-902)
canonical_layers.localize: Use age and anatomic compartment to frame the differential: congenital tract/cyst, nodal disease, salivary/thyroid, vascular malformation, neural tumor or sarcoma.
canonical_layers.workup: Ultrasound is often first-line for superficial masses; CT/MRI and tissue sampling are selected by depth/vascularity and malignancy risk. Avoid open biopsy before appropriate imaging and oncology planning when lymphoma/sarcoma is possible. **Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma**: the orbit is the primary site in about 10% of childhood RMS (mean age about 7). Tumors favor the superior orbit and are usually embryonal. They present with rapid proptosis, ptosis, or a lid or subconjunctival mass, and inflammatory signs can mimic orbital cellulitis. Intergroup RMS clinical grouping: I = completely resected. II = microscopic residual. III = gross residual after biopsy. IV = distant metastasis. Orbital embryonal tumors have about 94% 5-year survival versus about 74% for alveolar. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Ophthalmology", p 151) **RMS staging workup**: parameningeal primaries (nasopharynx, sinuses, middle ear, infratemporal fossa) need CT plus MRI and lumbar puncture with CSF cytology. Systemic workup includes chest imaging, bone scan, and bone marrow aspirate/biopsy (lung, bone, and marrow are the common metastatic sites). Clinically positive neck nodes occur in about 7% of non-orbital head and neck primaries but essentially never with orbital primaries. Distant metastases are present in about 13% overall versus about 4% for orbit. Staging uses the postsurgical IRS clinical group (I complete resection, II microscopic residual or resected nodes, III gross residual/biopsy only, IV distant metastases) plus pretreatment TNM in which orbit and nonparameningeal head and neck are favorable sites. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1812–1813) **Pediatric sinonasal malignancy profile**: In a single-center series, pediatric sinonasal cancer presented at a median age of 12. The maxillary sinus was the most common site, followed by ethmoid, nasal cavity, sphenoid and nasopharynx. Rhabdomyosarcoma made up over 70% of maxillary sinus tumors and 34% overall, followed by SCC and esthesioneuroblastoma. Treatment follows adult principles: resect with negative margins when feasible, then chemoradiation. In parameningeal RMS, surgery is mainly for diagnosis, debulking and salvage. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1937)
canonical_layers.manage: Treatment is histology-specific and often multidisciplinary. Preserve long-term growth, cranial nerve, swallowing, hearing and endocrine function whenever oncologically safe. **Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma**: it is the most common primary orbital malignancy of childhood (mean age ~7, rapid unilateral proptosis, often superonasal). Biopsy (or excision if it can be done without morbidity), then chemoradiation per Intergroup protocols. The globe is spared in over 90%, exenteration is reserved for resistant tumors, and 3-year survival is ~93%, the most favorable head and neck site. Radiation cataract is the common visual cost. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1011) **RMS treatment principles**: all children get multiagent chemotherapy. Resection is done only when it causes no major functional loss and would let radiation be omitted or reduced (often superficial nonparameningeal sites). Orbital RMS is treated with biopsy plus chemoradiation (3-year relapse-free survival about 91% in IRS I, versus 46% parameningeal and 75% other sites). For IRS group III disease, debulking adds nothing over biopsy. A clinically negative neck needs no treatment beyond chemotherapy. A positive neck gets neck dissection plus radiation. Radiation late effects include facial hypoplasia, malocclusion, dental disease, xerostomia, osteoradionecrosis, and second sarcomas. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1813–1814)
canonical_layers.operate: Plan biopsy/resection so the incision and tissue planes do not compromise definitive oncologic surgery; vascular lesions and skull-base tumors demand diagnosis before casual excision.
canonical_layers.teach: In children, the wrong biopsy can complicate the right cancer operation. Diagnose the compartment and histology before cutting. **Malignancy risk numbers**: about 11% of pediatric neck masses evaluated are malignant, and 29% of biopsied masses that looked benign proved malignant. Growth over days suggests infection. Steady growth over 4–8 weeks is the classic malignant tempo. An asymptomatic mass is the typical presentation, and systemic B symptoms are usually absent when lymphoma is confined to the neck. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neck Masses", p 1717, 1731) **Pediatric NPC numbers**: nasopharyngeal malignancy is about 1% of childhood cancers (mostly RMS and NPC). Pediatric NPC is mostly WHO type IIb undifferentiated nonkeratinizing, nearly always EBV-positive, more common in Black adolescents in US series, and over 80% present at AJCC stage IV with neck nodes after a median 4–5 months of symptoms mistaken for URI. Workup adds bone scan, chest/abdominal CT, marrow biopsy for advanced disease, and CSF cytology with skull-base invasion. Treatment combines chemotherapy with radiation (IMRT/proton to spare growth), yet 20–50% relapse, mostly within 1–2 years. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1825–1826) **Middle-ear rhabdomyosarcoma prognosis and therapy**: Although parameningeal, middle-ear and temporal bone RMS does better than other parameningeal sites (younger age, embryonal histology in up to 90%). 5-year survival was 88% in IRS-IV vs 42% in IRS-I, and 3-year survival was 48% with metastases. About 15% have distant metastases at diagnosis (lung most often), and nodes are involved in 5-20%. It spreads via the eustachian tube to the infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx, and through the fallopian canal to the IAC and posterior fossa. Dural or sigmoid involvement is a poor sign. On MRI it is T2 hyperintense and enhances, and desmin and muscle-specific actin confirm it. Therapy is VAC chemotherapy (vincristine, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide) with radiation. Resect only if complete removal is possible without mutilation, and do no prophylactic neck dissection. Late RT effects include growth or pituitary failure, cataract, and mandible/TMJ hypoplasia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 42, pp 895-899)

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Auditory deprivation changes central processing; duration and developmental timing influence how effectively restored peripheral input can be used. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Provide timely hearing access in children and avoid unnecessary prolonged deprivation in implant candidates; pair devices with auditory/language rehabilitation.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Cortical Neuroplasticity in Hearing Loss. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: a cochlear implant delivers signal; the brain still has to learn to use it.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Cortical Neuroplasticity in Hearing Loss

canonical_layers.recognize: Auditory deprivation changes central processing; duration and developmental timing influence how effectively restored peripheral input can be used.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the problem beyond the cochlea: brainstem/cortical networks adapt to altered sensory input and may reorganize with prolonged deprivation.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Workup**: integrate duration of loss, age at onset, language development, and hearing-device use with standard audiology when counseling rehabilitation.

**Also**: reconstruct onset, duration, consistency of auditory access, language exposure, aided use, and speech/language trajectory. In children, test functional communication in addition to thresholds. In adults with prolonged deprivation, include aided speech recognition and realistic counseling about central adaptation. **P1 CAEP biomarker**: The P1 cortical auditory evoked potential reflects input reaching the thalamus and primary auditory cortex. Its latency is about 300 ms in infancy, falls steeply over the first 2-3 years and reaches adult values by age 12-16. Later N1/P2 components (higher-order cortex) emerge in preadolescence. Children implanted before 3.5 years reach normal P1 latency within 6-8 months of implant use. About half of those implanted at 3.5-6.5 years do, while those implanted after 7 years stay delayed even 7-10 years later and rarely develop N1/P2. P1 can also confirm objectively that a hearing aid is benefiting the cortex in infants who cannot give behavioral responses. (Cummings 7e, Ch 132, p 1997-2000)
canonical_layers.manage:
**Manage**: provide timely hearing access in children and avoid unnecessary prolonged deprivation in implant candidates. Pair devices with auditory/language rehabilitation.

**Also**: provide stable auditory access early through amplification, bone-conduction technology, or cochlear implantation when indicated, paired with language-rich habilitation or rehabilitation. **Key trap**: device fitting without consistent use and therapy does not supply the repeated input required for cortical learning.
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery restores access, not learned auditory meaning. Postoperative programming and rehabilitation are part of the biologic treatment.
canonical_layers.teach:
**Teach**: a cochlear implant delivers signal -- the brain still has to learn to use it.

**Also**: plasticity explains both urgency and uncertainty. Early consistent input supports auditory-language network development, while long deprivation may limit later speech outcomes even when an implant produces excellent electrode function. **Key trap**: it is not a reason to deny evaluation -- it is a counseling and rehabilitation variable.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Frequent bacterial sinus infections, pneumonia, unusual organisms, poor vaccine response or refractory CRS despite appropriate therapy should raise humoral or broader immune deficiency. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Optimize topical CRS therapy, culture-directed antibiotics and immune-specific treatment such as vaccination strategy or immunoglobulin replacement when indicated by immunology.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Immunodeficiency-Associated Chronic Rhinosinusitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Refractory CRS plus recurrent lower-airway infection is an immune-history problem before it is a bigger-surgery problem.

canonical_layers.recognize: Frequent bacterial sinus infections, pneumonia, unusual organisms, poor vaccine response or refractory CRS despite appropriate therapy should raise humoral or broader immune deficiency. **Chronic granulomatous disease and phagocyte disorders**: CGD (about two thirds X-linked, one third autosomal recessive) impairs phagocyte oxidative killing, causing recurrent abscesses and granulomas from catalase-positive bacteria and fungi. Diagnose it with neutrophil function testing (dihydrorhodamine or nitroblue tetrazolium). Long-term care is directed by immunology and includes interferon gamma, avoidance of live vaccines (including BCG), and stem cell transplant for cure. Chédiak-Higashi (autosomal recessive: albinism, neutropenia, neuropathy) and Job (hyper-IgE with recurrent staphylococcal cold abscesses) belong in this differential. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 231-232)
canonical_layers.localize: The sinonasal disease is a consequence of impaired host defense rather than purely anatomic ostial obstruction; recurrent bacterial burden may coexist with structural disease.
canonical_layers.workup: Use infection history to guide quantitative immunoglobulins and functional antibody assessment, with immunology referral when abnormalities or strong suspicion persist. Avoid indiscriminate immune panels in ordinary CRS. **Pre-ESS immune screen in children**: obtain IgG, IgA, IgM (and IgE) plus vaccine titers (tetanus, Hib, pneumococcus) in any child being considered for sinus surgery. Interpret IgG subclass deficiency cautiously, because ~10% of the healthy population has an abnormal subclass level. If a deficiency is found, ESS can still improve symptoms, but families should expect that complete weaning from antibiotics is unlikely. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1059)
canonical_layers.manage: Optimize topical CRS therapy, culture-directed antibiotics and immune-specific treatment such as vaccination strategy or immunoglobulin replacement when indicated by immunology. **Rhinosinusitis in HIV**: Up to about 75% of untreated HIV patients develop rhinosinusitis. With a CD4 count above 200, organisms and management resemble those of immunocompetent hosts. Below 200, expect Pseudomonas, CMV, mycobacteria, fungi (including Mucor) and Pneumocystis. Have a low threshold for culture-directed therapy, early CT/endoscopy, biopsy (Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma) and early surgery. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 56)
canonical_layers.operate: FESS can improve drainage and topical access in refractory objective disease but should be integrated with immune management; surgery alone will not normalize infection susceptibility.
canonical_layers.teach: Refractory CRS plus recurrent lower-airway infection is an immune-history problem before it is a bigger-surgery problem.

candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Split- and full-thickness grafts differ in contraction, color/texture match, donor closure and take requirements. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Full-thickness grafts often suit smaller facial defects needing better match and less contraction; split-thickness grafts cover larger areas but contract more.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Skin Graft Selection. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: A graft is only as viable as its recipient bed; the operation is creating reliable contact with vascular tissue.

canonical_layers.recognize: Before choosing full- versus split-thickness skin, ask whether a skin graft is appropriate at all. **Requirements for take**: the defect needs a vascularized recipient bed, oncologic clearance when relevant, hemostasis, and a surface on which the graft can remain immobile while neovascularization occurs. The graft is transferred without its own vascular pedicle and therefore depends on a vascularized recipient bed for take. **Key trap**: if missing framework, exposed critical structures, dead space, or contour requirements demand vascularized tissue, a local/regional/free flap may be the better reconstruction.
canonical_layers.localize: **Principle**: recipient-bed biology drives take. **Good beds**: muscle, fascia, granulation tissue, intact perichondrium, and intact periosteum can support grafting. **Poor bed**: bare avascular cartilage or cortical bone stripped of perichondrium/periosteum is a poor bed and should trigger a plan to create vascularized coverage rather than simply choosing a thinner graft. On the face, also analyze aesthetic subunit, contour depth, eyelid/lip free-margin distortion risk, and donor color/texture/thickness/hair match.
canonical_layers.workup: Choose thickness by defect and reconstructive goal. **FULL-THICKNESS SKIN GRAFT (FTSG)**: contains epidermis plus the full dermis. It generally gives superior facial color/texture match and less secondary contraction, making it useful for smaller cosmetically sensitive defects. It requires a robust vascular bed, and the donor site usually must close primarily. **SPLIT-THICKNESS SKIN GRAFT (STSG)**: contains epidermis plus part of dermis. It can cover much larger areas, its donor site re-epithelializes, and it generally takes more readily. Secondary contraction, pigment/texture mismatch, and contour depression are greater concerns with STSG.
canonical_layers.manage: **Goal**: optimize TAKE, not just graft choice. Debride nonviable tissue, control infection and achieve meticulous hemostasis, contour the graft to full contact, eliminate hematoma/seroma and shear, and secure it with an appropriate bolster or other immobilizing dressing. **Risk factors**: smoking, irradiation, poor perfusion, and contaminated beds increase failure risk. Meshing STSG expands coverage and permits fluid egress but sacrifices surface texture. Sheet grafts are preferred when appearance is important and drainage can be managed. **EARLY TAKE-FAILURE RESCUE**: a tense hematoma/seroma, focal graft lift, or loss of graft-bed contact is a correctable mechanical emergency during the take window. Release the collection when clinically indicated, achieve hemostasis, restore intimate graft-to-bed contact, and re-secure/immobilize the graft rather than simply observing progressive separation. If the graft is clearly nonviable, debride nonviable tissue and reassess the recipient bed, infection/contamination, perfusion, dead space, and reconstructive requirement before repeating the same graft. **Key trap**: do not solve a persistently avascular bed by repeatedly changing graft thickness. **Composite graft size limit**: Conchal skin-cartilage composite grafts rebuild alar rim and columellar defects. Like skin grafts, they depend completely on the recipient bed, so they are contraindicated in irradiated or infected beds. Grafts up to about 1.5 cm can be used, but those 1 cm or smaller survive most reliably. Epidermolysis or a superficial slough in the first week is common and does not mean the graft has failed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, p 1058)
canonical_layers.operate: **Physiology**: early graft survival begins with PLASMATIC IMBIBITION, followed by INOSCULATION between graft and recipient vessels, and then NEOVASCULARIZATION/revascularization. Every technical step should protect that sequence. **Technique**: defat FTSGs enough for intimate bed contact without injuring the dermis, orient the best-matched donor skin, avoid tenting across concavities, fenestrate/pie-crust when needed for drainage, and prevent motion. **Key point**: a successful skin graft resurfaces a defect. It does not replace absent cartilage/bone support or obliterate meaningful dead space.
canonical_layers.teach: **BOARDS/CHIEF FRAME**: skin-graft selection asks, 'IS THE BED VASCULAR ENOUGH, how much surface must I cover, how much contraction can the site tolerate, and what donor gives the best match?' FTSG = better facial match/less secondary contraction but greater metabolic demand and limited harvest. STSG = larger/easier-take coverage but more secondary contraction and poorer texture/pigment match. Bare cartilage/bone without vascularized covering is a BED problem, not an indication to keep switching graft thickness. **CHIEF RESCUE FRAME**: early graft failure should trigger a cause-based diagnosis -- fluid under the graft, shear/motion, infection, inadequate hemostasis, or an avascular bed -- followed by correction of that mechanism before regrafting. **GRAFT-VERSUS-FLAP SEMANTIC RULE**: a skin graft arrives without an intrinsic blood supply and must revascularize from the recipient bed. A flap transfers tissue with its own blood supply (or a vascular pedicle/microvascular inflow). Therefore an avascular recipient surface is a reason to change the bed or reconstructive method, not a defining feature of skin-graft coverage.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Vestibular testing should answer a localization/functional question rather than be ordered as a fixed panel for every dizzy patient. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use results to guide rehabilitation, document unilateral/bilateral loss, support third-window/otolith diagnoses or decide whether destructive vestibular treatment is safe.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Vestibular Test Battery. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Know what frequency and organ each test interrogates. 'Abnormal VNG' is not a diagnosis.

canonical_layers.recognize: Vestibular testing should answer a localization/functional question rather than be ordered as a fixed panel for every dizzy patient. **Bedside and functional tests**: Dynamic visual acuity drops 2–3 Snellen lines with 2-Hz head oscillation when the VOR fails. Head-thrust is abnormal with more than about 50% reduced response. Fukuda stepping, Romberg, and past-pointing assess vestibulospinal function. Frenzel lenses remove fixation. Posturography quantifies function rather than localizing, and better scores on harder conditions suggest malingering. Cervical VEMP uses about 95 dB clicks and records the saccule–inferior vestibular nerve–SCM pathway. Superior canal dehiscence lowers its threshold by roughly 20 dB. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 409–410, 414)
canonical_layers.localize: VNG/calorics emphasize low-frequency horizontal semicircular canal/superior nerve function, vHIT evaluates high-frequency semicircular-canal VOR, VEMP assesses otolith pathways and posturography reflects integrated balance rather than a single end organ.
canonical_layers.workup: Choose tests from the suspected disorder and interpret discordant findings physiologically. Normal testing does not exclude vestibular migraine/PPPD, and an abnormal test may represent a compensated old lesion rather than the current symptom generator. **Caloric and rotary-chair interpretation**: Calorics: head up 30° to make the horizontal semicircular canal vertical. A side-to-side difference over about 20–25% is unilateral weakness, and a directional preponderance means nystagmus one way exceeds the other. Total slow-phase velocity for all four irrigations below roughly 12–24°/s indicates bilateral weakness. Failure of fixation suppression suggests a central lesion. Rotary chair: gain is eye/chair velocity (normal about 1). An acute unilateral loss gives low-frequency phase lead with high-frequency asymmetry, and loss of asymmetry signals compensation. Bilateral loss lowers low-frequency gain. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 412–414) **VEMP technique and interpretation**: cVEMP measures an inhibitory saccular-inferior vestibular nerve reflex recorded from the tonically contracted ipsilateral SCM (P13 about 12 ms, N23 about 19 ms) using 500-1000 Hz tone bursts or clicks. It is unaffected by SNHL but abolished by even small conductive losses, may be absent in normal people over 60, and needs adequate SCM contraction. Asymmetry ratio = 100 x (larger - smaller)/(larger + smaller), normal up to about 40%. Normal threshold is about 90 dB nHL. Responses below 80 dB nHL or a present VEMP despite an air-bone gap suggest a third window (superior canal dehiscence). oVEMP (N10 from inferior oblique, best with gaze about 30 degrees up) reflects utricle-superior vestibular nerve function. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 15, p 309-312) **Caloric cutoffs and mechanics**: Cutoffs vary by source and lab (Pasha about 20-25%, K.J. Lee 15-30%). Cummings counts unilateral weakness over 20% and directional preponderance over 25% (Jongkees formulas) as significant, with each lab setting its own norms. The patient lies with the head up 30 degrees, and convection produces about 75% of the response. Warm water excites the horizontal canal (ampullopetal flow). Directional preponderance usually reflects a spontaneous nystagmus that adds to or subtracts from each irrigation. Without one, it may be a central sign. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, pp 2508–2509) **Rotary chair: indications and time constant**: rotary chair is best for suspected bilateral loss, monitoring vestibulotoxic drugs, children who do not tolerate calorics, after meningitis, and genetic hearing-loss workups. It is not affected by the canal or cerumen. The cupula returns with a time constant of about 10 seconds, but velocity storage stretches the VOR time constant to about 20 seconds. Peripheral loss shortens the time constant and causes low-frequency phase lead and reduced gain. Bilateral loss lowers both gain and time constant. A compensated unilateral loss can have normal gain and phase, leaving only an asymmetry. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, p 2488, Ch 166, pp 2509–2510) **Posturography and subjective visual vertical**: the sensory organization test has six conditions. In conditions 1–3 the platform is fixed (eyes open, eyes closed, visual surround sway-referenced). In conditions 4–6 the platform is sway-referenced (eyes open, eyes closed, both sway-referenced). Falls on conditions 5 and 6 are the 'vestibular pattern'. A bedside version (CTSIB: foam plus a lantern over the head) correlates with it. After acute loss of utricular function, the subjective visual vertical is tilted about 10–15 degrees toward the lesioned side, but the test does not show which ear is affected unless done during off-axis rotation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, pp 2512–2513) **Bithermal caloric parameters**: water is delivered at 7°C above and below body temperature (44°C and 30°C) for 30 seconds. Air uses ±13°C (50°C and 24°C) for 60 seconds. Unilateral weakness = [(RW+RC)−(LW+LC)]/(sum of all four peak slow-phase velocities). A side difference above roughly 15–30% (lab dependent) is abnormal. Bilateral weakness is suggested when each ear's warm+cool total is under about 12°/s. Directional preponderance over 30% is reportable but of doubtful localizing value. Look in the ear first: remove cerumen, and use air (not water) with a perforation, expecting an exaggerated response on that side. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 322-323) **Rotary chair, vHIT and scleral coil specifics**: rotary chair tests the horizontal canals of both ears together at about 0.01–2 Hz (peak ~50°/s) and reports phase (often exaggerated in peripheral disease), gain (eye/chair velocity, low bilateral gain = bilateral loss) and symmetry (useful for tracking recovery). It finds residual function when calorics are absent, and off-vertical axis rotation probes the otoliths. vHIT uses a >250 Hz goggle camera. Gain of about 1 is normal. Overt (catch-up) saccades after the head stops are typical of an acute loss. Covert saccades during the turn suggest a compensated lesion. Goggle slippage limits vHIT above about 150–200°/s. The magnetic scleral search coil remains the gold standard and can record eye movements over 300°/s. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 323-324) **VEMP and SVV numbers**: VEMPs use a brief, loud (>90 dB SPL) 500 Hz tone burst. cVEMP is an ipsilateral inhibitory potential from the tensed SCM (P13/N23, saccule → inferior vestibular nerve → medial vestibulospinal tract → CN XI). oVEMP is a contralateral excitatory potential under the eye during upgaze (N10, utricle → superior vestibular nerve → MLF → CN III nucleus → inferior oblique). Amplitude asymmetry over 40% (after rectification) is abnormal. Conductive pathology, ossicular problems or age raise thresholds or abolish responses. A third window gives low cVEMP thresholds and oVEMP amplitudes over about 17 µV. VEMPs can be present in a deaf ear. Subjective visual vertical is normally within ±2–3°. Tilt is sensitive for acute utricular or brainstem injury, and a bucket test is a cheap version. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 324-325) **Computerized dynamic posturography**: the Sensory Organization Test measures anterior-posterior sway in six conditions that take away or sway-reference vision and the support surface, to separate visual, somatosensory and vestibular contributions to balance. The Motor Control Test measures automatic responses to sudden forward/backward platform translations, and the Adaptation Test measures responses to toes-up/toes-down platform rotation. CDP measures functional impairment (it tracks Dizziness Handicap Inventory scores) rather than localizing a lesion. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 325)
canonical_layers.manage: Use results to guide rehabilitation, document unilateral/bilateral loss, support third-window/otolith diagnoses or decide whether destructive vestibular treatment is safe.
canonical_layers.operate: Before vestibular-ablative surgery, confirm the target ear and contralateral reserve; before CI/skull-base surgery, baseline function can help counsel about postoperative imbalance.
canonical_layers.teach: Know what frequency and organ each test interrogates. 'Abnormal VNG' is not a diagnosis. **When formal vestibular testing is (and is not) needed**: order it when history and examination have not identified the side or site of the lesion, to select and monitor vestibular rehabilitation, to document recovery, to confirm contralateral function before a destructive procedure, and to check whether ablation (gentamicin, neurectomy) worked. Classic posterior canal BPPV with a positive Dix-Hallpike does not need it. No single test is a gold standard, otolith tests give only crude present/absent answers, and a normal battery does not exclude vestibular disease. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 316, 321)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. Chronic cough can persist after common pulmonary, sinonasal and reflux causes are addressed; throat tickle, talking/laughing triggers and sensory symptoms can suggest cough hypersensitivity. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat identified contributors and use behavioral cough-suppression/voice therapy for hypersensitivity phenotypes; selected refractory cases may warrant neuromodulatory or multidisciplinary management.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Chronic Cough / Laryngeal Hypersensitivity. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Chronic cough is a syndrome. Once dangerous and common causes are addressed, repeated empiric antibiotics or reflux therapy without evidence can become part of the problem rather than the solution.

canonical_layers.recognize: Chronic cough can persist after common pulmonary, sinonasal and reflux causes are addressed; throat tickle, talking/laughing triggers and sensory symptoms can suggest cough hypersensitivity. **Pediatric habit (psychogenic/somatic) cough**: a honking or barking cough, often with a chin-on-chest posture, typically starts after a URI and persists after other symptoms clear. It can occur many times a minute, disappears in sleep, lessens with distraction, and does not respond to antitussives, bronchodilators, or steroids. It accounts for 3%–10% of children with cough lasting more than 1 month. Spirometry and chest radiograph are normal. Distinguish it from a tic disorder, which has a premonitory urge and voluntary suppressibility. Paroxysmal (habit) sneezing, with eyes open and no sneezing in sleep, is a variant. Treat with reassurance, management of contributing conditions, and speech-therapy suppression techniques. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Psychiatric Disorders in Pediatric Otolaryngology", p 100–101) **Recurrent paroxysmal laryngospasm**: sudden episodes of laryngeal closure, often brought on by eating, steam or odors. They usually start during a URI or after RLN surgical trauma. Some cases come from reflux and respond to acid suppression; others reflect a hypersensitive closure reflex. Most resolve on their own within a few months, but a minority become chronic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 53, p 802)
canonical_layers.localize: The phenotype reflects an exaggerated laryngeal/cough reflex network rather than a single visible lesion; coexisting rhinitis, asthma, reflux or medication effects may still contribute.
canonical_layers.workup: Exclude red flags and common causes with targeted history/exam and appropriate pulmonary/sinonasal/laryngeal evaluation. Avoid endless empiric treatment when the phenotype and prior response no longer support it. **Chronic cough big four**: With a normal chest radiograph, cough over 8 weeks is usually from upper airway cough syndrome (sinonasal disease), asthma, GERD and ACE inhibitors; about a third have more than one cause. Difficult-to-treat asthma often has unrecognized sinonasal disease (proposed links: nasobronchial reflex, eosinophil activation, postnasal seeding, nasal obstruction), and vocal fold dysfunction mimics refractory asthma. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 144)
canonical_layers.manage: Treat identified contributors and use behavioral cough-suppression/voice therapy for hypersensitivity phenotypes; selected refractory cases may warrant neuromodulatory or multidisciplinary management. **Post-viral vagal neuropathy dosing**: give gabapentin starting at 100 mg three times daily and titrate to about 300 mg three times daily; success is about 37.5–80%. Amitriptyline, pregabalin, and tramadol are alternatives. TA-LCA botulinum toxin (about 2.5 U per side) can reduce refractory cough. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 56) **Superior laryngeal nerve block indications**: an office injection for refractory neurogenic cough (over 8 weeks, workup negative) or paralaryngeal pain, with about 80% response. The best candidates feel an irritative focus localized to one posterior thyrohyoid space, and palpation there triggers cough. Contraindications are an incomplete workup, local anesthetic or steroid allergy, and uncontrolled diabetes (steroid-induced hyperglycemia). (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 67, p 577-578)
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery is generally not the treatment. The advanced decision is recognizing when a structural laryngeal lesion, aspiration or airway disorder—not hypersensitivity—requires a procedural pathway. **SLN block technique and schedule**: mix 1 mL 0.5% bupivacaine with 1 mL triamcinolone 40 mg/mL just before use, and inject with a 27 g needle into the posterior thyrohyoid membrane just anterior to the superior cornu, aspirating first to avoid intravascular injection. Relief begins in 2-3 days; if there is none at 2 weeks, inject the other side, and stop if that also fails. Repeat responding blocks every 4-16 weeks. Drop the steroid if more than 3-4 blocks per year are needed, to limit adrenal suppression and skin atrophy. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 67, p 579-581)
canonical_layers.teach: Chronic cough is a syndrome. Once dangerous and common causes are addressed, repeated empiric antibiotics or reflux therapy without evidence can become part of the problem rather than the solution.

candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Spreader, batten, rim, lateral-crural-strut, septal-extension, dorsal and tip grafts solve different structural problems. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Septal cartilage is often preferred when adequate; auricular cartilage is useful for curved support, while rib is reserved for larger structural needs.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Rhinoplasty Graft Selection. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Do not memorize graft names as operations—name the mechanical failure first, then pick the graft.

canonical_layers.recognize: For structural nasal graft selection, start by naming the mechanical problem: midvault collapse/internal nasal valve narrowing, weak lateral wall or alar rim, inadequate caudal septal support, tip projection/rotation instability, dorsal deficiency, or major framework loss. Then choose graft geometry and donor material that can supply the required stiffness, shape, volume, and long-term stability. **Key trap**: do not choose a donor first and then invent a use for the harvested cartilage.
canonical_layers.localize: **Principle**: match graft to subunit and force. **Spreader grafts**: reconstruct/support the middle vault and can widen the internal nasal valve while restoring dorsal aesthetic lines. **Alar batten or lateral crural strut grafts**: reinforce a weak/collapsing lateral wall or malpositioned lateral crus. An alar-rim graft addresses rim support/contour rather than caudal septal strength. **Septal extension graft**: fixes tip support, projection, and rotation to the caudal septal complex more powerfully than a simple columellar strut. **Dorsal onlay/augmentation grafting**: restores height and contour but must be stable, smooth, and appropriately camouflaged.
canonical_layers.workup: **Analysis**: analyze the nose before selecting material -- external shape, tip support, middle-vault width, dynamic lateral-wall collapse, septal support/available cartilage, airway goals, skin-soft-tissue-envelope thickness, prior operations, scars, and prior grafts. In revision or post-traumatic cases, determine whether the native septum is depleted or structurally unsafe to harvest. **Key trap**: preserve an adequate dorsal/caudal L-strut and do not create iatrogenic septal instability merely to obtain graft material.
canonical_layers.manage: **Autograft hierarchy** is job-dependent. **Septal cartilage** is commonly preferred when available because it is straight, relatively stiff, and harvested in the same field. **Auricular/conchal cartilage** is curved and pliable, useful when contour or alar/lateral-wall shape is advantageous, but it supplies less straight load-bearing stock. **Costal cartilage** provides abundant strong material for major dorsal/caudal/septal reconstruction and revision noses when septum is inadequate, at the cost of a separate donor site and risks such as warping/calcification. Cadaveric costal cartilage or selected alloplastic material can be alternatives in appropriately selected patients, but material choice must account for structural demand, infection/extrusion/resorption/warping tradeoffs, and surgeon experience.
canonical_layers.operate: **At operation**, re-diagnose the deforming force after exposure. Do not solve every irregularity by stacking grafts. Harvest only what is needed while protecting donor-site function. Carve structural grafts with sufficient dimensions and stable fixation so the graft resists the force it is meant to correct. Bevel/camouflage edges where visibility is a risk. In rib grafting, anticipate warping and shape balanced segments deliberately. Confirm both airway and aesthetic consequences before closure, because a technically straight graft can still narrow another airway segment or create a visible contour. **Costal-cartilage harvest bailout**: stay directly on rib/perichondrial planes and treat an unexpected pleural violation as a separate physiologic problem, not as permission to continue harvesting blindly. Stop deeper dissection, obtain direct control/visualization of the defect, alert anesthesia, and assess ventilation/oxygenation and hemodynamics. If pleural injury or pneumothorax is suspected, use an appropriate leak/pneumothorax assessment and obtain chest imaging when the diagnosis is not already established clinically. Significant or symptomatic pneumothorax requires prompt pleural decompression/drainage rather than merely closing the donor incision. Re-establish a safe harvest plane -- or abandon further rib harvest if that plane cannot be trusted -- before proceeding with nasal reconstruction. **Spreader graft threshold and dorsal options**: when the dorsum is lowered more than about 3 mm, the middle vault roof is disrupted. Spreader grafts or flaps are advised to prevent an inverted-V deformity and internal valve collapse. For dorsal augmentation without a structural need, diced cartilage wrapped in temporalis fascia (DCF) is useful. Temporalis fascia alone camouflages irregularities and resorbs little. Gore-Tex has limited ingrowth, so it stays stable but can be removed. Extended spreader grafts fixed to a caudal septal extension graft or columellar strut control projection and rotation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 32, pp 519-521) **Costal cartilage handling**: harvest straight segments from the 6th to 8th ribs (inframammary incision in women). Carve concentrically from the central core, or use oblique symmetric cuts, to limit warping, the main complication. Soak in saline for about 30 minutes to reveal warping before placement. The ideal age for rib grafting is about 30 to 50 years. Younger cartilage is softer but warps more, and older cartilage may be calcified. Save perichondrium for camouflage. Irradiated homologous rib is an alternative. A warped rib graft usually needs replacement or recarving rather than observation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 33, p 534, 542) (Cummings 7e, Ch 34, p 546)
canonical_layers.teach: **Boards/chief frame**: rhinoplasty graft selection asks, 'What force or framework deficit am I correcting, what graft geometry solves it, and which donor material has the right mechanical properties?' Septum is often first-line straight structural stock. Concha is useful for curved/contour work. Rib is the high-volume/high-strength option when major reconstruction is required. This is not a wound-coverage decision and should never be conflated with FTSG-versus-STSG selection. **Chief commitment point**: the need for more cartilage never outranks donor-site safety. A suspected pleural entry converts the case from routine harvest to stop-assess-control-rescue -- do not keep dissecting for graft volume while the chest complication is unresolved.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Hyperacusis is abnormal intolerance of ordinary sound and differs from loudness recruitment, misophonia and phonophobia despite overlap. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Education, gradual sound desensitization and treatment of comorbid tinnitus/migraine/anxiety mechanisms are more useful than excessive sound avoidance in many patients.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Hyperacusis / Decreased Sound Tolerance. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: sound intolerance is a symptom family—name the phenotype before treating it.

canonical_layers.recognize: Hyperacusis is abnormal intolerance of ordinary sound and differs from loudness recruitment, misophonia and phonophobia despite overlap. **Hyperacusis prevalence, associations and TRT outcomes**: Hyperacusis affects about 6-8% of normal-hearing people and 18-80% of tinnitus patients, and its severity does not track audiometric thresholds, which separates it from recruitment. Associations include loss of the stapedial reflex with facial palsy, migraine, Lyme disease, benzodiazepine withdrawal and Williams syndrome; nearly half have a psychiatric disorder. Tinnitus retraining therapy raised loudness discomfort levels by about 12.5 dB and widened the dynamic range by about 11 dB, and helped hyperacusis (63%) more often than tinnitus (47%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 153, p 2332-2333)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the complaint to auditory gain/central processing after excluding active ear disease, third-window symptoms and neurologic/migraine context.
canonical_layers.workup: **Testing**: audiometry and loudness-tolerance testing may support assessment. **History**: should characterize triggers, pain, fear/avoidance, tinnitus, and functional impairment. **Also**: define whether ordinary sounds are uncomfortably loud (loudness hyperacusis), painful, fear-provoking (phonophobia), or trigger disproportionate anger/aversion (misophonia). Perform audiometry and uncomfortable-loudness levels when useful. Screen migraine, tinnitus, anxiety/PTSD, and facial-nerve/stapedius disorders, and investigate unilateral neurologic or middle-ear findings selectively.
canonical_layers.manage: **Approach**: education, gradual sound desensitization, and treatment of comorbid tinnitus/migraine/anxiety mechanisms are more useful than excessive sound avoidance in many patients. **Also**: counsel against continuous overprotection in safe environments because excessive earplug use can reinforce central gain and avoidance. Use gradual sound enrichment/desensitization, hearing protection for truly hazardous noise, migraine treatment when relevant, and audiology/behavioral-health support for distress and avoidance. Treat an identified otologic or neurologic cause rather than promising a single procedural cure.
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery has no routine role unless a specific structural disorder such as a third-window lesion explains the phenotype.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: sound intolerance is a symptom family—name the phenotype before treating it.

Hyperacusis, phonophobia, and misophonia overlap but are not interchangeable. The goal is safe sound tolerance and restored function—not eliminating all sound exposure or normalizing one uncomfortable-loudness number.
source_basis: Cummings 7e: Tinnitus and Hyperacusis

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Brief vertigo triggered by position change with reproducible canal-specific positional nystagmus is a mechanical otolith disorder. Persistent spontaneous vertigo or atypical neurologic nystagmus should trigger a different differential. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use the canal-appropriate repositioning maneuver and avoid chronic vestibular suppressants. Reassess persistent symptoms for wrong-canal localization, recurrence, cupulolithiasis or a central mimic.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of BPPV. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Name the canal before naming the maneuver. If you cannot describe the nystagmus, you have not localized the disease.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Presentation**: brief vertigo triggered by position change with reproducible canal-specific positional nystagmus is a mechanical otolith disorder. **Key trap**: persistent spontaneous vertigo or atypical neurologic nystagmus should trigger a different differential. **Mechanism**: BPPV results from otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) that have become dislodged from the utricular macula and migrated into a semicircular canal (most often posterior, given its dependent position), where their movement with head position abnormally stimulates the canal's cupula. **Associations**: most cases are idiopathic, but recognized associations include head trauma, prior vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis, prolonged bed rest or immobility, migraine, and age-related degeneration of the otolithic membrane. Inquire about these when a cause isn't obvious, since recurrent or atypical BPPV in a younger patient without an identifiable trigger warrants a closer look. **Events during repositioning**: posterior canal BPPV can convert to horizontal canal BPPV (usually resolves in days) or to apparent anterior canal BPPV; debris jamming at the common crus produces sustained pure torsional nystagmus because superior and posterior canal vertical components cancel. Persistent non-fatiguing horizontal positional nystagmus has been attributed to a 'light cupula,' a controversial entity that usually resolves within weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2520)
canonical_layers.localize: **Canal involvement**: the posterior semicircular canal is affected in the large majority of cases given its dependent anatomic position relative to the utricle. Horizontal and, rarely, anterior semicircular canal involvement produce distinct nystagmus patterns and require different repositioning maneuvers. **Canalithiasis vs. cupulolithiasis**: canalithiasis (free-floating debris, the more common pattern) produces nystagmus that is transient and fatigable. Cupulolithiasis (debris adherent to the cupula) produces more persistent, non-fatiguing nystagmus. **Superior (anterior) semicircular canal BPPV**: accounts for only about 2% of BPPV and produces downbeating nystagmus with a torsional component (upper pole toward the upward ear), which can be provoked on standard Dix-Hallpike testing because each superior canal is coplanar with the contralateral posterior canal. Its direction is opposite to that of posterior canal BPPV on the same test. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2520)
canonical_layers.workup: **Key tests**: Dix-Hallpike and supine roll testing are the key diagnostic tests. **Imaging/other testing**: routine MRI, CT, and vestibular testing are unnecessary in classic BPPV but become appropriate when the phenotype is atypical or neurologic signs are present. **Current evidence**: transient torsional upbeating nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike supports posterior-canal BPPV. If history is compatible but Dix-Hallpike is horizontal or negative, perform a supine roll test for horizontal-canal disease. Atypical, persistent/nonfatigable nystagmus or neurologic deficits should prompt reconsideration of a central cause. Routine imaging and vestibular suppressants are not indicated for otherwise typical BPPV.
canonical_layers.manage: **Treatment**: use the canal-appropriate repositioning maneuver and avoid chronic vestibular suppressants. **Reassessment**: reassess persistent symptoms for wrong-canal localization, recurrence, cupulolithiasis, or a central mimic. **Current evidence**: use a canalith-repositioning maneuver such as Epley for posterior-canal BPPV. For horizontal-canal disease, identify geotropic versus apogeotropic physiology and use an appropriate Lempert/barbecue-roll or Gufoni maneuver. Reassess persistent symptoms for unresolved/multicanal BPPV or an alternative peripheral/central diagnosis. **Maneuver details**: Epley clears posterior canal BPPV in more than 80%; the Semont (liberatory) maneuver also works but is harder to perform and somewhat less effective. Move head and body en bloc; avoid mastoid vibration in patients with prior retinal detachment or high myopia. Post-maneuver upright restrictions give at most a small benefit, and geotropic horizontal canal BPPV often clears by lying affected-ear-up for about 12 hours (forced prolonged positioning). (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2521)
canonical_layers.operate: BPPV almost never needs surgery. In truly intractable well-localized disease, rare occlusion procedures exist, but the advanced decision is usually better localization and repeated appropriate maneuvers rather than an operation. **Other maneuvers and surgery**: Semont (liberatory) is an alternative to Epley for posterior canal disease; Brandt-Daroff exercises work through habituation. Dix-Hallpike nystagmus has a 2–15 s latency and lasts 10–60 s; posterior canal is involved about 90%. For intractable cases, posterior semicircular canal occlusion has largely replaced singular (posterior ampullary) neurectomy and vestibular nerve section. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 412, 415–416) **Surgery for intractable BPPV**: posterior semicircular canal occlusion (plugging the canal lumen so it no longer senses angular acceleration) cured 94 of 97 reported cases, with transient postoperative hearing loss and permanent loss of that canal's function. Singular (posterior ampullary) neurectomy is effective but technically difficult, with hearing-loss risk reported up to 41%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2522)
canonical_layers.teach:
Name the canal before naming the maneuver. If you cannot describe the nystagmus, you have not localized the disease.

**Current evidence**: Dix-Hallpike with torsional upbeating nystagmus -> posterior semicircular canal -> Epley. Compatible history with horizontal/no Dix-Hallpike nystagmus -> supine roll -> horizontal-canal-specific maneuver.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Acute prolonged spontaneous vertigo lasting days with nausea, gait imbalance and no new hearing loss or focal neurologic deficit suggests this condition, but posterior-circulation stroke is the dangerous mimic. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Short-course vestibular suppressants/antiemetics are for the severe initial period only; begin early mobilization and vestibular rehabilitation. Prolonged suppressants delay central compensation.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Vestibular Neuritis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Acute vestibular syndrome is a stroke-localization problem first and a symptom-control problem second. Hearing should remain intact in classic neuritis.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Suspect** an acute unilateral peripheral vestibulopathy when a sustained acute vestibular syndrome presents with continuous vertigo/dizziness, spontaneous peripheral-pattern nystagmus, nausea, and gait unsteadiness, without acute cochlear symptoms or focal central neurologic signs. **Key trap**: these absences do NOT by themselves rule out posterior-circulation stroke. New hearing loss raises concern for labyrinthine disease AND for an AICA-territory stroke in the appropriate clinical setting. Assess hearing rather than assuming it guarantees a benign diagnosis. **Bedside signs of acute unilateral loss**: spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus beats toward the intact ear and is suppressed by fixation, so look with Frenzel lenses. *First-degree* nystagmus appears only on gaze toward the fast phase, *second-degree* also in primary gaze, and *third-degree* in every direction. After about 30 passive head shakes, the initial nystagmus beats toward the intact side and may then reverse. Mastoid or suboccipital vibration also drives nystagmus toward the intact side. An abnormal head impulse needs a fast thrust of only 10–20 degrees. The corrective saccade appears after thrusts toward the lesion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, p 2482, Ch 166, pp 2499, 2503–2504) **Course numbers and a red flag**: instability with some head movements can last months, and BPPV follows in up to 15% (often posterior canal, since the inferior division is spared). Fast phase beats away from the affected side, with caloric hypofunction in most patients. If the patient is not clearly improving after 2–3 weeks, rule out a central lesion such as cerebellar infarction. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 329)
canonical_layers.localize: **Vestibular testing**: can suggest superior-division, inferior-division, or combined unilateral vestibular hypofunction. **HINTS**: in adults with ongoing acute vestibular syndrome AND spontaneous nystagmus, HINTS is used to distinguish peripheral from central causes, ONLY by an examiner trained in the technique. Assessment of new hearing loss (HINTS-plus), focal findings, and gait instability adds safety. **Peripheral pattern**: typically an abnormal head impulse toward the affected ear, direction-fixed nystagmus, and no skew. **Central or equivocal pattern**: needs a stroke pathway and often MRI, recognizing early MRI may miss posterior fossa infarction. **Key trap**: HINTS is not a general test for episodic/positional vertigo or for patients without nystagmus.
canonical_layers.workup: For persistent acute vestibular syndrome, document nystagmus, gait, neurologic, and hearing findings. **HINTS**: trained clinicians may use it when spontaneous nystagmus is present. A central or equivocal finding, new unilateral hearing loss, or other concerning features warrants urgent stroke-oriented assessment and MRI as indicated. When nystagmus is absent, gait and other findings guide further workup instead of applying HINTS. **Key trap**: early diffusion MRI can be falsely negative for posterior-circulation infarction. Persistent concern requires clinical reassessment and appropriate imaging/neurology input. Audiometry can characterize new hearing loss but should not delay time-critical stroke assessment.
canonical_layers.manage: **Symptomatic treatment** (vestibular suppressants, antiemetics): used only briefly in the acute phase, since prolonged use slows central vestibular compensation. **Vestibular rehabilitation**: started early, as soon as acute nausea allows, speeds compensation and functional recovery. **Corticosteroids**: may modestly speed the rate of peripheral vestibular recovery in some patients when started early, though evidence for long-term functional benefit is mixed. **Steroids and antivirals**: in a placebo-controlled trial, valacyclovir had no effect. Methylprednisolone improved caloric recovery but pooled data show no proven benefit on symptoms, so evidence for steroids is weak (some limit use to starts within 3 days). Early ambulation is encouraged. If hearing loss accompanies the vertigo, treat and work up as sudden SNHL, including evaluation for a retrocochlear lesion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2522) **Expected course after acute loss**: spontaneous nystagmus resolves within days. Most patients have no vertigo at rest and can walk (perhaps with help) by about 2 weeks, and walk unaided and resume daily activities by about 1 month. Head-shaking and gaze-evoked nystagmus last longer, and fast head turns toward the lesion fail permanently if the nerve does not recover. Posterior canal BPPV develops later in 15–30% of patients, so new positional vertigo after recovery should prompt a Dix-Hallpike test rather than a diagnosis of relapse. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, pp 2492–2493)
canonical_layers.operate: There is no primary surgical treatment for vestibular neuritis. **Key skill**: selecting and correctly performing the examination. HINTS is for continuous acute vestibular syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus, in trained hands only. **Key trap**: do not use a seemingly peripheral result from an untrained or inapplicable examination to discharge a patient with possible stroke. Treat the confirmed peripheral disorder with short-term symptom relief and early vestibular rehabilitation.
canonical_layers.teach: **Board pearl**: continuous acute vertigo can be peripheral or stroke. In patients with spontaneous nystagmus, a TRAINED clinician can use HINTS plus hearing assessment. Central/equivocal findings or concerning clinical features warrant a stroke workup even if an early MRI is negative. **Key trap**: do not apply HINTS to episodic vertigo or absent nystagmus, and do not treat lack of hearing loss as proof against stroke.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Persistent imbalance after unilateral or bilateral vestibular loss often reflects incomplete compensation rather than persistent dangerous disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use adaptation, habituation, substitution and balance/gait training tailored to the deficit; prolonged vestibular suppressants can impede compensation in many chronic peripheral cases.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Vestibular Rehabilitation. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: vestibular rehab is targeted neuroplastic training, not generic balance exercise.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Vestibular and Balance Rehabilitation Therapy

canonical_layers.recognize: Persistent imbalance after unilateral or bilateral vestibular loss often reflects incomplete compensation rather than persistent dangerous disease.
canonical_layers.localize: Identify gaze-instability, motion sensitivity, balance/gait and positional components; different deficits require different exercises.
canonical_layers.workup: **Before prescribing**: document vestibular diagnosis, fall risk, vision/proprioception, neuropathy, and functional goals before prescribing therapy. **Also**: identify the impairment before prescribing exercises -- deficient vestibulo-ocular reflex, motion/visual sensitivity, positional vertigo, gait/balance limitation, or maladaptive avoidance. Measure fall risk and functional goals, and exclude an untreated fluctuating or central process that needs separate management. **Functional outcome measures and fall-risk cutoffs**: Track self-report and performance measures. DHI (0-100) scores self-perceived handicap, with 100 meaning severe. On the ABC scale, below 85% identifies likely fallers. On the Dynamic Gait Index, a score under 19/24 correlates with falls in older adults living in the community. A Functional Gait Assessment score of 22/30 or less predicts falls with 100% sensitivity and 72% specificity. A Timed Up and Go over about 11 seconds signals higher fall risk, and gait speed below 0.6 m/s suggests poor aging. If posturography is not available, the modified CTSIB tests four 30-second stances: eyes open or closed, on a firm or foam surface. (Cummings 7e, Ch 170, pp 2567, 2571)
canonical_layers.manage: **Approach**: use adaptation, habituation, substitution, and balance/gait training tailored to the deficit. **Key trap**: prolonged vestibular suppressants can impede compensation in many chronic peripheral cases. **Also**: use gaze-stabilization/adaptation exercises for vestibulo-ocular-reflex deficits, habituation for reproducible motion sensitivity, substitution when vestibular recovery is limited, and balance/gait training with graded exposure. Repositioning maneuvers treat BPPV and should not be replaced by generic exercises. Minimize long-term vestibular suppressants because they can delay compensation.
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery may remove the offending vestibular input but rehabilitation converts that stable deficit into usable function.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: vestibular rehab is targeted neuroplastic training, not generic balance exercise.

Rehabilitation must provoke a controlled, recoverable error signal to drive compensation; exercises that never challenge the impaired system do little, while excessive unsupervised provocation reduces adherence and fall safety. **Uncompensated stable lesion versus unstable labyrinth**: Before offering ablative surgery, decide whether symptoms come from poor central compensation after a stable lesion or from a fluctuating labyrinth. A single severe crisis followed by milder, motion-provoked or continuous unsteadiness suggests a stable but uncompensated lesion, so treat with rehabilitation. Spontaneous spells as bad as or worse than the first, or fluctuating SNHL, point to unstable disease. In the Michigan series of uncompensated vestibular neuritis, rehabilitation gave complete or dramatic improvement in 72%, versus 25% dramatic improvement, 25% no improvement and 5% worsening after vestibular nerve section. No improvement after 4-6 weeks of supervised therapy makes an unstable labyrinth (hydrops, fistula) more likely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, pp 2556-2557)
