candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Systemic autoimmune, infectious, metabolic, hematologic and skeletal disease can present with hearing loss, vestibular symptoms, middle-ear disease or temporal-bone findings. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the systemic driver with the relevant team plus symptom-specific hearing/vestibular rehabilitation; urgent sudden or rapidly progressive deficits keep their time-sensitive pathways.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Otologic Manifestations of Systemic Disease. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: a systemic diagnosis changes context, not the need to localize the ear problem.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Otologic Manifestations of Systemic Disease

canonical_layers.recognize: Systemic autoimmune, infectious, metabolic, hematologic and skeletal disease can present with hearing loss, vestibular symptoms, middle-ear disease or temporal-bone findings. **Fibro-osseous, histiocytic, and uveitic disorders**: Fibrous dysplasia replaces temporal bone marrow with ground-glass fibro-osseous tissue, narrowing the canal (canal cholesteatoma risk) and rarely the otic capsule. McCune-Albright adds precocious puberty and café-au-lait spots. Langerhans cell histiocytosis mimics chronic otitis with granulation and otorrhea. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome resembles Cogan syndrome (hearing loss and vertigo) but with granulomatous uveitis, poliosis/vitiligo, and aseptic meningitis. Cogan's keratitis is nonsyphilitic and interstitial. Middle-ear adenoma presents with conductive loss and is cured by excision. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 399, 420) **Langerhans cell histiocytosis forms**: LCH is a proliferation of histiocytes that contain Birbeck granules (tennis-racket organelles on electron microscopy) and stain CD1a/S100-positive. The localized form, eosinophilic granuloma, causes lytic temporal or frontal bone lesions in children and young adults. It mimics mastoiditis or otitis with granulation tissue and has an excellent prognosis after curettage, with radiation reserved for recurrence. Hand-Schüller-Christian disease is the chronic disseminated form, with lytic skull lesions, exophthalmos and diabetes insipidus. Letterer-Siwe is the acute disseminated infant form (under 3) with hepatosplenomegaly and rash and a very poor prognosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 615–616) **Bone dysplasias of the otic capsule**: *Osteogenesis imperfecta* (COL1A1/COL1A2 in about 90%, Sillence types I-IV and beyond, type I is van der Hoeve with blue sclerae, present in about 95% of those with CHL) causes hearing loss in about 20% of children by age 5 and about 90% of adults. The loss is mostly conductive from stapes involvement, and CT shows thickened, undermineralized capsule. *Osteopetrosis*: the infantile malignant recessive form (TCIRG1 in more than half, CLCN7) causes marrow failure, cranial nerve palsies, optic atrophy and foraminal stenosis of the carotid and jugular. It is treated with stem-cell transplant (5-year survival about 30-36%). The hearing loss is mainly conductive, and about a quarter develop SNHL from IAC narrowing. The dominant (Albers-Schönberg) form is milder. *Fibrous dysplasia* of the temporal bone causes CHL in about 80%, mostly from EAC narrowing, which carries a risk of canal cholesteatoma, and SNHL in about 17% from capsule or IAC involvement. Look for café-au-lait spots and endocrinopathy (McCune-Albright). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 871-873) **Eponymous immune syndromes with SNHL**: Susac syndrome is corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions, branch retinal artery occlusions, and progressive SNHL. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada is an autoimmune attack on melanocytes, with vertigo, SNHL, panuveitis or retinal detachment, and later skin depigmentation. Kearns-Sayre syndrome (an mtDNA deletion) is SNHL with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, heart block, and pigmentary retinopathy (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, pp 2091–2092). **Plasma cell and myeloid tumors of the temporal bone**: Multiple myeloma often replaces petrous marrow and makes punched-out lytic lesions that can rarely present with hearing loss, vertigo, otalgia or facial palsy. A solitary plasmacytoma of the temporal bone (M-protein in under 30%) is indolent and is treated with local radiation of about 40 Gy, with serial serum/urine protein studies and skeletal survey to detect conversion to myeloma. Granulocytic sarcoma (chloroma) is an extramedullary myeloid tumor that may precede, coincide with or follow AML/CML and can first present in the temporal bone. Leukemic infiltrates and hemorrhage in the middle and inner ear cause effusion, suppuration, mixed loss, sudden SNHL, vertigo and facial palsy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2300-2302) **IgG4-related disease of the mastoid**: IgG4-RD (usually men in their sixties-seventies, often multisystem) can involve the mastoid and look like chronic suppurative otitis media, though a mass lesion is more typical. Histology shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis, and it is easily missed unless the pathologist is asked to look. It responds well to corticosteroids, so making the diagnosis spares repeated surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2310) **Multiple sclerosis and the ear**: SNHL occurs in about 4-10% of patients with MS and is often sudden and unilateral, recovering over days to weeks. Word recognition may be poor out of proportion to thresholds and acoustic reflex patterns can be abnormal. ABR abnormalities (prolonged latencies, poor morphology, rate-sensitive changes) are common, and MRI may show plaques in the cochlear nucleus or inferior colliculus. Vertigo in MS usually reflects central vestibular pathway plaques with normal end organs. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2318, Ch 151, p 2309) **Lupus and Susac syndrome**: SNHL is reported in 15-66% of patients with SLE, typically bilateral, symmetric and high-frequency, often subclinical and unrelated to disease severity. Susac syndrome (RED-M: retinopathy with branch retinal artery occlusions, encephalopathy with corpus callosum lesions, deafness from microangiopathy) mostly affects women aged 20-40. The loss is fluctuating, asymmetric and worst in the low-mid frequencies because the apical cochlear arterioles are occluded. Neurologic features often burn out over 2-4 years, but hearing loss usually persists. Treatment is immunosuppression, with cochlear implantation if needed. (Cummings 7e, Ch 156, p 2368-2369, Ch 151, p 2309) **Otosyphilis and tuberculous otitis**: Otosyphilis causes fluctuating, often bilateral SNHL with tinnitus and vertigo, sometimes with a positive Hennebert sign and Tullio phenomenon. Screen with RPR/VDRL and confirm with FTA-ABS. K.J. Lee reserves IV penicillin for tertiary/neurosyphilis, but current CDC guidance treats otosyphilis at any stage as neurosyphilis (IV aqueous penicillin G for 10-14 days), usually with steroids, and the case is reported. Tuberculous otitis gives painless watery otorrhea with multiple TM perforations and pale granulation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 228-230)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the audiovestibular phenotype first, then connect it to systemic disease rather than attributing every symptom to the known diagnosis.
canonical_layers.workup:
Use targeted labs/imaging based on phenotype and systemic clues. Audiometry documents pattern and trajectory.

**Approach**: start with the audiovestibular phenotype and tempo, then use systemic clues to direct -- not shotgun -- testing. **Clues to consider**: autoimmune symptoms and fluctuating bilateral SNHL, vasculitic neurologic/renal/pulmonary findings, syphilis or Lyme exposure, granulomatous disease, hematologic hyperviscosity, or medication toxicity. Obtain targeted serology/imaging in partnership with the relevant specialty. **Otosyphilis testing**: nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) detect only about 70% of late disease, so use treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, MHA-TP), which detect 95% or more. Nontreponemal titers are used to follow treatment response. Lumbar puncture is positive in only about 5% and is not routinely required. Interstitial keratitis is present in about 90% of late otosyphilis, and Hutchinson's triad (SNHL, interstitial keratitis, notched incisors) marks late congenital syphilis. Hennebert sign and Tullio phenomenon are common in syphilis but not specific for it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2532) **GPA ear disease and ANCA yield**: The ear is involved in roughly 20-60% of GPA and can be the first or only site. It is unusual among autoimmune diseases in affecting both the middle ear (eustachian tube obstruction, effusion, granulation) and the inner ear, with SNHL in up to about a third of those with hearing loss. PR3/c-ANCA is more than 95% specific, and is positive in over 90% of active systemic disease but in only about 65-70% of limited (ear or head-and-neck only) disease, so a negative ANCA and a nondiagnostic small ear biopsy do not exclude it. Repeat biopsy and clinical correlation are often needed. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2295-2297, Ch 156, p 2368) **Temporal bone metastases and meningeal carcinomatosis**: Metastases arrive hematogenously, most often from breast, then lung, prostate and skin. They favor the petrous apex and IAC while the otic capsule resists invasion, and prostate or breast deposits may be osteoblastic. Meningeal carcinomatosis commonly presents with rapidly progressive SNHL that mimics a CPA tumor when unilateral or immune-mediated inner ear disease when bilateral. Diagnose with CSF cytology. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2301-2302)
canonical_layers.manage:
Treat the systemic driver with the relevant team plus symptom-specific hearing/vestibular rehabilitation. Urgent sudden or rapidly progressive deficits keep their time-sensitive pathways.

Treat urgent inner-ear loss promptly while pursuing the systemic cause, stop or modify ototoxic exposure when feasible, and coordinate immunosuppression or antimicrobial therapy with rheumatology, infectious disease, oncology, or primary teams. **Key trap**: do not label an isolated nonspecific positive autoimmune test as autoimmune inner-ear disease. **Otosyphilis treatment**: Cummings treats early disease with IM benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units (with a short steroid course) and late disease like neurosyphilis with prolonged penicillin plus probenecid (for example 3 weeks). **Current view (CDC 2021)**: otosyphilis at any stage is treated as neurosyphilis, with aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days (or procaine penicillin plus probenecid), with ID consultation. Prednisone 40-60 mg/day for at least 2 weeks before taper is commonly added. Hearing, especially word recognition, improves in about 35%-50%. Early otosyphilis (within 2 years) tends to present as sudden SNHL, while late disease mimics Ménière disease and can appear decades after exposure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2532) **Fibrous dysplasia of the temporal bone: management**: About 100 temporal bone cases are reported (70% monostotic, 23% polyostotic, 7% McCune-Albright), presenting in the second-third decade as painless bony swelling with canal stenosis. Surgery is limited to biopsy and relief of function. Restenosis after simple canalplasty is common, and a canal-wall-down mastoidectomy with wide canalplasty and skin grafting gives more durable patency. Radiotherapy is contraindicated because it raises the risk of sarcomatous change (baseline about 0.4%). Follow long term for facial nerve involvement and progression to SNHL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2305-2306) **Temporal bone fibrous dysplasia management and leukemia**: Fibrous dysplasia starts around age 10. It is monostotic in about 70%, and CT shows ground glass with the otic capsule 'floating'. *Never irradiate it*: radiation raises the sarcoma risk about 400-fold, against a baseline malignant change of about 1 in 200. Treat conservatively and recontour bone only for function or deformity. For canal stenosis, transcanal canalplasty restenosed in 89%, whereas postauricular canalplasty with (usually canal-wall-down) mastoidectomy, an oversized canal, skin grafting and a meatoplasty had no restenosis. *Leukemia* involves the temporal bone in about 20% (infiltration, hemorrhage, infection) and can present as otitis or mastoiditis. It is treated by treating the leukemia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 905-908)
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery is selective and anatomy-driven; systemic disease can alter healing, bone quality and recurrence risk. **Stapes surgery in osteogenesis imperfecta**: OI can mimic otosclerosis (early-onset conductive loss, high tympanometric compliance, childhood fractures that stop after puberty, blue sclerae). At surgery the footplate is typically thick, soft and chalky but fixed, the crura may be thin or fractured, and the incus long process and malleus may be fragile. Stapedectomy can match otosclerosis results but is delicate: crimping can fracture the incus, so a platinum-ribbon (rather than stainless-steel wire) prosthesis is preferred. Hearing loss occurs in about 30-50% of type I, about 50% of type III and 10-30% of type IV. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2303-2304)
canonical_layers.teach:
**Teach**: a systemic diagnosis changes context, not the need to localize the ear problem.

Systemic disease is a hypothesis generated by phenotype and associated findings. The ear may be the presenting organ, but treatment must address both time-sensitive hearing loss and the underlying disease, without allowing indiscriminate panels to replace clinical localization. **Osteopetrosis and recurrent facial palsy**: Any child or young adult with recurrent Bell-like facial palsy should be imaged for osteopetrosis: in the dominant adult (Albers-Schonberg, often CLCN7) form the temporal bone is sclerotic with narrowed eustachian tube, EAC and IAC, ossicles jammed by periosteal overgrowth and obliterated window niches, and each palsy tends to leave more residual weakness. Total facial nerve decompression has been advocated. In the malignant recessive infantile form (often TCIRG1), the tympanic facial nerve is consistently dehiscent and may herniate into the oval window niche, and bone marrow transplant is the only effective treatment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2305-2307)

What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the identified mechanism and use objective testing when it resolves a real question rather than as a routine prerequisite for every obstructed patient.

canonical_layers.recognize: Nasal obstruction is subjective; objective tests measure different components of airflow/geometry and do not perfectly substitute for symptoms.
canonical_layers.localize: Separate mucosal reversibility from fixed septal, valve or bony narrowing and from sensory mismatch where measured resistance is not the whole symptom.
canonical_layers.workup: Use validated symptom measures and exam/endoscopy first. Rhinomanometry, acoustic rhinometry or peak nasal inspiratory flow can answer selected physiologic/research questions, especially pre/post decongestion or intervention. **Saccharin clearance test**: A saccharin particle is placed on the anterior inferior turbinate, and the time until the patient tastes sweetness is recorded. A prolonged time suggests impaired mucociliary clearance, which points toward ciliary biopsy with electron microscopy, motility studies or nasal nitric oxide. Rhinomanometry gives an objective resistance value but is rarely used clinically because it is slow, costly and variable. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 16) **Rhinomanometry vs acoustic rhinometry**: rhinomanometry measures the transnasal pressure-flow relationship (resistance). Repeating it after maximal decongestion separates the mucosal component from the fixed structural one, but it cannot localize the site of obstruction. Acoustic rhinometry uses reflected sound to map cross-sectional area and volume by distance (it localizes) but says nothing about flow. The two are complementary, and acoustic rhinometry is feasible in newborns and young children. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Examination of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Face, and Orbit", p 949) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Examination of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, Face, and Orbit", p 950) **Peak nasal inspiratory flow (PNIF)**: a facemask Wright-type meter measures maximal forced nasal inspiration from residual volume. Take the best of 2 to 3 tries after practice. Typical adult norms are about 143 L/min (men) and 122 L/min (women), and about 80 L/min in children 6 and older. PNIF falls with age and rises with height and male sex. It is cheap, portable and reproducible, but effort- and lung-dependent (check peak expiratory flow), and alar collapse can lower it falsely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, p 607-608) **Rhinomanometry standards**: anterior active rhinomanometry (one nostril taped with a pressure tube while the other breathes) is the most common method. Nasal airway resistance is pressure divided by flow, reported in Pa/cm³/s (0.1 Pa/cm³/s = 1 cm H₂O/L/s). The international standard reports flow or resistance at 150 Pa or at radius 2. Normal unilateral resistance is about 0.24 to 0.26 Pa/cm³/s. On the pressure-flow plot, obstructed airways lie closer to the pressure axis, and distal flattening suggests valve collapse. Four-phase rhinomanometry (Vogt) reports vertex and effective resistance without needing a target pressure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, p 609-610) **Acoustic rhinometry**: reflected sound measures cross-sectional area along about the first 6 cm. The first notch is the nasal valve and the second the inferior turbinate head. One of these is the minimal cross-sectional area (MCA, about 0.5 to 0.6 cm² in adults, about 0.3 cm² at age 3 to 6). It needs only breath-holding, so it suits children, and it correlates with CT. It is unreliable past a severe narrowing, and nosepiece seal, swallowing and palate motion add error. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, p 612)
canonical_layers.manage: Treat the identified mechanism and use objective testing when it resolves a real question rather than as a routine prerequisite for every obstructed patient.
canonical_layers.operate: Surgical planning remains anatomy-driven; a number from an airflow test does not tell you which structure to modify.
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: symptom, anatomy and physiology are related but not identical. Concordance is useful; discordance is information.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. Posterior glottic granuloma on the vocal process often follows intubation, phonotrauma/throat clearing or laryngeal irritation and can cause throat discomfort, cough or dysphonia. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Reduce mechanical trauma with voice/cough therapy and treat relevant inflammatory contributors. Many lesions regress without surgery; recurrence is common when the inciting behavior persists.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Vocal Process Granuloma. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: If you remove the granuloma but leave the collision force, you have treated the consequence and preserved the cause.

canonical_layers.recognize: Posterior glottic granuloma on the vocal process often follows intubation, phonotrauma/throat clearing or laryngeal irritation and can cause throat discomfort, cough or dysphonia. **Intubation granuloma**: this lesion is more common in women, attaches directly to the vocal process, is often bilateral, and CT often shows arytenoid sclerosis. The voice can sound normal. Check fold motion first. With normal motion, use antireflux therapy and inhaled steroid. With impaired motion, which suggests posterior glottic injury or arytenoid fixation, consider microlaryngoscopic excision with steroid injection. Long intubation can also cause tissue loss, posterior glottic incompetence and interarytenoid synechia. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 887)
canonical_layers.localize: The lesion forms over the cartilaginous posterior glottis where mechanical contact pressure is high; this differs from a membranous vocal-fold mass.
canonical_layers.workup: Laryngoscopy establishes location; biopsy is reserved for atypical, progressive or suspicious lesions. Identify intubation history, hyperfunctional voice/cough and reflux-related symptoms without assuming reflux is always causal.
canonical_layers.manage: Reduce mechanical trauma with voice/cough therapy and treat relevant inflammatory contributors. Many lesions regress without surgery; recurrence is common when the inciting behavior persists. **Glottic insufficiency link**: compensatory hyperadduction from glottic insufficiency often drives recurrence, so augment at the same sitting as excision. About 75% respond to PPI but about 21% recur. For recurrence, give botulinum toxin to the ipsilateral TA-LCA about 3 days before excision. If laser is used, leave a cuff of granuloma over the perichondrium. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Vocal Fold Granuloma", p 181) **Contact granuloma specifics**: the lesion occurs mainly in men, often with a habitually low, held-back voice, throat clearing, and unilateral pain over the mid-thyroid cartilage referred to the ear. The opposite vocal process often fits into the cleft of a bilobed lesion. Start empiric antireflux therapy even without symptoms. Most granulomas mature, become pedunculated and fall off within 3–6 months. Office options are depot steroid injection into and around the base, or inhaled triamcinolone or mometasone, reassessed every 6–8 weeks. Surgery is a last resort because recurrence is predictable. If needed, remove only a mature pedunculated lesion and leave the base. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 885–887) **Toxin dosing for granuloma**: doses into one or both TA-LCA complexes range from 1.25 to 20 U, and 5 U on one side is usually enough. One treatment, alone or with excision, usually lets the granuloma resolve. Warn patients that the voice will be very weak and breathy for months. Toxin may backfire when glottic insufficiency drives the contact lesion. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 39, p 346)
canonical_layers.operate: Excision is reserved for airway compromise, diagnostic uncertainty or refractory symptomatic disease and should minimize further perichondrial trauma; adjunct botulinum toxin may be considered in selected recurrent contact lesions.
canonical_layers.teach:
**Board pearl**: if you remove the granuloma but leave the collision force, you have treated the consequence and preserved the cause.

**Treat** mechanical collision, cough/throat clearing, voice behavior, and clearly relevant inflammatory contributors. **Key trap**: evidence for empiric antireflux medication in an unselected contact-granuloma patient is mixed. Reflux therapy should not replace voice/cough-directed treatment or reassessment of an atypical lesion.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the ENT service. ENT reconstruction uses autograft, allograft and synthetic materials for support, lining, volume, ossicular conduction and implants. Material choice should match mechanical demand, infection risk and long-term biologic behavior. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Prefer the simplest durable material that restores function with acceptable donor morbidity. Counsel about resorption, extrusion, infection, calcification, warping and revision according to material/site.

canonical_layers.recognize: ENT reconstruction uses autograft, allograft and synthetic materials for support, lining, volume, ossicular conduction and implants. Material choice should match mechanical demand, infection risk and long-term biologic behavior.
canonical_layers.localize: Cartilage, fascia, bone, skin, nerve graft, vascularized flap and prosthetic implants each behave differently in mucosal, cutaneous, middle-ear and irradiated environments.
canonical_layers.workup: Define what is missing—structure, lining, cover, conductivity, nerve continuity or volume—and the quality of the recipient bed. Prior infection/radiation and contamination may make permanent foreign material less attractive.
canonical_layers.manage: Prefer the simplest durable material that restores function with acceptable donor morbidity. Counsel about resorption, extrusion, infection, calcification, warping and revision according to material/site.
canonical_layers.operate: Prepare a well-vascularized, tension-free recipient bed; avoid exposed implant edges and dead space. In contaminated or irradiated fields, vascularized autologous tissue often has a biologic advantage.
canonical_layers.teach: Choose a material by the job it must perform, not by habit. Support, lining, conduction and soft-tissue replacement are different reconstructive problems.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Chronic nonspinning dizziness/unsteadiness present most days for months and worsened by upright posture, motion, complex visual environments or busy stores/screens suggests PPPD, often after a vestibular, migraine, anxiety or medical trigger. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Education, graded vestibular rehabilitation, treatment of comorbid migraine/anxiety and selected serotonergic medication are commonly combined. Avoid chronic vestibular suppressants, which can reinforce compensation failure.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD). The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: PPPD is real dizziness without a single damaged end organ. The board/clinic pearl is persistent visually/posturally provoked symptoms after a trigger with no better structural explanation.

canonical_layers.recognize: Chronic nonspinning dizziness/unsteadiness present most days for months and worsened by upright posture, motion, complex visual environments or busy stores/screens suggests PPPD, often after a vestibular, migraine, anxiety or medical trigger.
canonical_layers.localize: PPPD is a functional sensory-integration disorder rather than a fixed unilateral vestibular lesion. The problem is maladaptive weighting of visual, vestibular and postural inputs plus heightened threat/vigilance.
canonical_layers.workup: Confirm the characteristic time course and triggers, then look for active vestibular, neurologic or cardiac disease that would better explain symptoms. Vestibular testing may be normal or may show a prior trigger disorder; abnormal tests do not exclude superimposed PPPD.
canonical_layers.manage: Education, graded vestibular rehabilitation, treatment of comorbid migraine/anxiety and selected serotonergic medication are commonly combined. Avoid chronic vestibular suppressants, which can reinforce compensation failure.
canonical_layers.operate: There is no operative treatment for PPPD. The advanced decision is recognizing when persistent symptoms are due to PPPD layered on top of a treated peripheral disorder rather than escalating to destructive vestibular procedures.
canonical_layers.teach: PPPD is real dizziness without a single damaged end organ. The board/clinic pearl is persistent visually/posturally provoked symptoms after a trigger with no better structural explanation. **Mal de debarquement versus PPPD and motion sickness**: After disembarking, a rocking feeling ('land sickness') is normal: it fades within 6 hours in more than 90% of people and within about 48 hours in most others. Mal de debarquement syndrome is rocking or swaying (not spinning) that lasts at least a month after a cruise, flight or long drive. It mostly affects women in their 40s and can last months to years. Unlike PPPD and motion sickness, symptoms improve while riding in a vehicle and return when motion stops. Meclizine and scopolamine do not help. Benzodiazepines (clonazepam), amitriptyline, readaptation to passive motion and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation may help. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2550)

candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Separate volume loss, skin texture/dyschromia, static rhytids, dynamic rhytids, ptosis/laxity and skeletal support; each requires a different treatment mechanism. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Neuromodulators address dynamic muscle activity; fillers restore selected volume/support; resurfacing targets skin; surgery repositions deeper tissues. Combine only when the anatomy and goals justify it.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Aging Face / Injectables / Resurfacing. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.

canonical_layers.recognize: Separate volume loss, skin texture/dyschromia, static rhytids, dynamic rhytids, ptosis/laxity, and skeletal support -- each requires a different treatment mechanism. **CHEMICAL PEEL DEPTH CLASSIFICATION** (high-yield boards framework): peels are classified by the histologic depth of injury they produce, not just by agent name. **SUPERFICIAL**: epidermis only, from stratum corneum to the basal layer. **MEDIUM-DEPTH**: full epidermis into the papillary dermis, occasionally upper reticular dermis. **DEEP**: mid-reticular dermis. Depth determines both efficacy for a given problem (fine rhytids/dyschromia vs. deeper rhytids/actinic damage vs. severe photoaging) and the complication profile (downtime, scarring risk, and systemic toxicity for deep peels). **Toxin complications by type**: local effects are pain, edema, erythema, ecchymosis, headache, short-term hyperesthesia and eyelid ptosis. Immunologic: an acute type 1 reaction. Systemic: nausea, fatigue, malaise, flulike symptoms and distant rash. Therapeutic failure comes from circulating neutralizing antibodies. Deep periorbital injection can also cause lagophthalmos. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1049; Cummings 7e, Ch 26)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize aging change by tissue plane and facial danger zones, especially vascular territories and motor-nerve relationships. **SUPERFICIAL AGENTS**: glycolic acid (~20-70%, an alpha-hydroxy acid), salicylic acid (~20-30%, a beta-hydroxy acid, useful in acne-prone/oilier skin since it is lipophilic), Jessner solution (resorcinol, salicylic acid, and lactic acid in ethanol -- itself superficial in 1-2 coats but becomes a MEDIUM-depth combination when layered with TCA), and lower-concentration TCA (<=20-30%). **MEDIUM-DEPTH AGENTS**: TCA 30-35% alone, or -- because higher-concentration TCA alone above ~35% has an unacceptably high scarring risk -- TCA 35% COMBINED with a priming agent such as Jessner solution (Monheit combination peel) or 70% glycolic acid (Coleman combination peel), which reach medium depth more safely by disrupting the epidermal barrier first. **DEEP AGENTS**: phenol-croton oil formulations, classically the Baker-Gordon formula (USP phenol, croton oil, septisol/soap, and distilled water). Croton oil concentration is now recognized as the primary driver of depth (lower croton oil = shallower, more controllable peels), which is why modified/diluted phenol-croton formulas have largely replaced the original fixed-ratio Baker-Gordon recipe in modern practice.
canonical_layers.workup: **Workup**: standardized photos, medication/bleeding history, prior filler/device history, and ocular/facial-nerve function guide safe planning. Match peel depth to the problem and to Fitzpatrick skin type before selecting an agent. Fine rhytids, mild dyschromia, and actinic keratoses respond to superficial-to-medium peels. Deeper rhytids and more severe photodamage may need medium or deep peels. **Higher Fitzpatrick phototypes (IV-VI)** carry a higher risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with medium and deep peels, which favors more conservative depth selection, pretreatment skin priming (e.g., topical retinoid and/or hydroquinone to reduce post-peel dyschromia), and closer follow-up in this population. Herpes simplex prophylaxis is standard before medium and deep peels given the risk of reactivation with dermal injury. **ISOTRETINOIN**: the classic, still-tested teaching is to avoid medium and deep chemical peels (and other resurfacing/dermabrasion procedures) for roughly 6-12 months after isotretinoin use because of concern for abnormal wound healing and atypical scarring. A 2017 ASDS consensus found limited evidence to support this restriction for purely superficial procedures, but the traditional waiting period remains the expected board answer, especially for medium/deep peels. **Fitzpatrick and Glogau**: Fitzpatrick types run from I (always burns, never tans) to VI (never burns). Types I to III are the safest for peels and lasers. Types III and IV often show lines of demarcation, and types V and VI tend to develop hyperpigmentation lasting 18 to 24 months, so most surgeons avoid deep peeling there. The Glogau scale grades photoaging: I mild (little wrinkling, no keratoses, about 28 to 35 years); II moderate (early wrinkling, sallow color, early actinic keratoses, about 35 to 50); III advanced; IV severe. The ideal resurfacing patient is a fair, thin-skinned woman with fine rhytids. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 351-352, 359) **Laser resurfacing contraindications and complications**: Avoid ablative resurfacing after isotretinoin within the prior 1-2 years, in scleroderma, active acne, prior facial burns, or prior head and neck radiation (all impair reepithelialization). This is the book view. The 2017 ASDS consensus found insufficient evidence to delay superficial peels, nonablative lasers or fractional ablative lasers after isotretinoin, but still advises against fully ablative laser and mechanical dermabrasion on or soon after it. Complications are prolonged erythema, scarring and dyschromia, with higher pigmentary risk in Fitzpatrick III and darker skin. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 72) **Peel contraindications**: These include confirmed malignancy (except very superficial BCC), unstable psychiatric status and true allergy. For phenol, add cardiac, hepatic or renal disease. In the book, isotretinoin taken within the prior 6 months contraindicates dermabrasion, because it reduces the pilosebaceous units needed for healing, and some wait a full year before any facial resurfacing. The 2017 ASDS consensus still advises against mechanical dermabrasion on or soon after isotretinoin but found no evidence to delay superficial peels. Telangiectasias and large pores do not improve and may look worse. Nevi can darken. Port-wine stains, hemangiomas and neurofibromas do not respond. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 352-353, 360)
canonical_layers.manage: **Modality mapping**: neuromodulators address dynamic muscle activity, fillers restore selected volume/support, resurfacing targets skin, and surgery repositions deeper tissues. Combine only when the anatomy and goals justify it. **FACELIFT HEMATOMA COMMITMENT POINT**: after rhytidectomy/facelift, new asymmetric or rapidly progressive facial/neck swelling, increasing pain or pressure, tense ecchymosis, brisk drain output, skin-flap duskiness, or progressive dysphagia/airway symptoms should trigger immediate assessment for an expanding hematoma. A small, stable, nonexpanding collection is not the same problem as a tense or enlarging hematoma. **Key trap**: the latter can compromise skin-flap perfusion and, when the cervical component is substantial, can threaten the airway -- do not passively observe a progressive tension hematoma while waiting for routine imaging. Reassess blood pressure and contributing anticoagulant/coagulopathy issues in parallel, because perioperative hypertension is a reproducible hematoma risk factor, but medical correction does not replace source control once a major hematoma is present. **ENDPOINTS BY DEPTH** (how you tell how deep you are, in real time): SUPERFICIAL peels show a patchy, stringy white 'pseudofrost' that can be wiped away, or simple erythema. MEDIUM-DEPTH peels show a uniform, solid WHITE FROST WITH ERYTHEMA VISIBLE THROUGH IT (frosting from coagulated epidermal/papillary dermal protein while the dermal vasculature still shows through) -- the 'accordion sign' (skin sliding freely when stretched) confirms adequate but not excessive depth. DEEP (phenol-croton oil) peels progress to a SOLID, OPAQUE WHITE FROST WITHOUT VISIBLE ERYTHEMA, reflecting full-thickness epidermal and papillary/upper-reticular dermal coagulation. Titrate agent, concentration, and number of coats to the desired endpoint rather than to a fixed time. **Resurfacing lasers**: CO2 (10,600 nm, water chromophore) ablates about 20-60 microns on the first pass, re-epithelializes in about 8 days with 3-6 months of erythema, and gives more collagen tightening. Hypopigmentation is its most common complication. Er:YAG (2940 nm) has 12-18 times more water absorption. Pasha quotes 3-5 microns of ablation, a figure that applies per J/cm2 of fluence, so per-pass depth depends on settings (K.J. Lee quotes about 25-30 microns per pass). Er:YAG heals in about 5 days with 3-4 weeks of erythema and less tightening. Dermabrasion stops at the papillary dermis (pinpoint bleeding) and must spare the adnexa of the reticular layer. Pretreat with tretinoin and give antiviral prophylaxis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 508–510) **Filler specifics**: Hyaluronic acid lasts about 6-12 months and is reversible with hyaluronidase. Calcium hydroxyapatite (Radiesse) is deep dermal, lasts about 12 months and has no reversal agent. Poly-L-lactic acid (Sculptra) stimulates collagen over multiple sessions and is used for HIV lipoatrophy. PMMA (Bellafill/ArteFill) is permanent. Vascular compromise presents with pain and blanching or a violaceous pattern away from the site. Stop injecting and treat at once, ideally within hours rather than waiting toward the 24-48 hours sometimes quoted, with high-dose hyaluronidase (repeated as needed), warm compresses, massage and aspirin, with nitropaste as an adjunct. Visual symptoms need emergency ophthalmology. Delayed nodules may respond to triamcinolone. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 513–515) **Peel complications**: hyperpigmentation is the most common complication after TCA/superficial peels (sunscreen, hydroquinone, tretinoin); hypopigmentation is expected after deep phenol peels. HSV reactivation appears within about 24 hours (prophylactic antivirals). Phenol cannot be combined with an undermined rhytidectomy flap (necrosis) and is contraindicated on irradiated skin lacking adnexa. Milia peak about 1 month after dermabrasion. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 512–513) **Dermabrasion**: it is best for acne, traumatic and surgical scars, and is the treatment of choice for rhinophyma. Perioral dermabrasion matches CO2 laser results but heals in about half the time. Expect only 50% to 80% improvement of rhytids and 30% to 40% of severe acne scars. Healing takes 10 to 14 days, and erythema lasts 8 to 12 weeks. Wait 12 months before repeating. Treat to the jawline, hairline and orbital rims but not across them, and never dermabrade the neck. Pinpoint bleeding marks the papillary dermis. Milia and acne flares are common afterward. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 359-362) **Ablative laser resurfacing: CO2 versus Er:YAG**: CO2 removes roughly 50-100 µm per pass, coagulates small vessels for a nearly bloodless field and reepithelializes in about 2 weeks. Er:YAG removes only about 25-30 µm, bleeds more, suits mild epidermal aging and heals in 5-7 days. Nonablative rejuvenation (for example 1.32 µm Nd:YAG) heats the dermis to stimulate fibroblasts without ablating epidermis. Give perioperative HSV antiviral prophylaxis (eg, valacyclovir starting the day before and continuing to about day 10). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 72) **Peel preparation**: give tretinoin nightly starting 4 to 6 weeks before medium/deep peels and stop it about 2 weeks before. Tretinoin thins the stratum corneum and deepens a peel, so avoid it right before a Baker phenol peel. Use 4% hydroquinone for Fitzpatrick III or higher before and after. Give antiviral prophylaxis to every medium/deep resurfacing patient (e.g., acyclovir 800 mg three times daily), starting before the procedure and continuing until reepithelialization. Use SPF 30 or more for 9 to 12 months. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 353, 359) **Nonablative and maintenance options**: nonablative devices heat the dermis to about 65 to 75°C to denature collagen without wounding the epidermis. They need multiple sessions (every 4 to 12 weeks) but avoid hypopigmentation and scarring. Microdermabrasion causes only stratum corneum turnover. Tretinoin is the best-proven topical antiphotoaging agent. Laser resurfacing can also treat widespread actinic keratoses. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 366-370) **Toxin contraindications and interactions**: avoid toxin in pregnancy or lactation, albumin hypersensitivity, and neuromuscular junction disease (myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton). Drugs that add to junctional blockade (aminoglycosides, penicillamine, quinine, calcium channel blockers) are listed as contraindications, and aspirin or anticoagulation raises bruising risk. Unrealistic expectations are a contraindication too. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1049)
canonical_layers.operate: **Know**: vascular occlusion, ocular ischemia, skin necrosis, ectropion, nerve injury, and pigment/scar complications -- and have a rescue plan before treatment. **EXPANDING-HEMATOMA BAILOUT**: a rapidly expanding or tense post-facelift hematoma with threatened flap viability, active bleeding, severe pain/pressure, or airway progression requires prompt decompression and definitive hemostasis rather than repeated needle aspiration alone. Coordinate airway support when cervical swelling is compromising ventilation or access. **Sequence**: release constricting dressings/closure as needed for urgent decompression, return to the operative field for evacuation when indicated, remove clot enough to expose the bleeding bed, identify and control the source, irrigate and perform a deliberate hemostasis check, then reassess flap color, capillary refill/tension, and the need for drainage before reclosure. Treat severe hypertension, nausea/retching, and correctable coagulopathy concurrently -- none should delay evacuation of a clearly expanding tension hematoma. After evacuation, continue close surveillance for reaccumulation and skin-flap ischemia/necrosis. **DEEP PEEL SAFETY REQUIREMENT**: phenol is directly cardiotoxic (arrhythmogenic, most often ventricular ectopy/arrhythmia) and hepato/nephrotoxic with rapid mucocutaneous absorption. Full phenol-croton oil (Baker-Gordon-type) peels therefore require continuous cardiac monitoring, IV access and hydration, and staged application (typically treating cosmetic subunits over a defined interval, e.g., roughly every 10-15 minutes) to limit the systemic phenol load absorbed at any one time. This monitoring requirement is unique to deep/phenol peels and is not needed for superficial or TCA-based medium peels, which are not systemically absorbed to a clinically significant degree. **Neuromodulator technique**: The Dysport to Botox dose ratio is about 2.5:1 (Dysport spreads more and starts sooner). Inject the frontalis at least about 2 cm above the brow, the corrugator belly and tail for vertical glabellar lines, and the procerus for horizontal glabellar lines. Inject crow's feet about 1 cm lateral to the orbital rim. Upper lid ptosis comes from toxin diffusing to the levator, mostly after glabellar or brow injections, and apraclonidine treats it by stimulating Muller muscle. Medial spread from crow's feet injections instead weakens the lower lid or causes diplopia. Perioral injections stay within 5 mm of the vermilion (lip flip). Avoid rubbing for several hours after injection. Phenol peel limits in Pasha are under 25% of the face at a time with about 10-minute intervals, whereas Cummings advises 15-30 minutes between facial units. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 512, 516–517) **Phenol toxicity numbers**: toxic doses are about 8 to 15 g in adults, with cardiac, hepatic and renal effects. Phenol is cleared by the kidneys (largely within about 20 minutes), so renal disease contraindicates it. Before a deep peel, get CBC, liver and renal panels, electrolytes and a baseline ECG. Run IV fluids (500 to 1000 mL), wait at least 15 to 30 minutes between facial units, and treat no more than half the face at once. Monitor the heart for at least 30 minutes afterward with ACLS staff present. Arrhythmia is the main danger. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 357-358) **Rhytidectomy complications by the numbers**: Hematoma is the most common complication (about 3-15%) and needs prompt evacuation. Skin necrosis is most common postauricularly and more frequent in smokers. The great auricular nerve is the most often injured nerve (about 7%). Temporal or marginal mandibular neurapraxia occurs in about 1%, and permanent motor injury in about 0.1%. Over-resecting subplatysmal fat without platysmaplasty produces a cobra-neck deformity. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1036-1037)
canonical_layers.teach: **Teach**: match the aging layer to the treatment layer -- muscle, volume, skin, and ptosis are not interchangeable problems. **CHIEF RESCUE FRAME**: SMALL/STABLE COLLECTION may be managed selectively; EXPANDING/TENSE HEMATOMA is a different entity. Recognize progressive swelling/pressure and flap compromise -> assess airway and hemodynamics -> DECOMPRESS/EVACUATE when major -> FIND AND CONTROL THE BLEEDING SOURCE -> correct BP/coagulopathy/nausea in parallel -> reassess flap perfusion and recurrence. The resident should know why this is time-sensitive: sustained subflap pressure can impair perfusion and convert a reversible bleeding complication into skin-flap necrosis. **Boards/chief framework**: depth of injury, not agent brand name, is what to reason from. SUPERFICIAL (epidermis: glycolic, salicylic, light TCA, Jessner alone) -> minimal downtime, treats fine texture/mild dyschromia. MEDIUM (papillary dermis: TCA 35% alone or combined with Jessner/glycolic priming) -> uniform white frost with erythema showing through, treats moderate rhytids/actinic damage/lentigines. DEEP (reticular dermis: phenol-croton oil) -> solid opaque frost, treats severe photoaging/deep rhytids but requires cardiac monitoring for phenol toxicity and carries the highest scarring/pigment-change risk, especially in darker Fitzpatrick types. A combination peel (Jessner+TCA or glycolic+TCA) exists precisely because high-concentration TCA alone is a poor way to reach medium depth safely. **Expected sequelae vs complications**: pigment change, usually hypopigmentation, is the most common peel sequela and usually appears in the first 3 months. Treat early hyperpigmentation with tretinoin 0.1%, hydroquinone 4% and triamcinolone. Withhold estrogens 4 weeks before and 6 to 8 weeks after a peel. Wait at least 4 months to repeat a deep peel and 1 year to repeat a medium peel. Multiple superficial peels do not equal one medium or deep peel. A breakthrough herpetic outbreak is treated with high-dose acyclovir. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 356, 358-359)

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Acute vestibular syndrome with hearing loss suggests labyrinthine involvement rather than isolated vestibular neuritis; bacterial extension from otitis/mastoid disease can be destructive. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the underlying infection/inflammation urgently when bacterial disease is possible, manage vertigo briefly when needed and begin hearing/vestibular rehabilitation as the acute phase resolves.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Labyrinthitis / Infections of the Labyrinth. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: vestibular neuritis should not cause a new cochlear hearing loss; that clue changes localization.

canonical_layers.recognize: Acute vestibular syndrome with hearing loss suggests labyrinthine involvement rather than isolated vestibular neuritis; bacterial extension from otitis/mastoid disease can be destructive. **Nystagmus direction by labyrinthitis type**: Serous (toxic) labyrinthitis gives irritative nystagmus beating toward the affected ear with usually recoverable hearing, while suppurative bacterial labyrinthitis destroys function, so nystagmus beats away, hearing loss is typically permanent, and labyrinthitis ossificans or meningitis can follow. Syphilitic labyrinthitis may show Tullio and Hennebert signs. Viral labyrinthitis differs from vestibular neuritis by the presence of hearing loss. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 383–384)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize to cochlea + vestibular labyrinth and determine whether spread is viral/inflammatory, meningogenic or tympanogenic.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Essential**: audiometry and otologic/neurologic exam. Imaging and infectious workup are driven by meningitis, mastoiditis, cholesteatoma, or intracranial concern.

**Also**: differentiate **vestibular neuritis** (acute vestibular syndrome without new cochlear loss) from **labyrinthitis** (vertigo plus new sensorineural hearing loss). **Red flags**: otitis media/mastoiditis, meningitis, fever, neurologic deficits, severe headache, or immunocompromise raises concern for suppurative/intracranial disease and warrants urgent audiometry, imaging, cultures, and specialty evaluation rather than a benign neuritis label. **Congenital syphilis, rubella, toxoplasmosis and HSV**: Infants of mothers with reactive treponemal tests need a quantitative RPR/VDRL; an infant titer more than fourfold the mother's suggests severe disease and needs CSF analysis plus HIV testing, and CDC treatment is 10 days of IV aqueous penicillin G. Rubella infection in the first trimester carries the highest risk, yet 10-20% of infants infected later develop SNHL (bilateral, often cookie-bite, from cochleosaccular degeneration). Congenital toxoplasmosis (about 1 in 10,000) causes hearing loss in up to 26%, and neonatal HSV in about 10%, though routine HSV screening for unexplained neonatal SNHL is not recommended. (Cummings 7e, Ch 155, p 2359-2360) **Postmeningitic ossification specifics**: Bacteria spread from the meninges through the cochlear aqueduct, which opens into the basal turn of the scala tympani near the round window. That is where ossification is most severe, and it keeps advancing for years. The risk is highest after *S. pneumoniae* meningitis, in males, and when intracranial pressure was raised. Early fibrous or osteoid obliteration is missed on CT and is seen as loss of fluid signal on high-resolution T2 fast-spin-echo MRI. Monitor postmeningitic children with progressive loss closely with imaging, so they can be implanted before the cochlea ossifies. Basal-turn drill-out allows insertion in ossified cochleae. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 873-874)
canonical_layers.manage:
**Manage**: treat the underlying infection/inflammation urgently when bacterial disease is possible, manage vertigo briefly when needed, and begin hearing/vestibular rehabilitation as the acute phase resolves.

**Also**: use brief vestibular suppressants only during the most disabling acute period, then mobilize and begin vestibular rehabilitation. Treat bacterial otogenic or meningitic disease urgently with IV antibiotics and source control as indicated. **Key trap**: steroids/antivirals follow the specific hearing-loss or viral syndrome rather than being automatic for every acute vertigo presentation. **Post-meningitic ossification and imaging**: Up to 35% of children develop hearing loss after bacterial meningitis, and up to 70% of those with SNHL show some labyrinthine ossification, which can begin within days to 3 weeks; pneumococcus causes more SNHL, but ossification rates do not differ by organism. Steroids at diagnosis were associated with less labyrinthitis ossificans in one study. Use heavily T2-weighted MRI to show early fibrous obliteration that CT misses, and expedite implant evaluation (bilateral simultaneous implantation may be offered). Cryptococcal meningitis, the most common fungal meningitis, causes SNHL in up to 30%, with organisms in the IAC and modiolus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 155, p 2360-2362) **Serous labyrinthitis and congenital window defects**: With AOM, do tympanocentesis, myringotomy and a tube, and give parenteral therapy covering pneumococcus, H. influenzae and Moraxella. Labyrinthectomy is never indicated for serous labyrinthitis. Suspect a congenital perilymphatic/CSF fistula when a child with otitis has mixed loss, vertigo or nystagmus. In Pittsburgh, 64% of children explored for fistula had otitis media, and 93% of those had a fistula. CT shows an inner- or middle-ear anomaly (e.g., Mondini, large vestibular aqueduct) in only about half. Once the ear is dry, explore, and pack both windows with temporalis muscle or connective tissue even if no leak is seen. Typical findings are a laterally facing round window, a deformed stapes or a window fissure. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt is an option for refractory leaks. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 798-799) **Suppurative and chronic labyrinthitis**: Suppurative disease presents with sudden vertigo, vomiting, deep pain and severe SNHL. Nystagmus first beats toward the affected ear and then away once function is lost. MRI shows the labyrinthitis, CT shows predisposing defects, and CSF is normal without meningitis. Facial palsy, meningitis and later cerebellar abscess may follow. Treat with myringotomy and a tube, a cortical mastoidectomy for osteitis, or a modified radical mastoidectomy for cholesteatoma or CSOM, plus gram-negative coverage (Pseudomonas, Proteus). Perform labyrinthectomy only for complete loss of function or meningeal spread despite antibiotics. Delay major surgery until meningitis is controlled. Chronic labyrinthitis usually comes from a cholesteatoma fistula of the lateral semicircular canal, with slowly progressive loss. Recurrent meningitis needs CT and MRI to look for an inner-to-middle-ear defect. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 799-801)
canonical_layers.operate: Source control may require mastoid/middle-ear surgery when suppurative disease or cholesteatoma drives labyrinthine infection.
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: vestibular neuritis should not cause a new cochlear hearing loss; that clue changes localization.

New hearing loss is the branch point: pure vestibular neuritis should not cause it. Suppurative labyrinthitis is an otologic/intracranial emergency and may permanently destroy hearing and vestibular function.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Sound- or pressure-induced vertigo/oscillopsia, autophony, internal body-sound amplification and an apparent low-frequency conductive gap with intact middle ear suggest a third-window syndrome. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Observe mild symptoms and counsel trigger avoidance; consider surgical plugging/resurfacing for disabling, physiologically confirmed syndrome after excluding mimics such as patulous ET and ossicular disease.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Superior Canal Dehiscence. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Third-window disease can mimic conductive hearing loss with a normal middle ear. Symptoms + physiology + dedicated CT must agree before surgery.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Mechanism**: superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome (SCDS) arises from a true bony defect over the superior semicircular canal that forms a third mobile window. **Qualifying symptoms (2021 Bárány Society criteria)**: bone-conduction hyperacusis, sound- or pressure-induced vertigo/oscillopsia time-locked to the stimulus, or pulsatile tinnitus. **Key trap**: thin bone or an apparent defect on CT alone is not enough. Imaging can overcall dehiscence, and symptoms and physiology must agree. **Direction of evoked eye movements**: loud sound, positive canal pressure, or Valsalva against pinched nostrils excite the affected superior semicircular canal (upward slow phase, upper pole of the eye torting away from that ear). Negative canal pressure, Valsalva against a closed glottis, or jugular compression give the opposite movement. Patients may hear their eye movements, pulse, or a tuning fork on the lateral malleolus. Weber lateralizes to the affected ear. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2529)
canonical_layers.localize: **Physiologic hallmark**: the dehiscence sits in the plane of the superior semicircular canal, so eye movements provoked by sound or pressure changes occur in that canal's plane. This distinguishes SCDS from other third-window or conductive-hearing-loss conditions. **Supporting non-imaging findings**: a low-frequency air-bone gap with normal middle ear function (normal tympanogram, present acoustic reflexes) on audiometry, or abnormally low cervical VEMP thresholds/elevated ocular VEMP amplitudes on the affected side.
canonical_layers.workup: **Diagnostic criteria (2021 Bárány Society, requires ALL)**: (1) at least one qualifying third-window symptom; (2) at least one supporting physiologic sign -- sound/pressure-evoked superior-canal-plane eye movements, abnormally low-frequency or negative bone-conduction thresholds, or enhanced VEMP responses (low cVEMP threshold/high oVEMP amplitude); (3) high-resolution temporal bone CT reconstructed in and orthogonal to the superior canal plane showing a defect; and (4) no better alternative explanation. **Key trap**: a low-frequency air-bone gap with normal tympanometry/reflexes can suggest the mechanism, but is not itself a substitute for the consensus physiologic criteria. **Interpretation note**: interpret VEMPs using laboratory-specific norms. **Imaging and objective tests**: standard 1-mm temporal bone CT overcalls dehiscence because of partial volume. Use 0.5-mm collimated scans reformatted in the plane of the superior semicircular canal (Pöschl) and perpendicular to it (Stenver), and never diagnose from CT alone. Supporting findings are lowered cVEMP thresholds, enlarged oVEMP amplitudes and bone conduction thresholds below 0 dB, producing an air-bone gap despite normal air conduction. 'Near-dehiscence' with these objective findings can be treated like true dehiscence. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2530) **VEMP numbers**: In dehiscence, cervical VEMP thresholds are abnormally low (this text uses 65 dB HL or less, versus the 85-95 dB HL normally needed). In confirmed cases the mean threshold was about 67 dB (plus or minus 10) vs about 82 dB HL (plus or minus 5) in unaffected ears. Cervical VEMP tests the saccule and inferior vestibular nerve, and ocular VEMP tests the utricle and superior vestibular nerve, so together they can show which nerve division is involved. For example, ocular VEMP is lost after superior vestibular nerve section while cervical VEMP remains. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2032)
canonical_layers.manage: **Asymptomatic**: observe patients with an incidental radiographic dehiscence and no symptoms. **Symptomatic, non-surgical**: counsel symptomatic patients to avoid known triggers (loud sound exposure, straining/Valsalva maneuvers) where practical. **Surgical threshold**: reserve surgery for patients with symptoms that are functionally impairing and whose findings meet the full diagnostic criteria, since symptom severity does not always correlate with dehiscence size on imaging.
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: functionally impairing SCDS symptoms meeting full diagnostic criteria, refractory to observation/trigger avoidance. **Setup**: choose middle fossa craniotomy (direct visualization, better for anteriorly located or larger dehiscences) or transmastoid approach (less invasive, avoids craniotomy, but more limited exposure of the canal) based on dehiscence location and surgeon experience. **Key steps**: repair by plugging the canal lumen, resurfacing the bony defect over an intact membranous canal, or a combination. Plugging obliterates canal function and is generally more durable; resurfacing preserves canal function but has a higher reported recurrence rate. **Danger structures**: the superior semicircular canal itself (inadvertent opening into the membranous labyrinth risks sensorineural hearing loss), the facial nerve, and the temporal lobe dura during middle fossa exposure. **Failure mode**: repairing a radiographically obvious dehiscence in a patient whose symptoms do not actually match the third-mobile-window pattern, or in whom VEMP/audiometric findings do not corroborate the diagnosis -- symptoms may then persist post-repair from a different, unaddressed cause. **Postoperative plan**: expect resolution of sound/pressure-induced vertigo when the correct ear is repaired. Monitor hearing, since surgery itself carries a real risk of sensorineural hearing loss. **Repair options**: middle fossa plugging is standard. Transmastoid plugging has more failures (better for vestibular than auditory symptoms) and suits patients who are poor middle fossa candidates. Round window plugging is generally not appropriate because it does not treat the third window, objective improvement is rare, and hearing often worsens. A tympanostomy tube can help mainly pressure-induced symptoms. Posterior canal dehiscence (at the jugular bulb) and lateral canal dehiscence (cholesteatoma, surgery) also occur. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2531) **Plugging outcomes and intraoperative ECochG**: Plugging is more reliable than resurfacing. It relieves vertigo and lowers superior semicircular canal VOR gain by about 44%, with a modest 10% fall in ipsilateral posterior canal gain. Hearing improvement is less predictable than relief of the auditory symptoms. The ECochG SP/AP ratio is usually high, rises further when the dehiscence is exposed, and normalizes right after an adequate plug, so it can guide surgery. Do not suction perilymph at the defect. Plug with fascia or periosteum supported by bone chips or bone pate. Use a transmastoid route for poor craniotomy candidates. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, pp 2553-2554)
canonical_layers.teach: SCDS requires concordant third-window symptoms, a qualifying physiologic finding and high-resolution canal-plane CT, with other diagnoses excluded. An air-bone gap is a clue, not a stand-alone consensus criterion; CT dehiscence alone should not trigger surgery.

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Recurrent painful unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling in a child, often beginning in early childhood and resolving by adolescence, suggests this condition after excluding suppurative infection, stones and autoimmune disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Acute episodes are treated with hydration, massage, analgesia and antibiotics only when bacterial infection is suspected. Recurrent severe disease may benefit from sialendoscopy with irrigation/dilation.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Most children improve with age. The management goal is reducing morbidity while preserving the gland, not escalating every recurrence to surgery.

canonical_layers.recognize: Recurrent painful unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling in a child, often beginning in early childhood and resolving by adolescence, suggests juvenile recurrent parotitis after excluding suppurative infection, stones and autoimmune disease. **Key epidemiology**: It is the second most common pediatric inflammatory salivary disorder after mumps. Boys are affected more than girls; episodes start by age 1–2 years, recur every 3–4 months, and the diagnosis is usually made at ages 3–6 years. Reported associations include IgA or IgG3 deficiency, early juvenile Sjögren syndrome, and HIV (about 20% of HIV-infected children). Glands can lose 50–80% of function, even though most cases resolve at puberty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1163) **JRP and its mimics**: JRP has a bimodal onset (peaks at about 3-6 and about 10 years), nonpurulent secretions from Stensen duct, elevated serum amylase, and sialectasis on ultrasound, MR sialography or sialography. Juvenile Sjögren syndrome usually presents as recurrent parotid swelling (parotid involvement in about 70%) rather than dry eyes and mouth. Check ESR, ANA, RF, anti-SSA/SSB and immunoglobulins, and consider a labial or parotid biopsy. Pneumoparotitis is air insufflated up Stensen duct, either self-induced or from wind instruments, glassblowing, diving, spirometry or coughing. Diagnose it with ultrasound, plain film or CT, treat it by removing the trigger, and reserve duct ligation for chronic cases. Postoperative 'anesthesia mumps' is transient gland swelling after surgery that rarely threatens the airway. (Cummings 7e, Ch 205, pp 3045-3047)
canonical_layers.localize: The disorder affects intraparotid ductal/acinar function and can show sialectatic change; recurrent episodes do not necessarily imply a fixed obstructing stone.
canonical_layers.workup: Ultrasound is useful to confirm parotid changes and exclude abscess/stone. Broader autoimmune/immunologic testing is selective for atypical, severe or systemic presentations.
canonical_layers.manage: Acute episodes are treated with hydration, massage, analgesia and antibiotics only when bacterial infection is suspected. Recurrent severe disease may benefit from sialendoscopy with irrigation/dilation. **Sialendoscopy for JRP**: In pediatric sialendoscopy series, JRP is the leading indication (about 69%), followed by stones (about 15%). Ductal perforation is the most common complication. Thresholds for scoping range from two episodes in 6 months to two in a year. Endoscopy typically shows a pale white duct lining that has lost its normal vascular pattern. In a meta-analysis, about 73% had no further episodes after ductal irrigation with steroid (with or without antibiotic). Most children still outgrow JRP by puberty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 205, pp 3040, 3046)
canonical_layers.operate: Sialendoscopy is gland-preserving and favored over parotidectomy for refractory disease; identify stenotic/inflammatory ducts and avoid unnecessary gland sacrifice. **When surgery is needed**: Recurrent parotitis usually stops by puberty with hydration, sialogogues, massage, and sialendoscopy in selected cases. In the rare refractory case that needs gland surgery, a total rather than superficial parotidectomy is generally required, because leftover deep-lobe tissue keeps getting infected. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1282)
canonical_layers.teach: Most children improve with age. The management goal is reducing morbidity while preserving the gland, not escalating every recurrence to surgery.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Recurrent vertigo, motion sensitivity or visually induced dizziness with migraine history/features can represent this condition even when headache is absent during some attacks. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use migraine education, sleep/exercise/trigger management and preventive or acute migraine therapy tailored to attack frequency and comorbidity. Vestibular rehabilitation can help persistent motion/visual sensitivity.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Vestibular Migraine. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: The pearl is that normal interictal vestibular testing does not rule out vestibular migraine. Treat the migraine network and avoid forcing every dizzy patient into a peripheral lesion.

canonical_layers.recognize: Recurrent vertigo, motion sensitivity or visually induced dizziness with migraine history/features can represent vestibular migraine even when headache is absent during some attacks. **Epidemiology and timing numbers**: Migraine affects about 25% of women, 15% of men and 5% of children, and the female excess in vestibular migraine may reach 4:1, with mean onset in middle age. Vertigo comes before the headache in only about 15%. It occurs during the headache in about 47% and in the headache-free interval in about 36%. Motion sickness is much more common with migraine (about 51% vs 20% with tension headache). The lifetime prevalence of migraine is 56% in Ménière disease versus 25% in controls. At about 9 years of follow-up, the diagnosis was confirmed with a positive predictive value of 85%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2537-2540)
canonical_layers.localize: This is a central sensory-network disorder rather than a fixed peripheral vestibular lesion; exam and vestibular testing may be normal between episodes.
canonical_layers.workup: Diagnosis is clinical after confirming compatible migraine/vestibular episodes and excluding alternative peripheral or central causes when red flags exist. Do not order extensive vestibular imaging/labs solely because dizziness is persistent.
canonical_layers.manage: Use migraine education, sleep/exercise/trigger management and preventive or acute migraine therapy tailored to attack frequency and comorbidity. Vestibular rehabilitation can help persistent motion/visual sensitivity. **Prophylaxis doses and drug-class details**: Start with lifestyle measures (migraine diet, regular sleep, aerobic exercise), and add prophylaxis if symptoms persist after 6-8 weeks. Typical starting and target doses: propranolol 60 mg/day to 120-180 mg/day. Nortriptyline 5-10 mg/day up to 50-200 mg/day (less sedating than amitriptyline, which is 10-25 mg at bedtime up to 50-100 mg). Venlafaxine 37.5 mg/day to 75-225 mg/day. Gabapentin 300 mg/day to 1200-2400 mg/day in divided doses. Zonisamide 25 mg/day up to 100-400 mg/day, often better tolerated than topiramate. Only beta-blockers without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity work (acebutolol does not). Verapamil has a modest effect, and diltiazem has none. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2538, 2540)
canonical_layers.operate: There is no operative treatment for vestibular migraine. Advanced decision-making is recognizing comorbid BPPV/Ménière disease or a central red flag rather than escalating to ablative vestibular surgery.
canonical_layers.teach: The pearl is that normal interictal vestibular testing does not rule out vestibular migraine. Treat the migraine network and avoid forcing every dizzy patient into a peripheral lesion.
