candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Hypernasality, nasal air emission and reduced oral pressure after cleft/palatal or neuromuscular disease suggests velopharyngeal dysfunction; distinguish structural insufficiency from mislearning/articulation errors. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Speech therapy treats articulation/mislearning but not a structural gap. Surgery or prosthetic management is selected for persistent structural dysfunction according to closure pattern and airway risk.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Velopharyngeal Insufficiency. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Treat the closure pattern, not just the word 'hypernasal.' A good speech operation can be a bad sleep operation if airway risk is ignored.

canonical_layers.recognize: Hypernasality, nasal air emission and reduced oral pressure after cleft/palatal or neuromuscular disease suggests velopharyngeal dysfunction; distinguish structural insufficiency from mislearning/articulation errors. **Phoneme-specific VPD and other bedside clues**: In phoneme-specific (mislearned) VPD, the child closes the port for most oral sounds but makes /s/, /sh/, /z/ (rarely /f/) as a nasal fricative. It is often mistaken for global VPD, it responds to articulation therapy, and it rarely needs surgery. Hyponasality turns /m/ into /b/, /n/ into /d/ and /ng/ into /g/. Facial grimacing (pinching the nares on oral sounds) is a compensatory sign of VPD. Speech that worsens as a task is repeated over minutes suggests fatigue, as in myasthenia gravis. VPD follows about 1 in 1500 adenoidectomies. Test any child with VPD of unknown cause for 22q11.2 deletion (FISH or chromosomal microarray, FISH can miss deletions under about 40 kb). In one series of VPD after adenotonsillectomy, more than half carried the deletion, 28% without obvious features. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2851-2853)
canonical_layers.localize: Closure depends on palate length/motion, lateral pharyngeal-wall motion and posterior wall; gap pattern and size determine procedure selection.
canonical_layers.workup: Perceptual speech evaluation plus nasendoscopy and/or videofluoroscopy defines closure pattern. Sleep history matters because pharyngeal surgery can worsen OSA. **Instrumental assessment specifics**: Nasometry calculates nasalance, the ratio of nasal to total (nasal plus oral) acoustic energy. Multiview videofluoroscopy needs frontal and base views because the lateral view misses a unilateral gap. Nasendoscopy is done after topical decongestant and 2% lidocaine, through the middle meatus, viewing the port from above during recorded connected speech. It requires some cooperation, and adding laryngoscopy screens for compensatory vocal nodules. A Passavant ridge occurs in about 20% of people and usually sits below the plane of closure. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1962, 1966-1967) **Nasometry and aerodynamics**: nasalance is nasal acoustic energy divided by nasal plus oral energy. Hypernasality is usually perceived above about 25–33% on a passage with no nasal sounds, and hyponasality below about 50% on nasal sentences. Use regional or dialect norms, because nasalance correlates only moderately with perceived hypernasality. High nasal airflow with low intraoral pressure on pressure consonants indicates velopharyngeal incompetence. (Cummings 7e, Ch 55, p 822) **Choosing VPD tests**: Perceptual speech analysis by an experienced speech pathologist is still the gold standard. Nasometry (nasal-to-oral sound energy ratio against normative passages) and pressure-flow testing are indirect measures. Speech endoscopy is the usual first-line direct study. Most children over about 3 years tolerate it. Pass the scope through the middle meatus rather than along the floor so it sits high in the nasopharynx, and record audio with the video. Speech videofluoroscopy needs at least two, ideally three, views (lateral, frontal, and en face such as Towne or base view), costs radiation, and can miss small fistulas. Closure during swallowing tells you nothing about closure for speech. More than 40% of children with VPD are also dysphonic, which can hide mild VPD. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2853-2854)
canonical_layers.manage: Speech therapy treats articulation/mislearning but not a structural gap. Surgery or prosthetic management is selected for persistent structural dysfunction according to closure pattern and airway risk. **Submucous cleft rarely needs surgery**: Only a minority of children with an overt submucous cleft (bifid uvula, zona pellucida, notched posterior hard palate) develop VPI. When surgery is needed, gap size, palate length, lateral wall motion and closure pattern guide the choice. The Furlow Z-plasty is the most-reported repair, with pharyngeal flap or intravelar veloplasty as alternatives. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1167) **Prosthetic management**: A speech bulb obturator fills the velopharyngeal port when the velum is too short. A palatal lift holds a long but poorly moving velum up and back, typically in neurologically impaired patients with poor timing and coordination. Prostheses can be tuned under nasendoscopy and suit poor surgical candidates. Drawbacks are frequent refitting as the child grows, poor tolerance, and loss of the device. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1967-1968) **Prosthetic options**: A palatal lift pushes a palate of adequate length up and back, and a speech bulb (acrylic obturator) fills the port for a short or immobile palate. Gradual bulb reduction can sometimes wean the patient as wall motion improves. Prostheses hang on the maxillary teeth, so they need adequate dentition and a cooperative child. They cannot be used during active orthodontics, with loose deciduous teeth or during rapid maxillary expansion. They suit adolescents and adults, poor surgical candidates, temporary VPD after stroke or brain injury, and patients with OSA, because the device comes out at night. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2855-2856) **Awake posterior pharyngeal wall augmentation in adults**: for partial or unilateral VPI (after stroke, cancer resection or radiation) when open palatal surgery is not appropriate. Complete or bilateral palatal weakness is a contraindication. With a transnasal scope, map the gap dynamically, then inject submucosally at the level of Passavant ridge (transnasally, or perorally with a bent needle) as superficially as possible, through as few sites as possible because each adds extrusion risk, slightly overinjecting. Trial a temporary hyaluronic acid or CMC gel first, then calcium hydroxylapatite (about 12 months, repeatable). Aspirate before injecting laterally to avoid the carotid. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 63, p 549-552)
canonical_layers.operate: Pharyngeal flap, sphincter pharyngoplasty, palatal lengthening/Furlow-type procedures and augmentation solve different patterns. Preserve an airway appropriate to the patient's baseline OSA risk. **Closure-pattern frequencies and 22q11 safety**: closure patterns are coronal (about 55%), sagittal (10–15%), circular (10–20%) and circular with a Passavant ridge (15–20%). Give at least 3–6 months of speech therapy to correct compensatory articulation before surgery. Severe cases can be repaired as early as about age 4. Before a pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty in 22q11 deletion, palpate the posterior pharyngeal wall and consider MRA, because the internal carotids can be medialized. Nasometry adds objective resonance data. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 624) **22q11.2 deletion before pharyngeal surgery**: 22q11.2 deletion is the most common genetic cause of VPI, and up to about 8% of children with isolated cleft palate carry it. About 93% of deletions are de novo, and TBX1 is the key gene. Medially displaced, tortuous internal carotid arteries in the posterior pharyngeal wall are a recognized hazard, so many surgeons image the vessels (e.g., MRA) before a pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty. The syndrome also brings cardiac defects (up to 85%), immune and calcium problems, and a higher rate of adult psychiatric illness. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 54–55) **Medialized carotids in 22q11.2 deletion**: Velocardiofacial syndrome (22q11.2 microdeletion, diagnosed by FISH or microarray) is the most common syndrome with a palatal anomaly as a key feature, although only about 9% have an overt cleft. The internal carotid arteries may run medially behind the posterior pharyngeal wall, so image the course of the vessels before a pharyngeal flap, sphincter pharyngoplasty or tonsil surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Malformations of the Mouth and Pharynx: Orofacial Clefts and Related Syndromes", p 1170) **Pharyngeal flap: airway safety and technique**: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the most common problem complicating recovery from a pharyngeal flap. Remove enlarged tonsils and adenoids first and wait 4-6 weeks. In retrognathic children, especially those who needed a tracheotomy in infancy, get a sleep study and consider waiting for growth. Otherwise the flap may need takedown, CPAP or tracheotomy. The superiorly based flap is raised on prevertebral fascia with its base near the C1 arch and is sized to the gap. A flap that is too narrow leaves VPI, and one that is too wide or whose ports scar down causes hyponasality and OSA. Poor lateral wall motion before surgery is not a contraindication. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1968) **Small gaps: augmentation and injection**: For small gaps, an obstructing flap is excessive. A rolled pharyngeal flap (muscle rolled into a bulge under replaced mucosa) or posterior wall injection (autologous fat, collagen, hydroxyapatite) suits gaps of no more than about 2 mm AP, or tenuous closure such as in wind instrument players. Injected materials last only about 3-6 months, though the speech benefit can persist. None is FDA approved for this site. Teflon is abandoned because of infection, granuloma, migration and embolic risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1968-1969) **Sphincter pharyngoplasty, Furlow and revision**: Sphincter pharyngoplasty transposes superiorly based palatopharyngeus myomucosal flaps into a transverse incision at the level of closure. It suits poor lateral wall motion or deep lateral recesses when central closure is present, and it carries much lower OSA risk than a pharyngeal flap. Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty rebuilds the levator sling and lengthens the palate, mainly for submucous cleft. A failed flap can be redone 6-12 months later, lined with nasal mucosa flaps from the soft palate. Reassess resonance objectively 3-6 months after any VPI operation. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1969) **Matching the operation to the gap**: Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty or intravelar veloplasty re-orient a longitudinal levator. In the Furlow, both myomucosal flaps are posteriorly based and both mucosal flaps anteriorly based. A superiorly based pharyngeal flap fills the midline and suits sagittal or circular patterns with good lateral wall motion. Sphincter pharyngoplasty (lateral myomucosal flaps inset at the level of maximal palatal excursion) suits coronal or circular patterns with reasonable palatal motion, and narrower flaps with less overlap are used when the palate moves well. A large gap with poor wall motion ('black hole') may need Furlow plus sphincter pharyngoplasty. Posterior wall augmentation (fat, hyaluronic acid, calcium hydroxylapatite, or a rolled pharyngeal flap) is only for a small central gap and often does not last. A randomized trial found no outcome difference between pharyngeal flap and sphincter pharyngoplasty. Every procedure needs postoperative airway monitoring, and CPAP can bridge the airway while edema settles. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2856-2858)
canonical_layers.teach: Treat the closure pattern, not just the word 'hypernasal.' A good speech operation can be a bad sleep operation if airway risk is ignored.

candidates.canonical_topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Early severe CRS, nasal polyposis, chronic wet cough, bronchiectasis, recurrent otitis or neonatal respiratory history should raise CF or PCD rather than isolated idiopathic CRS. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use aggressive saline/topical therapy and disease-specific pulmonary management. Antibiotics are culture/phenotype driven. Surgery may improve drainage/topical access but cannot correct the underlying clearance defect.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: When CRS starts early and the lungs/ears are involved, think mucociliary disease. The sinus operation treats consequences, not the genetic mechanism.

canonical_layers.recognize: Early severe CRS, nasal polyposis, chronic wet cough, bronchiectasis, recurrent otitis or neonatal respiratory history should raise CF or PCD rather than isolated idiopathic CRS. **PCD versus CF clues**: PCD is autosomal recessive (about 1 in 15,000–30,000, likely underdiagnosed). Kartagener syndrome is the triad of bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and situs inversus. Suspect PCD with nasal congestion from birth, chronic wet cough, and severe recurrent otitis and sinusitis. Unlike CF, clubbing and nasal polyps are uncommon. Associations include complex congenital heart disease, polycystic kidney, biliary atresia, hydrocephalus, and infertility. Screening uses nasal or exhaled nitric oxide (low in PCD, often high in asthma) or the saccharin transit test. Ciliary ultrastructure or function studies confirm the diagnosis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Pulmonology", p 229–230)
canonical_layers.localize: Abnormal mucus composition or mucociliary clearance creates diffuse upper- and lower-airway disease; sinus disease is part of a systemic airway phenotype.
canonical_layers.workup: Coordinate sweat/genetic testing for CF or specialized ciliary/nasal nitric oxide/genetic assessment for PCD when suspected. CT/endoscopy define sinonasal burden but do not establish the systemic diagnosis. **CF diagnostics and numbers**: CF is autosomal recessive. About 1 in 25 white individuals are carriers, incidence is about 1 in 3,000, and ΔF508 is by far the most common variant. US newborn screening measures immunoreactive trypsinogen, with or without CFTR variant testing (sensitivity and specificity near 99%), followed by a confirmatory sweat chloride test by pilocarpine iontophoresis. A level of 60 mmol/L or higher is diagnostic. The book calls values below 40 normal and 40–60 borderline, and says infants under 6 months above 30 remain at risk. Current CF Foundation criteria call ≤29 unlikely and 30–59 intermediate. Nasal potential difference testing is a specialized adjunct. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Pulmonology", p 227) **Mucociliary and PCD testing (Cummings)**: each ciliated cell has about 200 cilia (9+2 axoneme with dynein arms) beating at 8 to 20 Hz; in vitro the beat frequency is about 8 Hz at room temperature and 12 Hz at 37°C. On the saccharin test (particle on the inferior turbinate), normal transit is about 10 minutes; over 30 minutes is abnormal, and normal transport effectively excludes PCD. Nasal nitric oxide is about 10-fold lower in PCD and is a useful screen from about age 5, but cannot prove or exclude PCD. A beat frequency under about 11 Hz on high-speed video prompts electron microscopy. An abnormal EM is diagnostic, but a normal EM does not exclude PCD. Air-liquid interface culture separates inherited from acquired defects. PCD is mostly autosomal recessive (X-linked forms: RPGR, PIH1D3); more than 30 genes are known, so next-generation sequencing is preferred. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, pp 603-606)
canonical_layers.manage: Use aggressive saline/topical therapy and disease-specific pulmonary management. Antibiotics are culture/phenotype driven. Surgery may improve drainage/topical access but cannot correct the underlying clearance defect. **PCD specifics and surgery**: Missing outer dynein arms are the most common ultrastructural defect. Kartagener's triad (sinusitis, bronchiectasis, situs inversus) occurs in about half of patients. Male infertility from sperm dysmotility and chronic otitis are common. Because the cilia do not clear mucus toward the natural ostium, a standard middle-meatal antrostomy may fail. A gravity-dependent drainage operation (inferior antrostomy or endoscopic medial maxillectomy) can be considered for refractory disease, along with aggressive irrigation, and ear tubes for OME. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 57-58) **Sinus–lung interface in CF**: Pseudomonas aeruginosa from a child's sinus culture should prompt CF evaluation. Choose sinus antibiotics with the lower-airway flora in mind (S. aureus and H. influenzae in younger children, Pseudomonas later; about 80% of adults are colonized). Sinus surgery improves symptoms and quality of life but has not consistently improved lung function or prevented exacerbations, and polyps recur often. Chronic azithromycin and inhaled tobramycin each reduce pulmonary exacerbations. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Pulmonology", p 228–229)
canonical_layers.operate: FESS should create durable, maintainable cavities for irrigation while respecting pediatric anatomy; recurrence is common if postoperative topical therapy is not sustained. **CF sinus surgery precautions**: almost all CF patients have pansinusitis, and about 10% have obstructive polyps. Operate for obstruction, mucocele, refractory pain or fever, fungal disease, or pulmonary exacerbations linked to sinus disease; it is not curative. Correct vitamin K deficiency before surgery, because fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption raises bleeding risk. Keep anesthesia short (aim for under about 1 hour) because retained pulmonary secretions make long anesthetics risky. Preserve landmarks, consider wide antrostomy or endoscopic medial maxillectomy for irrigation access, and plan inpatient recovery with aggressive irrigation and debridement. A sweat chloride above about 60 mmol/L is diagnostic. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 555–556)
canonical_layers.teach: When CRS starts early and the lungs/ears are involved, think mucociliary disease. The sinus operation treats consequences, not the genetic mechanism.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. Persistent dysphonia with reduced mucosal wave, stiffness, spindle gap or a linear furrow despite otherwise normal mobility suggests sulcus/scar. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Voice therapy addresses compensatory hyperfunction but does not restore missing lamina propria. Injection/augmentation or scar-directed phonosurgery is individualized because predictable restoration of normal mucosal wave is difficult.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Vocal Fold Sulcus / Scar. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Scar is a material-property problem, not simply a gap. A perfectly medialized stiff fold may still vibrate poorly.

canonical_layers.recognize: Persistent dysphonia with reduced mucosal wave, stiffness, spindle gap or a linear furrow despite otherwise normal mobility suggests sulcus/scar. **Ford sulcus types**: these are three distinct entities, not grades. Type 1 is a physiologic sulcus (often with atrophy, minimal dysphonia). Type 2 is sulcus vergeture, with epithelium adherent to the ligament along the fold. It is likely developmental and familial cases are all type 2. Type 3 is a focal epithelial-lined pit, likely ruptured cyst, often with cyst, fibrous mass, or mucosal bridge (diplophonia). Subepithelial hydrodissection maps the defect. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Vocal Fold Scar and Sulcus Deformities of the Vocal Fold", p 207)
canonical_layers.localize: The lesion disrupts the superficial lamina propria/vocal-ligament interface, impairing pliability even when gross glottic closure is acceptable.
canonical_layers.workup: High-quality stroboscopy is essential to characterize mucosal-wave loss, closure and contralateral compensation. Voice assessment defines functional burden; imaging rarely diagnoses superficial scar. **Sulcus classification**: type I is a physiologic groove into the superficial lamina propria. Type II (sulcus vergeture) has loss of SLP with mucosa adherent to the vocal ligament. Type III (sulcus vocalis) extends into the ligament or deeper. Voice is often worse than the exam suggests. Stroboscopy shows reduced mucosal wave, and microlaryngoscopy with palpation may be needed for diagnosis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 100)
canonical_layers.manage: Voice therapy addresses compensatory hyperfunction but does not restore missing lamina propria. Injection/augmentation or scar-directed phonosurgery is individualized because predictable restoration of normal mucosal wave is difficult. **Iatrogenic postoperative dysphonia**: this usually follows stripping or vaporization, with adherence of mucosa to ligament or a margin divot. First-line treatment is voice building rather than rest: vigorous singing across the full range for about 10 minutes, 2–3 times a day, using /oo/ and starting from whatever pitch works. It can help even more than a year out. Wait 9–12 months before revision. Remove an iatrogenic granuloma only if it persists beyond about 6 months. Limited elevation of mucosa along a line of adherence can relieve diplophonia, whereas collagen injection gives only modest, inconsistent gains. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 885)
canonical_layers.operate: Set realistic goals: improve closure and/or pliability without creating additional scar. Avoid repeated aggressive epithelial manipulation in a stiff fold. **Gray minithyrotomy access**: it reaches the subepithelial plane of the membranous fold without an epithelial incision, through a 2-3 cm neck incision with microlaryngoscopic video guidance. A fine needle through the midline thyroid cartilage localizes the glottis, then a 1-3 mm drill tunnel is made about 3-5 mm off midline, angled along the fold's long axis rather than perpendicular to the lamina. Tympanoplasty instruments release the adhesion and create a pocket confined to the scar. It does not treat epithelium and gives little medialization. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 56, p 487-490) **Gray minithyrotomy grafting and recovery**: implant fat strips (8-15 mm long, about 1-2 mL per fold), and do not undercorrect, since too little fat is the usual cause of failure. Fascia, perichondrium and acellular dermis have also been used. Pinhole epithelial perforations are acceptable, but a large tear means stopping and returning after healing. Expect about a week of voice rest and roughly 1 month of phonatory recovery. Late deterioration is blamed on poor fat-graft survival. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 56, p 489-492)
canonical_layers.teach: Scar is a material-property problem, not simply a gap. A perfectly medialized stiff fold may still vibrate poorly.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the ENT service. Oral ulceration, bullae, white/red lesions, xerostomia, periodontal change and exposed necrotic bone can reflect systemic autoimmune, infectious, hematologic, metabolic or medication-related disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat the underlying disorder with the appropriate specialty while addressing pain, infection, oral hygiene, xerostomia and nutrition. Persistent or suspicious red/white/ulcerative lesions still need malignancy exclusion.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Oral Manifestations of Systemic Disease. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: oral mucosa is a window into systemic disease, but a systemic explanation never excuses failure to exclude cancer when the lesion is persistent or atypical.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Oral Manifestations of Systemic Diseases

canonical_layers.recognize: Oral ulceration, bullae, white/red lesions, xerostomia, periodontal change and exposed necrotic bone can reflect systemic autoimmune, infectious, hematologic, metabolic or medication-related disease. **Oral hairy leukoplakia**: corrugated white plaques on the lateral tongue that do not scrape off, caused by Epstein-Barr virus and almost always a marker of immunosuppression (most often HIV). Confirm with biopsy and EBV in situ hybridization, test for HIV, and expect regression with antiretroviral therapy; it is not premalignant. **Color clues to systemic disease**: a blue-gray gingival line (Burton line) means lead poisoning. Perioral and labial melanotic macules suggest Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (GI hamartomatous polyps). Diffuse mucosal hyperpigmentation suggests Addison disease. Mucosal telangiectasias suggest HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu). Generalized pallor suggests anemia or thalassemia, and generalized redness suggests polycythemia or liver failure. Small yellow papules are Fordyce granules (ectopic sebaceous glands, normal). Black hairy tongue is elongated filiform papillae. Black-brown discoloration can follow bismuth or arsenic. **Amyloidosis**: the tongue is the most common head and neck site (macroglossia). Congo red staining shows apple-green birefringence. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 187, 194) **HIV oral disease in children**: About half of HIV-infected patients have an oral complaint at diagnosis. In children the common findings are candidiasis (which can mark antiretroviral failure), recurrent HSV or large aphthous ulcers lasting more than a month, and bilateral parotid enlargement, whereas hairy leukoplakia and Kaposi sarcoma are uncommon. In one study, oral Candida was the earliest sign of HIV in infants younger than 15 months. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1269) **GI, polyposis and nutritional clues**: Crohn disease causes cobblestoned buccal mucosa, deep linear ulcers, lip swelling and mucosal tags. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome causes flat brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa. Gardner syndrome causes jaw osteomas, supernumerary or unerupted teeth and odontomas. Plummer-Vinson syndrome is iron deficiency, glossitis and dysphagia from esophageal webs, with a raised risk of pharyngeal and esophageal carcinoma. Niacin deficiency gives a beefy red tongue, riboflavin deficiency a magenta tongue, zinc deficiency hypogeusia, and scurvy a hemorrhagic gingivitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1274) **Hematologic and immunodeficiency clues**: About 10% of leukemias show oral infiltrates, such as spongy gingival hyperplasia (seen in at least a third of children with leukemia), petechiae and ulcers. Oral GVHD (lichenoid lesions) occurs in up to 80% after bone marrow transplant. ITP presents with gingival bleeding and sublingual hematoma. Clues to primary immunodeficiency include severe early periodontitis with tooth loss (leukocyte adhesion deficiency, Chediak-Higashi, Kostmann), a double row of teeth from retained primary teeth plus candidiasis (hyper-IgE syndrome), and conical teeth or hypodontia (ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1276) **Immune-mediated mucosal disease**: lichen planus shows Wickham striae (reticular) or erosive lesions on the buccal mucosa, gingiva and tongue. It carries a small malignant-transformation risk, so recheck erosive lesions. Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies with suprabasal acantholysis and a positive Nikolsky sign. Mucous membrane pemphigoid is subepithelial, causes desquamative gingivitis and can scar the conjunctiva to blindness. Erythema multiforme (often HSV-triggered) causes target skin lesions and crusted lips. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is usually drug-induced. (Cummings 7e, Ch 12, p 193) **Systemic clues in the mouth**: Addison disease causes diffuse mucocutaneous pigmentation (not seen in secondary adrenal insufficiency). Crohn disease causes cobblestoning and deep granulomatous ulcers. Ulcerative colitis can cause pyostomatitis. Dialysis patients get uremic stomatitis and brown tumors (giant cell lesions) from hyperparathyroidism. Pregnancy gingivitis affects about two-thirds of pregnancies, and pyogenic granuloma (pregnancy tumor) under 10%. Leukemia can first present with gingival hyperplasia, bleeding or petechiae. (Cummings 7e, Ch 12, p 190-197) **Vesiculobullous and ulcerative disease (DIF patterns)**: pemphigus vulgaris (anti-desmoglein 3, age 50+) causes suprabasilar acantholysis with a 'tombstone' basal layer and intercellular IgG/C3 ('chicken-wire') on DIF. Mucous membrane pemphigoid is subepithelial with linear basement-membrane IgG/IgA/C3, threatens the eyes and larynx, and is treated with topical steroids, dapsone or systemic immunosuppression. Oral lichen planus shows Wickham striae, Civatte bodies, a T-cell band and fibrinogen on DIF. It is linked to hepatitis C and carries a 0-10% SCC risk (erosive form). Erythema multiforme is triggered mainly by HSV, and also by sulfonamides, anticonvulsants and quinolones, and progresses to SJS/TEN. Aphthous ulcers are minor (under 1 cm, heal within 2 weeks), major (over 1 cm, up to 6 weeks, posterior) or herpetiform (multiple, under 2 mm). Associations include Behçet, Crohn, celiac, PFAPA, Sweet syndrome and B12/folate deficiency. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 36, pp 649-650, 654) **Oral candidiasis forms and treatment threshold**: Four forms: pseudomembranous (thrush, wipes off to raw red base, most common), atrophic/erythematous (red depapillated tongue), angular cheilitis, and hyperplastic (thick plaque that does not wipe off, rarest). Confirm with KOH or PAS. With CD4 over 200 use topical nystatin. Under 200 use systemic fluconazole, watching for azole resistance after repeated courses. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 208) **HIV periodontal disease and oral histoplasmosis**: Linear gingival erythema (fiery marginal band out of proportion to plaque) and necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis strongly suggest HIV. Treat with chlorhexidine, debridement and dental care, and biopsy when bone loss exceeds mucosal disease (lymphoma, bacillary angiomatosis). Oral histoplasmosis (Ohio River valley) produces painful granulomatous ulcers, is AIDS-defining, and needs biopsy/culture and amphotericin or itraconazole. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 208-209) **Lobular capillary hemangioma (pyogenic granuloma)**: A friable, bleeding, noninfectious lobular capillary proliferation of gingiva, lip, tongue or nasal septum, often after trauma and hormonally driven in pregnancy (pregnancy lesions usually regress postpartum). Otherwise excise, cauterize or laser, completely to prevent recurrence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 225)
canonical_layers.localize: Describe the exact oral subsite, mucosal layer/pattern, salivary status, dental/alveolar involvement and whether disease is localized or multisite.
canonical_layers.workup: Medication review, systemic review, dental evaluation and appropriately handled biopsy are central. Suspected immunobullous disease requires the correct perilesional specimen strategy; MRONJ requires exposure history and jaw assessment. **Immunobullous disease: histology and immunofluorescence**: pemphigus vulgaris is intraepithelial (suprabasilar) acantholysis from anti-desmoglein 1/3 antibodies, with a 'row of tombstones' basal layer and Tzanck cells. DIF shows intercellular deposits, serum IIF is positive, and it is often fatal untreated. Mucous membrane (cicatricial) pemphigoid is a subepithelial split with linear basement-membrane DIF and usually negative IIF. It favors the attached gingiva in women in their 50s-60s, and ocular involvement (about 50-70%) can cause symblepharon and blindness, so it needs ophthalmology referral. Bullous pemphigoid affects older adults, is mainly cutaneous, and is rarely oral. The Nikolsky sign is classically positive in pemphigus and can also be positive in mucous membrane pemphigoid. Send perilesional tissue for DIF in Michel medium, not formalin. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 188, 190-191)
canonical_layers.manage: Treat the underlying disorder with the appropriate specialty while addressing pain, infection, oral hygiene, xerostomia and nutrition. Persistent or suspicious red/white/ulcerative lesions still need malignancy exclusion. **Drug-induced gingival overgrowth and stomatitis**: Generalized gingival overgrowth is caused by phenytoin, cyclosporine and calcium channel blockers, as well as leukemia, Sturge-Weber syndrome and hereditary gingival fibromatosis (autosomal dominant, appearing as the permanent teeth erupt). Phenytoin overgrowth appears within months and regresses after the drug is stopped. Heavy metals (lead, bismuth) leave a gingival line. Broad-spectrum antibiotics can cause a beefy, depapillated tongue from Candida overgrowth. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Mouth and Pharynx", p 1305, Ch "Inflammatory Disease of the Mouth and Pharynx", p 1186) **MRONJ risk**: Cummings quotes about 0.4% with oral bisphosphonates for osteoporosis and 5-20% with IV antiresorptive therapy. **Current view**: the AAOMS 2022 position paper gives much lower estimates, under about 0.05% at osteoporosis doses and roughly 1-5% for cancer patients on zoledronic acid or denosumab. Treatment ranges from local debridement to resection, and nonvascularized bone grafts are not recommended. Head and neck cancer patients need dental evaluation and treatment before surgery or radiation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 12, p 189) **Recurrent aphthous stomatitis**: Affects 20-50% of people. Potent topical steroids (0.05% clobetasol or fluocinonide) outperform triamcinolone. Tetracycline rinses reduce ulcer size and pain. Amlexanox 5% paste speeds healing without preventing recurrences. Viscous lidocaine for pain. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 200)
canonical_layers.operate: Operative intervention is selective: biopsy, debridement/source control or management of complications rather than reflex excision of inflammatory disease.
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: oral mucosa is a window into systemic disease, but a systemic explanation never excuses failure to exclude cancer when the lesion is persistent or atypical.
source_basis: Cummings 7e: Oral Manifestations of Systemic Diseases

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. Task-specific strained/strangled voice breaks on voiced speech suggest adductor laryngeal dystonia; breathy breaks on voiceless contexts suggest abductor phenotype. Tremor and muscle-tension dysphonia are common mimics/comorbidities. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Botulinum toxin injection is standard symptomatic treatment for many patients, with dose/muscle/laterality individualized over repeated cycles; voice therapy helps compensatory behaviors but does not cure dystonia.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Spasmodic Dysphonia. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Spasmodic dysphonia is task-specific. Listen to the phonetic context of the break instead of diagnosing every strained voice as dystonia.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Definition**: spasmodic dysphonia (now often termed laryngeal dystonia in the broader movement-disorder literature) is a task-specific focal laryngeal dystonia. **Pattern**: it causes involuntary spasms during specific voicing tasks, classically speech, while other laryngeal tasks (singing, laughing, coughing) can be relatively spared. **Key trap**: this task-specificity is itself a diagnostic clue that distinguishes it from a structural or paralytic voice disorder. **Laryngeal dystonia subtypes**: about 80% of cases are adductor and about 20% abductor, and some are mixed. Two rare forms are adductor breathing dystonia and singer's dystonia. In adductor breathing dystonia the folds close on inspiration, causing stridor and dyspnea, but it is self-limited, does not cause hypoxia, and does not need a surgical airway. Singer's dystonia affects only singing in professional singers and may later spread to speech. Meige syndrome combines blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and torticollis with SD. Sensory tricks (pinching the nose, pressing the occiput or abdomen) and better voicing after a yawn, sneeze, singing or yelling are typical. (Cummings 7e, Ch 57, p 834) **Neurologic dysphonia by pattern**: hypoadducted, weak breathy voice with poor cough suggests myasthenia, muscular dystrophy, Parkinson disease, Shy-Drager (multiple system atrophy), post-polio syndrome, TBI or abductor SD. Strained/staccato hyperfunction suggests adductor SD, pseudobulbar palsy or Huntington disease. Mixed patterns occur in MS, ataxic (cerebellar) dysphonia and ALS. Palatal involvement (VPI) suggests myasthenia, ALS or high vagal paralysis. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 2, p 13)
canonical_layers.localize: **Adductor type** (far more common): strained, strangled, effortful voice with abrupt voice breaks from excessive thyroarytenoid/lateral cricoarytenoid (adductor) muscle activity during vowel production. **Abductor type** (less common): breathy voice breaks from involuntary posterior cricoarytenoid (abductor) spasm during voiceless consonants. **Mixed forms** exist. **Key trap**: a coexisting vocal tremor is common and can be mistaken for essential tremor affecting the voice -- tremor and spasmodic dysphonia often occur together and are treated somewhat differently. **PCA injection route**: rotate the larynx by hand, pass the EMG needle behind the posterior edge of the thyroid lamina and advance it to the cricoid. The alternative is a transcricoid pass. A sniff fires the PCA and produces an EMG burst, and the toxin is given at that point. Adductor injections go through the cricothyroid membrane into the TA-vocalis complex. (Cummings 7e, Ch 57)
canonical_layers.workup: **Diagnosis**: clinical, based on perceptual voice characteristics during connected speech, not sustained vowels alone, since spasms are task-specific. **Also required**: laryngoscopy to exclude a structural cause (mass, paralysis, scar) that could mimic the voice quality. **Board pearl**: a multidisciplinary laryngology/speech-language pathology evaluation is standard, given how easily this is misattributed to a purely psychogenic or functional voice disorder. **Elicitation phrases**: adductor SD worsens on voiced, vowel-initial phrases (count 80-90, 'We eat eggs every day'). Abductor SD worsens on voiceless consonant-vowel transitions (count 60-70, 'The puppy bit the tape'). Symptoms typically worsen with stress and improve with alcohol. Whispering, singing, and laughing are often spared. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, p 106) **Speech tasks during exam**: 'taxi' and other voiceless-consonant words bring out abductor SD breaks. 'kaa' tests palatal lift and closure. 'maa' and /m/, /n/ test nasal resonance for hyper- or hyponasality. The rainbow passage contains every English phoneme and is the standard recorded sample for tracking change. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 2, p 14)
canonical_layers.manage: **First-line**: botulinum toxin injection into the affected laryngeal muscles (thyroarytenoid for adductor type, posterior cricoarytenoid for abductor type). **Effect**: provides temporary (typically 3-4 month) symptomatic relief by weakening the involuntary spasm. **Key trap**: it requires repeat injection indefinitely since it does not address the underlying central dystonic process. **Adjunct**: voice therapy alone is generally insufficient as monotherapy but is a useful adjunct. **Botulinum details**: a typical start for adductor LD is about 1 U per TA-LCA side, in a small volume (0.1 mL) under EMG with a prephonatory burst. For abductor LD, inject one PCA (5–7.5 U) and stage the other side after about 2 weeks because of airway risk. Supraglottic false fold injection (5–7.5 U per side) causes little breathiness but lasts only 8–10 weeks. Contraindications are pregnancy, breastfeeding, myasthenia, and aminoglycosides. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Botulinum Toxin Injection of the Larynx", p 344) **Botulinum toxin outcome numbers**: in adductor SD, TA injection restores about 60–100% of normal function (mean about 90%) for 3–4 months. Side effects are a mild breathy voice for under 2 weeks (about 45%) and choking on liquids for a few days (about 22%). In abductor SD, PCA injection restores about 70% of normal function, with mild dysphagia or exertional stridor as the cost. Supraglottic squeeze that persists despite therapy can be treated by injecting the supraglottic part of the LCA through the thyrohyoid membrane. Avoid injection in pregnancy and lactation, and be cautious in myasthenia, Lambert-Eaton and motor neuron disease. RLN section has been abandoned: at 3 years only 36% kept some benefit and 3% had a normal voice. (Cummings 7e, Ch 57, p 833–834) **Dose range and bilateral versus unilateral injection**: there is no standard dose. Bilateral adductor doses range from about 0.3 to 15 U per TA-LCA complex, but most patients are controlled with 0.625-2.5 U per side. Unilateral injection can give similar relief, usually at a higher dose and for a shorter time. Bilateral PCA injection is usually staggered, although simultaneous injection with unequal doses has been reported as reasonably safe. After the first PCA injection, the dose for the second side is lowered in proportion to the weakness seen. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 39, p 345) **Aftercare and the nonresponder**: patients go home right away with no voice restrictions, but nothing by mouth for 60-90 minutes after laryngeal anesthesia. Warn them about breathiness and dysphagia to liquids after TA-LCA injection, and about dyspnea and stridor after the second PCA side. Failure is usually technical. Antibody resistance is very rare. Test with an antibody assay or a frontalis test injection. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 39, p 344, 348)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: adductor spasmodic dysphonia inadequately controlled by or intolerant of botulinum toxin, or seeking a longer-lasting alternative. **Setup/key steps**: selective laryngeal adductor denervation-reinnervation (interrupting the recurrent laryngeal nerve's adductor branches and reinnervating with a branch of the ansa cervicalis) is the most established surgical alternative. It aims to weaken involuntary adductor spasm while preserving reinnervated muscle tone. Type II thyroplasty (midline laryngoplasty to widen the glottis) is an alternative for adductor-type disease in selected patients. **Danger structures**: the recurrent laryngeal nerve itself is the target of denervation-reinnervation, so precise identification of the adductor branches is essential to avoid unintended vocal fold paralysis instead of the intended selective weakening. **Failure mode**: treating spasmodic dysphonia as a structural problem needing vocal fold surgery rather than a dystonic movement disorder needing neuromodulation (botulinum toxin) or nerve-directed surgery. **Postoperative plan**: voice therapy and staged reassessment, since denervation-reinnervation results evolve over months as reinnervation matures. **SLAD-R outcomes**: selective laryngeal adductor denervation-reinnervation gives favorable voice in more than 90% long term. About 25% still have some breaks and a minority relapse. RLN section was abandoned because of recurrence and worse voice. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 54) **SLAD-R technique**: the operation is bilateral. Through an inferiorly based thyroid cartilage window (keeping a posterior strut with the cricothyroid joint to protect the main RLN and PCA branch), the TA adductor branch is divided distal to the PCA branches and its distal stump is reinnervated with an ansa cervicalis branch (sternohyoid or sternothyroid) using 7-0/8-0 epineural sutures. The LCA branch is cut and a partial LCA myotomy of only 15-30% of the muscle is added. A full myotomy causes a posterior glottic chink, especially in men. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 53, p 464-467) **Laryngeal toxin preparation**: reconstitute the 100 U Botox vial with preservative-free saline to the needed concentration (insert range about 1.25-10 U per 0.1 mL). Inject 0.1 mL per fold (0.2 mL is acceptable and does not threaten the airway). Mix and transfer with a 21 g or larger needle, then inject through an insulated 26-27 g EMG needle. Laryngoscopy-guided injection without EMG needs slightly higher doses. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 39, p 345-347)
canonical_layers.teach: Task-specific voice breaks (worse in connected speech, better singing/laughing) point toward spasmodic dysphonia/laryngeal dystonia, not a structural lesion. Botulinum toxin, not phonosurgery, is first-line. **SLAD-R candidacy and recovery**: the best candidates are young, respond well to botulinum toxin and have little tremor. Contraindications are abductor or mixed SD, functional dysphonia or MTD, relative age over 65, and prominent tremor, which does not improve. The voice is breathy for 3-6 months (like a large bilateral TA toxin dose), and thin-liquid dysphagia is common in the first days. Strength improves by 9-12 months, and over 75% end with a normal voice. True recurrence appears within 12 months and responds to toxin, while persistent breathiness is treated with augmentation. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 53, p 464, 469-470) **The breathy phase is the price of duration**: after injection there are several days of marked weakness, then a 3-4 month plateau of milder weakness that gives the benefit. In adductor SD, the length of the breathy phase roughly tracks the length of benefit, so cutting the dose to shorten breathiness also shortens relief. Supraglottic injection avoids the breathy phase in up to 76% and suits professional voice users. Abductor SD carries the risk of dyspnea instead. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 39, p 344-345)

candidates.canonical_topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the ENT service. Persistent crusting, septal perforation, subglottic stenosis, salivary enlargement, chronic otitis, facial paralysis, oral lesions or cervical adenopathy can be the presenting manifestation of systemic autoimmune, granulomatous, infectious or infiltrative disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Coordinate disease-specific immunologic/infectious/oncologic therapy while treating local functional consequences. Avoid irreversible local surgery during uncontrolled destructive inflammatory disease unless airway or other urgent function requires it.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: When ENT disease appears in multiple unrelated sites, stop creating separate diagnoses and ask whether one systemic process connects them.

canonical_layers.recognize: Persistent crusting, septal perforation, subglottic stenosis, salivary enlargement, chronic otitis, facial paralysis, oral lesions or cervical adenopathy can be the presenting manifestation of systemic autoimmune, granulomatous, infectious or infiltrative disease. **Sarcoidosis in the head and neck**: cervical adenopathy is the most common head and neck presentation (about 25-50%). Laryngeal sarcoid is classically a pale, diffuse supraglottic swelling, especially of the epiglottis. Other sites include the sinonasal tract (crusting, nodules, septal perforation), lacrimal glands, and orbit. Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever) is uveitis, parotid enlargement, facial palsy (about 50%), and fever. Workup includes CXR (bilateral hilar adenopathy), serum ACE, calcium, and biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas. About 40% are asymptomatic at diagnosis. Treat symptomatic or organ-threatening disease with steroids. Intralesional steroid or debulking is used for obstructing laryngeal disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 204-205, 241) **Syphilis**: primary syphilis is a painless chancre with adenopathy. Secondary syphilis comes about 4-6 weeks later with rash, mucous patches, and condylomata lata. Tertiary syphilis brings gummas, neurosyphilis, and aortitis. Otosyphilis can cause fluctuating or sudden SNHL with vertigo and positive Hennebert or Tullio signs. Congenital syphilis: Hutchinson triad (notched incisors, interstitial keratitis, deafness), mulberry molars, saddle nose, and Clutton joints. Screen with RPR or VDRL and confirm with a treponemal test (FTA-ABS). Penicillin G treats all stages, with steroids added for otologic disease. Desensitize penicillin-allergic patients when penicillin is essential. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 242) **Giant cell arteritis**: it is the most common systemic vasculitis. It typically affects patients over 50, usually women, and about half have polymyalgia rheumatica. Features are new headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw or tongue claudication (claudication can mimic TMJ or dental pain), with visual symptoms. About one-third of untreated patients go blind. ESR and CRP are elevated. Start high-dose steroids immediately. Do not wait for the biopsy. Temporal artery biopsy is the reference standard, but skip lesions cause false negatives (up to about 40%), so take a long segment (Pasha says 2-5 cm). Pasha advises a contralateral biopsy if the first is negative. Current ACR guidance starts unilateral and adds vascular ultrasound or imaging. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 248) **Connective tissue disease in the head and neck**: rheumatoid arthritis involves the TMJ in about 50% (usually bilateral). Cricoarytenoid arthritis or ankylosis causes hoarseness, globus, or stridor and must be told apart from bilateral vocal fold paralysis (palpate the arytenoids or use LEMG). Ossicular joint involvement is rare. RA is linked to secondary Sjogren syndrome. SLE causes oral ulcers with an erythematous halo, septal perforation, autoimmune SNHL, parotid swelling, and cricoarytenoid disease. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific. ANA is a sensitive screen. Discoid lupus affects skin and oral mucosa without visceral disease. Mixed connective tissue disease has overlap features with high-titer anti-U1 RNP. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 245-247) **Cervicofacial actinomycosis**: Actinomyces israelii is an oral commensal that becomes invasive after dental work, poor hygiene or radiation, always with companion bacteria. It forms a slowly enlarging, woody, relatively painless mass with multiple sinus tracts draining sulfur granules, and it crosses tissue planes. Treatment is prolonged high-dose penicillin (often 6 weeks IV, then months of oral therapy), with doxycycline as the alternative for penicillin allergy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Salivary Glands", p 1283) **Laryngeal amyloidosis**: usually localized light-chain disease. It most often involves the true and false folds and ventricles, causing hoarseness and sometimes stridor. Diagnose with biopsy showing apple-green birefringence with Congo red. Screen for myeloma (CBC, renal and liver tests, urine Bence Jones protein). Treat with microdebrider or CO2 laser excision. Recurrence is common, so follow long term. Survival matches the general population. (Cummings 7e, Ch 11, p 181-182) **Laryngeal granulomatous and autoimmune disease**: GPA presents with subglottic stenosis in 10-20% and can be ANCA-negative in up to 20% with airway disease. Sarcoidosis favors the supraglottis (epiglottis first) with pale, turban-like thickening and spares the cords. Rheumatoid arthritis involves the larynx in 25-30%, causing cricoarytenoid ankylosis that can fix both cords or submucosal rheumatoid nodules. In pemphigus of the larynx, bullae are rarely seen. Look for tan fibrinous erosions with an erythematous halo on the supraglottis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 11, p 180-182) **Infectious laryngitis that mimics cancer**: laryngeal TB now usually occurs without pulmonary symptoms (the PPD is usually positive). Test these patients for HIV. Histoplasmosis and blastomycosis (Ohio and Mississippi valleys) form exophytic or ulcerative lesions. Blastomycosis shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and broad-based budding yeast. Cryptococcus affects the true folds in immunocompromised hosts. Biopsy with fungal and AFB stains before calling SCC. (Cummings 7e, Ch 11, p 183-184) **Granulomatous infections of the nose**: rhinoscleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) passes through catarrhal (atrophic, honey-colored crusts), granulomatous and sclerotic stages, mostly on the turbinates. Mikulicz cells (vacuolated macrophages containing bacilli) and Russell bodies are diagnostic, culture on MacConkey agar is positive in only 50–60%, and ciprofloxacin is first-line. Nasal TB favors the cartilaginous septum (caseating granulomas, AFB, lupus vulgaris). Test for HIV. Leprosy causes atrophy of the anterior nasal spine and premaxilla. Actinomycosis forms a hard mass with sinus tracts and sulfur granules (drainage plus prolonged penicillin-class therapy). Rhinosporidiosis (R. seeberi, from contaminated water) gives a polypoid mass treated by excision plus dapsone. Syphilis causes chancre or gumma (FTA-ABS, penicillin G) (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, pp 793–794). **Kimura and Rosai-Dorfman disease**: Kimura disease typically affects young Asian men: painless, often itchy cervicofacial and periauricular masses, sometimes in the parotid, with peripheral eosinophilia and high IgE that track disease activity. Treatment options include observation, excision, steroids, cyclosporine, or radiation. Rosai-Dorfman disease presents with massive painless bilateral cervical adenopathy. It involves the salivary glands in about 30% of cases, and its histiocytes are S-100-positive. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1170) **Sarcoidosis head and neck patterns**: Laryngeal sarcoid is a pale, diffuse submucosal supraglottic (epiglottic) swelling. Sinonasal disease gives crusting and 'cobblestone' mucosa. Lupus pernio (violaceous plaques on nose, cheeks and ears) is pathognomonic. Löfgren syndrome is acute arthralgia, erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar adenopathy. Labs: elevated ACE, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria. Biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas with Schaumann bodies. Chest staging 0-IV runs from no thoracic disease through hilar adenopathy and parenchymal involvement to fibrosis. Supraglottic lesions are observed unless obstructive. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 222-223) **Laryngeal rheumatologic disease**: 25–53% of RA patients have laryngeal involvement, either cricoarytenoid arthritis (hypomobility) or 'bamboo nodes', which are transverse submucosal bands on the mid-fold. Treat bamboo nodes systemically first, with optional local steroid. Excision is difficult and scars. In SLE, laryngeal edema occurs in up to 28% and fold paralysis in 11%. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 53) **Heerfordt syndrome**: Uveoparotid fever: a sarcoidosis variant with fever, bilateral parotid enlargement and uveitis, frequently with facial nerve palsy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 16) **Sturge-Weber syndrome**: V1-distribution port-wine stain with ipsilateral leptomeningeal venous angiomatosis causing seizures, hemiparesis, glaucoma and tram-track intracranial calcifications. Oral and nasal mucosal angiomatous involvement may bleed during surgery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 32) **Multiple sclerosis in ENT**: Relapsing CNS demyelination (peak about 35 years, women) presenting to ENT as trigeminal neuralgia in a young patient, vertigo, sudden hearing loss or internuclear ophthalmoplegia. MRI shows T2/FLAIR periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers) with open-ring enhancement. CSF shows oligoclonal bands and IgG index over 0.7. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 126-127) **Lupus and Behçet in the head and neck**: SLE can cause laryngotracheal perichondritis with vocal fold thickening, nasal crusting and septal perforation. Discoid lupus affects only skin/mucosa. Specific serology is anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm. Behçet disease requires recurrent oral aphthae (3 or more per year) plus two of genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions (erythema nodosum) or a positive pathergy test. It can cause progressive SNHL and vasculitis of vessels of any size. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 221-222)
canonical_layers.localize: Patterns such as destructive sinonasal disease plus airway stenosis, multisite glandular disease or multiple cranial neuropathies suggest a systemic process rather than isolated local pathology. **Laryngeal site signatures of systemic disease**: sarcoidosis favors the supraglottis (pale, turban-like epiglottis). GPA favors the subglottis (biphasic stridor). Amyloidosis presents as a smooth submucosal (often subglottic/ventricular) mass treated by endoscopic debulking when symptomatic. Rheumatoid arthritis affects the cricoarytenoid joint (pain, hoarseness, fixation that mimics paralysis). (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 94-95)
canonical_layers.workup: Use history/exam to target serology, chest/renal evaluation, biopsy and infectious testing rather than ordering broad panels indiscriminately. Biopsy the safest active site when tissue diagnosis is needed. **Tuberculosis**: cervical TB (scrofula) is the most common head and neck form. Laryngeal TB favors the posterior glottis (interarytenoid area), epiglottis, and vocal folds and can mimic cancer. TB otitis causes painless watery otorrhea with multiple TM perforations. Screen with an IGRA (unaffected by BCG) or a PPD. PPD induration is positive at 5 mm or more in HIV, immunosuppression, or close contacts. At 10 mm or more in health care workers, IV drug users, residents of congregate settings, and children under 4. And at 15 mm or more in low-risk people. Diagnose nodal disease by FNA (AFB, culture, PCR) or excisional biopsy. Avoid incision and drainage, which leaves a chronic draining sinus. Treat with multidrug therapy and isolate active pulmonary disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 243) **Relapsing polychondritis (McAdam criteria)**: diagnose with 3 of 6 criteria: bilateral auricular chondritis, nonerosive seronegative polyarthritis, nasal chondritis, audiovestibular damage, respiratory tract chondritis and ocular inflammation. Alternatively, 1 criterion plus positive histology, or chondritis at 2 or more separate sites that responds to steroids or dapsone, is enough (Damiani). Auricular chondritis is the most common presentation (40%). Saddle nose is present in 24% at diagnosis and 53% later, airway involvement in about 25%, and eye disease in over 50%. HLA-DR4 doubles risk, and anti-type II collagen antibodies track flares. Five-year survival is 66–74%, or 45% with vasculitis. Treat with NSAIDs for mild disease and steroids (80–100 mg/day in severe flares) with dapsone, methotrexate or cyclosporine (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 792). **Relapsing polychondritis criteria**: Episodic painful chondritis (attacks resolve within about a week): auricular in about 50% with lobule sparing, nasal 15% (saddle nose), laryngotracheal 15% (airway collapse may need tracheostomy), nonerosive arthritis 50%, ocular 15%. McAdam criteria: bilateral auricular chondritis, nasal chondritis, laryngotracheal chondritis, seronegative nonerosive polyarthritis, ocular inflammation, cochleovestibular damage. Diagnose with 3 or more criteria, or 1 plus biopsy, or chondritis at 2 sites responding to steroids or dapsone. Treat with steroids, dapsone, colchicine or NSAIDs. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 221) **EGPA (Churg-Strauss) criteria**: Asthma typically precedes vasculitis by 3-9 years, progressing through allergic, eosinophilic (Loeffler-type) and vasculitic phases. About 70% have sinonasal disease. pANCA/MPO is positive in only about 50%. ACR 1990 criteria (4 of 6): asthma, eosinophils over 10%, mononeuropathy/polyneuropathy, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, paranasal sinus abnormality, and extravascular eosinophils on biopsy. The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria now replace the 1990 set: obstructive airway disease +3, nasal polyps +3, mononeuritis multiplex +1, eosinophils at least 1×10⁹/L +5, extravascular eosinophilic inflammation on biopsy +2, cANCA/PR3 −3 and hematuria −1, with a score of 6 or more classifying EGPA. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 220)
canonical_layers.manage: Coordinate disease-specific immunologic/infectious/oncologic therapy while treating local functional consequences. Avoid irreversible local surgery during uncontrolled destructive inflammatory disease unless airway or other urgent function requires it. **Tuberculous cervical adenitis (scrofula due to M. tuberculosis)**: older children, often with a TB contact, bilateral nodes, and abnormal chest film. Unlike NTM it is treated medically—isoniazid and rifampin with pyrazinamide for the first 2 months, completing 6 months when culture confirms—not by excision alone. AFB stains are positive in under 50%, three early-morning gastric aspirates yield organisms in up to 70% of young children, residual nodes over 10 mm persist in 30% after therapy, and all children with TB should be offered HIV testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cervical Adenopathy", p 1755) **GPA workup and treatment**: Classic triad: necrotizing granulomas of the airway, systemic small/medium-vessel vasculitis and focal glomerulonephritis (rapidly progressive GN in about 75%). Rhinitis/crusting is the most common presenting symptom. Workup: cANCA/PR3 (supportive, not definitive), ESR/CRP, urinalysis for RBC casts or over 5 RBC/HPF, chest imaging and biopsy showing necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis. Induce remission with high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab. Maintain with methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 219-220) **Biologics for vasculitides**: Rituximab (anti-CD20, B-cell depletion) is now standard for moderate-severe granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) is approved for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) for giant cell arteritis. Infliximab (anti-TNF) is used in relapsing polychondritis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 190)
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery is often reconstructive or rescue rather than curative; active vasculitis/granulomatous disease increases restenosis and wound-failure risk. Time elective reconstruction to disease control when possible.
canonical_layers.teach: When ENT disease appears in multiple unrelated sites, stop creating separate diagnoses and ask whether one systemic process connects them. **Endemic mycoses that mimic laryngeal and oral cancer**: histoplasmosis (Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, bird and bat droppings) causes painful ulcerative lesions with heaped edges, mostly in disseminated disease. Blastomycosis (Midwest/Great Lakes) causes verrucous laryngeal or skin lesions with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and broad-based budding yeast. Coccidioidomycosis (desert Southwest, 'valley fever') shows spherules filled with endospores. Cryptococcosis (pigeon droppings, immunosuppression) causes meningitis with SNHL and is seen as an encapsulated yeast on India ink. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia can be misread as SCC, so request fungal stains and cultures. Treatment is an azole or amphotericin B. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 244) **GPA by the numbers**: sinonasal disease is the most common head and neck finding (about 60-90%). Other rates: nasopharyngeal ulceration about 75%, laryngeal ulceration about 25%, subglottic stenosis under about 20%, serous otitis media/CHL about 20-25%, and ocular disease about 40%. Lungs are involved in about 90%, and renal disease causes most deaths. c-ANCA/PR3 supports the diagnosis. Nasal biopsies have low yield (necrosis and inflammation), so take deep, generous tissue. Kidney, lung, or skin biopsies have higher yield. Treat with induction immunosuppression (steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide), then maintenance. Use saline irrigation and debridement for local care. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 247-248)
