candidates.canonical_topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Most facial pressure/headache is not automatically sinus disease. Migraine and other primary headache disorders commonly mimic 'sinus headache.'. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat proven sinonasal inflammation when present and route primary headache/TMJ/neuralgia to the correct pathway. Avoid antibiotics or ESS for imaging findings that do not fit the syndrome.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: 'pain over the sinus' is anatomy, not etiology.

canonical_layers.recognize: Most facial pressure/headache is **not** automatically sinus disease. Migraine and other primary headache disorders commonly mimic 'sinus headache.' **Foundation**: 'sinus headache' is a symptom label, not a diagnosis. The related phrase 'rhinogenic headache' should likewise trigger a causation question rather than be accepted as a diagnosis by itself. Facial pressure, frontal pain, nasal congestion, tearing, or weather sensitivity can occur with migraine and other primary headache disorders as well as sinonasal disease. **Key point**: a rhinogenic attribution requires a compatible sinonasal disorder plus objective evidence and a credible causal relationship. Reopen migraine, tension-type headache, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, trigeminal neuralgia/other neuropathic pain, dental disease, and temporomandibular disorder when the pain phenotype or objective nasal evaluation does not fit inflammatory sinus disease. **Pediatric 'sinus headache' data**: in a case-control study of children with chronic or recurrent headache, only ~7% of headaches were attributable to sinusitis, yet 54% had previously been labeled sinus headache. URI, ABRS and strep pharyngitis are the commonest causes of acute pediatric headache in the ED. Red flags for intracranial disease and neuroimaging include an occipital location, inability to describe the pain, focal neurologic signs, morning or sleep-waking headache, and worsening when lying down. Isolated sphenoid sinusitis is rare in children and gives retro-orbital, vertex or occipital pain that wakes the child, sometimes with visual or cranial nerve signs. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 990) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 991) **Cluster headache**: Severe strictly unilateral orbital/temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes, up to 8 times a day, often nocturnal, with ipsilateral tearing, conjunctival injection, congestion, rhinorrhea, sweating, miosis and ptosis. The episodic form has remissions of at least 3 months, and the chronic form does not. Abort attacks with 100% oxygen or triptans (intranasal or injected). K.J. Lee gives oxygen at about 8 L/min for 10 min, but current AHS guidance uses 12-15 L/min by non-rebreather mask for about 15 minutes. Verapamil is the main preventive, with lithium and topiramate. Refractory cases may get occipital nerve block, sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation or hypothalamic deep brain stimulation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 122-123) **Neuropathic facial pains**: Trigeminal neuralgia is brief electric attacks triggered by innocuous stimuli in V divisions, mostly in women over 50, with normal sensation. Get an MRI for MS, CPA tumor or vascular loop; carbamazepine is first line (baclofen, lamotrigine and pimozide are possible alternatives), with microvascular decompression or ablation for refractory cases. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia causes seconds-to-2-minute stabbing pain in the tonsil, tongue base, ear or mandibular angle, triggered by swallowing, coughing or yawning. Image it (demyelination, CPA tumor, carotid aneurysm), and treat with carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine or microvascular decompression (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, p 797). **Postherpetic and other chronic pains**: about 30% of people get zoster, and V1 is the most common cranial site. Antivirals within 72 hours shorten the rash but do not prevent postherpetic neuralgia (pain more than 3 months after the rash heals), which is very common after age 50. Treat with 5% lidocaine, 8% (not 0.075%) capsaicin, gabapentin/pregabalin (a 50% pain reduction may take 2–3 months) or TCAs. Persistent idiopathic facial pain is daily pain for more than 2 hours a day over more than 3 months, poorly localized, not in one nerve's distribution and without deficit. It often starts after minor dental or ENT procedures and has psychiatric comorbidity; use low-dose amitriptyline or anticonvulsants, not surgery. Posttraumatic trigeminal neuropathic pain follows injury to the inferior alveolar, lingual or mental nerve (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 797–798).
canonical_layers.localize: Localize pain by time course, autonomic/migrainous features, triggers, neurologic findings and objective sinonasal inflammation rather than pain location alone. **Application**: localize from the pain phenotype instead of the word 'sinus.' Rhinosinusitis-associated pain should track a real inflammatory process; unilateral inflammatory disease can produce ipsilateral pain, but laterality alone is not proof. Brief electric-shock attacks with triggers suggest trigeminal neuralgia; strictly unilateral severe orbital/temporal attacks with prominent autonomic features demand a trigeminal-autonomic differential; jaw/dental provocation redirects toward odontogenic/TMJ disease. **Red flags**: severe focal pain with cranial neuropathy, orbital deficit, epistaxis, necrosis, or destructive imaging reopens neoplasm, invasive fungal disease, skull-base disease, and other dangerous secondary causes.
canonical_layers.workup: Endoscopy and CT are used when sinus disease is clinically plausible, but incidental mucosal thickening does not prove causality. Red flags may require neurologic/dental/ophthalmic workup. **Senior workup**: first ask whether there is **objective sinonasal disease** on nasal endoscopy and/or appropriate imaging, then ask whether the pain behaves causally with that disease. **ICHD-3** requires more than coincidental mucosal thickening: timing, worsening/improvement in parallel with rhinosinusitis, localization concordance, and exclusion of a better headache diagnosis matter. **Key trap**: incidental CT opacification or a septal spur/contact point that merely occupies the same side as pain is not sufficient by itself. When endoscopy and CT are normal or discordant with disabling pain, stop escalating antibiotics or sinus procedures and pursue the neurologic, dental, TMJ, ophthalmic, or other pathway suggested by the phenotype. **ICHD criteria in children**: pediatric migraine allows attacks of 2-72 hours under current ICHD-3 (the book cites the older 1-72 hours, versus 4-72 in adults), may be bilateral, and photophobia/phonophobia may be inferred from behavior. Episodic tension-type headache needs at least 10 attacks that are bilateral, pressing and not worsened by activity, without nausea. Cluster headache involves unilateral orbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis/miosis). The American Academy of Neurology recommends neuroimaging for recurrent pediatric headache when the neurologic exam is abnormal. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 989) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 990) **Primary headache criteria**: Migraine: attacks of 4-72 hours with two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, or worsened by activity, plus nausea/vomiting or photophobia and phonophobia; aura is usually visual. Tension-type: bilateral pressing/tightening (bifrontal or occipitonuchal), mild-moderate, not worsened by activity, without nausea or photo/phonophobia, lasting up to 7 days. Imaging is unnecessary with a stable pattern and normal neurologic exam; MRI is preferred over CT outside emergencies. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 120-122) **ICHD-3 migraine criteria**: migraine without aura needs at least 5 attacks of 4–72 hours with at least 2 of: unilateral, pulsating, moderate/severe, worsened by routine activity. At least 1 of nausea/vomiting or photophobia plus phonophobia must also be present. Migraine with aura needs at least 2 attacks of fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor, brainstem or retinal aura (each 5–60 minutes, spreading over at least 5 minutes) followed within 60 minutes by headache. Red flags for expedited workup and admission are mental status change, seizure, acute vision change, neck stiffness, temporal artery tenderness, field loss, diplopia, cranial neuropathy and unilateral rhinorrhea (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 795–796).
canonical_layers.manage: Treat proven sinonasal inflammation when present and route primary headache/TMJ/neuralgia to the correct pathway. Avoid antibiotics or ESS for imaging findings that do not fit the syndrome. **Management**: treat proven acute or chronic rhinosinusitis according to its actual phenotype, but do not use treatment response as a license to keep relabeling recurrent migraine as infection. If objective CRS is present yet facial pain is disproportionate or persists despite successful inflammatory control, manage the CRS for its own indications and separately evaluate the residual headache disorder. Counsel patients explicitly that nasal/autonomic symptoms can accompany migraine. **Key trap**: for proposed 'contact-point headache,' acknowledge that selected patients may improve after carefully chosen nasal surgery, but contact on CT/endoscopy is common and causation is uncertain -- do not promise pain cure from anatomy alone. **Trigeminal neuralgia in children**: rare, with case reports from infancy onward. MRI with MRA of the root entry zone is needed to look for vascular compression or tumor (an epidermoid has been found). Carbamazepine is first-line, then oxcarbazepine. Microvascular decompression is the most effective option when drugs fail; in the largest pediatric series (n = 23), venous compression and long delay to surgery predicted poorer results. Herpes zoster in healthy children is usually mild, and postherpetic neuralgia is uncommon and short-lived. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral and Facial Neuropathic Pain in Children", p 995) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral and Facial Neuropathic Pain in Children", p 996) **Trigeminal neuralgia**: Brief electric-shock paroxysms (seconds to 2 minutes) in V2/V3 (V1 under 5%) triggered by chewing, talking, touch or cold air, with a normal neurologic exam; usually from superior cerebellar artery compression at the root entry zone, or MS demyelination in younger patients. Carbamazepine is first line (a response supports the diagnosis; about 75% are controlled medically), then oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, baclofen or gabapentin. Procedures: percutaneous glycerol, radiofrequency or balloon rhizotomy, gamma knife, and microvascular decompression (most durable; not for MS). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 123-124, 133) **Migraine abortive and preventive therapy**: Abortives (triptans, ergots, NSAIDs, combination analgesics, antiemetics) work best within about 15 minutes of onset. Avoid opioids and butalbital as first line and limit OTC analgesic overuse. Prophylaxis is indicated for frequent attacks (more than 2 per month or abortives more than twice weekly), prolonged or disabling attacks, or abortive failure. Options are antiepileptics (topiramate), beta blockers, tricyclics, calcium channel blockers and botulinum toxin (for chronic migraine), and supplements include magnesium, riboflavin and coenzyme Q10. The book predates CGRP-targeted drugs: current AHS guidance adds CGRP monoclonal antibodies for prevention and gepants for acute treatment and prevention. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 121) **Treating the mimics**: for mild/moderate migraine, NSAIDs or acetaminophen are first line. Triptans (serotonin agonists that vasoconstrict) are for moderate/severe migraine and are contraindicated in cardiovascular disease; ondansetron can itself cause headache. For TMD (5–10% of people; 82% present with ear pain), use a night occlusal splint, a 2-week NSAID trial (ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily), a soft diet and muscle relaxants, and refer refractory cases to oral surgery; MRI is not routine (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 796–797).
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery is appropriate when a defined sinonasal disease process and symptom relationship support it -- not as an empiric headache procedure. **Operative decision/bailout**: FESS is not a diagnostic trial for unexplained facial pain. Operate when objective sinonasal disease and the total clinical picture support a reasonable expectation that surgery will improve the rhinologic disease. **Key trap**: do not perform or revise technically patent sinus surgery simply because facial pressure persists. Likewise, septoplasty/turbinate surgery for a presumed contact-point mechanism requires a coherent, carefully selected case rather than imaging contact alone. **Escalate urgently** and stop the routine-rhinology pathway for new neurologic deficit, vision change/ophthalmoplegia, thunderclap or rapidly progressive headache, meningismus, cranial neuropathy, necrotic tissue, or destructive/skull-base findings. **Contact-point surgery criteria**: offer surgery only when a mucosal contact point on endoscopy/CT is shown to drive the pain, for example by clear relief with topical decongestant/anesthetic or a diagnostic block, after neurologic evaluation and failed medical therapy. Contact points are common in pain-free people. One series reported 91% lower intensity and 85% lower frequency, but results vary, surgery can worsen headache, and at least 1 year of follow-up is needed to call it a success (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 688).
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: 'pain over the sinus' is anatomy, not etiology. **Chief rule**: prove DISEASE, then prove CONCORDANCE. Objective endoscopy/CT can support rhinosinusitis, but it does not by itself prove the sinus abnormality caused the headache. 'Sinus headache' with a migraine phenotype and no objective inflammatory disease is migraine until another diagnosis is established. **Key point**: the senior move is often knowing when NOT to prescribe another antibiotic, obtain another low-value sinus scan, or offer FESS. **Numbers against 'sinus headache'**: of nearly 3,000 patients with self- or physician-diagnosed 'sinus headache,' more than 80% met migraine criteria. Only 20–30% of patients with endoscopic or radiologic sinus disease report facial pain. CT mucosal thickening appears in 30–40% of asymptomatic people. Contact points are as common without pain as with it, and nearly 50% of facial-pain patients have their contact point on the opposite side (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 795–796).

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Asymmetric SNHL, unilateral tinnitus or disproportionate word-recognition loss should prompt retrocochlear thinking; larger tumors may cause imbalance, facial/trigeminal symptoms or brainstem/cerebellar effects. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Observation, stereotactic radiation and microsurgery are all valid in selected patients. Decide from age/comorbidity, size/growth, symptoms, hearing, brainstem effect and patient preference rather than tumor diameter alone.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Vestibular Schwannoma. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: The treatment question is not 'How do we remove it?' It is 'What outcome matters most—tumor control, hearing, facial function—and which strategy best balances those goals?'

canonical_layers.recognize: **Red flags**: asymmetric SNHL, unilateral tinnitus, or disproportionate word-recognition loss should prompt retrocochlear thinking. Larger tumors may cause imbalance, facial/trigeminal symptoms, or brainstem/cerebellar effects. **Foundation refinement**: suspect a retrocochlear process when unilateral or asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss, unilateral tinnitus, unexpectedly poor speech discrimination, disequilibrium, or progressive cranial-neuropathy symptoms do not fit a simple cochlear explanation. **Key trap**: these findings are clues, not a diagnosis -- most asymmetric hearing loss is not vestibular schwannoma, and normal bedside vestibular findings do not exclude a small intracanalicular lesion. **Presentation details**: Asymmetric high-frequency SNHL is the usual presentation, but 10–20% present with sudden SNHL. The Hitselberger sign is reduced sensation of the posterosuperior canal and concha from pressure on CN VII sensory fibers. Clinically significant facial weakness occurs in under 5% of vestibular schwannomas, versus over half of facial nerve schwannomas. Histology shows dense Antoni A (Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas. About 95% are sporadic and 5% NF2-related. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 395, 427, 434) **NF2 classic criteria taught in this text**: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or a first-degree relative with NF2 plus either a unilateral schwannoma before age 30 or two of meningioma, glioma, schwannoma, or juvenile posterior subcapsular lens opacity. Incidence ~1 in 40,000-90,000. Merlin gene on 22q12. Current practice uses the 2022 revised criteria for NF2-related schwannomatosis, which add molecular (NF2 variant) criteria. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 477) **Bruns nystagmus**: seen in about 10% of vestibular schwannomas. Large CPA tumors compress the flocculus and brainstem, producing coarse, large-amplitude nystagmus on gaze toward the lesion (gaze-paretic) and fine nystagmus on gaze away (vestibular) (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, p 2090). **Compensation and hyperventilation clues**: slow tumor growth lets the brain compensate gradually, so many patients only notice brief imbalance on quick turns toward the tumor side. Patients whose vestibular function is preserved until surgery often have severe postoperative vertigo and an ocular tilt reaction, with vertical diplopia from skew. Hyperventilation can transiently restore conduction in a demyelinated nerve (schwannoma, vascular compression, MS). The result is an excitatory nystagmus whose fast phase beats toward the affected ear, whereas peripheral hypofunction usually beats away from it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, pp 2490, 2493, Ch 166, p 2505) **Symptom order and the sudden-loss rule**: In descending order, the common symptoms are SNHL, tinnitus, dysequilibrium and facial hypesthesia, with a median duration of about 2 years. About 1-3% of patients with sudden SNHL turn out to have a vestibular schwannoma (up to 10% in some MRI series), and up to 20% of tumors present with sudden loss, so image every unexplained sudden or asymmetric loss even after full recovery. Patients rarely report imbalance, but on the Fukuda stepping test they often turn more than 90 degrees toward the tumor, and the head impulse test may show catch-up saccades to that side. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, p 2701)
canonical_layers.localize: **Origin**: vestibular schwannoma usually arises from the vestibular nerve within the IAC and may extend into the CPA. Tumor size, fundal extension, brainstem contact, and residual hearing shape management. **Anatomy refinement**: localize the lesion along the vestibular nerve within the internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle, tracking relationships to the facial nerve, cochlear nerve, brainstem, cerebellum, and nearby AICA vascular loops. **Key trap**: with increasing CPA size, distinguish isolated CN VIII symptoms from CN V/VII dysfunction, cerebellar signs, brainstem compression, and hydrocephalus -- these change urgency and management rather than merely increasing a size label.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Diagnostic test**: MRI with IAC protocol is diagnostic. Document pure-tone thresholds, word recognition, vestibular/facial function, and tumor growth on serial imaging when observing. **Key trap**: broad laboratory testing is not the workup. **Application refinement**: obtain complete audiometry with speech measures and contrast-enhanced MRI of the IAC/CPA when retrocochlear disease is suspected. MRI, not an isolated audiogram pattern or ABR, is the diagnostic imaging foundation. Characterize intracanalicular versus CPA extension, maximal/volumetric size, cystic features, brainstem effect, and serial growth. During observation, compare standardized serial MRI and hearing trajectories rather than treating a single millimeter change or one audiogram as definitive progression. **Koos grading** (for documentation and comparison): I = intracanalicular; II = CPA extension without brainstem contact; III = occupies the CPA cistern without brainstem displacement; IV = brainstem/cranial-nerve displacement, often with compression or hydrocephalus. **AAO-HNS hearing classes** use pure-tone average (PTA) and speech discrimination/word recognition: A = PTA <=30 dB and score >=70%; B = PTA 31-50 dB and score >=50%; C = PTA >50 dB and score >=50%; D = score <50%. A/B are generally serviceable. Measure tumor diameter on comparable contrast MRI sequences and monitor serial audiograms. Reproducible growth around >=2 mm on serial imaging or meaningful hearing decline warrants reconsideration of observation, but no single annual growth threshold automatically mandates treatment. Account for measurement error, interval, symptoms, age, and tumor volume.

**Grading scale**: the **Gardner-Robertson hearing classification** is the standard scale for reporting hearing in vestibular schwannoma, distinct from but conceptually related to the AAO-HNS class above. Class I (good): PTA 0-30 dB with speech discrimination 70-100%. Class II (serviceable): PTA 31-50 dB with 50-69% discrimination. Class III (non-serviceable): PTA 51-90 dB with 5-49% discrimination. Class IV (poor): PTA 90-100 dB with 1-4% discrimination. Class V (deaf): no measurable hearing. **Key trap**: Classes I-II are considered serviceable hearing; III-V are not -- this distinction drives hearing-preservation candidacy discussions. **Imaging and test details**: Contrast CT can miss tumors under about 1.5 cm, whereas gadolinium MRI detects lesions as small as 1.5 mm. Watch for false positives from vessels or neuritis. Noncontrast high-resolution T2 sequences can screen and can follow known tumors, detecting a 2-mm change about as reliably as contrast MRI (except in cystic tumors) without repeated gadolinium. Calorics (superior nerve) and cVEMP (inferior nerve) can suggest which nerve the tumor comes from, which bears on hearing-preservation odds, but are not screening tests. About 85% of schwannomas meet the bone at an acute angle, while about 75% of meningiomas meet it at an obtuse angle. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2702–2703)
canonical_layers.manage: **Options**: observation, stereotactic radiosurgery (radiation), and microsurgery are all valid in selected patients. Decide from age/comorbidity, size/growth, symptoms, hearing, brainstem effect, and patient preference rather than tumor diameter alone. **Senior decision refinement**: integrate tumor size and growth, serviceable hearing, symptoms, age/comorbidity, brainstem or CSF-pathway effect, prior treatment, anatomy, and patient goals. Counsel separately for tumor control, facial-nerve function, and hearing preservation, because success in one domain does not guarantee the others. After SRS, distinguish expected treatment-related enlargement/pseudoprogression from durable serial growth before labeling failure, when the clinical situation permits surveillance. **Size-driven defaults**: observation with serial MRI and audiometry is reasonable for small asymptomatic Koos I-II tumors. SRS is an alternative for selected small/medium growing or symptomatic tumors without significant mass effect. **Dosing**: contemporary single-fraction SRS marginal doses are commonly 11-14 Gy (often 12-13 Gy). Selected series report about 90-99% five-year tumor control and 95-100% facial-nerve preservation, while hearing preservation varies substantially with baseline hearing, size, cochlear dose, and follow-up. Large tumors causing substantial brainstem compression or hydrocephalus generally require microsurgical decompression; an intentionally retained remnant may be observed or treated with subsequent SRS. **Key trap**: Koos grade or a 2.5-cm cutoff alone is not a treatment mandate. **NF2**: NF2-related schwannomatosis requires multidisciplinary bilateral-hearing planning; bevacizumab is an option in selected progressive NF2-related tumors. **Hearing prognosis on observation**: word recognition (speech discrimination) at diagnosis is the best predictor of long-term serviceable hearing. In the Danish wait-and-scan cohort (Stangerup 2010), 69% of patients with 100% speech discrimination at diagnosis kept good hearing after more than 10 years of observation, compared with 38% of those with even a small discrimination loss. Tumor size, intracanalicular location and age have not consistently predicted hearing outcome, and hearing can decline without tumor growth, so follow audiograms as well as MRI and revisit the treatment discussion if word recognition falls. **Natural history and surveillance interval**: Average growth is about 1–2 mm per year and roughly half of small tumors do not grow for long periods, though hearing can decline without growth. Pasha's observation schedule: MRI every 6 months for the first year, then yearly for 2 years, then every other year indefinitely. Observation is typical for tumors under about 1.5 cm, and radiosurgery is usually offered for growing tumors under about 2.5 cm. Radiation risks include delayed hearing loss years later and very rare malignant change (<0.1%). (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 395–396) **Hearing rehabilitation in NF2**: if the cochlear nerve is anatomically intact (untreated or radiated tumor, or after hearing-preservation surgery), try a CI first. It gives open-set speech in up to about 70%, which an ABI rarely achieves. Assess nerve status with promontory stimulation no sooner than 6–8 weeks after surgery. An absent response does not rule out CI benefit. About one third of ears develop cochlear ossification after translabyrinthine surgery, which favors a CI placed at the same operation. If the nerve is lost, place an ABI at the first-side resection as a 'sleeper' device. (Cummings 7e, Ch 163, p 2449) **Postoperative complications**: After translabyrinthine surgery, CSF rhinorrhea occurs in under 5% and usually stops with a fresh compression dressing. A persistent leak usually seals after about 3 days of lumbar drainage, or closing the ear canal with eustachian tube obliteration works at once. Meningitis appears at a mean of about postoperative day 8. Vital-sign changes during brainstem dissection signal AICA-territory ischemia, so pause. Changes that persist or recur mean the operation should end, because complete AICA loss causes Atkinson syndrome (lateral pontine tegmental infarction, often fatal). When facial palsy and corneal anesthesia occur together and the palsy is expected to last more than about 6 months, protect the eye early with a gold weight or spring and a brow lift. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, p 2727) **Radiosurgery dose and selection limits**: Cutting the marginal dose below 16 Gy dropped facial neuropathy to about 15%, and at 13 Gy or less facial injury is rare and usually transient. Keeping the cochlear dose under about 4 Gy helps preserve hearing. Even so, PTA usually falls 15–20 dB over the first 6–12 months and keeps declining for years. Radiation is generally contraindicated for tumors over about 3 cm in the posterior fossa, or with brainstem compression or non-auditory cranial neuropathies, because of swelling, hydrocephalus and radionecrosis. Cystic tumors respond less predictably. (Cummings 7e, Ch 181, pp 2750–2751)
canonical_layers.operate: **Approaches**: retrosigmoid, middle-fossa, and translabyrinthine approaches trade exposure and hearing goals differently. **Endpoint**: facial nerve preservation is a major endpoint -- continuous monitoring and careful tumor-nerve dissection matter more than forcing gross-total resection when nerve function is threatened. **OR decision refinement**: choose the operative corridor for the actual objective and anatomy. Middle fossa or retrosigmoid may support hearing-preservation attempts in selected small tumors with useful hearing, whereas translabyrinthine exposure accepts hearing sacrifice when hearing preservation is not a realistic objective and provides direct IAC access. Use facial-nerve monitoring and, when hearing preservation is attempted, cochlear/auditory monitoring appropriate to the case. Preserve arachnoid planes and avoid traction or thermal injury to CN VII/VIII and brainstem/AICA structures. **Key trap**: if the capsule is densely inseparable from the facial nerve, cochlear nerve, brainstem, or critical vasculature, stop escalating dissection -- leave an intentional residual and plan MRI surveillance with selective adjuvant SRS rather than pursuing unsafe gross-total resection at the cost of function. **Approach selection by hearing and extent**: middle fossa is a hearing-preservation option chiefly for appropriately selected small intracanalicular tumors with good preoperative hearing; retrosigmoid may permit hearing preservation in selected small CPA tumors. Translabyrinthine surgery sacrifices hearing, offers broad IAC exposure, and is appropriate when ipsilateral hearing is nonserviceable or preservation is not a realistic goal. Tumor anatomy, fundal extension, brainstem effect, facial-nerve course, and team experience -- not Koos class alone -- determine approach. **Facial nerve risk by approach**: the middle cranial fossa approach carries the highest risk of facial weakness, because from above the facial nerve lies in the anterosuperior internal auditory canal, in the surgeon's path to a tumor that usually arises from the inferior vestibular nerve; much of this weakness is early and temporary. It remains the best route for hearing preservation in small intracanalicular tumors with good hearing. The translabyrinthine route exposes the nerve reliably at the fundus without crossing it, and the retrosigmoid route reaches the tumor from behind. **Choosing the approach: hearing first, then size and location.** *Step 1, is hearing serviceable?* Use AAO-HNS class A or B, or the 50/50 rule (pure-tone average 50 dB or better and word recognition 50% or better); word recognition matters most. *Serviceable hearing:* (a) **Intracanalicular or small tumor (CPA component up to about 1 cm) that reaches the fundus**: middle cranial fossa, which exposes the whole internal auditory canal including the fundus without entering the labyrinth; best for younger, healthier patients and for tumors of the superior vestibular nerve, at the cost of the highest facial nerve risk and temporal lobe retraction (thinner, more adherent dura in older patients). (b) **Small to medium tumor (up to about 1.5 to 2 cm) centered in the CPA or medial canal with a CSF cap at the fundus**: retrosigmoid, which handles the CPA well but cannot clear the lateral third of the canal without risking the posterior semicircular canal and vestibule. (c) Hearing preservation is rarely realistic above about 2 cm, so the goal shifts to tumor control and facial function. *Nonserviceable hearing:* **any size, translabyrinthine** is the most direct route, finds the facial nerve at the fundus, avoids cerebellar retraction and has the lowest headache burden; retrosigmoid remains an option, especially for large tumors with wide posterior fossa extension or by surgeon preference. *Large tumors (over about 3 cm or brainstem compression)*: translabyrinthine or retrosigmoid, with planned near-total resection when the capsule is stuck to the facial nerve. *Favorable signs for hearing preservation*: small tumor, excellent word recognition, CSF at the fundus, preserved ABR waveforms and superior vestibular nerve origin. *Only-hearing ear, NF2 or high surgical risk*: observation or radiosurgery is usually favored over attempting hearing-preservation surgery. **Translabyrinthine steps that protect nerves**: Leave an island of bone over the sigmoid sinus (Bill's island) and divide the mastoid emissary vein. Finish all bone work before opening dura, skeletonizing the IAC through about 270 degrees. Expose the inferior border first, using the cochlear aqueduct as the inferior limit to protect the lower cranial nerves, and the superior border last, because the facial nerve is most at risk there. At the fundus, Bill's bar marks the facial nerve: reflect and divide the superior vestibular nerve lateral to it to find the plane, and debulk large tumors from inside before dissecting the capsule off CN VII. Close by removing the incus, cutting the tensor tendon, packing the eustachian tube, and filling the defect with strips of abdominal fat. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2716–2719)
canonical_layers.teach: **Board pearl**: the treatment question is not 'How do we remove it?' It is 'What outcome matters most -- tumor control, hearing, facial function -- and which strategy best balances those goals?' **Chief framework**: 1) recognize asymmetric auditory findings as a retrocochlear prompt, not a tumor diagnosis; 2) map IAC/CPA anatomy and neurologic consequences before choosing treatment; 3) use MRI growth, hearing, symptoms, and patient goals to choose observation, SRS, or surgery; 4) choose middle fossa, retrosigmoid, or translabyrinthine exposure by hearing objective and anatomy rather than habit; 5) counsel tumor control, facial function, and hearing as separate outcomes; 6) recognize SRS pseudoprogression; 7) prefer planned functional preservation and an intentional residual over destructive dissection when the facial nerve, brainstem, or critical vessels become the limiting plane. **NF2 criteria and the child with one acoustic neuroma**: NF2 is defined by bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or by a first-degree relative with NF2 plus either a unilateral vestibular schwannoma or two of the following: neurofibroma, meningioma, glioma, schwannoma, or juvenile posterior subcapsular lens opacity. In a child, an isolated unilateral vestibular schwannoma does not by itself establish NF2, but it raises suspicion, so offer NF2 genetic testing. If other neurogenic tumors are present, the risk of NF2 and of a contralateral tumor is high, so image routinely. Current practice uses the 2022 revised criteria for NF2-related schwannomatosis, which add molecular (NF2 variant) criteria. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 139) **Realistic hearing-preservation counseling**: In a pooled review of 621 attempted hearing-preservation operations, hearing was preserved in only about 33%, and much less often when useful or serviceable hearing is the standard rather than any measurable hearing. About 56% of patients later lose much of the hearing that was saved. Hearing preservation is unlikely by any approach once the tumor is over about 2 cm. Because translabyrinthine removal has a slightly higher facial-nerve preservation rate, many eligible patients choose it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2716, 2726) **Pseudoprogression numbers**: About 23% of tumors swell after radiation, usually 2–4 mm (occasionally up to 10 mm), mostly 6–24 months after treatment but sometimes up to 5 years. About half lose central enhancement. Do not call treatment a failure before about 2–3 years. The swelling itself can raise the risk of hydrocephalus, hearing loss and facial or trigeminal symptoms. (Cummings 7e, Ch 181, p 2749) **Late radiation risks and salvage surgery**: Hydrocephalus occurs in about 3.4–5.6% and is treated with a VP shunt. Malignant change in a sporadic tumor is roughly 1 in 1000 (about 0.1–0.3%), but about 4.7% in NF2, a 10-fold rise. Half of reported cases are in NF2, so avoid radiation in children and tumor-prone syndromes when possible. Failures can occur after 5 years, so follow-up is lifelong. Surgery after failed radiation is harder: the tumor is densely stuck to the facial nerve in 89% vs 63%, and HB I–II results fall to 37% vs 70%, which favors planned subtotal removal. (Cummings 7e, Ch 181, pp 2751–2752)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Persistent nasal obstruction/discharge and cough in a child for ≥12 weeks with objective disease suggests pediatric CRS; adenoid disease, allergy, asthma, reflux symptoms and recurrent viral illness commonly overlap. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Saline and intranasal anti-inflammatory therapy are foundational; prolonged or repeated antibiotics should be phenotype-driven rather than automatic. Adenoidectomy is often the first surgical step in appropriate younger children before full FESS.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Pediatric Chronic Rhinosinusitis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Pediatric CRS is not simply adult CRS in a small nose. The adenoid and underlying systemic disease matter much more.

canonical_layers.recognize: Persistent nasal obstruction/discharge and cough in a child for **>=12 weeks** with objective disease suggests pediatric CRS. Adenoid disease, allergy, asthma, reflux symptoms, and recurrent viral illness commonly overlap. **Pediatric refinement -- key trap**: do not equate weeks of nasal symptoms in a child with CRS. **Differential**: separate persistent inflammatory disease from serial viral URIs, chronic adenoiditis/adenoid hypertrophy, allergic/nonallergic rhinitis, reflux/irritant symptoms, and foreign body. **Diagnostic requirement**: pediatric CRS requires a compatible chronic symptom pattern plus objective evidence of sinonasal inflammation. Symptom-free intervals instead suggest recurrent acute episodes rather than CRS. **Pediatric CRS clues**: daytime cough (often worse at night) or throat clearing may dominate over discharge because posterior ethmoid drainage goes to the pharynx. Fever is uncommon, and nonspecific complaints (fatigue, poor school performance) should not be attributed to sinusitis without respiratory symptoms. Widening of the nasal bridge (pseudohypertelorism) has been described. Polyps point to CF or allergy, and any polyp in a child under 12 warrants a sweat chloride test. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1043) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1111)
canonical_layers.localize: Disease involves sinonasal mucosa, but the **adenoid** can act as an inflammatory/biofilm reservoir, especially in younger children. **CF, PCD, and immune deficiency** change the phenotype. **Age-specific refinement**: localize both the sinonasal disease and the driver. Adenoids can function as an inflammatory/bacterial reservoir even when they are not massively obstructive. **Key point**: map which sinuses are actually developed and diseased, rather than importing an adult 'full-house' template. **Red flags** that should reopen CF, PCD, or immune evaluation: nasal polyps, severe/refractory diffuse disease, bronchiectasis/chronic wet cough, neonatal respiratory distress, recurrent otitis, poor growth, unusual infections, or family history.
canonical_layers.workup: Confirm persistent symptoms and use nasal exam/endoscopy when feasible. **CT** is generally reserved for refractory disease or surgical planning. Evaluate allergy, CF/PCD, or immune disorder when history suggests unusually severe/recurrent disease. **Application refinement**: confirm that symptoms are chronic and concordant with endoscopy and/or appropriate imaging before escalating treatment. **Endoscopy**: can document purulence, edema, polyps, and adenoid disease. **Key trap**: CT is most useful when symptoms persist despite appropriate treatment, complications/atypical disease are suspected, or surgery is being planned -- not as a reflex test for every child with congestion. **Culture**: selectively, when refractory, unusual, or host-factor disease makes microbiology actionable. **Red flag**: nasal polyposis or a strong lower-airway/systemic phenotype should trigger targeted host-disease evaluation instead of repeated empiric antibiotics. **Pediatric sinusitis definitions and CT triggers**: Pasha suspects bacterial rhinosinusitis when symptoms persist beyond 10 days. The current AAP (2013) guideline also counts a worsening course after initial improvement or a severe onset (fever of 39 °C or more with purulent discharge for at least 3 days). Acute disease resolves completely within 30 days, chronic disease lasts over 12 weeks, and recurrent acute disease has symptom-free intervals. The sphenoid starts to pneumatize at about 3 years and the frontal sinus is not radiographically distinct until about 6-8 years, so frontal and sphenoid disease is uncommon in young children. Obtain CT for a toxic child, an acute episode not improving after 48–72 hours of treatment, immunocompromise or suspected complications. Polyps in a child should prompt CF testing. Recurrent sinusitis with pneumonia or bronchiectasis should prompt an immune workup. Adenoidectomy improves symptoms in up to about half of children. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 554–555) **Lund-Mackay thresholds in children**: Asymptomatic children average a Lund-Mackay score of about 2.8, so incidental opacification is common (18-45% of children scanned for other reasons). A score of 2 or less has an excellent negative predictive value, and a score of 5 or more strongly predicts CRS (sensitivity about 86%, specificity about 85%). The score also predicts how well adenoidectomy works: in one series, 1-year success was about 65% with scores under 5 (adenoiditis) vs 43% with scores of 5 or more (true CRS). For cultures, middle meatal suction aspirates outperform swabs (87% vs 66% accuracy). Under general anesthesia, maxillary antral puncture remains the gold standard and lets you irrigate at the same time. (Cummings 7e, Ch 200, pp 2974, 2977)
canonical_layers.manage: **Foundational**: saline and intranasal anti-inflammatory therapy. Prolonged or repeated antibiotics should be phenotype-driven rather than automatic. **Adenoidectomy** is often the first surgical step in appropriate younger children before full FESS. **Child-specific sequencing**: begin with appropriate medical management and treatment of contributing rhinitis/host disease -- avoid simply repeating broad antibiotic courses without verifying the phenotype. **When to operate**: when an otherwise uncomplicated child remains symptomatic after adequate medical therapy, **adenoidectomy** is generally the first surgical step because it addresses an important pediatric reservoir and may improve CRS even without dramatic obstructive hypertrophy. **If symptoms persist after adenoidectomy**: reassess the diagnosis, adherence, allergy, dental/focal disease, and CF/PCD/immune context before escalating. **Key trap**: balloon dilation is not a default substitute for this sequence -- evidence remains less robust and cost-effectiveness is unfavorable compared with established adenoidectomy/ESS pathways. **Medical therapy evidence**: Antibiotic evidence in pediatric CRS is weak. In a placebo-controlled trial after tap and washout, cefaclor and placebo had similar resolution rates (about 65% vs 53%). AAO-HNS consensus nonetheless supports about 21 days when antibiotics are used. In a randomized trial, adding an oral methylprednisolone taper to 30 days of amoxicillin-clavulanate improved symptoms and CT scores over antibiotics alone. Saline irrigation is the mainstay, and more than 80% of children tolerate it. Culture-directed IV antibiotics are not justified on their own, because the reported success came alongside irrigation and adenoidectomy. Reserve antihistamines and leukotriene antagonists for documented allergy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 200, pp 2975-2977)
canonical_layers.operate:
If disease persists after appropriate medical/adenoid management, **limited FESS** is tailored to involved sinuses and age/anatomy. Protect orbit/skull base and preserve mucosa for long-term sinus development/function. **Senior operative refinement**: perform ESS for a defined refractory target -- persistent, objectively confirmed disease after appropriate medical therapy and usually adenoid-directed treatment, significant anatomic/focal disease, complications, or selected CF/PCD/other high-burden phenotypes. **Key point**: tailor the extent to the child's diseased, developed sinuses and the goal of drainage/topical access, rather than automatically performing adult-style complete ESS. **Counseling**: in very young children or systemic mucociliary disease, counsel that surgery improves ventilation/access but does not cure the underlying host defect. **Key trap**: orbital/intracranial complications follow the separate urgent source-control pathway and should not be delayed by the elective CRS sequence.

**Pediatric CRS surgical ladder**: first confirm persistent pediatric CRS rather than recurrent viral URIs/adenoiditis, and address appropriate medical therapy and important modifiers such as allergy, asthma, immune deficiency, cystic fibrosis, or primary ciliary dyskinesia when the history suggests them. For uncomplicated medically refractory pediatric CRS, **adenoidectomy** is generally the first-line operation, particularly in younger/pre-adolescent children, because the adenoid can function as an inflammatory/bacterial reservoir -- adenoid size alone is not the criterion. Persistent objective/symptomatic CRS after appropriate medical management and adenoidectomy is the usual pathway to **endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS)**, with CT obtained for operative planning and extent tailored to involved sinuses/anatomy rather than a mandatory **Lund-Mackay** cutoff. ESS may reasonably move earlier in children with cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, significant nasal polyposis, or complications when disease biology and clinical need justify it. **Key trap**: balloon dilation is not a required step between adenoidectomy and ESS -- current evidence has not established it as a superior or mandatory first-line pediatric CRS operation. There is likewise no evidence-based universal number of antibiotic weeks or single age threshold that must be met before surgery: document persistent symptoms plus objective disease, prior therapy, comorbidity, and expected benefit instead of using a ritual checklist. **Outcome numbers for counseling**: adenoidectomy alone succeeds in roughly 50-69% of children with medically refractory CRS (meta-analysis 69%), works best under ~5-6 years, and is the first operation for most pediatric otolaryngologists (~81%). Pediatric ESS, usually anterior ethmoidectomy plus maxillary antrostomy, has a pooled success of ~89% (range 77-100%, 882 children). Results are worse with immunodeficiency, CF, ciliary dyskinesia, younger age and smoke exposure, and revision rates are around 10%. Absorbable packing has made routine second-look anesthesia unnecessary, and most surgeons (~89%) no longer perform it. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Rhinitis and Acute and Chronic Sinusitis", p 1050) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1057) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1061) **Absolute indications for pediatric ESS**: (1) complete nasal obstruction from CF polyposis, (2) antrochoanal polyp, (3) intracranial complications, (4) mucocele/mucopyocele, (5) orbital abscess, (6) traumatic optic canal injury, (7) dacryocystorhinitis from refractory sinusitis, (8) fungal sinusitis, and selected (9) meningoencephaloceles and (10) neoplasms. Refractory CRS and recurrent acute sinusitis are relative indications that follow failed medical therapy and adenoidectomy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1059) **Stepwise surgery and why FESS fails**: Adenoidectomy alone helped about 61% at 12 months vs about 88% when combined with a maxillary sinus wash, and the wash helps most in children with asthma and high CT scores. Children younger than 7 and those with asthma more often fail adenoidectomy and need FESS. AAO-HNS consensus supports adenoidectomy as the first operation up to age 12, with no consensus for teens 13 and older. There is no consensus that balloon maxillary dilation adds anything beyond irrigation with adenoidectomy, and it raised charges without saving OR time. Conservative pediatric FESS succeeds in about 88%. When revision is needed (13% in one series), the usual findings are adhesions (57%) and a stenotic or missed natural maxillary ostium (52%). Go straight to FESS for CF, polyps, antrochoanal polyp or allergic fungal sinusitis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 200, p 2977)
canonical_layers.teach: Pediatric CRS is not simply adult CRS in a small nose -- the adenoid and underlying systemic disease matter much more. **Chief framework -- pediatric CRS**: prove the phenotype, find the driver, escalate in child-specific order. (1) Distinguish persistent CRS from serial URI/adenoiditis/rhinitis. (2) Use objective disease, not symptoms alone. (3) Screen selectively for CF/PCD/immune disease when the phenotype demands it. (4) After medical therapy, adenoidectomy is commonly the first operation. (5) Persistent disease earns diagnostic reassessment before ESS. (6) When ESS is needed, operate on the child's actual developed/diseased sinuses and a defined goal. (7) Do not turn balloon dilation or adult-style full-house ESS into automatic shortcuts. **Key point**: preserve the older PCD/CF senior case as the host-disease branch of this framework. **Facial growth and ESS**: an age-matched 10-year cohort (Bothwell) found no quantitative or qualitative facial growth difference after pediatric ESS, despite growth disturbance in piglet models. Families can be told there is no evidence of clinically significant growth effects. Still, be very conservative in the developing frontal recess (do not strip it or dissect above the middle turbinate insertion), and enter the pediatric sphenoid through the posterior ethmoid or superior meatus rather than by enlarging the ostium from the narrow sphenoethmoidal recess. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1060) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis", p 1062)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. CRS requires ≥12 weeks of compatible symptoms plus objective inflammation; phenotyping by polyps, eosinophilic/type-2 features, asthma/AERD, fungal disease and other modifiers is more useful than treating all CRS as one infection. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Saline and topical intranasal corticosteroid therapy are foundational. Add short systemic therapy, biologics or surgery according to phenotype, severity and prior response rather than requiring a rigid 'maximal medical therapy' checklist.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of CRS Phenotyping. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: CRS management is phenotype → objective disease → treatment response → individualized surgery/biologic decision, not repeated antibiotics for a CT scan.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Definition**: recognize chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) as persistent sinonasal inflammation, not a synonym for recurrent 'sinus infections.' **Diagnostic requirement**: symptoms must fit a chronic CRS syndrome and be paired with objective inflammatory evidence on nasal endoscopy and/or CT. **Next step**: phenotype the disease rather than stopping at the label. **Phenotypes/modifiers**: CRSsNP, CRSwNP, AFRS, and clinically important modifiers such as asthma, AERD, immune dysfunction, ciliary disease, or odontogenic disease behave differently. **Why it matters**: these change counseling, recurrence risk, and treatment choices.
canonical_layers.localize: **Localization**: CRS involves the sinonasal mucosa and drainage pathways. **Phenotype vs endotype**: separate the two. **Phenotype** is the clinically observable pattern, such as polyps versus no polyps or AFRS. **Endotype** refers to the dominant inflammatory biology, commonly type-2 inflammation in many Western CRSwNP patients but not universally. **Key trap**: do not equate a single biomarker with a complete endotype, and do not assume all polyps share identical biology. **Concept**: structural narrowing can worsen ventilation/topical access, but CRS is fundamentally an inflammatory disease rather than simply blocked plumbing.
canonical_layers.workup: **Principle**: confirm objective disease before committing a patient to long-term CRS treatment or surgery. **Endoscopy**: document edema, purulence, polyps, and postoperative anatomy. **CT**: obtain when it will confirm extent/anatomy or guide surgery, not as a symptom-only screening test. **History**: ask specifically about asthma, NSAID reactions/AERD, prior surgery, smell loss, allergy, immune deficiency clues, dental source, and unilateral red flags. **Testing**: allergy or immune testing is selective. **Biomarkers**: interpret eosinophils, total IgE, and other biomarkers as context rather than stand-alone diagnostic labels. **Diagnostic criteria and outcome tool**: Adult CRS requires at least 2 of 4 cardinal symptoms (nasal obstruction, mucopurulent drainage, facial pain or pressure, reduced smell) for 12 weeks or more, plus objective inflammation on endoscopy or CT. ABRS is 4 weeks or less. The SNOT-22 is the standard validated patient-reported measure of CRS symptom burden and is used to track response to medical therapy, surgery or biologics. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 51, 54) **Tissue eosinophilia cutoffs**: in research, eosinophilic CRSwNP is defined by more than 5 eosinophils per high-power field, or by a tissue ECP/MPO ratio above 1. A cutoff of more than 10 eosinophils/HPF is the clinically meaningful threshold for quality-of-life impact. Higher tissue or blood eosinophils and comorbid asthma predict worse quality of life, more severe disease and polyp recurrence after surgery; IgE, ECP and IL-5 also predict recurrence (Cummings 7e, Ch 41, p 657). **CT patterns and secretions**: in 500 screening CTs, Babbel found an infundibular pattern in 26% (maxillary only), an ostiomeatal-unit pattern in 25% (maxillary, frontal and anterior ethmoid), a sphenoethmoidal recess pattern in 6%, and a polyposis pattern in 10%. Acute secretions measure about 10 to 25 HU on CT and chronic inspissated secretions about 30 to 60 HU. On MRI, T2 signal falls as protein concentration rises; secretions above about 30% protein can appear as signal voids that mimic air. Fungal ball and allergic fungal mucin are T2-dark. Up to a third of asymptomatic people show mucosal thickening on CT, and symptom severity does not track CT extent. (Cummings 7e, Ch 38, p 625-627)
canonical_layers.manage: **Approach**: treat the phenotype and the patient's goals. **Baseline therapy**: **saline irrigation** plus **topical intranasal corticosteroid** are durable baseline treatments. **Key trap**: systemic antibiotics are not reflexive chronic anti-inflammatory therapy merely because the CT is abnormal. **Steroids**: short systemic steroid courses may be useful selectively, especially for severe polyp inflammation, after weighing risk. **Recalcitrant CRSwNP**: integrate asthma/AERD status, prior ESS, systemic-steroid burden, smell loss, and quality of life when discussing revision surgery versus a biologic. **Board pearl**: contemporary guidance does NOT support biologics for routine CRS without nasal polyps.
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: offer ESS when symptoms, objective disease, phenotype, and prior appropriate therapy support a reasonable expectation of benefit -- not after an arbitrary one-size-fits-all antibiotic checklist. **Goal**: disease-appropriate clearance and creation of durable access for ventilation, surveillance, and **topical therapy**. **Boundaries to preserve**: orbit, skull base, carotid, and optic nerve. **Extent**: should match disease burden and anatomy; recalcitrant inflammatory phenotypes may require broader access than limited focal disease. **Key trap**: surgery modifies anatomy and inflammatory burden but does not erase the underlying inflammatory tendency.
canonical_layers.teach: **Senior model**: diagnose CRS with **symptoms + objective inflammation**, then ask which phenotype, which modifiers, which prior treatment, and what outcome matters. **Phenotype vs endotype**: phenotype guides prognosis and treatment; endotype may refine biologic thinking but is not a magic single-test answer. **Key trap**: treating every CT opacity as infection, every polyp patient as identical, or every refractory patient as either 'needs surgery' or 'needs a biologic' without integrating disease type, asthma/AERD, prior ESS, steroid burden, and patient preference. **Ethnic and genetic pearls**: Asian CRSwNP is often Th1/Th17 and neutrophilic, with lower IL-5, less eosinophilia and less asthma than Western CRSwNP. Polymorphisms of the bitter taste receptor T2R38 (expressed on sinonasal epithelium and solitary chemosensory cells, where it boosts ciliary beat and antimicrobial release) may affect CRS susceptibility. Low vitamin D has been linked to deficient Treg activity in CRSwNP (Cummings 7e, Ch 41, pp 652, 655).
