candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. First distinguish upper from lower motor-neuron weakness, complete from incomplete paralysis, immediate from delayed onset, and flaccid paralysis from synkinesis. Ear vesicles, trauma, tumor signs, recurrent episodes or progressive weakness are not routine Bell palsy. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Eye protection is immediate. Treat idiopathic acute palsy promptly with corticosteroids; manage Ramsay Hunt, infection, trauma or neoplasm according to cause. Persistent weakness evolves into rehabilitation, synkinesis treatment and reanimation planning.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Facial Paralysis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Facial paralysis is not one disease. Every presentation should be classified by lesion level, cause, completeness and time since denervation because those variables determine both prognosis and reconstruction.

canonical_layers.recognize: First distinguish upper from lower motor-neuron weakness, complete from incomplete paralysis, immediate from delayed onset, and flaccid paralysis from synkinesis. Ear vesicles, trauma, tumor signs, recurrent episodes or progressive weakness are not routine Bell palsy. **Neoplastic and neurologic causes**: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the parotid tumor most often causing facial palsy (by prevalence), though adenoid cystic has the highest perineural rate. Facial nerve schwannoma presents with paralysis or spasm in over half of cases. Guillain-Barré is a common cause of acute bilateral facial palsy; myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness with ptosis; stroke spares the forehead. Möbius syndrome and myotonic dystrophy are congenital/hereditary causes. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 427–428, 433–434) **Congenital and neonatal facial palsy**: birth trauma (forceps, prolonged labor, large infant) is the most common cause of unilateral neonatal facial paralysis. The pediatric nerve is exposed because the mastoid tip does not develop until about age 2. Hemotympanum or periauricular bruising supports a traumatic cause, and most traumatic palsies recover with observation. Electrophysiologic testing (EMG/ENoG) helps separate traumatic from developmental palsy, and an ABR screens for associated hearing loss. Congenital unilateral lower lip palsy (asymmetric crying facies, from depressor anguli oris hypoplasia) is the most common congenital cause and carries about a 10% rate of cardiac defects. Möbius syndrome combines CN VI and VII palsies, sometimes bilateral, with limb anomalies (club foot), micrognathia and tongue weakness. Osteopetrosis (Albers-Schönberg) can compress CN VII and VIII in a narrowed IAC. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 594–595) **Pediatric Lyme facial palsy**: in endemic areas, Lyme disease is a leading cause of childhood facial palsy (peak age 5-9 years). Headache at presentation predicts Lyme, palsy can be bilateral, and erythema migrans may be absent. Confirm with a two-tier test (ELISA/IFA, then Western blot). The book treats with oral doxycycline for children 8 and older or amoxicillin under 8, for longer courses (21-28 days) for isolated palsy, and says corticosteroids are contraindicated. Current IDSA/AAP guidance allows short doxycycline courses at any age, generally for about 14-21 days, and does not recommend routine steroids. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Headaches", p 990) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral and Facial Neuropathic Pain in Children", p 998) **Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome**: Recurrent facial palsy with orofacial (usually lip) swelling and a fissured tongue is Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome. It belongs to the orofacial granulomatosis spectrum, with chronic granulomatous cheilitis (cheilitis granulomatosa of Miescher). In a child it can be the first sign of Crohn disease, so get a GI evaluation, and include sarcoidosis (Heerfordt syndrome: uveitis, parotid swelling, facial palsy) in the differential for recurrent palsy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Oral Cavity and Oropharyngeal Manifestations of Systemic Disease", p 1274) **Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome**: Triad of recurrent orofacial (lip) swelling, recurrent unilateral or bilateral facial paralysis, and fissured tongue (lingua plicata); a granulomatous process (orofacial granulomatosis/cheilitis granulomatosa) that may raise serum ACE. Treatment targets the palsy and edema; steroids and nerve decompression have limited success. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 22) **Möbius syndrome**: Nonprogressive congenital facial diplegia, usually bilateral, with abducens palsy (loss of lateral gaze), often other cranial neuropathies, limb anomalies and pectoral/brachial muscle aplasia (Poland overlap). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 22) **Bilateral facial paralysis**: Simultaneous or sequential bilateral palsy (0.3%-2% of cases) is far more often systemic than unilateral palsy. Causes include Guillain-Barre syndrome (CN VII is the third most often involved cranial nerve after IX and X; high CSF protein with a normal cell count), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis and Heerfordt syndrome, leukemia, syphilis, bacterial meningitis, mononucleosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, benign intracranial hypertension, and brainstem or prepontine tumor. Work up with a full neurologic exam, lumbar puncture with cytology, VDRL, Lyme serology, autoantibodies and MRI. Eye care is critical, and the disability is far greater than with unilateral palsy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, p 2594) **Recurrent, familial and progressive palsy**: About 9%-11% of Bell palsy patients have had a prior episode, on either side, and familial cases make up 6%-8%. A second palsy on the same side revealed a tumor in about 20% (8 of 40), so image recurrent ipsilateral palsy. Slowly progressive weakness is not Bell palsy. Palsy that progresses beyond 3 weeks, or shows no return of function by 6 months, should be presumed to be tumor (facial schwannoma, hemangioma, meningioma, perineural metastasis) until proven otherwise, with CT and gadolinium MRI and serial imaging if the first studies are negative. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, p 2594; Ch 173, p 2609) **Pregnancy, barotrauma and other special settings**: Bell palsy is about 3.3 times more common in pregnancy, mainly in the third trimester or just after delivery; preeclampsia is about 6 times more frequent among these patients, outcomes may be worse, and prednisone is considered low risk late in pregnancy. Facial baroparesis is a transient palsy, sometimes with taste loss, on ascent in a plane or car (about 8000-10,000 ft) or when diving. It is caused by middle-ear pressure acting on a dehiscent nerve and is prevented with a tympanostomy tube. In Kawasaki disease, facial palsy may mark more severe disease. In HIV, early palsy resembles Bell palsy, but consider lymphoma, zoster and Guillain-Barre syndrome. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2595-2597) **Congenital versus birth-trauma palsy numbers**: Neonatal facial palsy occurs in about 0.23% of live births, and about 78% is due to birth trauma, split evenly between forceps and nonforceps deliveries (pressure from the maternal sacrum). Facial bruising, swelling or hemotympanum favor trauma. Other cranial neuropathies or a prolonged ABR I-III or I-V interval favor a developmental cause. Congenital unilateral lower lip palsy (absent depressor labii inferioris) is the mildest form. In CHARGE syndrome, 75% have at least one cranial neuropathy (CN VIII about 60%, VII 43%, IX/X 30%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2592-2593) **Synchronous bilateral facial paralysis**: the main causes are Lyme disease, Möbius syndrome, NF2, brainstem lesions (cavernous hemangioma), bilateral temporal bone fractures, Guillain-Barré and HIV. Bilateral simultaneous palsy is rarely Bell palsy and needs a directed workup. Lyme palsy often comes with headache, fever, rash, arthralgia and fatigue. Treat it with antibiotics and eye care; adding steroids may worsen outcomes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 21, p 394-395) **Neonatal facial palsy**: Traumatic neonatal palsy is linked to first births, high birth weight, prolonged labor, and forceps or vacuum delivery, often with local bruising. About 90% recover spontaneously. Distinguish it from developmental palsy (Moebius, hemifacial microsomia, CHARGE), which lacks trauma signs, may be bilateral or segmental, and does not recover. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 1024)
canonical_layers.localize: Use forehead involvement, taste/lacrimation symptoms, hyperacusis, ear disease and other cranial neuropathies to localize along the facial nerve from brainstem to parotid branches.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Imaging**: typical acute Bell palsy often needs no imaging; atypical, recurrent, progressive, traumatic, or tumor-associated palsy requires targeted MRI/CT and etiologic evaluation. Document severity serially with a consistent facial grading system and ocular status.

**Also**: grade function serially with a named scale such as **House-Brackmann** (I normal; II mild; III moderate with complete eye closure; IV moderately severe with incomplete/weak closure; V barely perceptible motion; VI no movement), and separately document ocular protection and synkinesis. Typical new Bell palsy does not require routine imaging, but progressive, recurrent, segmental, traumatic, or tumor-associated weakness does.

**Grading scale**: the **Sunnybrook Facial Grading System** is a complementary, more granular alternative to House-Brackmann, scoring resting symmetry, voluntary movement of five facial actions, and synkinesis separately to produce a composite score out of 100 (100 = normal). It is especially useful when synkinesis needs to be tracked over time, which House-Brackmann does not capture well. **Electrodiagnostic timing details**: ENoG is only meaningful in complete (HB VI) paralysis and not until Wallerian degeneration has occurred (after about 24–72 hours); it compares compound action potential amplitude with the normal side. EMG shows fibrillations 1–2 weeks after denervation and polyphasic potentials with reinnervation; any voluntary motor units mean some nerve continuity. Older tests: nerve excitability test (side difference ≥3.5 mA is significant) and maximal stimulation test are subjective and rarely used; topognostic tests (Schirmer, stapedial reflex, salivary flow) have been replaced. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 427–430) **Pediatric facial palsy specifics**: Bell palsy is the most common cause of acute unilateral facial weakness in children, and most recover nearly fully within weeks. Lyme disease is a major association in endemic areas, so order serology with Western blot confirmation. Recurrence occurs in about 7%. Bilateral palsy (<1%) should prompt a search for a systemic cause, such as Lyme, sarcoidosis (chest imaging, serum and CSF ACE), Guillain–Barré, or other polyneuropathy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Neurology", p 140) **Electrodiagnostic test criteria and pitfalls**: These tests apply only to complete paralysis, from about day 3 (after Wallerian degeneration) until recovery begins or excitability is lost. A nerve excitability test difference above 3.5 mA suggests degeneration, though 38% of such patients still recover fully. On the maximal stimulation test, an equal response predicts complete recovery in about 92%, and a markedly reduced or absent response predicts incomplete recovery in about 86%. ENoG compares the nasolabial CMAP between sides; healthy sides differ by about 3%, and test-retest error is about 20%, so average repeated trials. Degeneration above 90% within 14 days leaves only about a 30% chance of spontaneous good recovery. Always follow over 90% ENoG with voluntary EMG: motor units or polyphasic potentials mean dyssynchrony (false-positive ENoG) and an excellent prognosis. Patients who cannot cooperate are treated as complete and tested with MST after 72 hours. (Cummings 7e, Ch 171, pp 2579-2582) **Late EMG and nerve-repair failure**: Fibrillation potentials appear 10-14 days after denervation and predict incomplete recovery in about 81%. Polyphasic reinnervation potentials can appear as early as 4-6 weeks, before visible movement, and predict fair to good recovery. After 14 days, EMG predicts outcome better than ENoG. After a nerve repair or anastomosis, no clinical recovery and no polyphasic potentials by 15 months (18 months at the latest) means failure, and another procedure such as hypoglossal-facial transfer should be considered. (Cummings 7e, Ch 171, pp 2581-2582) **ENoG mechanics**: Supramaximal stimulation at the stylomastoid foramen with recording at the nasolabial fold; % response = involved/uninvolved amplitude x 100 and % degeneration = 100 minus that. It is valid from day 3 (after Wallerian degeneration) to about day 21, repeated every 3-5 days to plateau; it cannot distinguish axonotmesis from neurotmesis. A response of 10% or less of the normal side (90% or more degeneration) predicts over 50% chance of incomplete recovery; ENoG predicts spontaneous recovery with 80-100% accuracy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 15, p 312-313) **Electrodiagnostic timing**: MST and ENoG are useful from about 3 days to 2-3 weeks, because a cut nerve still conducts distally for 48-72 hours. EMG fibrillations appear at only 10-21 days, but volitional motor-unit potentials on EMG mean the nerve is intact despite an absent ENoG response (deblocking). Fisch's criteria for surgical exposure are ENoG 10% or less of normal within 6 days for trauma, within 2 weeks for Bell palsy, and despite drainage and antibiotics for AOM. Gantz found no benefit from middle fossa decompression after 14 days. Incomplete palsy with ENoG above 10% after day 14 gives about 90% satisfactory recovery. Complete palsy with ENoG of 10% or less in the first 14 days gives under 50%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 857-858)
canonical_layers.manage:
**Immediate**: eye protection. Treat idiopathic acute palsy promptly with corticosteroids; manage Ramsay Hunt, infection, trauma, or neoplasm according to cause. Persistent weakness evolves into rehabilitation, synkinesis treatment, and reanimation planning.

**Also**: for new Bell palsy, start oral corticosteroids promptly when not contraindicated and protect the eye. **Key trap**: antiviral monotherapy is not recommended; combination antiviral plus steroid may be offered selectively, because any added benefit is modest/uncertain. **Red flags**: vesicles, severe pain, hearing/vestibular symptoms, or other cranial neuropathies redirect evaluation toward Ramsay Hunt or another cause. **Bell, Ramsay Hunt, Lyme and Melkersson-Rosenthal prognosis**: Bell palsy: about 70–85% recover fully by 6 months, 7–12% recur, and any residual movement predicts a good outcome; decompression (middle fossa, covering meatal foramen, labyrinthine segment, and geniculate) is considered only for >90% ENoG degeneration with no voluntary EMG activity within 2 weeks. Ramsay Hunt leaves residual weakness in 30–50%. Lyme disease involves the facial nerve in about 10% (sometimes bilaterally) and typically recovers fully over 6–12 months with antibiotics. Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is recurrent facial edema, recurrent facial palsy, and fissured tongue starting in youth, with granulomas on lip biopsy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 430–432) **Traumatic and iatrogenic injury**: Complete paralysis after a penetrating facial wound should be explored and repaired within about 48–72 hours, while distal branches can still be stimulated; injuries medial to a vertical line through the lateral canthus usually recover without repair. With contamination or tissue loss, tag the ends and repair in a second stage at about 3–4 weeks. For paralysis noticed right after ear surgery, wait 2–3 hours for local anesthetic to wear off; if the nerve was seen intact, give steroids and follow electrically, and consider re-exploration for complete paralysis in selected cases. Delayed-onset or incomplete weakness usually recovers fully. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 433) **Facial palsy complicating AOM in children**: Half of the cases occur at age 3 or younger, often with a dehiscent tympanic segment. In acute otitis without osteitis, treat with tympanocentesis or myringotomy (a tube if there is recurrent AOM, underlying chronic OME, or prolonged drainage is needed) plus IV antibiotics covering pneumococcus and H. influenzae. Recovery is usually rapid without mastoidectomy or decompression. Perform mastoidectomy only for coalescent osteitis, CSOM or cholesteatoma. Decompression is considered for complete paralysis with electrophysiologic degeneration. In contrast, facial palsy with *CSOM or cholesteatoma* needs immediate surgical exploration. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 802-803) **Lyme facial palsy: antibiotics yes, steroids no**: Facial palsy is the most common otologic manifestation of Lyme disease (about 3-11% of cases, bilateral in about 25%) and occurs in early disseminated (second-stage) disease, sometimes as the only neurologic sign. Recovery is usually spontaneous and complete over weeks to months; antibiotics (doxycycline first line) do not change the palsy outcome but are given to treat the infection and prevent late arthritis and neurologic disease. Corticosteroids have not shown benefit, and one retrospective series found worse long-term outcomes with more synkinesis when steroids were added. A red-violet earlobe nodule (borrelial lymphocytoma) is another second-stage ear sign. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2298-2299) **Bell palsy evidence numbers**: Untreated, 80%-90% recover completely, and in the Peitersen series none of 1505 untreated patients was left with permanent complete paralysis; patients whose palsy never becomes complete recover in 95%-100%. Steroids raise the chance of complete recovery by about 17%, and starting within 48 hours (829-patient RCT) gave higher recovery and less synkinesis. The AAN estimates that adding an antiviral increases recovery by no more than 7%. Poor prognostic factors include hyperacusis, reduced tearing, age over 60, diabetes, hypertension and severe pain. Transmastoid decompression has been abandoned because the lesion is at the meatal foramen (about 0.68 mm wide, versus 1.02-1.53 mm elsewhere in the canal). (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2589, 2591) **Lyme and otitis media palsy**: Facial palsy occurs in 0.9%-4.5% of Lyme disease and can come before seroconversion or occur without erythema migrans or a known tick bite; confirm a positive ELISA with IgM and IgG immunoblots. Treat with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14-21 days. Adding corticosteroids was associated with worse long-term facial outcomes than antibiotics alone. Otitis media causes about 3.1% of acute palsies. In acute otitis media, give parenteral antibiotics and do a wide myringotomy without manipulating the nerve. Palsy with chronic otitis, usually gradual, suggests cholesteatoma and needs surgery, with decompression that leaves the perineurium intact. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2596-2597) **Textbook acute-palsy algorithm**: Bell palsy (15–30/100,000) should be fully evolved by 72 hours. Give prednisone within 48–72 hours (about 60 mg for 5 days, then a 5-day taper), with or without an antiviral, plus eye care. Consider ENoG within about 12 days for complete paralysis; decompression is debated for under 10% residual response with no voluntary EMG units. Temporal bone fracture: immediate-onset palsy → consider exploration; delayed onset → serial ENoG, with decompression if below 10%. Iatrogenic palsy with unknown continuity: explore unless ENoG proves continuity. Repair tension-free; graft with great auricular (avoid if neck metastasis is possible), sural (longest) or medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (branching pattern suits multiple distal branches). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 21, p 395-396) **Unexpected facial palsy after ear surgery**: The facial nerve is most often injured at the second genu, then at the anterior epitympanum. If the patient wakes with a paralysis, wait about 2 hours for local anesthetic to wear off and loosen the mastoid dressing. If the nerve was clearly seen and intact (or only its sheath was breached and decompressed), do not explore. If immediate complete paralysis follows surgery in which the nerve was *not* identified, exploration is mandatory, and it can be planned for the next day. At exploration, decompress several millimeters proximal and distal to the injury. A frayed sheath with intact contents needs decompression only. A transected nerve is freshened and repaired primarily or with an interposition graft. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 863)
canonical_layers.operate: Timing determines the reconstructive toolbox: primary repair/cable graft when nerve continuity is lost acutely, nerve transfer while native muscle remains viable, and regional/free muscle transfer when chronic denervation has eliminated useful motor endplates. **Middle fossa decompression for Bell palsy**: The criteria are ENoG degeneration over 90% within 14 days of complete paralysis plus no voluntary EMG motor units. In the Iowa and Gantz series, about 91%-92% reached HB I-II after middle fossa decompression of the meatal foramen, labyrinthine segment and geniculate, versus about 42% with steroids alone. Find the IAC about 60 degrees anterior to the blue line of the superior semicircular canal. Only about 120 degrees of the lateral IAC circumference can be opened safely, because the cochlea may lie within 1 mm below and the superior canal ampulla just behind. Bill's bar separates the nerve from the superior vestibular nerve. Risks include about a 30-dB conductive loss, SNHL, CSF leak and, most serious, AICA injury, so offer it only where the approach is done routinely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, p 2592; Ch 173, pp 2603-2605) **Facial palsy from chronic otitis**: dehiscence of the tympanic segment (up to about 30% congenitally) or erosion lets exotoxins and inflammation injure the nerve. Palsy from AOM starts abruptly, is usually incomplete and recovers with antibiotics plus myringotomy or a tube. Palsy from COM progresses slowly and often persists. Treat it with tympanomastoidectomy, clearing matrix and granulation off the epineurium and decompressing proximal and distal to the involved segment. Open the sheath only if cholesteatoma has invaded it. HB I–II recovery is reported in 52–83%. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 422-423)
canonical_layers.teach: Facial paralysis is not one disease. Every presentation should be classified by lesion level, cause, completeness and time since denervation because those variables determine both prognosis and reconstruction. **Recovery timing, recurrence and tumor red flags**: Bell palsy in children recovers completely in about 90% (adults: 71% complete, 84% HB I-II). If recovery begins before 3 weeks it is almost always complete. If it begins at 3 weeks to 2 months it is usually satisfactory. If it is delayed to 2-4 months, fewer than 30% reach HB I-II. Progression from paresis to complete paralysis over 3-10 days predicts degeneration in about 75%. Bell palsy recurs in about 10%, two-thirds on the opposite side. About 10% of *ipsilateral* recurrences are tumors, mostly facial neuromas. Suspect a tumor with no recovery by 6 months, slow progression beyond 3 weeks, ipsilateral recurrence, twitching before the weakness, or other neurologic signs. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 858, 860-861, 864) **Grading reliability and FNGS 2.0**: House-Brackmann is AAO-HNS endorsed and weights maximal effort, but full agreement among examiners ranges from only about 33% to 80%, and it handles regional and secondary deficits poorly. Facial Nerve Grading System 2.0 scores the brow, eye, nasolabial fold and oral commissure separately (1-6 each) and adds a secondary-movement score for synkinesis and contracture. In acute palsy, where synkinesis cannot yet exist, grade by percentage of function: II = 75%-99%, III = 50%-75%, IV = 25%-50%, V = 1%-25%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 171, pp 2575-2576) **Otitic facial palsy is often mislabeled Bell palsy**: Facial paralysis complicated 0.5% of AOM before antibiotics vs about 0.005% now (Denmark). Children with acute facial palsy are frequently misdiagnosed with Bell palsy in the ED, so every child needs a full ENT exam with pneumatic otoscopy. An underlying disease such as leukemia should be considered when palsy develops during otitis. In a Washington series, incomplete palsies resolved with myringotomy and IV antibiotics alone. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 802-803)

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Progressive bilateral hearing difficulty—often speech-in-noise first—in an older adult should trigger formal hearing evaluation rather than being dismissed as normal aging. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Counsel on communication strategies and hearing-assistive technology; offer or refer for hearing aids when appropriate. Reassess benefit and escalate to cochlear-implant evaluation when appropriately fitted amplification does not provide adequate speech understanding.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Age-Related Hearing Loss / Presbycusis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Do not normalize disability because of age. The goal is function: identify hearing loss, treat remediable causes, provide amplification/assistive strategies and recognize when hearing aids are no longer enough.

canonical_layers.recognize: Progressive bilateral hearing difficulty—often speech-in-noise first—in an older adult should trigger formal hearing evaluation rather than being dismissed as normal aging.
canonical_layers.localize: Usually bilateral sensorineural dysfunction from age-related cochlear/neural changes; asymmetry, conductive findings, sudden change or focal neurologic symptoms require a different localization pathway.
canonical_layers.workup: Perform otoscopy and audiologic evaluation. Ask about communication goals, tinnitus, falls/cognition and functional impact; pursue additional workup when asymmetry or other atypical findings suggest a non-age-related cause.
canonical_layers.manage:
Counsel on communication strategies and hearing-assistive technology. Offer or refer for hearing aids when appropriate. Reassess benefit and escalate to cochlear-implant evaluation when appropriately fitted amplification does not provide adequate speech understanding.

**Pathway**: follow a function-centered pathway. Counsel on communication strategies, offer appropriately fitted amplification and assistive technology, verify benefit rather than merely documenting device purchase, and refer for cochlear-implant evaluation when aided speech understanding remains inadequate. **Key trap**: asymmetry, sudden change, conductive findings, or focal neurologic symptoms require diagnostic workup beyond an age-related label.
canonical_layers.operate: The advanced procedural decision is not routine ear surgery; it is recognizing when severe functional hearing loss warrants implant evaluation and when asymmetric or conductive disease needs a different diagnostic pathway.
canonical_layers.teach: Do not normalize disability because of age. The goal is function: identify hearing loss, treat remediable causes, provide amplification/assistive strategies and recognize when hearing aids are no longer enough. **Hearing loss and dementia numbers**: In cohort studies, mild hearing loss doubles dementia risk, moderate loss triples it and severe loss raises it about fivefold, and an effect is seen from as young as 55. Over 11 years of follow-up, hazard ratios rose from 1.89 to 4.94 from mild to severe loss, and each 25 dB of loss equaled about 7 years of cognitive aging. The 2017 Lancet Commission ranked age-related hearing loss as the largest potentially modifiable dementia risk factor, and the 2024 update kept it among the largest. Cummings 7e notes that randomized proof that treatment prevents decline was still lacking at the time. The ACHIEVE trial (2023) then found that a hearing intervention did not slow 3-year cognitive decline overall, but slowed it by about 48% in older adults at higher dementia risk. (Cummings 7e, Ch 133, p 2013) (Cummings 7e, Ch 132, p 2007)

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Permanent congenital/early-onset SNHL should trigger etiologic thinking early because genetic diagnosis can predict progression, syndromic risks and cochlear-implant considerations. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Ensure early language access through amplification, CI evaluation and educational support while the etiologic workup proceeds. A genetic result can guide surveillance of vision, thyroid, renal, cardiac or neurologic disease in syndromic conditions.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Congenital Hearing Loss Genetics. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: The goal of genetics is not just naming a mutation; it can predict progression, syndromic surveillance and expected auditory rehabilitation.

canonical_layers.recognize: Use this card for the **molecular etiology** pathway once congenital/early-onset hearing loss is confirmed. Genetic hearing loss may be syndromic or nonsyndromic, recessive, dominant, X-linked, mitochondrial, de novo, or variably penetrant. **Key trap**: the absence of affected parents does NOT make a genetic cause unlikely. **Workup approach**: pattern the phenotype before ordering tests -- congenital versus delayed/progressive, unilateral versus bilateral, severity/configuration, vestibular symptoms, family history/consanguinity, pigmentation, vision, renal/branchial, thyroid, cardiac, craniofacial, neurologic, and skeletal findings. **Usher syndrome subtypes**: Usher is the most common autosomal recessive syndromic hearing loss and the leading cause of combined deafness and blindness. Type I has profound congenital SNHL, absent vestibular function and retinitis pigmentosa beginning before adolescence; these children walk late and are early CI candidates. Type II, the most common, has moderate to severe congenital SNHL, normal vestibular function and later RP. Type III has progressive SNHL with variable vestibular loss. Diagnosis uses an ophthalmologic exam with electroretinography plus genetics. Pendred is the second most common recessive syndrome and Jervell and Lange-Nielsen the third. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 587) **Audioprofile clues in dominant nonsyndromic loss**: dominant loss is usually postlingual and progressive. Low-frequency (upsloping) loss points to WFS1 (DFNA6/14/38; ~75% of dominant low-frequency loss). A congenital, nonprogressive mid-frequency 'cookie-bite' loss points to TECTA (DFNA8/12). High-frequency progressive loss has many genes, classically KCNQ4 (DFNA2). DFNA9 (COCH) is distinctive for accompanying vestibular failure, which can precede and progress faster than the hearing loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 472-474, 491) **Craniofacial syndromes and their ear findings**: *Treacher Collins* (TCOF1, autosomal dominant, about 60% new mutations; a neural-crest migration defect of the first and second arches) gives bilateral, symmetric moderate-to-severe conductive loss. It comes from ossicular deformity in a small, fibrous epitympanum, and the inner ear is usually normal. *Crouzon* and *Apert* (FGFR2): about a third of Crouzon patients have a nonprogressive conductive loss, and Apert classically has congenital stapes footplate fixation. Both have eustachian tube dysfunction and OME. *Osteogenesis imperfecta* (COL1A1/COL1A2, type I with blue sclerae): conductive loss from thin, fragile stapes crura and from otosclerosis that is often aggressive. *Osteopetrosis* (malignant recessive form): mixed loss, facial palsy, optic atrophy and choanal atresia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 570, 572, 575-577) **Chromosomal and other syndromes**: *Turner* (45,X, about 1 in 5000 females) has persistent OME that often progresses to chronic otitis media. A characteristic midfrequency ('cookie-bite') SNHL can progress in the teens, so these children need lifelong audiometry. *Noonan* (PTPN11 and others; normal karyotype; males and females; pulmonary stenosis) has a Turner-like phenotype with conductive or sensorineural loss. *Wildervanck (cervico-oculo-acoustic) syndrome* is Klippel-Feil fusion plus Duane retraction plus congenital SNHL, almost entirely in females. *Möbius* is congenital bilateral facial (and abducens) palsy, with hearing loss in 15-25%. *Hurler* (mucopolysaccharidosis I) causes mixed loss from mesenchyme filling the middle ear, plus OME. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 563, 567, 571, 572, 574, 576) **Branchio-oto-renal (Melnick–Fraser) syndrome**: autosomal dominant (EYA1), with bilateral preauricular pits/sinuses, cervical branchial fistulas or cysts, auricular malformation up to microtia, inner-ear anomalies such as Mondini dysplasia, and hearing loss that may be conductive, sensorineural, mixed, or sudden, plus renal anomalies ranging from mild to severe. An isolated preauricular pit carries only about a 1-in-200 chance of hearing loss, but a pit or branchial anomaly plus hearing loss is a strong indication for renal ultrasound and EYA1 testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Cysts and Sinuses of the Head and Neck", p 1740) **Dominant audioprofiles**: Dominant nonsyndromic loss is usually postlingual, progressive and milder than recessive loss, and several genes have signature audiograms: WFS1 (DFNA6/14/38) gives low-frequency loss; TECTA (DFNA8/12) gives a congenital, nonprogressive midfrequency 'cookie-bite' loss; KCNQ4 (DFNA2) gives progressive high-frequency loss through outer hair cell death. Recessive TECTA (DFNB21) instead causes severe-to-profound loss. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2283-2286) **Usher syndrome types**: Usher = SNHL plus retinitis pigmentosa, often with vestibular loss; it accounts for 3-6% of congenital deafness and about half of combined deaf-blindness. Type 1: congenital severe-to-profound loss, absent vestibular function, RP in childhood (USH1B/MYO7A is 75% of type 1). Type 2: moderate-to-severe congenital loss, normal vestibular function, RP starting in the 3rd-4th decade (USH2A is the most common Usher form overall). Type 3: progressive loss with variable vestibular and RP onset. It presents as an apparent nonsyndromic loss (a 'nonsyndromic mimic'), so panels include Usher genes; a congenitally deaf child who walks late suggests type 1. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2288-2289) **Waardenburg types**: WS1 (PAX3) is SNHL, white forelock, iris heterochromia and dystopia canthorum. WS2 (MITF, SNAI2) is WS1 without dystopia canthorum and with a higher rate of hearing loss (57-85% vs 36-67%). WS3 (Klein-Waardenburg, PAX3) is WS1 plus upper-limb hypoplasia or contractures. WS4 (Shah-Waardenburg) is WS plus Hirschsprung disease, usually recessive with EDNRB or EDN3 and dominant with SOX10. Hearing loss is usually profound, bilateral and stable, and temporal bone imaging is usually normal. The cause is absent strial melanocytes from a neural crest defect. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2288) **Stickler syndrome**: Dominant type II/XI collagen disorder (COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2), about 1 in 10,000. Diagnosis needs a congenital vitreous anomaly plus 3 of: myopia before age 6, retinal detachment or lattice degeneration, joint hypermobility, SNHL, or midline clefting. Robin sequence and cleft occur in 28-65%, often submucous. Hearing loss can be conductive (from ET dysfunction), sensorineural or mixed. The COL11A2 type has no eye findings because that gene is not expressed in the vitreous. Retinal detachment, in about 50%, is the most serious problem, so these children need ophthalmology follow-up. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2287) **Alport syndrome**: Type IV collagen disease (COL4A5, X-linked in ~80%; COL4A3/4 autosomal) with hematuric nephritis progressing to ESRD in all males, progressive symmetric high-frequency SNHL detectable by late childhood, and eye lesions (anterior lenticonus, macular flecks). Diagnosis needs 3 of 4: family history of hematuria/renal failure, progressive high-frequency SNHL, the typical eye lesion, and glomerular basement membrane changes. Anterior lenticonus predicts ESRD before age 30. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2289) **Branchio-oto-renal syndrome numbers**: Dominant, nearly full penetrance, 1 in 40,000, and about 2% of profoundly deaf children. Hearing loss occurs in ~90% (mixed 50%, conductive 30%, sensorineural 20%). Preauricular pits occur in 82%, auricular malformations in 32%, branchial fistulas or cysts are common, and renal anomalies occur in about 25%. Inner ear findings include cochlear hypoplasia, an enlarged vestibular or cochlear aqueduct, and a hypoplastic lateral semicircular canal. Genes are EYA1 (about 25% of cases), SIX1 and SIX5, so a child with ear pits and hearing loss needs a renal ultrasound. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2286) **Mitochondrial syndromes**: Mitochondrial disorders are maternally inherited with no father-to-child transmission; severity tracks heteroplasmy. Hearing loss occurs in ~70% of syndromic forms. MELAS and MIDD (maternally inherited diabetes and deafness, 0.5-2.8% of diabetics) are caused by m.3243A>G and give progressive high-frequency SNHL from strial atrophy. MERRF causes hearing loss with myoclonus, ataxia and optic atrophy. Kearns-Sayre syndrome (large mtDNA deletions) causes ophthalmoplegia, retinopathy and heart block before age 20, with SNHL in 50%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2289-2290) **Chromosomal disorders and hearing**: About 75% of children with trisomy 21 have hearing loss (conductive, sensorineural or mixed). Trisomy 13 is usually profound deafness with cleft lip and palate. Turner syndrome (45,X) has frequent otitis media and common mild-to-moderate SNHL. About 20% of boys with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) have mild SNHL. Loss in Turner and Klinefelter is often missed unless specifically tested. (Cummings 7e, Ch 149, p 2271) **Less common X-linked syndromes**: *Norrie syndrome* (Xp11.4) is retinal pseudotumor/dysplasia leading to congenital blindness, with progressive SNHL starting in the 2nd–3rd decade in about a third, plus intellectual disturbance. *Otopalatodigital syndrome* (Xq28) is hypertelorism, a prominent supraorbital ridge, cleft palate, short stature, broad digits with a wide first toe web, and conductive loss from ossicular malformation (full disease in males). *X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth* (connexin 32/GJB1, Xq13) is peripheral neuropathy with 'champagne-bottle' calves and sometimes SNHL. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 17, p 341-342)
canonical_layers.localize: **Approach**: localize the phenotype to a gene/syndrome family rather than memorizing a disconnected gene list. **GJB2/GJB6-related DFNB1**: a classic nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive cause. **SLC26A4**: can produce Pendred/DFNB4 with enlarged vestibular aqueduct. **Usher syndrome**: couples hearing loss with retinal disease +/- vestibular dysfunction. **Branchio-oto-renal syndromes**: link ear/branchial findings with renal disease. **Jervell-Lange-Nielsen**: links congenital severe SNHL with long-QT risk. **Mitochondrial variants**: can confer aminoglycoside susceptibility. Imaging anatomy such as EVA or cochlear malformation can therefore sharpen -- not replace -- the genetic differential. **Dominant and X-linked syndromes**: the mnemonic WANT BCS covers the dominant syndromes. Waardenburg causes SNHL. Its causative genes are PAX3 (types I and III) or MITF (type II). Type I has dystopia canthorum, with about 50% SNHL. Type II lacks dystopia but has about 80% SNHL. Type III adds limb anomalies and type IV adds Hirschsprung disease. Stickler (COL2A1) causes progressive SNHL with myopia, retinal detachment, joint laxity and Pierre Robin sequence. Branchio-oto-renal syndrome (EYA1) causes mixed loss with pits/tags and renal anomalies, so order a renal ultrasound. Alport syndrome is mostly X-linked COL4A5. It causes progressive SNHL in the first decade with nephritis and lenticonus or myopia. X-linked POU3F4 causes congenital stapes fixation with a gusher; avoid routine stapedotomy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 588–590)
canonical_layers.workup: **Sequence**: after diagnostic audiology, obtain a three-generation family history and syndrome-directed examination, then use contemporary comprehensive genetic testing rather than reflexively stopping after a single connexin assay. **ACMG's** etiologic-evaluation framework supports genetic evaluation because a molecular diagnosis can change prognosis, recurrence counseling, surveillance for extra-auditory disease, and management. A broad hearing-loss panel with copy-number and relevant mitochondrial analysis is often higher-yield than serial single-gene testing. Targeted testing is reasonable when the phenotype strongly points to one diagnosis. Order ECG, ophthalmology, renal studies, thyroid assessment, or other tests when the phenotype/gene result makes them actionable rather than as an indiscriminate laboratory battery. **Key trap**: in a neonate, do not let genetic testing delay time-sensitive cCMV testing. **First-tier test in the dysmorphic child**: chromosomal microarray (array CGH) is now recommended as the first-line genetic screen, in place of karyotype, for children with unexplained developmental delay and dysmorphic or craniofacial features. It detects gains and losses of about 300–500 kb, compared with 3–5 Mb for high-resolution karyotype. Exome sequencing is reserved for cases where tiered testing is negative (clinical diagnostic yield about 25%). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetics, Syndromology, and Craniofacial Anomalies", p 31, 57) **Classic testing sequence taught by this text**: screen GJB2 first (if biallelic, no further testing needed); if CT/MRI shows EVA or incomplete partition, test SLC26A4 (Pendred/DFNB4); consider Usher genes next in severe-to-profound congenital loss (3-6% of such children, second to GJB2 among congenitally deaf CI users). Order MRI for suspected NF2, progressive loss or retrocochlear audiology. Up to 30% have no cause after history and examination. Modern practice replaces serial single-gene testing with comprehensive panels, but the phenotype logic still applies. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 490) **Pendred testing**: Pendrin (SLC26A4, chromosome 7) is a chloride/iodide transporter. Pendred syndrome is euthyroid goiter with SNHL and is diagnosed classically by an abnormal *potassium perchlorate discharge test* (an organification defect). It is the most common syndromic cause of SNHL, at about 10% of syndromic cases. Up to 80% of patients have inner-ear anomalies (EVA with or without IP-II). The goiter usually appears in adolescence, so a child can have SLC26A4-related EVA (DFNB4) with normal thyroid function. Many experts screen SLC26A4 in every patient with EVA. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 525) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 537-538) **CHARGE audiogram and BOR numbers**: The hearing loss in CHARGE is typically mixed, with a 'wedge-shaped' audiogram: the bone-conduction curve slopes down and meets a flat air-conduction curve in the low frequencies. Chronic OME and ossicular anomalies add a conductive component, and cochlear-nerve aplasia can cause profound loss. In BOR (about 1 in 40,000, autosomal dominant), the loss is mixed in about 50%, conductive in 30% and sensorineural in 20%, and may begin in childhood. Cervical sinuses open anterior to the SCM below the hyoid, and severe renal dysplasia occurs in about 6%, so renal ultrasound is required. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 564, 570) **Pendred syndrome details**: Pendred is the most common syndromic hereditary SNHL (recessive, SLC26A4/pendrin, which can account for up to ~10% of hereditary deafness). The goiter appears in the 2nd decade and patients usually stay euthyroid. Most patients have a temporal bone anomaly on imaging (enlarged vestibular aqueduct, often with Mondini/IP-II). The perchlorate discharge test is positive when more than 10% of radioiodine washes out, but its sensitivity is low, so genetic testing is preferred. Nonsyndromic SLC26A4 loss is DFNB4. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2288) **Genetic testing yield and counseling numbers**: Comprehensive multigene panels (massively parallel sequencing) are now standard of care and diagnose about 40% overall, rising to about 60% in a newborn with bilateral congenital profound loss. Yield is higher with young age, early onset, symmetric loss and family history. For normal-hearing parents of one deaf child, the risk of a second deaf child is about 17.5%. If the familial variant is known, prenatal testing is possible by chorionic villus sampling (10-12 weeks) or amniocentesis (15-18 weeks). (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2290-2291)
canonical_layers.manage: A genetic diagnosis is clinically useful only if it **changes counseling or care**. Explain inheritance and recurrence risk with genetics professionals. Identify relatives who need testing or audiology. Anticipate progression and vestibular risk. Institute syndrome-specific surveillance (for example retinal, renal, thyroid, or cardiac evaluation when indicated), and avoid preventable exposures when a genotype creates susceptibility. **Key trap**: do not promise auditory outcome from genotype alone -- hearing phenotype and progression can vary even within families. Continue standard early hearing intervention in parallel with etiologic testing; children should not wait for a molecular answer before receiving amplification, language access, educational support, or CI evaluation. **Usher syndrome urgency**: Usher syndrome (autosomal recessive) causes about half of deaf-blindness and about 3-6% of congenital severe-to-profound SNHL (some estimates reach 10%). Type 1 combines profound congenital SNHL with absent vestibular function (delayed sitting and walking), and retinitis pigmentosa appears later. Bilateral cochlear implants are indicated before age 2. Type 2 is the most common, with milder loss and normal vestibular function. Type 3 is progressive and is seen mainly in Finnish and Ashkenazi populations. ERG detects retinopathy before fundus changes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Ophthalmology", p 151) **Surveillance schedule after confirmed childhood SNHL**: Do audiologic testing about every 3 months in the first year, every 6 months through the preschool years, then yearly during school. Early amplification is the goal. JCIH sets 1-3-6 benchmarks (screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3, intervene by 6), and JCIH 2019 encourages 1-2-3 month targets where states already meet 1-3-6. A GJB2 diagnosis needs no additional specialty referral because it has no comorbidity, whereas JLNS needs cardiology and beta-blockade and Usher needs close ophthalmology follow-up. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 490-491) **Jervell and Lange-Nielsen**: Recessive KCNQ1 (KVLQT1) or KCNE1 potassium-channel defect causing congenital bilateral severe-to-profound SNHL with long QT, syncope and sudden death. It is found in about 0.21% of congenitally deaf children (other estimates reach about 0.6%). Beta-blockers lower mortality from about 71% to 6%. The dominant long-QT form without deafness is Romano-Ward syndrome. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2288) **Treatable metabolic causes**: Biotinidase deficiency (seizures, hypotonia, ataxia, rash, alopecia) causes SNHL in at least 75% of symptomatic untreated children. Biotin reverses the neurologic and skin findings but not established hearing loss or optic atrophy, so it must start early. Refsum disease (PHYH or PEX7; postlingual progressive SNHL, retinitis pigmentosa, neuropathy, ataxia, high CSF protein without extra cells) is diagnosed by serum phytanic acid and treated with diet and plasmapheresis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2289)
canonical_layers.operate: For cochlear implantation, the genetic result can refine **expectations** and associated-risk planning but rarely replaces audiologic candidacy. Some cochlear-limited genetic causes have favorable CI performance because the auditory nerve and central pathways are preserved, whereas syndromes with neuropathy, major neurodevelopmental disease, cochlear nerve deficiency, or complex malformation require individualized counseling and surgical planning. Use CT/MRI when anatomy or CI planning requires it. **Key trap**: a gene result does not justify prophylactic ear surgery and does not eliminate the need to evaluate an unexpected asymmetric/progressive course for acquired causes such as cCMV.
canonical_layers.teach: **Chief/boards discriminator**: genetic congenital hearing loss = phenotype -> pedigree -> molecular diagnosis -> actionable syndrome/recurrence counseling. **GJB2** is important, but "Connexin 26 negative" is not the endpoint of modern evaluation. Use multigene testing when appropriate and chase extra-auditory findings selectively. **Key trap**: etiologies are not mutually exclusive -- a child can have cCMV plus a genetic contributor, so a discordant course deserves reconsideration rather than diagnostic anchoring. **Recurrence and prenatal counseling**: the empiric recurrence chance for a hearing couple who already have one deaf child is about 17.5% (higher than the older estimate of ~10%). Prenatal molecular diagnosis requires the familial variant to be known first; fetal DNA comes from chorionic villus sampling at 10-12 weeks or amniocentesis at 15-18 weeks, and preimplantation diagnosis is possible with IVF. Genetic counseling should occur before and after testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Genetic Hearing Loss and Inner Ear Diseases", p 491) **GJB2 numbers**: GJB2 causes up to 50% of severe-to-profound congenital recessive nonsyndromic deafness. Founder variants: 35delG in Europeans (about 2.5% carrier rate in the US Midwest), 167delT in Ashkenazi Jews (about 4% carriers), 235delC in Japanese. Truncating variants usually give moderate-to-profound loss; missense variants can be mild. Loss is usually symmetric and stable, temporal bone anatomy is normal (routine imaging not needed), there are no associated comorbidities, and implant results are very good. GJB2 and the adjacent GJB6 deletion can act together in trans (digenic). (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2283; Ch 149, p 2275) **1555A>G numbers**: The m.1555A>G variant in the 12S rRNA gene (MTRNR1) is found in 17-33% of people with aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss and in about 2% of a US NICU cohort. Loss follows normal doses, can appear months after exposure, and starts in the basal outer hair cells. Without exposure, the same variant causes a later-onset, progressive, mild high-frequency nonsyndromic loss. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2286)

candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Start after the fracture has already been identified. Read the mandible as a loaded ring: displacement reflects muscle pull, fracture geometry, dentition, and whether the segment is favorable or unfavorable under function. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Sequence reduction around restoration of facial width, height, and reproducible occlusion. Choose closed treatment, load-sharing miniplate concepts, or load-bearing reconstruction based on stability, comminution, infection, atrophy, and patient factors rather than a one-plate-fits-all rule.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Mandibular Biomechanics and Occlusion. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: A mandible plate is not just hardware across a crack. Explain what force the construct is resisting, whether bone is sharing the load, and how you know the restored occlusion is mechanically trustworthy.

canonical_layers.recognize: Treat the mandible as a curved load-bearing beam exposed to bending, torsion, and muscle-driven distraction. **Force pattern**: during common functional loading, the tooth-bearing/alveolar border often experiences distracting (tension) forces while the inferior border is relatively compressed. The exact force pattern changes with fracture site and loading. **Key question**: the fixation question is therefore not 'which plate do I always use?' but 'what forces remain after reduction, how much bone can share them, and where can fixation safely neutralize them?'
canonical_layers.localize: **Key concept**: localize the mechanical failure mode. Simple, well-reduced fractures with broad bony contact can share functional load with smaller fixation. Comminution, segmental defects, severe atrophy, infected bone after debridement, or inadequate buttressing behave as load-bearing problems, because the plate must bridge forces the bone cannot transmit. In the anterior mandible, curvature and muscular loading add torsion, so a single weak point of fixation can permit lingual splay/rotation. At the angle, elevator/depressor forces create combined tension, compression, and torsion. Translate CT geometry into the force vector before selecting hardware.
canonical_layers.workup: **Four inputs**: build the fixation plan from baseline occlusion, bone contact/quality, fracture geometry, and safe screw corridors. Use wear facets, dental midlines, preinjury photographs/dental records when available, and the maxillary dentition as a template. Angle class is descriptive, not a command to 'normalize' a patient's longstanding bite. **Decide**: whether an arch bar/MMF will function only as temporary reduction assistance or also as a tension band. Map tooth roots, mental foramina, and the inferior alveolar canal before choosing monocortical versus bicortical screw corridors. For multiple fractures, decide which large stable segments will restore mandibular width and continuity first.
canonical_layers.manage: **Load sharing**: the reduced bone buttresses across the fracture and transmits part of functional force, allowing appropriately placed miniplates/lag screws in suitable simple patterns. Champy's ideal osteosynthesis lines are a load-sharing concept, not permission to use one miniplate for every fracture. **Load bearing**: the reconstruction construct must carry essentially all functional load across an unstable/comminuted/defect/markedly atrophic segment. Use a sufficiently rigid bridging construct fixed into healthy bone. **Key trap**: if reduction leaves a gap or the inferior border is not buttressed, ask whether the case has silently converted from load sharing to load bearing.
canonical_layers.operate: **Mechanical sequence**: reproduce occlusion with temporary MMF/elastics -> reduce bone without letting the fixation device create distraction -> control rotation/width -> apply fixation along safe force-neutralizing corridors -> release MMF and stress-test the result by checking bilateral posterior contacts, midlines, mandibular excursion, and fracture stability. In body/angle simple patterns, an appropriately placed superior monocortical miniplate can neutralize the tension zone when the basal cortex is well reduced. In symphyseal/parasymphyseal fractures, torsion usually requires two points of stabilization, unless a sufficiently rigid load-bearing construct is used. Lag screws compress only when their geometry truly creates gliding and purchase across appropriate fragments -- otherwise tightening can displace the reduction.
canonical_layers.teach: **Boards/mechanics algorithm**: 1) establish the patient's bite; 2) reduce the fracture so bone can share load when possible; 3) identify tension/compression/torsion; 4) ask whether bone stock/buttressing permits load sharing; 5) if not, bridge with load-bearing fixation; 6) protect roots and the inferior alveolar nerve; 7) release MMF and verify occlusion before closure. AO CMF specifically treats severely atrophic, comminuted, and defect patterns as load-bearing problems, while simple buttressed fractures can use load-sharing constructs. **Key trap**: an occlusal error after rigid fixation is not something elastics should be expected to rescue if the skeleton was fixed in the wrong position. **Adenoid facies and dentofacial growth**: Chronic nasal obstruction from adenotonsillar hypertrophy is associated with long-face syndrome: increased lower facial height and gonial angle, a high narrow palate and posterior crossbite. Cause and effect has never been proven in humans, so adenotonsillectomy for orthodontic reasons alone is considered only with significant hypertrophy. Adenoid facies is an open mouth, flat midface and dark circles under the eyes. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1194)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Adult-onset asthma, CRSwNP and respiratory reactions to COX-1 inhibitors form this condition. Severe recurrent polyposis and anosmia may precede a clearly recognized NSAID reaction history. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use topical sinonasal therapy, guideline-based asthma care and appropriately selected biologic therapy. Aspirin desensitization followed by maintenance therapy is an option in selected patients; FESS is often coordinated to improve sinus access and disease control.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of AERD. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: AERD is a chronic upper-and-lower-airway inflammatory syndrome. The operation is one component of a medical-surgical disease-control plan.

canonical_layers.recognize: **AERD (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, also NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease)** is the clinical combination of asthma, typically severe/recurrent **CRSwNP**, and reproducible upper/lower respiratory reactions to **COX-1-inhibiting NSAIDs**. **Key trap**: it is NOT simply a vague 'aspirin allergy.' **History**: ask what drug caused the reaction, the timing, respiratory features, alcohol sensitivity, asthma control, smell loss, prior polyp surgery, and how rapidly polyps recur.
canonical_layers.localize: **Mechanism**: dysregulated arachidonic-acid/eicosanoid biology with excess cysteinyl-leukotriene signaling in a type-2 inflammatory airway phenotype. **Key concept**: the **united airway** -- the nose/sinuses and asthma must be managed together. Cross-reactivity is driven largely by **COX-1 inhibition**. **Key trap**: do not teach that every NSAID carries identical risk. **Counseling**: distinguish strong COX-1 inhibitors from appropriately selected alternatives, and use specialist-supervised challenge when needed.
canonical_layers.workup: A convincing history of asthma plus CRSwNP plus stereotyped respiratory reactions to COX-1 NSAIDs can establish the syndrome clinically. **If uncertain**: when the history is unclear and the answer will change management, refer for a **controlled aspirin/NSAID challenge** in an appropriate setting rather than advising an unsupervised trial. Assess asthma control before challenge/desensitization, and document sinonasal burden objectively. **Key trap**: do not diagnose AERD from nasal polyps plus an unrelated rash or GI intolerance to aspirin.
canonical_layers.manage: **Treat both airways**: topical sinonasal corticosteroid therapy and saline, guideline-based asthma treatment, and often a leukotriene-pathway agent. **For persistent disease**: discuss **aspirin desensitization followed by aspirin therapy (ATAD)** versus a **biologic**, based on asthma/polyp severity, bleeding/GI risk, pregnancy plans, adherence, cost/access, and patient goals. Current evidence supports both strategies in selected patients. **Key trap**: there is no universal rule that every AERD patient must receive ATAD, or that a biologic always replaces it.
canonical_layers.operate: **ESS** is often important when polyp burden and sinus disease remain substantial. It clears inflammatory load and creates access for postoperative topical therapy. In patients pursuing ATAD, surgery is commonly optimized before desensitization when clinically appropriate. **Key trap**: do not present surgery as curative -- AERD carries a high recurrence tendency and requires longitudinal anti-inflammatory management. **Escalate planning** when asthma is poorly controlled or the history suggests severe NSAID reactions.
canonical_layers.teach: **Board discriminator**: AERD = asthma + CRSwNP + COX-1 NSAID respiratory reaction. The senior decision is not merely 'avoid aspirin' -- decide whether the patient needs disease-control optimization, ESS, ATAD, biologic therapy, or a combination, and know why. **Key trap**: calling any aspirin adverse effect AERD, challenging an unstable asthmatic, or forgetting that recurrent sinonasal disease and asthma are one inflammatory airway problem.

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Episodic spontaneous vertigo with fluctuating unilateral sensorineural hearing symptoms, tinnitus and aural pressure suggests this condition; duration and audiometric documentation matter. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Educate about episodic disease, hearing rehabilitation and trigger/lifestyle measures; use vestibular suppressants only for acute attacks. Escalate from medical prevention to intratympanic therapy and, in disabling refractory disease, ablative options based on hearing status and goals.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Ménière Disease. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Do not label every patient with vertigo+tinnitus as Ménière disease. The syndrome requires a coherent episodic pattern plus hearing evidence, and treatment escalates according to disability and hearing preservation.

canonical_layers.recognize: Episodic spontaneous vertigo with fluctuating unilateral sensorineural hearing symptoms, tinnitus and aural pressure suggests Ménière disease; duration and audiometric documentation matter. **Variants and bilaterality**: Cochlear hydrops has hearing loss, fullness, and tinnitus without vertigo. Vestibular hydrops has episodic vertigo without auditory symptoms. Lermoyez syndrome is worsening hearing and tinnitus that improve abruptly after a vertigo attack. Tumarkin otolithic crisis is a sudden drop attack without loss of consciousness. Delayed endolymphatic hydrops follows an earlier profound loss in one ear with later Ménière symptoms. Disease becomes bilateral in about 25–30%, and the glycerol dehydration test (rarely used) improves hearing in active hydrops. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 417–418) **Crises of Tumarkin**: otolithic drop attacks. The patient suddenly loses postural control and falls without losing consciousness, often feeling pushed to the ground. They are attributed to high endolymphatic pressure acting on the otolith organs and usually signal advanced disease (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, p 2090). **Natural history and variants**: attacks most often last 2-3 hours. Vertigo stops spontaneously in about 57% by 2 years and 71% by 8 years, and only 1%-2% progress to profound deafness. Bilateral disease is roughly 19%-24%, familial in 10%-20%, and HLA-B8/DR3 and Cw7 are associated. Tumarkin otolithic crises (sudden drop attacks without loss of consciousness or vertigo) occur in 2%-6%. In Lermoyez syndrome, hearing and tinnitus worsen before the vertigo and then improve when it begins. The audiogram may be 'tent-shaped' (low-frequency fluctuating loss with a peak at 2 kHz), and diplacusis is common. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2525) **Recurrent vestibulopathy as a differential**: recurrent Ménière-like vertigo spells without hearing loss or neurologic signs (vestibular Ménière). Over about 8.5 years, roughly 60% remit, 15% develop Ménière disease, 10% keep having attacks, 10% develop BPPV and 5% another peripheral disorder. Treat symptoms only. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 329) **Nystagmus during an attack and ECoG cutoff**: early in a spell, irritative nystagmus beats toward the affected ear. In the paralytic phase it beats toward the healthy ear. In the recovery phase it often reverses toward the affected ear again. The direction therefore depends on timing and does not reliably lateralize. ECoG SP/AP ratio above about 0.35 is considered abnormal. Hydrops can bulge the saccule against the footplate (vestibulofibrosis), producing a positive fistula test with an intact drum. The other causes of that sign are SCDS, otosyphilis and perilymph fistula. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 327-328, 330) **Lermoyez syndrome**: A Ménière variant in which fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus worsen first and then improve after the vertigo attack (the reverse of the usual pattern). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 20)
canonical_layers.localize: The clinical syndrome reflects inner-ear dysfunction associated with endolymphatic hydrops, but hydrops is not synonymous with the diagnosis. Vestibular migraine and other episodic vestibular disorders can mimic it.
canonical_layers.workup:
**Workup**: obtain audiometry and assess alternative causes based on atypical features. MRI is used when asymmetric SNHL or neurologic features warrant retrocochlear exclusion. Vestibular tests support function but are not a single diagnostic gold standard.

**Grading scale**: stage disease severity with the AAO-HNS 1995 Committee on Hearing and Equilibrium four-tone (0.5, 1, 2, 3 kHz) pure-tone-average system, using the worst audiogram obtained during the 6-month interval before treatment. Stage I ≤25 dB, Stage II 26-40 dB, Stage III 41-70 dB, Stage IV >70 dB. **Key trap**: staging is for reporting/comparing outcomes and counseling, not a substitute for the clinical diagnostic criteria themselves. **Diagnostic criteria**: Cummings presents the AAO-HNS 1995 scheme, in which 'definite' Ménière disease needs 2 or more spontaneous vertigo spells of at least 20 minutes, audiometric hearing loss on at least one occasion, and tinnitus or fullness in that ear, 'probable' needs one definitive spell, 'possible' is vertigo without documented loss or fluctuating loss without definite spells, and 'certain' needs histopathology. **Current view**: the 2015 Bárány Society/AAO-HNS criteria, used in the 2020 AAO-HNS Ménière guideline, replace it. Definite disease is 2 or more spells lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, audiometric low-to-mid-frequency SNHL in the affected ear on at least one occasion, and fluctuating aural symptoms. Probable disease is 2 or more spells of 20 minutes to 24 hours with fluctuating aural symptoms but no audiometric proof. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2525) **Test performance**: caloric weakness occurs in 48%-74% (absent response in 6%-11%). Head impulse asymmetry in only 29%. ECochG SP/AP ratio is elevated in about 62% of patients but also in 21% of controls. cVEMP shows elevated thresholds, reduced amplitude and flattened tuning (normal best frequency about 500 Hz) but individual variation limits diagnostic use. Gadolinium MRI can show hydrops but is not part of diagnostic criteria. MRI's role is to exclude vestibular schwannoma or endolymphatic sac tumor. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2526)
canonical_layers.manage: Educate about episodic disease, hearing rehabilitation and trigger/lifestyle measures; use vestibular suppressants only for acute attacks. Escalate from medical prevention to intratympanic therapy and, in disabling refractory disease, ablative options based on hearing status and goals. **Medical and device therapy evidence**: salt restriction and diuretics remain reasonable first-line despite no placebo-controlled proof. Acetazolamide is no better than other diuretics. Betahistine was no better than placebo in a large European multicenter trial. The Meniett pressure device (needs a ventilation tube) helped only for the first 3 months versus placebo and is rarely used. A ventilation tube alone helps some patients. Intratympanic dexamethasone (typically 10 mg/mL, often repeated about every 3 months) gave complete vertigo control in 82% vs 57% with saline. Gentamicin was superior to dexamethasone in an RCT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2527) **Intratympanic gentamicin protocols compared**: In a meta-analysis, titration dosing (daily or weekly until vestibular symptoms or hearing change) gave the best complete vertigo control (about 82%), low-dose one-or-two-injection regimens the worst (about 67%), multiple daily dosing the most hearing loss (about 35%) and weekly dosing the least (about 13%). Because the vestibular deafferentation reaction appears 3-5 days after an injection, space injections at least a week apart. Adult 40 mg/mL gentamicin is often buffered to about 30 mg/mL. Severe hearing loss usually shows up within the first month, and poor pretreatment hearing is the main risk factor. (Cummings 7e, Ch 158, p 2390-2391) **IT steroids versus gentamicin and spontaneous remission**: In a double-blind trial, intratympanic methylprednisolone cut vertigo attacks by about 90% versus about 87% for gentamicin, so a nonablative steroid series is a reasonable first step when hearing must be preserved, with gentamicin for those who accept hearing risk or cannot return for repeat injections. Interpret all vertigo outcomes against the 60-80% spontaneous remission of Meniere disease over 2-8 years. A single sustained-release dexamethasone dose (OTO-104) also reduced vertigo in an early RCT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 158, p 2386-2387)
canonical_layers.operate: Procedural choices intentionally trade vertigo control against hearing/vestibular function. Intratympanic gentamicin, labyrinthectomy and vestibular neurectomy are not equivalent; residual useful hearing and contralateral vestibular reserve matter. **Surgical options with success rates**: About 10–15% of patients need surgery. Endolymphatic sac decompression or shunt preserves hearing and balance with low morbidity, with 60–80% vertigo control (close to the spontaneous remission rate). Vestibular nerve section via craniotomy spares hearing and controls vertigo in about 90%. Labyrinthectomy controls vertigo in up to about 90% but is limited to nonserviceable hearing (worse than about 50–60 dB or <50% word recognition) and is avoided if the other labyrinth is weak or contralateral disease is likely. Diet: sodium below about 1.5 g/day with even meal spacing. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 418–419) **Ablative/surgical outcomes**: titrated intratympanic gentamicin (single injection, repeat only if needed) controls vertigo in about 83%-90%, with profound loss around 3%-10%. Ablating caloric function as an endpoint caused severe-to-profound loss in 58%. Endolymphatic sac surgery has weak evidence (Thomsen sham-mastoidectomy trial, shunt no better than a tube). Vestibular nerve section controls vertigo in 85%-95% with hearing kept in 80%-90%. Labyrinthectomy gives the highest control and is favored when there is no useful hearing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2528) **Cochleosacculotomy and endolymphatic sac surgery details**: In cochleosacculotomy, a 3-mm right-angle pick is passed through the round window to fracture the osseous spiral lamina, creating a permanent endolymph-perilymph shunt. It relieves vertigo in about 70% but causes high-frequency SNHL in about 25% and profound loss in about 10%, so it is an alternative to labyrinthectomy in elderly patients who already have poor hearing. The endolymphatic sac always lies below Donaldson's line (drawn along the horizontal semicircular canal through the posterior canal), bounded by the sigmoid sinus, jugular bulb and mastoid facial nerve. A Cochrane review of two RCTs found no significant benefit from sac surgery. A sac-to-subarachnoid shunt is conceptually flawed and raises CSF leak risk. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, pp 2554-2555)
canonical_layers.teach: Do not label every patient with vertigo+tinnitus as Ménière disease. The syndrome requires a coherent episodic pattern plus hearing evidence, and treatment escalates according to disability and hearing preservation. **AAO-HNS outcome reporting**: assess treatment no sooner than 24 months. The vertigo numeric value is post-treatment spells/month divided by pretreatment spells/month x 100 (Class A = 0, complete control, B 1-40, C 41-80, D 81-120, E >120, F = secondary treatment started). Hearing change is significant if the 4-tone PTA changes by more than 10 dB or word recognition by more than 15%. A 6-point functional level scale grades disability. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2526)

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Oral Allergy Syndrome (Pollen-Food Syndrome). Recognize oral allergy syndrome (OAS, also called pollen-food syndrome) from a reproducible history of rapid-onset, LOCALIZED lip/mouth/throat itching or mild swelling within minutes of eating a specific RAW fruit, vegetable, or nut, resolving within minutes and rarely progressing beyond the oropharynx. The trigger foods are predictable from the patient's pollen sensitization: TREE pollen peaks in SPRING (oak, birch, cedar/juniper, maple, elm), GRASS pollen in LATE SPRING-SUMMER (timothy, Bermuda, Kentucky bluegrass), WEED pollen (dominated by ragweed) in FALL (worsening until first frost), and MOLD spores more variably (often warm/damp conditions, persisting indoors year-round). A patient with seasonal allergic rhinitis who also reports itching with specific raw produce is describing OAS before any testing is done. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Counsel avoidance of the specific RAW trigger foods; cooking, peeling, canning, or baking usually denatures the causative protein and restores tolerance for most patients, so blanket food-allergy-style restriction of cooked/processed forms is unnecessary and overly restrictive.
