canonical_layers.recognize: Infantile hemangiomas appear in early infancy, proliferate, then involute; large segmental face or scalp lesions raise concern for PHACE rather than representing only a cosmetic problem. **Parotid hemangioma**: hemangioma is the most common salivary gland tumor in children; it appears in the first weeks of life as a soft, compressible preauricular mass, often with bluish overlying skin. It proliferates for about 6-12 months, then involutes. About half of patients have coexisting cutaneous hemangiomas. Do not mistake it for a solid parotid neoplasm requiring parotidectomy: imaging and clinical course usually settle the diagnosis, and propranolol is first-line when treatment is needed. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, p 211) **Natural history and classification**: infantile hemangioma is about 3 times more common in girls. It may be absent at birth or show only a premonitory pale or red macule (herald patch). Rapid growth occurs in the first months, with most growth done by about 4–6 months and a plateau near 1 year. Classic teaching is 50% involution by age 5 and 70% by age 7; newer series show most involution finished by about age 4. Lesions are focal, segmental or multifocal. Segmental lesions in a beard (V3) distribution carry about a 60% risk of airway hemangioma and warrant a low threshold for endoscopy. More than 5 cutaneous lesions warrants abdominal ultrasound for hepatic hemangiomas. Maffucci syndrome is multiple venous-type vascular lesions with enchondromas, with about a 25% risk of chondrosarcoma. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 543–545) **PHACE components and natural-history numbers**: PHACE(S) comprises posterior fossa malformations, segmental head/neck hemangioma, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects (coarctation), eye anomalies and sternal/supraumbilical defects; because intracranial arterial anomalies can cause strokes, brain MRI/MRA screening is required. Infantile hemangiomas are 3 times more common in girls, 60% occur in the head and neck, proliferate for about 6-10 months, and about 50% have involuted by age 5 and 70% by age 7; multiple cutaneous lesions should prompt a search for visceral (especially hepatic) hemangiomas. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Laryngeal Anomalies", p 1527) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1642) **Multiple and segmental hemangiomas**: up to 20% of infants have multiple lesions. The book uses six or more cutaneous hemangiomas, and current AAP 2019 guidance uses five or more, as the trigger for screening for visceral (especially hepatic) hemangiomas with abdominal ultrasound and thyroid tests. Hepatic lesions can cause hepatomegaly, GI bleeding, high-output heart failure, anemia or profound consumptive hypothyroidism. Segmental lesions are plaque-like, proliferate up to about 18 months, ulcerate more, rarely involute completely, and carry PHACE risk (posterior fossa anomalies such as Dandy–Walker, hemangioma, arterial anomalies, cardiac/aortic arch defects, eye anomalies, sternal cleft or supraumbilical raphe), with neurologic sequelae in over 50%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Hemangiomas and Vascular Malformations", p 1901, 1904–1905) **High-risk sites**: about 65% of beard-distribution hemangiomas (chin, jawline, preauricular) have airway involvement, usually supraglottic or subglottic, and they often involve the parotid and parapharyngeal space with a 12–16 month proliferative phase, airway compression, and recurrent otitis media. Periocular lesions cause astigmatic, strabismic, or deprivation amblyopia (deprivation can occur after as little as 1 week; untreated children over age 1 reach 75% amblyopia), so refer to ophthalmology immediately. Nasal tip lesions (about 16% of facial hemangiomas) splay the medial crura and are often excised before school age; ear lesions can occlude the canal, and lip lesions ulcerate and impair feeding. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Hemangiomas and Vascular Malformations", p 1905–1906) **Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon belongs to KHE/tufted angioma, not infantile hemangioma**: profound thrombocytopenia in an infant with a violaceous, infiltrative vascular tumor points to kaposiform hemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma. Diagnosis needs incisional biopsy; extensive or symptomatic lesions need antiangiogenic therapy, with sirolimus now a key agent. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, pp 3006-3007) **Functional complications that force early treatment**: subglottic lesions cause biphasic stridor; periocular lesions cause deprivation amblyopia or, if they distort the globe before about 6 months, astigmatic amblyopia; lip and neck-fold lesions ulcerate (brown crust, then pain and bleeding) and impair feeding; large parotid/scalp lesions can cause high-output heart failure. About 80% of salivary hemangiomas are parotid. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, p 3007; Ch 205, p 3048)
canonical_layers.localize: These GLUT-1-positive vascular tumors differ from malformations present fully formed at birth. Segmental distribution can accompany posterior-fossa, arterial, cardiac, eye, and ventral developmental anomalies.
canonical_layers.workup: Typical focal lesions are clinical diagnoses. For PHACE risk, obtain MRI/MRA of head and neck, echocardiography/aortic-arch assessment, ophthalmologic examination, and multidisciplinary review before treatment decisions. **Congenital hemangiomas are GLUT-1 negative**: RICH and NICH are fully formed at birth, lack GLUT-1 staining (unlike infantile hemangioma) and do not respond to propranolol or other medical therapy. RICH is observed; NICH may need laser or excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, p 3006)
canonical_layers.manage: Observe uncomplicated lesions. Oral propranolol is first-line systemic therapy for high-risk hemangiomas; in PHACE, assess cerebrovascular/cardiac anatomy and use individualized cautious initiation and titration. Topical timolol suits selected thin superficial lesions. **Treatment triggers and propranolol cautions**: treat for complications such as threatened vision or hearing, airway compromise, impaired feeding, ulceration or cosmetically important sites, or high-output heart failure. Before starting propranolol, check vital signs and do a cardiopulmonary exam; ECG and glucose screening are not needed when the exam is normal. Response usually comes within 2–12 weeks. Continue until at least age 1, then taper, and watch for rebound. Contraindications include cardiogenic shock, sinus bradycardia, hypotension, heart block beyond first degree, heart failure and bronchial asthma. PHACES arterial anomalies raise stroke risk. Lesions that do not respond to propranolol should raise suspicion for a different vascular tumor such as KHE. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, p 545) **Nasal and periocular hemangiomas**: nasal tip hemangiomas involute slowly and can deform developing alar cartilages, leaving fibrofatty residua, so earlier treatment or surgery may be justified. Periorbital (often superonasal) hemangiomas threaten amblyopia from visual-axis occlusion or astigmatism, which is an indication for treatment. Intranasal hemangiomas present with unilateral obstruction and epistaxis. The book lists Kasabach-Merritt consumptive coagulopathy among hemangioma complications; current understanding attributes it to kaposiform hemangioendothelioma/tufted angioma rather than common infantile hemangioma. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Orbital Swellings", p 1010) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1109) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Nose, Paranasal Sinuses, and Nasopharynx", p 1110) **Ulceration and older therapies**: ulceration is the most common complication (nose, lips, periorbital, during rapid growth)—treat with analgesia, gentle cleansing, topical antibiotic, occlusive dressings, oral antibiotics for cellulitis, and PDL or excision for refractory ulcers. This 2014 chapter still lists corticosteroids as first line (oral prednisolone 2–3 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks then taper; intralesional triamcinolone/betamethasone up to about 2.5 mL with a 70–90% response but risk of retinal artery embolization in periocular injection; topical clobetasol for small lesions), with vincristine and interferon (spastic diplegia in 10–30%) as salvage and propranolol described as an emerging option. Current AAP 2019 guidance makes oral propranolol first-line systemic therapy (and topical timolol for small superficial lesions), with steroids second line. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Hemangiomas and Vascular Malformations", p 1909–1910)
canonical_layers.operate: Surgery or laser has selected roles for urgent focal compromise, residual deformity, ulceration, or lesions unsuitable for medication; airway disease requires direct airway assessment and coordinated control.
canonical_layers.teach: A large segmental facial hemangioma is a syndrome marker. Propranolol is highly effective, but PHACE arterial disease changes pretreatment evaluation and dosing precautions.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Subacute (de Quervain) Thyroiditis. A painful tender thyroid after a viral-like illness, fever, and transient thyrotoxic symptoms suggests subacute granulomatous thyroiditis. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treat pain with NSAIDs and use corticosteroids for severe or refractory inflammation. Beta blockade treats adrenergic symptoms; antithyroid drugs do not help. Follow for the transient hypothyroid phase and uncommon permanent hypothyroidism. Check TSH/free hormones and ESR or CRP. Low radioactive-iodine uptake during thyrotoxicosis distinguishes destructive thyroiditis from Graves disease; ultrasound or biopsy is reserved for atypical or focal findings.

canonical_layers.recognize: A painful tender thyroid after a viral-like illness, fever, and transient thyrotoxic symptoms suggests subacute granulomatous thyroiditis. **Other thyroiditides to differentiate**: painless (silent/postpartum) thyroiditis mimics subacute thyroiditis without pain. Acute suppurative thyroiditis is rare, painful, and febrile (look for a piriform sinus fistula, usually left, in children) and needs IV antibiotics/drainage. Riedel thyroiditis is a rock-hard fibrotic gland (now linked to IgG4-related disease) causing compression and hypothyroidism, treated with hormone replacement and isthmus division for airway compromise. (Pasha 6e, Ch 3, p 145) **Other thyroiditides**: painless (silent/postpartum, subacute lymphocytic) thyroiditis is autoimmune and painless, occurs in up to 5% of postpartum women, causes self-limited thyrotoxicosis and leaves about 20% permanently hypothyroid. Acute suppurative thyroiditis (Staph, Strep, Enterobacter) often follows a URI. In children, recurrent left-sided episodes suggest a pyriform sinus fistula, so after treatment (antibiotics, drainage) evaluate with barium swallow, CT or endoscopy. Drug-induced thyroiditis is caused by amiodarone (type 1 iodine-induced hyperthyroidism vs type 2 destructive thyroiditis), interferon-alpha, IL-2, lithium and minocycline. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 38, p 698-699) **Thyroiditis spectrum**: Painless (silent) thyroiditis affects both sexes and has no viral prodrome. Thyrotoxicosis lasts 2-6 weeks, then hypothyroidism for 2-8 weeks, and about half later develop chronic autoimmune thyroiditis. The postpartum form behaves the same way. RAI-induced thyroiditis flares 1-2 weeks after treatment. Amiodarone causes either iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (in nodular glands) or a destructive thyroiditis, and about 2% of patients on interferon-alpha develop thyrotoxicosis. Exogenous hormone use shows no goiter, low uptake and low thyroglobulin. In de Quervain thyroiditis, treat with salicylates 2.4-3.6 g/day or NSAIDs, and use prednisone about 40 mg/day for 3-4 weeks for severe pain. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1861) (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1862)
canonical_layers.localize: Inflammatory follicular disruption releases stored hormone; this is destructive thyroiditis, not increased hormone synthesis.
canonical_layers.workup: Check TSH/free hormones and ESR or CRP. Low radioactive-iodine uptake during thyrotoxicosis distinguishes destructive thyroiditis from Graves disease; ultrasound or biopsy is reserved for atypical or focal findings.
canonical_layers.manage: Treat pain with NSAIDs and use corticosteroids for severe or refractory inflammation. Beta blockade treats adrenergic symptoms; antithyroid drugs do not help. Follow for the transient hypothyroid phase and uncommon permanent hypothyroidism. **Acute suppurative thyroiditis**: Usually caused by S. aureus, streptococci or S. pneumoniae. It is commonest in children (suspect a piriform sinus fistula) and presents with severe pain, torticollis-like posture, high WBC, normal thyroid function and often normal ESR, which distinguishes it from de Quervain thyroiditis. Give antistaphylococcal and anaerobic coverage. Abscesses need drainage, sometimes partial thyroidectomy, with antibiotics for at least 2 weeks after drainage. Thyroid dysfunction is rare. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1861) (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1862)
canonical_layers.operate: There is no routine surgical role. Failure to follow the expected course, a persistent focal lesion, abscess concern, or compressive progression should reopen the diagnosis.
canonical_layers.teach: Pain, high inflammatory markers, thyrotoxicosis, and low uptake form the classic pattern; anticipate the thyrotoxic-to-hypothyroid-to-recovery sequence.

canonical_layers.recognize: Lemierre syndrome is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after an oropharyngeal/deep-neck infection. It classically occurs in an otherwise healthy adolescent or young adult and is commonly associated with Fusobacterium necrophorum. **Red flag pattern**: think of it when a recent sore throat initially improves or seems routine but is followed by recurrent high fever, unilateral neck pain/swelling, toxicity, pleuritic symptoms, or pulmonary septic emboli.
canonical_layers.localize: **Spread pattern**: infection typically spreads from tonsillar/peritonsillar or parapharyngeal tissue into the carotid sheath/internal jugular vein. Septic thrombus can shower the lungs, causing multiple peripheral nodules, cavitation, effusions, or empyema, and can less commonly seed joints or other organs. **Key point**: because the IJV lies near the carotid artery and lower cranial nerves, extensive parapharyngeal infection can produce additional vascular/neural complications.
canonical_layers.workup: Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when this does not delay treatment, along with CBC/metabolic/inflammatory assessment, contrast CT neck to evaluate IJV thrombosis and deep-neck source, and chest imaging for septic emboli. **Key trap**: ultrasound can identify accessible IJV thrombosis but may miss high skull-base or low thoracic segments. Culture/drain any abscess. A negative throat culture does not exclude Lemierre syndrome, because the relevant infection is deep/vascular.
canonical_layers.manage:
Treat promptly with prolonged systemic antibiotics covering anaerobes and oral flora, adjusted to cultures and clinical response. Drain peritonsillar/parapharyngeal or other collections when present. **Anticoagulation** is individualized rather than automatic -- consider it with extensive/progressive thrombosis, intracranial extension, persistent embolization, or other selected circumstances in multidisciplinary discussion. Persistent fever should trigger reassessment for undrained source, resistant organism, or ongoing septic thrombosis. DURATION: plan roughly **4-6 weeks** of systemic antibiotics for Lemierre syndrome, given the endovascular septic source, longer than a typical pharyngitis/abscess course, adjusted to clinical response, source control, and any residual thrombosis/emboli.

Start prompt IV therapy active against Fusobacterium and oral anaerobes, drain the primary/deep-neck or thoracic source when indicated, and narrow with cultures and response. Duration is not a universal fixed 4-6 weeks: tailor IV-to-oral transition and total course to source control, internal-jugular thrombus, metastatic infection, complications, and clinical/radiographic response. Anticoagulation remains individualized for progression, extensive clot, cerebral-sinus extension, or poor response rather than routine for every patient.
canonical_layers.operate: **Goal**: surgery targets the infectious source, not routine removal of the thrombosed IJV. Drain accessible abscesses and secure the airway when swelling/trismus threatens it. IJV ligation/excision is rarely required in the antibiotic/endovascular era and is reserved for uncontrolled septic source or hemorrhagic/vascular complications not manageable otherwise. Thoracic drainage may be needed for empyema or other metastatic infection.
canonical_layers.teach: Boards/chief framework: young patient + recent pharyngitis + recurrent fever/neck tenderness + septic pulmonary lesions = Lemierre until disproven. Diagnose the deep infection and IJV thrombosis, treat anaerobes, and drain source control. The thrombosed vein is usually treated medically; the abscess is what you operate on.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis is a noninvasive, usually type-2/eosinophilic inflammatory phenotype occurring in immunocompetent patients, often with nasal polyposis, thick eosinophilic mucin, asthma/atopy, heterogeneous sinus opacification and bony expansion/remodeling. The dramatic CT appearance can mimic invasive fungal disease, but this condition does not require fungal tissue invasion. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Treatment combines complete surgical clearance of obstructing allergic mucin with durable sinus access plus postoperative anti-inflammatory therapy, especially topical corticosteroid irrigations and selected systemic steroids. Long-term endoscopic surveillance matters because recurrence is common. Antifungal drugs are not the central treatment for classic noninvasive AFRS, and a positive fungal culture should not trigger an invasive-fungal regimen without tissue invasion or the appropriate host/clinical syndrome.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of AFRS. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Boards/chief framework: AFRS can erode bone without invading tissue. Immunocompetent patient + polyps + allergic mucin + expansile heterogeneous sinus disease suggests AFRS; high-risk host + necrosis/cranial neuropathy + histologic invasion suggests AIFR. The pathology word that changes the emergency is invasion.

canonical_layers.recognize: **AFRS (allergic fungal rhinosinusitis)** is a distinct, usually highly inflammatory polypoid CRS phenotype characterized by atopy/type-2 inflammation, eosinophilic 'allergic' mucin containing fungal elements, and often striking heterogeneous/hyperattenuating sinus material with expansion or bony remodeling. **Key trap**: it is NOT invasive fungal sinusitis -- the defining process is allergic/inflammatory rather than tissue-invasive fungal necrosis.
canonical_layers.localize: AFRS localizes to sinuses packed with tenacious eosinophilic mucin and fungal debris, often with polyposis and anatomic distortion. **Key trap**: expansion, thinning, or erosion can occur from chronic pressure/inflammation and does NOT by itself prove invasive fungal disease. **Red flags**: tissue invasion, vascular invasion, necrosis, cranial neuropathy, or an immunocompromised host should immediately reopen the differential toward invasive fungal rhinosinusitis.
canonical_layers.workup: **Approach**: integrate endoscopy, CT pattern, atopic history, and operative/pathologic findings rather than relying on a fungal culture alone, because fungi can colonize sinonasal cavities without causing AFRS. **Pathology**: should assess eosinophilic mucin/fungal elements and, critically, absence of tissue invasion when AFRS is the diagnosis. **Imaging**: define orbital/skull-base distortion on CT before surgery; consider MRI when extension or the relationship to orbit/skull base cannot be adequately characterized on CT. **Bent and Kuhn criteria**: There are five major criteria: nasal polyposis, type I hypersensitivity to fungi (skin test or specific IgE), characteristic CT (heterogeneous, serpiginous hyperattenuation), eosinophilic mucin, and noninvasive fungal elements on staining. Minor criteria are bone erosion, unilateral predominance, Charcot-Leyden crystals, peripheral eosinophilia and a positive fungal culture. The usual organisms are dematiaceous molds (Bipolaris, Curvularia, Alternaria), then Aspergillus. Postoperative antifungals are not indicated. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 55) **Bent and Kuhn criteria (1994)**: diagnosis requires all 5 major criteria. These are type I hypersensitivity to fungi; nasal polyposis; characteristic CT (heterogeneous hyperattenuation, expansion or erosion); eosinophilic mucin without tissue invasion; and a positive fungal stain. The minor criteria support the diagnosis: asthma, unilateral predominance, bone erosion, positive fungal culture, Charcot-Leyden crystals and serum eosinophilia. An aspirate of eosinophilic mucin is the most sensitive specimen. On MRI the mucin is T1 iso-to-hypointense with a T2 signal void, and the mucosa enhances peripherally while the mucin does not. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 30, pp 531-533)
canonical_layers.manage: Long-term control requires anti-inflammatory therapy and surveillance after clearance of the obstructing mucin burden. **First line**: topical corticosteroid therapy, often facilitated by postoperative sinus access. **Selective**: systemic corticosteroids may be used selectively for severe inflammatory flares while minimizing cumulative toxicity. **Key trap**: do not teach routine systemic antifungal therapy as a universal cornerstone. **Board pearl**: biologic therapy has evolved beyond the core textbooks -- **dupilumab** received a specific U.S. **FDA AFRS indication in February 2026**. Contemporary counseling should distinguish that new option from older evidence and still individualize treatment by severity, age, prior surgery, steroid burden, and comorbidity.
canonical_layers.operate: **ESS** is central when substantial AFRS burden is present: remove allergic mucin and polyps, ventilate involved sinuses, and create durable access for topical therapy and postoperative debridement/surveillance. **Danger**: expect distorted anatomy and protect orbit/skull base -- extensive expansion or erosion may make landmarks unreliable. **Technique**: senior-level planning emphasizes image review, navigation when appropriate, and stopping/reorienting rather than following diseased anatomy blindly. **Key trap**: surgery reduces burden but does not eliminate the underlying inflammatory tendency. **AFRS surgery specifics**: bony expansion and erosion often leave dura and periorbita stuck to the overlying mucosa, so avoid or use the microdebrider very carefully near dehiscences. Remove all tenacious allergic mucin, because residual debris drives recurrence and revision. Perioperative systemic steroids help but recurrence follows their withdrawal, so long-term steroid irrigations are preferred (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 704).
canonical_layers.teach: **Board discriminator**: AFRS = allergic/inflammatory fungal-associated CRS with eosinophilic mucin, typically polyps, and characteristic imaging. Invasive fungal sinusitis = tissue invasion/necrosis and a very different emergency. **Key trap**: calling bone erosion 'invasion,' treating a positive fungal culture as diagnostic by itself, or prescribing antifungals while neglecting surgical clearance and long-term anti-inflammatory control. **Board pearl**: a specific **dupilumab AFRS indication arrived in 2026**, after the core textbooks.

canonical_layers.recognize: Acute unilateral facial weakness with severe otalgia and vesicles of the pinna, canal, or oropharynx suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome; hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo may coexist, and rash may follow the palsy or be absent. **Prognosis and timing numbers**: VZV causes about 4.5%-9% of peripheral facial palsies and is the second most common cause. Incidence rises sharply after age 60 as cell-mediated immunity declines. In older, largely untreated series, complete recovery occurred in only about 16%-22% overall: about 10% after complete paralysis versus about 66% after incomplete paralysis. The rash appears before the palsy in about 25%, and these patients do better, while in about 10% the vesicles appear well after the palsy. Zoster sine herpete shows fourfold-raised anti-VZV IgG and responds better to prednisone plus an antiviral than to prednisone alone. Combined steroid and antiviral therapy is the consensus, and starting it within 3 days gave complete recovery in about 75% in one series. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2589, 2592)
canonical_layers.localize: Varicella-zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion inflames the facial nerve in the fallopian canal; adjacent vestibulocochlear involvement explains audiovestibular symptoms.
canonical_layers.workup: The diagnosis is clinical. Examine the ear and oropharynx, document House-Brackmann grade and eye closure, and obtain audiometry when hearing symptoms are present; use MRI or electrodiagnostics for atypical, severe, or nonrecovering cases rather than routinely.
canonical_layers.manage: Start meticulous corneal protection immediately. Early corticosteroid plus antiviral therapy is commonly recommended despite limited comparative evidence; provide analgesia and short-term vestibular symptom control followed by rehabilitation when needed. **Regimen and sequelae**: start an antiviral early (e.g., valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days). Add prednisone about 1 mg/kg/day when there is facial palsy or SNHL, although high-quality evidence for either drug is lacking. Facial recovery is worse than in Bell palsy. Refer to ophthalmology if V1 or the cornea is involved. Postherpetic neuralgia is more common over age 60, and gabapentin is the preferred agent (Cummings 7e, Ch 138, p 2098). **Textbook regimen and prognosis**: only about 60% regain normal facial function, worse than Bell palsy. Give high-dose steroid (about 1 mg/kg/day for 14 days) when there is facial palsy or SNHL, plus valacyclovir 1 g every 8 hours for 7 days. Decompression is not advised, because degeneration is diffuse rather than confined to the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion. Use gabapentin for postherpetic neuralgia. A Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells) or viral titers can support the diagnosis. Check for herpetic keratitis. Other cranial nerves (V, IX–XII) can be involved. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 403-404)
canonical_layers.operate: Facial nerve decompression is not routine because evidence is insufficient. Persistent deficits are managed later with exposure protection, rehabilitation, chemodenervation, or facial reanimation according to recovery and denervation duration.
canonical_layers.teach: Ramsay Hunt generally has a worse facial recovery prognosis than Bell palsy. Ear pain plus palsy warrants a careful search for vesicles, but their absence does not exclude zoster sine herpete.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Radioiodine-Refractory Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. RAI-REFRACTORY DTC is not synonymous with 'any recurrence after I-131' and does not automatically mean 'start a TKI.' Establish that structural disease has lost clinically meaningful iodine responsiveness—for example disease that does not concentrate RAI, loses uptake, progresses despite appropriate RAI, or has mixed/nonresponsive clinically important lesions—and stop repeating empiric RAI when expected benefit is negligible and cumulative toxicity rises. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Do not treat radiographic existence alone. Stable/asymptomatic RAIR disease can often be monitored; oligoprogressive or symptomatic focal disease may be controlled with surgery, directed radiation or image-guided ablation to defer systemic toxicity. Start systemic therapy when disease is clinically meaningful, progressive/symptomatic or threatening and not adequately controllable locally. When no preferred actionable target exists, lenvatinib is generally favored over sorafenib as first-line multikinase therapy.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Key trap**: RAI-refractory DTC is not synonymous with "any recurrence after I-131" and does not automatically mean "start a TKI." **Definition**: establish that structural disease has lost clinically meaningful iodine responsiveness -- for example, disease that does not concentrate RAI, loses uptake, progresses despite appropriate RAI, or has mixed/nonresponsive clinically important lesions. Stop repeating empiric RAI when expected benefit is negligible and cumulative toxicity rises.
canonical_layers.localize: **Approach**: map the tempo and THREAT, not merely the number of metastases. Distinguish indolent asymptomatic lesions from focal disease threatening airway, esophagus, spinal cord, brain, major vessels, or weight-bearing bone, and from diffuse objectively progressive disease. **Imaging**: FDG-PET/CT can be useful in the classic Tg-positive/iodine-scan-negative setting and for biologically dedifferentiated disease. **Key concept**: a single enlarging lesion in otherwise stable metastatic disease may be a LOCAL-THERAPY problem rather than a reason to expose the whole patient to indefinite systemic therapy.
canonical_layers.workup: **Before systemic therapy**: confirm structural progression and its pace on comparable imaging, symptoms, performance status, prior RAI dose/uptake history, and whether surgery, external-beam/stereotactic radiation, ablation, or another focal treatment can control the threatening site. **Key step**: obtain comprehensive tumor molecular profiling BEFORE choosing first-line systemic treatment, because actionable RET or NTRK fusions and other targetable alterations can move a selective inhibitor ahead of a nonspecific multikinase inhibitor in the 2025 ATA framework.
canonical_layers.manage: **Key trap**: do not treat radiographic existence alone. **Stable/asymptomatic** RAIR disease can often be monitored. **Oligoprogressive or symptomatic focal disease** may be controlled with surgery, directed radiation, or image-guided ablation to defer systemic toxicity. **Systemic therapy**: start it when disease is clinically meaningful, progressive/symptomatic or threatening, and not adequately controllable locally. When no preferred actionable target exists, **lenvatinib** is generally favored over **sorafenib** as first-line multikinase therapy. Choose/sequence agents with endocrinology/medical oncology around comorbidity, prior therapy, mutation profile, and toxicity.
canonical_layers.operate: **Role of the H&N surgeon**: remains relevant after RAIR designation. Resect accessible locoregional disease when it offers durable control or prevents airway/esophageal/vascular catastrophe, and integrate focal surgery with radiation/ablation rather than treating systemic therapy as the only remaining modality. **Before invasive rescue**: define whether the goal is cure, durable local control, prevention of a specific complication, or palliation. **Key trap**: redifferentiation strategies that may restore iodine uptake are specialist/molecular-tumor-board decisions -- not a reason to give serial empiric RAI blindly.
canonical_layers.teach: **Chief framework**: RAIR is a BIOLOGY/RESPONSE state, not simply metastatic DTC. **Ask four questions in order**: Is the disease truly iodine-nonresponsive? Is it actually progressing or threatening? Can the important site be controlled LOCALLY? What molecular target should determine systemic therapy if systemic treatment is now justified? **The 2025 shift**: LOCAL THERAPY FIRST when feasible, plus MOLECULAR PROFILING BEFORE first-line systemic therapy.

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Confirm that reported 'strep' or sore-throat episodes were true qualifying tonsillitis episodes. Frequency alone is insufficient without severity features and documentation. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Below the usual thresholds, favor watchful waiting: fewer than 7 episodes in 1 year, fewer than 5/year for 2 years, or fewer than 3/year for 3 years. Tonsillectomy may be offered when ≥7 in 1 year, ≥5/year for 2 years, or ≥3/year for 3 years are documented with qualifying features. Consider modifying factors such as PFAPA, multiple antibiotic intolerance/allergy or >1 peritonsillar abscess.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Recurrent Tonsillitis Decision-Making. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: The classic error is equating 'seven sore throats' with seven qualifying episodes. Teach the 7/5/3 framework, documentation requirements, and the modifying factors that can change a watchful-waiting recommendation.

canonical_layers.recognize: Confirm that reported 'strep' or sore-throat episodes were true qualifying tonsillitis episodes. Frequency alone is insufficient without severity features and documentation. **PFAPA**: the most common cause of recurrent fever in children. Fevers of 38.5-41°C last 3-6 days, recur every 2-8 weeks with well intervals, and come with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis or cervical adenitis. Corticosteroids such as prednisolone stop most attacks within 24 hours, NSAIDs do not help, and tonsillectomy is an option for selected children with severe pharyngitis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, p 2982)
canonical_layers.localize: This is recurrent tonsillar/oropharyngeal inflammatory disease; distinguish it from chronic throat symptoms, reflux, viral URI burden, PFAPA and peritonsillar infection.
canonical_layers.workup: Reconstruct the documented episode history. A guideline-supported episode includes sore throat plus qualifying findings such as fever >38.3°C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate or positive group-A streptococcal testing. PSG is not a recurrent-infection test. **Strep diagnostics and carriers**: Rapid antigen testing is highly specific but has only moderate sensitivity (about 60-90%), so a negative rapid test should be followed by culture when strep is suspected. An ASO titer above about 333 Todd units, or a 2-fold rise, confirms recent infection. Titers peak at 3-6 weeks. GAS carriage affects about 5-40% of children. Carriers rarely spread disease or develop sequelae, so do not test children with clearly viral features such as cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, hoarseness or oral ulcers. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1199)
canonical_layers.manage: **Watchful waiting thresholds**: favor watchful waiting below fewer than 7 episodes in 1 year, fewer than 5/year for 2 years, or fewer than 3/year for 3 years. **Tonsillectomy may be offered when**: ≥7 in 1 year, ≥5/year for 2 years, or ≥3/year for 3 years are documented with qualifying features. **Modifying factors to consider**: PFAPA, multiple antibiotic intolerance/allergy, or >1 peritonsillar abscess. **When to treat strep carriage**: Eradication (e.g., clindamycin or rifampin-containing regimens), and tonsillectomy if that fails, is reserved for carriers with a family history of rheumatic fever, ping-pong spread within the family, a personal history of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, or a school outbreak. In the Paradise trial, untreated control children averaged only 1.17, 1.03 and 0.45 episodes in years 1-3, which shows how often recurrent tonsillitis resolves on its own. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy", p 1202)
canonical_layers.operate: When surgery is chosen, the advanced decision includes expected benefit versus postoperative pain, dehydration and hemorrhage risk, plus perioperative OSA/comorbidity considerations when relevant. The indication must survive chart review before the operation starts.
canonical_layers.teach: The classic error is equating 'seven sore throats' with seven qualifying episodes. Teach the 7/5/3 framework, documentation requirements, and the modifying factors that can change a watchful-waiting recommendation. **PANDAS criteria and the tonsillectomy question**: PANDAS requires OCD and/or tics starting between age 3 and puberty, an episodic course with abrupt onset or dramatic flares, a documented temporal link to culture-proven GABHS infection, and neurologic findings (motor hyperactivity, adventitious movements without frank chorea). Supportive features are remission on antibiotics, high streptococcal titers and clumsiness. Steroids, plasma exchange and IVIG have been tried. Tonsillectomy has been proposed, but there is no good evidence that it reduces symptoms or prevents episodes, so PANDAS alone is not a standard indication. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, pp 2982-2983)

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Allergy Testing & Interpretation. Recognize that a positive skin or serum specific-IgE test documents SENSITIZATION, not automatically clinically causal allergy. Testing is most useful when the exposure history and symptom pattern make IgE-mediated disease plausible and the result will change avoidance, medication strategy, diagnosis, or allergen-immunotherapy selection. Do not equate total IgE, eosinophilia, or broad screening panels with identification of a culprit allergen. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use results to change care, not to accumulate sensitization labels. Counsel avoidance only for clinically relevant exposures; optimize disease-directed pharmacotherapy and reserve AIT consideration for patients with clinically meaningful allergic disease plus confirmed relevant sensitization. Do not order serial skin or serum testing merely to prove that ongoing immunotherapy is working when symptoms and exposures are stable; the 2024 inhalant-immunotherapy guideline advises against routine efficacy retesting unless clinical circumstances change.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Allergy Testing & Interpretation. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Senior model: first ask whether the history predicts IgE-mediated disease and whether the answer will change management. Then select an interpretable test and require CLINICAL RELEVANCE before acting. A positive test without exposure-linked symptoms is sensitization; a negative systemic test with compelling localized symptoms may require phenotype refinement, not diagnostic closure. Testing is a decision tool, not a diagnosis generator.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Recognize** that a positive skin or serum specific-IgE test documents **sensitization**, not automatically clinically causal allergy. Testing is most useful when the exposure history and symptom pattern make IgE-mediated disease plausible and the result will change avoidance, medication strategy, diagnosis, or allergen-immunotherapy selection. **Key trap**: do not equate total IgE, eosinophilia, or broad screening panels with identification of a culprit allergen.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the diagnostic question before choosing a test: seasonal/perennial exposure correlation, upper-airway versus asthma manifestations, and whether systemic sensitization is expected. **Key trap**: negative conventional systemic testing does not by itself prove nonallergic rhinitis -- strongly allergen-linked symptoms can raise local allergic rhinitis, while NARES and nonallergic rhinopathy remain distinct competing phenotypes.
canonical_layers.workup:
Choose **skin-prick testing (SPT)** or **serum allergen-specific IgE** selectively. Skin testing provides rapid in-vivo assessment but requires interpretable controls and consideration of medications/skin disease that can blunt results. Serum specific-IgE is useful when skin testing is unsafe, impractical, or uninterpretable. Interpret either test against the clinical exposure history. **Avoid**: indiscriminate inhalant or food panels, and do not use total IgE or eosinophil counts as substitute culprit-allergen tests. When systemic tests are negative despite a compelling localized allergen history, consider specialist evaluation for local allergic rhinitis rather than simply labeling the patient nonallergic.

**SPT technique and positive criteria**: apply a drop of allergen extract and prick through it into the epidermis, always alongside a **histamine positive control** and a **saline/diluent negative control**. Read at **15-20 minutes**. A **positive SPT** is a wheal **at least 3 mm larger than the negative control**, typically with surrounding erythema/flare; a negative histamine control invalidates the test (antihistamine effect or technique failure).

**Intradermal (dilutional) testing**: more sensitive than SPT but less specific, with a higher false-positive and systemic-reaction rate -- reserve it for inhalant allergens with a negative or equivocal SPT plus a compelling history, and avoid it for food allergens given the anaphylaxis risk. **Technique**: inject a small volume (about **0.01-0.02 mL**) intradermally, starting several logs more dilute than the SPT concentrate (classic skin end-point titration protocols start in the range of a **1:500-1:1000 dilution** of the SPT extract), producing a small (**~4 mm**) bleb, then step up in concentration if negative. **Positive intradermal test**: a wheal that has **grown at least 2 mm in diameter** compared with the injected bleb, with confluent erythema, read at **10-15 minutes**. **Skin end-point titration (SET)** uses this stepwise wheal-growth pattern to identify a safe, effective starting concentration for immunotherapy, rather than treating a single dilution as simply positive or negative. **Safety**: because of the higher systemic-reaction risk, perform intradermal testing only where epinephrine and resuscitation equipment are immediately available, and observe the patient afterward. **Skin endpoint titration (SET) scheme**: Make serial 5-fold dilutions (1 mL of the stronger solution plus 4 mL of diluent). Pasha starts from a 1:100 w/v extract, so #1 = 1:500, #2 = 1:2,500, #3 = 1:12,500, #4 = 1:62,500, #5 = 1:312,500 and #6 = 1:1,562,500. The AAOA convention instead starts from a 1:20 concentrate, so its #1 = 1:100; check which numbering a question uses. Each intradermal bleb starts at about 4 mm and grows to about 5 mm when negative. A wheal of 7 mm or more (at least 2 mm larger than the previous negative) is positive. The endpoint is the first positive dilution that is followed by a confirming wheal at least 2 mm larger at the next stronger dilution (for example 5-5-7-9). The endpoint dilution is a safe starting dose for immunotherapy. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 38-39) **Test preparation and in vitro role**: Hold oral antihistamines before skin testing, generally for about 3-7 days depending on the agent (Pasha's 48-72 hours is too short for most second-generation drugs). Beta-blockers are a relative contraindication because they blunt rescue epinephrine. In vitro specific IgE (RAST/ELISA/ImmunoCAP) is indicated for dermatographism or eczema, high anaphylaxis risk, uncooperative young children, unstoppable medications, or equivocal skin results. A negative skin test alone is NOT an indication. In vitro tests are highly specific and carry no anaphylaxis risk, but they are less sensitive, slower and more costly. (Pasha 6e, Ch 1, p 38-39) **Medications that blunt skin tests**: stop oral H1 antihistamines 2 to 7 days before testing, depending on half-life. Topical azelastine, H2 blockers (e.g., ranitidine) and some tricyclic antidepressants also suppress the wheal and flare. Omalizumab must be stopped about 8 weeks before. Montelukast does not affect skin tests and can be continued. Contraindications to skin-prick testing include severe cardiopulmonary disease, including poorly controlled asthma. Do not test over active dermatitis. A large reaction at the negative control (dermatographism) makes results unreliable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 577) **Skin test rules and MQT**: SPT contraindications: uncontrolled asthma, unstable cardiovascular disease, current beta-blocker use and pregnancy. Space sites at least 2 cm apart; sensitivity and specificity are roughly 80%. In dilutional intradermal testing, never accept a #1 endpoint, because reactions at that strength are likely irritant. Modified quantitative testing (SPT followed by a single intradermal test) estimates the starting dose with fewer supplies. It correlates well with full IDT but gives a conservative, slightly weaker starting dose. Desloratadine can suppress wheals for 10-14 days, longer than other second-generation antihistamines (about 7 days). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1129-1132) **Intradermal and MQT criteria in Cummings**: skin-prick lancets penetrate about 1 mm and are read at 15 to 20 minutes. A single intradermal test is read at 10 minutes and is positive with a wheal of 7 mm or more that is at least 2 mm wider than the negative control. Modified quantitative testing (MQT) combines a prick test with one or two intradermal dilutions to find an endpoint, confirmed when the next stronger concentration produces a wheal at least 2 mm larger. MQT is faster and cheaper than full dilutional testing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 577) **Newer diagnostics**: component-resolved diagnosis measures IgE to individual allergen molecules. For example, Can f 5 is a prostatic protein made only by male dogs, and up to 38% of dog-allergic patients react only to it, so they may tolerate female dogs. The basophil activation test detects CD63/CD203c by flow cytometry and can help diagnose local allergic rhinitis. Nasal provocation testing helps when systemic tests are negative but suspicion is high. Nasal cytology separates allergic rhinitis (eosinophils, mast cells, basophils) from NARES and other rhinitides. Total IgE mainly flags atopy when markedly elevated. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 578-579)
canonical_layers.manage: Use results to change care, not to accumulate sensitization labels. If obstruction, polyposis, CRS, septal deviation, or valve dysfunction is present, decide surgery on the objective structural/inflammatory disease and expected benefit, not on the size of a wheal or a serum IgE class. **Key trap**: a positive allergy test should never distract from unilateral bleeding, mass, CSF leak, or other dangerous alternatives requiring separate workup.

Multi-test devices show poor reproducibility. Food testing is not indicated for isolated rhinitis without a convincing history of immediate reactions. Skin and serum testing are both sensitive but only moderately specific, so test only plausible allergens. Back skin is often used in young children. CN XII (tongue) is spared -- its involvement instead defines Collet-Sicard syndrome.
canonical_layers.localize: **Location**: the lesion sits at the jugular foramen itself, where IX, X, and XI exit the skull base together. CN XII exits separately through the hypoglossal canal. **Related syndromes**: adding hypoglossal (XII) involvement to this picture is Collet-Sicard syndrome. Further extension into the retroparotid/parapharyngeal space with injury to the adjacent cervical sympathetic chain (producing Horner syndrome) is Villaret syndrome. **Typical causes**: glomus jugulare paraganglioma, lower-cranial-nerve schwannoma, metastasis, or skull-base meningioma.
canonical_layers.workup: Contrast MRI/MRA/CTA of the skull base characterizes the jugular foramen mass and its vascularity; paraganglioma workup includes catheter angiography and embolization planning when appropriate. Add direct laryngoscopy to confirm vocal-fold mobility and a formal swallow evaluation.
canonical_layers.manage: Decide between observation (favored for small, asymptomatic, slow-growing lesions, especially in older or comorbid patients, since resection risks worsening existing lower-cranial-neuropathy), stereotactic radiosurgery, or surgical resection based on lesion type, growth, and symptom burden. **Jugular foramen schwannoma strategy**: These tumors arise in the pars nervosa, anteromedial to the jugular bulb. Unlike the irregular erosion of a paraganglioma, they cause smooth, well-corticated enlargement of the foramen. A mainly intracranial tumor is removed most easily through a suboccipital (retrosigmoid) approach. Intraforaminal and dumbbell tumors need a Fisch infratemporal approach. Avoid transposing the facial nerve when possible, because of permanent weakness. Stereotactic radiosurgery has controlled more than 94% in several series. In one Gamma Knife series, 20% of affected lower cranial nerves improved and 77% stayed stable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, p 2682, Ch 179, p 2707, Ch 181, p 2753)
canonical_layers.operate: **Key trap**: vascular imaging is mandatory before biopsying a suspected paraganglioma given its hypervascularity. **Approach**: depends on the specific lesion (for example, infratemporal fossa approaches for jugular foramen tumors). **Danger structures**: protect the remaining lower cranial nerves and the jugular bulb/sigmoid sinus. **Perioperative plan**: plan for perioperative airway/aspiration management (possible vocal-fold medialization, feeding plan) since resection can worsen voice and swallow function.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR). Chronic hoarseness, throat clearing, globus, cough, or irritation may be reflux-associated, but this symptom cluster is nonspecific and commonly overlaps allergy, voice-use, sensory neuropathy, and other laryngeal disorders. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Use meal timing, weight and trigger modification when relevant. A time-limited PPI trial is reasonable when typical GERD symptoms coexist, but response is not diagnostic; stop escalation and reconsider the phenotype when treatment fails. Perform laryngeal examination and assess competing causes and alarm features. Posterior erythema or edema alone cannot diagnose LPR. For isolated extraesophageal symptoms without typical GERD, favor objective ambulatory reflux testing before prolonged PPI therapy; tailor endoscopy to GI indications.

canonical_layers.recognize: Chronic hoarseness, throat clearing, globus, cough, or irritation may be reflux-associated, but this symptom cluster is nonspecific and commonly overlaps allergy, voice-use, sensory neuropathy, and other laryngeal disorders.
canonical_layers.localize: Proximal refluxate exposure may injure pharyngolaryngeal mucosa, but no symptom or laryngoscopic sign uniquely localizes symptoms to reflux.
canonical_layers.workup: Perform laryngeal examination and assess competing causes and alarm features. Posterior erythema or edema alone cannot diagnose LPR. For isolated extraesophageal symptoms without typical GERD, favor objective ambulatory reflux testing before prolonged PPI therapy; tailor endoscopy to GI indications. **Validated LPR scores**: Reflux Symptom Index has 9 items scored 0-5 (total 0-45), abnormal >13; Reflux Finding Score has 8 laryngoscopic items (subglottic edema/pseudosulcus, ventricular obliteration, erythema, fold edema, diffuse edema, posterior commissure hypertrophy, granuloma, thick mucus) scored 0-26, abnormal >7. Dual-probe pH testing places probes 5 cm above the LES and just above the UES; DeMeester score >14.7 is abnormal; impedance detects nonacid and gaseous reflux. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 91-92, 117) **pH testing numbers**: a reflux event is esophageal pH below 4.0 (pepsin is active below this); the key metric is percent time pH below 4, abnormal when over about 4.2% of the study. Distal probe sits 5 cm above the manometric LES; proximal esophageal probe 15–20 cm above the LES (normal under 1%); hypopharyngeal probe 2 cm above the UES (more than 2–3 events abnormal). Off-therapy testing requires stopping PPI for 1 week, H2 blockers 48 hours, antacids 2 hours. Wireless (Bravo) capsule is placed 6 cm above the GEJ and records 48–96 hours. Impedance-pH detects nonacid and gas reflux. Symptom index of 50% or more indicates good correlation. pH studies are normal in about 25% of erosive esophagitis and only about 50% of patients with laryngeal 'reflux' signs have abnormal acid exposure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 969–972, 980) **Testing specifics**: dual-probe hypopharyngeal-esophageal impedance-pH (HEMII-pH) is abnormal with 6 or more proximal esophageal or 2 or more hypopharyngeal events. GI reports that use distal GERD norms may miss LPR. The Bravo capsule detects acid only. The oropharyngeal (Restech) probe does not directly measure reflux events. Barium swallow and EGD do not diagnose LPR. This chapter calls an RSI over 10 abnormal, but the validated cutoff is over 13. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Laryngopharyngeal Reflux Disease", p 64)
canonical_layers.manage: Use meal timing, weight and trigger modification when relevant. A time-limited PPI trial is reasonable when typical GERD symptoms coexist, but response is not diagnostic; stop escalation and reconsider the phenotype when treatment fails. **Medication pearls**: PPIs taken 30-60 minutes before meals (twice daily if needed); H2 blockers for uncomplicated GERD; prokinetics (metoclopramide raises LES pressure but risks tardive dyskinesia; erythromycin is a motilin agonist); sucralfate coats ulcerated mucosa; liquid antacids after meals for mild disease. Agents that lower LES tone include nitrates, calcium channel blockers, beta-agonists, alcohol, nicotine, chocolate, fat, and mint. Fundoplication success is best predicted by prior response to acid suppression. (Pasha 6e, Ch 2, pp 115, 117-118) **Evidence pearls**: 87% of healthy volunteers had at least one 'reflux' laryngeal sign (interarytenoid bar, medial arytenoid erythema, posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning), so findings are nonspecific. Recommended approach: empiric twice-daily PPI, taper to daily on response; pH/impedance testing if no response. PPIs heal erosive esophagitis in about 90% and keep remission in 80% (H2 blockers about 50%). GERD is the third most common cause of chronic cough (after postnasal drip and asthma; about 21%), and 43–75% of such patients lack heartburn; a PPI trial for cough should last about 3 months. Antireflux surgery is not advised for PPI-unresponsive patients without objective acid or nonacid reflux. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 979–981) **PPI nuances**: about 36% of empiric-PPI failures still have nonacid LPR, so treatment failure does not exclude reflux. Taper PPIs, because about 25% get rebound acid hypersecretion. Alginates help nonacid reflux. Fundoplication chosen by full-column impedance helps about 80%. Consider Barrett screening even without heartburn. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Laryngopharyngeal Reflux Disease", p 63)
canonical_layers.operate: Antireflux surgery is reserved for objectively proven reflux with appropriate symptom correlation and foregut evaluation, not unexplained throat symptoms alone.
canonical_layers.teach: Avoid turning nonspecific throat symptoms or erythema into a reflex diagnosis. Establish whether reflux is objectively or clinically plausible before committing to long-term acid suppression.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Keratosis Obturans. Keratosis obturans is accumulation of a dense laminated keratin plug within the external auditory canal, typically causing marked otalgia, aural fullness, and conductive hearing loss. Removal may reveal a widened or ballooned bony canal with inflamed epithelium. It can be unilateral or bilateral and has reported associations with chronic sinus/pulmonary disease such as bronchiectasis, but the diagnosis rests on the canal phenotype rather than an associated condition. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: The mainstay is meticulous removal of accumulated keratin under microscopy, often staged when the canal is exquisitely painful or inflamed, followed by topical anti-inflammatory treatment when indicated and scheduled aural toilet because recurrence is common. Avoid traumatic blind removal that strips canal epithelium. Patients with recurrent disease need a long-term cleaning plan rather than repeated treatment as bacterial otitis externa. Diagnosis is usually made by otomicroscopy during careful removal of the keratin plug.

candidates.board_pearl: Keratosis obturans is plug-and-widening disease; EACC is focal erosion disease. canonical_layers.recognize: **Definition**: keratosis obturans is accumulation of a dense laminated keratin plug within the external auditory canal, typically causing marked otalgia, aural fullness, and conductive hearing loss. Removal may reveal a widened or ballooned bony canal with inflamed epithelium. It can be unilateral or bilateral and has reported associations with chronic sinus/pulmonary disease such as bronchiectasis. **Key trap**: the diagnosis rests on the canal phenotype rather than an associated condition.
canonical_layers.localize: **Process**: abnormal epithelial migration and keratin accumulation throughout the canal, rather than a single focal erosive pocket. The canal may become diffusely and smoothly widened from chronic pressure. The tympanic membrane can be obscured by the plug but is not the primary site of disease. **Key trap**: focal sequestration and localized bone destruction should shift concern toward EACC or another destructive canal process.
canonical_layers.workup: **Diagnosis**: usually made by otomicroscopy during careful removal of the keratin plug. Audiometry can document conductive loss when hearing symptoms are significant. **CT**: not required for every straightforward case, but useful when debridement is incomplete, anatomy is atypical, there is focal erosion or granulation, recurrent severe disease, or concern for EACC, canal stenosis, malignancy, or middle-ear extension.
canonical_layers.manage: **Mainstay**: meticulous removal of accumulated keratin under microscopy, often staged when the canal is exquisitely painful or inflamed, followed by topical anti-inflammatory treatment when indicated and scheduled aural toilet, because recurrence is common. **Key trap**: avoid traumatic blind removal that strips canal epithelium. Patients with recurrent disease need a long-term cleaning plan rather than repeated treatment as bacterial otitis externa. **Topical regimen**: Keratosis obturans is usually bilateral and seen in young and middle-aged patients. Removing a long-standing cast can be painful and may need repeated sessions. Between debridements, agents that slow epithelial turnover or soften the keratin reduce how fast it builds up: steroid drops, mineral oil, acetic-acid rinses, a betamethasone-urea preparation, and topical 5-fluorouracil. Under the cast the canal skin looks shiny, red and atrophic. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 622)
canonical_layers.operate: **Management**: most keratosis obturans is managed nonoperatively with serial debridement. **Surgical option**: canalplasty or meatoplasty is reserved for unusual refractory cases in which anatomic narrowing, repeated severe accumulation, or inability to maintain a clean self-draining canal defeats conservative care. **Key trap**: the presence of true focal bony necrosis/erosion should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis before labeling the case refractory keratosis obturans.

Both contain keratin and can cause conductive loss, so the distinction comes from the canal wall after the debris is removed: diffuse smooth widening favors keratosis obturans, while localized osteitis, sequestration, or a focal crater favors EACC.

candidates.prompt: A patient's presentation is consistent with Sialolithiasis. Recognize salivary duct obstruction from the history before reaching for imaging. The classic presentation is recurrent unilateral submandibular swelling and colicky pain that begins or worsens with meals as stimulated saliva backs up behind an obstruction. Examine the floor of mouth and Wharton duct for a palpable stone, reduced salivary flow, or turbid/purulent saliva. Fever, persistent tenderness, erythema, or pus suggests secondary acute bacterial sialadenitis on top of the obstruction rather than uncomplicated stone disease. PAROTID STONES: parotid (Stensen duct) stones are far less common than submandibular stones (roughly 80-90% of sialoliths are submandibular) because parotid saliva is more serous/less mucinous and Stensen duct has no antigravity segment. They present with the same meal-provoked pattern but as preauricular/cheek swelling; palpate along the duct's course from the papilla opposite the second maxillary molar back across the masseter. What is the initial recognition and management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
candidates.answer_text: Match treatment to obstruction and infection rather than excising the gland by habit. During uncomplicated episodes, hydration, gland massage, warm compresses, analgesia, and sialogogues can improve flow. Superimposed suppurative sialadenitis needs appropriate antibiotics and drainage/source control if an abscess forms. Definitive treatment is gland-preserving whenever feasible: distal palpable submandibular stones are often removed transorally; mobile small duct stones may be retrieved endoscopically; proximal/hilar disease may require sialendoscopy-assisted or combined transoral approaches.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Sialolithiasis. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Boards/chief framework: MEAL-RELATED swelling means think obstruction; PUS means obstruction may now be infected. First localize distal versus hilar/proximal disease, then choose the least destructive route that clears the obstruction. Modern management is gland-preserving: a submandibular stone is not synonymous with submandibular gland excision.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Approach**: recognize salivary duct obstruction from the history before reaching for imaging. **Classic presentation**: recurrent unilateral submandibular swelling and colicky pain that begins or worsens with meals, as stimulated saliva backs up behind an obstruction. **Exam**: examine the floor of mouth and Wharton duct for a palpable stone, reduced salivary flow, or turbid/purulent saliva. **Infection clue**: fever, persistent tenderness, erythema, or pus suggests secondary acute bacterial sialadenitis on top of the obstruction rather than uncomplicated stone disease. **Parotid stones**: parotid (Stensen duct) stones are far less common than submandibular stones -- roughly **80-90%** of sialoliths are submandibular -- because parotid saliva is more serous/less mucinous and Stensen duct has no antigravity segment. They present with the same meal-provoked pattern but as preauricular/cheek swelling. Palpate along the duct's course from the papilla opposite the second maxillary molar back across the masseter.
canonical_layers.localize: **Approach**: localize the obstruction by gland, duct segment, and cause. **Why submandibular stones predominate**: Wharton duct is long and ascends against gravity, and submandibular saliva is relatively mucinous and mineral rich. **Stone location**: anterior/distal duct stones may be palpable in the floor of mouth; hilar/proximal stones sit near the posterior mylohyoid border and gland. **Key trap**: not every obstructed gland contains a stone -- duct stenosis, mucus plugs, scar, or less commonly a mass can produce the same meal-provoked physiology. **Parotid anatomy**: Stensen duct runs across the masseter, then turns medially through buccinator to pierce the buccal mucosa. Parotid stones can lodge anywhere from the papilla to the hilum. **Decisive difference**: the facial nerve's buccal and zygomatic branches interdigitate directly over and around the parotid gland and duct, so any open approach aimed at the duct or gland carries a facial-nerve risk that transoral Wharton duct surgery does not share.
canonical_layers.workup: **Exam**: evaluate the duct and gland deliberately -- inspect the papilla, bimanually palpate the entire floor of mouth, and massage the gland while observing the quantity and quality of saliva. **Imaging**: ultrasound is a useful radiation-free first study for many stones and gland inflammation. Thin-cut noncontrast CT is highly sensitive for calcified stones and helps when the stone is deep, proximal, multiple, or the diagnosis is uncertain. Contrast CT is favored when abscess or deep-space infection is a concern. **When imaging is negative**: persistent obstructive symptoms with negative stone imaging should prompt consideration of stenosis or another ductal lesion, often evaluated directly with sialendoscopy. **Parotid stones**: the same ultrasound-first, CT-when-needed approach applies. Define stone size, mobility, number, and distance from the papilla, since these determine whether pure endoscopic retrieval is realistic for either gland. **Textbook stone numbers**: about 80-90% of stones form in the submandibular gland. About 90% of submandibular stones are radiopaque and about 90% of parotid stones are radiolucent, so plain films miss most parotid stones. Use ultrasound or noncontrast CT. Gout (urate stones) and smoking are associations. Sialendoscopic basket retrieval works for small stones (about 3 mm or less in the parotid, 4 mm or less in the submandibular gland). Stones of about 5-10 mm usually need intraductal laser or mechanical fragmentation. Palpable stones over about 1 cm near the hilum are removed transorally, and the gland is excised for intraparenchymal or multiple stones not reachable transorally. Sialography is contraindicated during acute infection. (Pasha 6e, Ch 5, pp 202, 204)
canonical_layers.manage: **Principle**: match treatment to obstruction and infection rather than excising the gland by habit. **Uncomplicated episodes**: hydration, gland massage, warm compresses, analgesia, and sialogogues can improve flow. **Infection**: superimposed suppurative sialadenitis needs appropriate antibiotics and drainage/source control if an abscess forms. **Gland-preserving options**: definitive treatment is gland-preserving whenever feasible. Distal palpable submandibular stones are often removed transorally. Mobile small duct stones may be retrieved endoscopically. Proximal/hilar disease may require sialendoscopy-assisted or combined transoral approaches. **Parotid-specific management**: escalate from least to most invasive rather than defaulting to open surgery. Sialendoscopy is first-line definitive treatment for accessible parotid stones. **Why open sialolithotomy is a poor choice for parotid stones** (incising the duct to remove a stone), for reasons distinct from submandibular disease: (1) the buccal and zygomatic facial-nerve branches cross directly over Stensen duct, so open dissection down to the duct risks facial nerve injury with no equivalent risk in transoral submandibular duct surgery; (2) only the short distal segment of Stensen duct is reachable without deep parotid dissection, so many parotid stones sit more proximally within or near the gland -- an open approach for a proximal parotid stone effectively commits to parotid-level dissection rather than the simple, low-morbidity duct-slitting used for distal submandibular stones; (3) duct injury, stricture, and salivary fistula after open parotid duct surgery are proportionally harder to salvage than after submandibular duct work. **Lithotripsy**: indicated for either gland when a stone is too large or too adherent/impacted for intact basket capture, rather than forcing repeated traumatic basket attempts that risk duct avulsion.
canonical_layers.operate: **Corridor selection**: choose the operative corridor from stone location and duct anatomy. **Transoral submandibular duct surgery**: identify the duct and remember that the lingual nerve loops beneath/around Wharton duct in the posterior floor of mouth -- proximal dissection therefore carries lingual-nerve risk. **Sialendoscopy**: can dilate stenoses, retrieve selected stones, and guide combined approaches while preserving the gland. **Submandibular gland excision**: reserved for selected irretrievable intraparenchymal/proximal disease, severely damaged glands, or recurrent disease not amenable to gland-preserving care. Its risks include marginal mandibular, lingual, and hypoglossal nerve injury. **Parotid stones**: sialendoscopic basket or wire retrieval handles small, mobile stones. Add intracorporeal lithotripsy (holmium or pulsed-dye laser fragmentation, or pneumatic lithotripsy) under direct endoscopic vision for larger or impacted stones, fragmenting them into basket-retrievable pieces in the same setting. Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL) is an older, less widely available alternative largely supplanted by intracorporeal technique. **Combined approach**: endoscopic localization plus limited transfacial or intraoral access with facial-nerve monitoring when a facial incision is used, reserved for very proximal or partially intraparenchymal parotid stones. Formal parotidectomy is the last resort. **Transoral stone removal indications**: The key questions are whether the stone is palpable and whether it is mobile or impacted. Absolute indications are failed sialendoscopy or conservative care, a palpable impacted stone, or a stone 5 mm or larger with no way to fragment it. Relative indications are nonpalpable stones, or a patient who wants one operation instead of repeated fragmentation. Contraindications are a fully atrophic gland, very deep intraparenchymal stones and multiple impacted intraparenchymal stones. (H&N Surgery Atlas 2024, Ch 18, p 183)
canonical_layers.teach: **Boards/chief framework**: meal-related swelling means think obstruction; pus means obstruction may now be infected. First localize distal versus hilar/proximal disease, then choose the least destructive route that clears the obstruction. **Key trap**: modern management is gland-preserving -- a submandibular stone is not synonymous with submandibular gland excision. A negative CT for stone does not end the workup when the history is convincingly obstructive -- stenosis and noncalcified duct pathology remain possibilities. **Boards/chief framework for parotid stones specifically**: escalate hydration/massage -> sialendoscopy alone -> sialendoscopy plus intracorporeal lithotripsy -> combined endoscopic-assisted transfacial approach with nerve monitoring -> parotidectomy (last resort). **Key trap**: open sialolithotomy is the wrong reflex for parotid stones, because it exposes facial nerve branches for a problem sialendoscopy usually solves. It remains reasonable for accessible distal submandibular (Wharton duct) stones, where only the lingual nerve, and only in the posterior floor of mouth, is at risk.
