candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. You are considering Audiogram Interpretation. First decide reliability, then air vs bone thresholds, conductive vs SN vs mixed pattern, symmetry, configuration, speech reception/word recognition and whether results fit the exam. When is Audiogram Interpretation the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
candidates.answer_text: Pair pure tones with speech testing and tympanometry; asymmetric SN loss or unexpectedly poor speech performance can trigger retrocochlear evaluation.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the workup layer of Audiogram Interpretation. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Never interpret a single threshold in isolation; the audiogram is a localization test.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Step 1 -- reliability**: reading an audiogram starts with test reliability (consistent thresholds, appropriate masking). **Step 2 -- air-bone relationship**: then assess the air-bone relationship at each frequency to classify conductive, sensorineural, or mixed loss. **Step 3 -- symmetry and shape**: then evaluate symmetry between ears and the shape (configuration) of the loss across frequencies -- flat, sloping, cookie-bite, or notched. Each of these narrows the differential before you even consider speech scores. **Degree of hearing loss and masking numbers**: Adult degree categories used by Pasha: ≤25 dB normal, 26–40 mild, 41–55 moderate, 56–70 moderately severe, 71–90 severe, ≥91 profound. Interaural attenuation is about 70 dB for insert earphones, about 40 dB for supra-aural earphones, and 0 dB for bone conduction. The maximal pure conductive loss is about 60 dB (as with ossicular discontinuity behind an intact drum); a gap beyond that implies a sensorineural component. Rollover (word score falling at higher intensity) and tone decay suggest retrocochlear disease. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 349–350) **Pseudohypacusis checks**: SRT and the 500/1000/2000-Hz PTA should agree within about 5 dB. An SRT much better than the PTA suggests functional loss, as do normal voice level and articulation in someone claiming severe bilateral loss. Every unilateral loss should get a pure-tone Stenger test. The same tone is played to the better ear about 10 dB above threshold and to the poorer ear about 10 dB below the admitted threshold. A patient with a true loss still responds, because the tone is heard in the good ear. A malingerer perceives the tone only in the 'bad' ear and denies hearing it. Many patients with functional loss also have a real underlying loss, so true thresholds still need to be established. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2037)
canonical_layers.localize: **Air-bone gap**: localizes pathology to the outer/middle ear (conductive component). **Bone-conduction elevation**: localizes to the cochlea or beyond (sensorineural component). **Retrocochlear red flag**: a word recognition score disproportionately worse than the pure-tone average predicts, or striking interaural asymmetry, localizes suspicion toward a retrocochlear process (e.g., vestibular schwannoma) rather than routine cochlear disease. **Behavioral site-of-lesion tests**: Largely replaced by MRI and ABR but still tested: tone decay over 25 dB, rollover ratio of 0.30 or more on the performance-intensity function, and acoustic reflex decay (amplitude falls by half within 5 seconds at 10 dB above reflex threshold, usually at 1000 Hz) suggest retrocochlear disease. Historic: SISI score of 70% or more indicates cochlear and 30% or less neural lesion; ABLB recruitment indicates cochlear; Békésy type III/IV indicates neural and type V pseudohypacusis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 280-281, 292)
canonical_layers.workup: Pair pure tones with speech testing and tympanometry; asymmetric SN loss or unexpectedly poor speech performance can trigger retrocochlear evaluation. **Pseudohypacusis tests**: Clues: test–retest variability beyond 5 dB, SRT more than 10 dB better than the PTA, present acoustic reflexes despite claimed severe loss, and no crossover (shadow curve) in a claimed dead ear. The Stenger test presents the same tone to both ears, louder in the claimed bad ear; a malingerer denies hearing anything because the sound is perceived only in the louder ear. The Lombard test (voice rises when masking noise is added) and delayed auditory feedback (speech disrupted by hearing one's own delayed voice) also expose functional loss; ABR/ASSR confirm true thresholds. (Pasha 6e, Ch 7, pp 353–354) **Tuning-fork estimate of the air-bone gap**: a Rinne negative only at 256 Hz suggests a gap of about 20–30 dB. Negative at 256 and 512 Hz suggests 30–45 dB. Negative at 256, 512, and 1024 Hz suggests 45–60 dB (Cummings 7e, Ch 145, p 2188). **When to mask**: Interaural attenuation is about 40-65 dB for supra-aural earphones, about 70 dB or more for inserts, and 0-10 dB for bone conduction. Mask the nontest ear for air conduction when the test-ear stimulus exceeds the nontest-ear bone threshold by 40 dB or more (70 dB with inserts), and for bone conduction whenever the test ear shows an air-bone gap over 10 dB. Use narrow-band noise for tones and speech-spectrum noise for speech. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 267) **Pseudohypacusis red flags and the Stenger test**: Clues: SRT better than PTA by over 10 dB, poor test-retest reliability (over 5 dB), acoustic reflexes at or within 5 dB of admitted thresholds, present OAEs (TEOAEs imply cochlear thresholds no worse than about 30-40 dB HL), a unilateral 'dead ear' without crossover responses, and half-word responses. The Stenger test (for interaural differences of at least 30 dB) presents a tone 5 dB above threshold in the good ear and 5 dB below admitted threshold in the poor ear; failure to respond is positive. False or exaggerated loss is about twice as common in children (typically about age 11, girls) and may signal psychosocial stress; ABR/ASSR estimates true thresholds. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 290-292) **Masking rules with numbers**: Interaural attenuation is about 0 dB for bone conduction, 35-50 dB for supra-aural headphones and 60-65 dB for insert earphones, and it is greater at higher frequencies. Inserts therefore let you mask harder with less overmasking. Mask air conduction when the test-ear air threshold exceeds the non-test ear's air or bone threshold by the interaural attenuation. Mask bone conduction whenever thresholds are asymmetric. For speech, mask when the test-ear SRT differs from the non-test ear's SRT or PTA by 45 dB or more, or when word-recognition testing is presented 45 dB or more above them. Unmasked crossover produces a shadow curve. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2024) **Speech audiometry cross-checks**: SRT (spondees repeated 50% of the time) should agree within 10 dB of the 500/1000/2000 Hz pure-tone average (use the best two-frequency average in steep configurations). Word recognition is tested about 25-35 dB SL above SRT to find the maximum score: 90-100% normal, 76-88% slight, 60-74% moderate, 40-58% poor, under 40% very poor difficulty. Conversational speech is about 50-60 dB HL, so presentation level matters when comparing scores. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 272-273) **Tuning fork details**: Use a 512-Hz fork struck gently (lower forks are felt as vibration). Rinne turns negative only once the air-bone gap reaches roughly 20 dB or more. Bing: occluding the canal makes the tone louder (occlusion effect) in normal or SNHL ears but not with conductive loss. Schwabach compares the patient's bone conduction duration with the examiner's: prolonged in conductive loss, shortened in SNHL. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 263-264)
canonical_layers.manage: Treat the cause when reversible; otherwise match amplification, surgery or implantable rehabilitation to type/severity and goals.
canonical_layers.operate: **Role**: the audiogram itself is not operated on, but it is the decision instrument for nearly every otologic procedure. It defines candidacy thresholds -- stapedotomy for a conductive/mixed loss with adequate cochlear reserve, cochlear implantation for severe-to-profound loss with limited aided benefit. It confirms whether a planned procedure is even addressing the loss present (for example, don't plan a conductive-repair operation on a purely sensorineural pattern). It also provides the baseline against which postoperative hearing results are judged. **Failure mode**: reading a single threshold or a single visit's audiogram in isolation and using it to justify a procedure, instead of confirming the pattern is reproducible, fits the exam, and is the kind of loss the planned intervention can actually be expected to improve.
canonical_layers.teach: Never interpret a single threshold in isolation; the audiogram is a localization test. **Degree scales and the AMA impairment formula**: Adults: normal to 25 dB HL, mild 26-40, moderate 41-55, moderately severe 56-70, severe 71-90, profound over 90; children use stricter limits (normal to 15 dB HL, slight 15-25). AMA monaural impairment = (average of 500, 1000, 2000, 3000 Hz minus 25) x 1.5%; binaural = (5 x better-ear % + poorer-ear %)/6. Percentages serve medicolegal purposes; descriptive terms better predict communication impact. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 276-278)

candidates.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. You are considering Tympanometry / Acoustic Reflexes. Type A tympanogram reflects near-normal middle-ear pressure/compliance; type B is flat and requires ear-canal volume interpretation; type C indicates negative middle-ear pressure. Acoustic reflex presence/absence adds information about the conductive pathway, cochlea, CN VIII, brainstem and CN VII. When is Tympanometry / Acoustic Reflexes the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
candidates.answer_text: Interpret tympanometry with otoscopy and audiogram. For a type B tracing, normal canal volume suggests middle-ear effusion while large volume suggests a patent tube/perforation; small volume suggests probe obstruction or canal occlusion.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the workup layer of Tympanometry / Acoustic Reflexes. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Never say 'type B equals fluid' without checking canal volume. Tympanometry measures mechanics; reflex testing interrogates a neural-mechanical arc.

canonical_layers.recognize: Type A tympanogram reflects near-normal middle-ear pressure/compliance; type B is flat and requires ear-canal volume interpretation; type C indicates negative middle-ear pressure. Acoustic reflex presence/absence adds information about the conductive pathway, cochlea, CN VIII, brainstem and CN VII.
canonical_layers.localize: A conductive lesion can abolish measured reflexes by preventing stimulus delivery or recording of stapedius contraction. Retrocochlear/facial-nerve patterns depend on which ear is stimulated and which ear records the response.
canonical_layers.workup: Interpret tympanometry with otoscopy and audiogram. For a type B tracing, normal canal volume suggests middle-ear effusion while large volume suggests a patent tube/perforation; small volume suggests probe obstruction or canal occlusion. **Quantitative tympanometry in children**: tympanometric width (gradient) and peak compensated admittance are the best single predictors of effusion. Width greater than ~200-250 daPa is highly specific for effusion, and peak admittance of 0.1 mmho or less strongly suggests fluid, whereas more than 0.6 mmho makes effusion unlikely. Width widens as disease worsens until the tracing becomes flat. Jerger letter types ignore gradient. Type C is sometimes split at -100 to -200 daPa (C1) versus beyond -200 daPa (C2). Compare canal volume with the other ear when a perforation is suspected. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "The Assessment of Hearing and Middle-Ear Function in Children", p 327-331) **Canal volume and reflex decay numbers**: Normal equivalent ear-canal volume is 0.5-1.0 mL in children and 0.6-2.0 mL in adults. Volumes above about 2.0 mL in children or 2.5 mL in adults with a flat tracing mean a perforation or a patent tube. In reflex decay testing, a tone 10 dB above reflex threshold is held for 10 seconds, and it is abnormal if amplitude falls to half or less within 5 seconds. Test at 500 and 1000 Hz, because decay at higher frequencies is common in normal ears. Absent contralateral reflexes with intact ipsilateral reflexes point to a lesion of the crossed brainstem pathways. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2025-2026) **Normative values and reflex rules**: Adult norms: static admittance 0.3-1.7 mL, tympanometric width 50-114 daPa, ear canal volume 0.9-2.0 mL (children 3-10 y: 0.25-1.05 mL, 80-160 daPa, 0.3-0.9 mL). A broad width marks reduced mobility, and type C is peak pressure below -100 daPa (adults) or -150 daPa (children). Reflex thresholds are normally 70-100 dB HL (about 70 dB SL). A reflex is absent if there is any significant conductive loss in the probe ear or over about 65 dB HL loss in the stimulated ear. Ossicular discontinuity can give an Ad tracing with a high-frequency-predominant conductive loss. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 274-276)
canonical_layers.manage: Use immittance to refine diagnosis rather than treating the tracing itself. It can confirm effusion, support ossicular/tympanic pathology and identify when additional retrocochlear/facial evaluation is needed.
canonical_layers.operate: Preoperative middle-ear assessment helps determine whether a conductive hearing deficit is due to effusion, TM, ossicles or ventilation. After tube placement, a large-volume flat tympanogram can confirm a patent pathway.
canonical_layers.teach: Never say 'type B equals fluid' without checking canal volume. Tympanometry measures mechanics; reflex testing interrogates a neural-mechanical arc.

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the ENT service. You are considering Evidence Interpretation / Outcomes Research. A paper can be statistically positive yet clinically unimportant, or clinically important yet underpowered. First identify the question, population, comparator, outcome and study design before trusting a P value. When is Evidence Interpretation / Outcomes Research the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
candidates.answer_text: Read absolute event rates, effect size and confidence intervals before P values. Look for selection bias, confounding, loss to follow-up, inappropriate comparison groups, multiplicity and whether the study is powered for its claimed conclusion.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the workup layer of Evidence Interpretation / Outcomes Research. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Teach: effect size + uncertainty + applicability beats 'P < .05.' A negative study without adequate power does not prove equivalence.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Outcomes Research; Interpreting Medical Data; Evidence-Based Performance Measurement

canonical_layers.recognize: A paper can be statistically positive yet clinically unimportant, or clinically important yet underpowered. First identify the question, population, comparator, outcome and study design before trusting a P value.
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the inference problem: diagnosis, prognosis, treatment effect, harm, or time-to-event. Match the data type and study design to the claim being made.
canonical_layers.workup: Read absolute event rates, effect size and confidence intervals before P values. Look for selection bias, confounding, loss to follow-up, inappropriate comparison groups, multiplicity and whether the study is powered for its claimed conclusion. **Validating a patient-reported outcome instrument**: a usable quality-of-life questionnaire must show convergent validity (correlates with measures of the same construct), discriminant validity (does not track unrelated constructs), reliability (stable scores when disease impact is unchanged), and responsiveness (scores move when disease impact changes). Global instruments (e.g., the parent-completed Child Health Questionnaire) are often paired with disease-specific ones such as the OM-6, which caregivers complete for children 6 months to 12 years with chronic or recurrent otitis, rating 6 domains on a 1–7 scale plus a 0–10 global score. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Outcomes and Evidence-Based Medicine in Pediatric Otolaryngology", p 61)
canonical_layers.manage: Translate evidence into action by combining magnitude/certainty of benefit, harms, patient values and applicability. Distinguish guideline recommendation strength from evidence level and recognize when observational data are the best feasible evidence for surgical questions.
canonical_layers.operate: For operative literature, ask whether technique, surgeon experience, selection criteria and follow-up make the result transportable to your practice. Surgical case series can teach feasibility but rarely establish superiority.
canonical_layers.teach: Teach: effect size + uncertainty + applicability beats 'P < .05.' A negative study without adequate power does not prove equivalence. **Intention-to-treat and validity trade-offs**: intention-to-treat analyzes subjects in the arm they were randomized to regardless of crossover or dropout, protecting the balance that randomization created. Internal validity (is the effect real within the study) and external validity (does it generalize) trade off: tightly controlled trials gain internal validity but may not reflect real practice. Power (1 − beta, conventionally 80%–90%) rises with sample size, alpha, and the size of the difference judged clinically meaningful. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Outcomes and Evidence-Based Medicine in Pediatric Otolaryngology", p 62–63) **Choosing the statistical test**: pick by independent vs paired samples and data scale. Independent numeric data use the t test (Mann-Whitney U if nonparametric); paired numeric data use the paired t test (Wilcoxon signed rank); dichotomous independent data use chi-squared or Fisher exact; paired dichotomous data use McNemar; three or more groups use ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if nonparametric); censored time-to-event data use log-rank with Cox regression for predictors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 2, p 14)

candidates.prompt: A patient is evaluated in laryngology clinic. You are considering Benign Vocal Fold Lesions. Benign phonotraumatic lesions are not interchangeable. Nodules are typically bilateral symmetric callus-like lesions at the mid-membranous striking zone and strongly linked to repetitive phonotrauma. Polyps are usually unilateral, often hemorrhagic or translucent, and may follow acute or chronic phonotrauma. When is Benign Vocal Fold Lesions the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
candidates.answer_text: Use flexible laryngoscopy with videostroboscopy when available to assess lesion morphology, symmetry, mucosal wave, closure pattern and surrounding inflammation. Ask about occupational voice demands, acute phonotrauma, smoking, anticoagulation, reflux/rhinitis symptoms and prior surgery. Persistent unilateral irregular, leukoplakic, ulcerative or vascular lesions require a neoplasm/dysplasia pathway rather than being labeled a benign polyp by appearance alone.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the workup layer of Benign Vocal Fold Lesions. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Boards/chief framework: nodules = usually bilateral and therapy-responsive; polyp = usually unilateral phonotraumatic mass; cyst = subepithelial stiffness with reduced wave and often a surgical lesion when symptomatic. The operative goal is not 'take the bump off'—it is preserve the vibratory cover while eliminating pathology.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Key point**: benign phonotraumatic lesions are not interchangeable. **Nodules**: typically bilateral, symmetric, callus-like lesions at the mid-membranous striking zone, strongly linked to repetitive phonotrauma. **Polyps**: usually unilateral, often hemorrhagic or translucent, and may follow acute or chronic phonotrauma. **Cysts**: subepithelial lesions (mucus-retention or epidermoid) that can markedly impair mucosal wave and are less likely than nodules to resolve with voice therapy alone. **Reinke edema**: a separate diffuse superficial-lamina-propria process strongly associated with smoking/irritants. **Granular cell tumor and laryngeal neurogenic tumors**: Granular cell tumor is a Schwann-cell-derived lesion most common on the tongue; the larynx is involved in about 7-10%. In adults about half show pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, so a superficial biopsy can be misread as squamous cell carcinoma; it is multicentric in 10-15%, recurs in 2-8% after endoscopic excision, and is malignant in 1-3%. Pediatric granular cell tumors favor the glottis and subglottis, and laryngeal neurofibromas (often with NF1) arise on the arytenoid or aryepiglottic fold, with plexiform lesions infiltrating and recurring, so subtotal debulking is acceptable. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Larynx, Trachea, and Bronchi", p 1646) **Rosen nine-lesion classification**: mid-membranous lesions are defined by morphology, stroboscopic wave, response to voice rest/therapy, and operative findings. The nine are nodules, subepithelial cyst, ligament cyst, subepithelial fibrous mass, ligament fibrous mass, polyp, reactive lesion, pseudocyst, and nonspecific vocal fold lesion. Nodules and reactive lesions respond to therapy; cysts, fibrous masses, and polyps do not. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Pathological Conditions of the Vocal Fold", p 25) **Symptom-to-lesion clues**: roughness points to free-edge pathology (mass, laryngitis); breathiness to incomplete closure (paralysis, ankylosis, dislocation, scar, atrophy); strain to hyperfunction (primary or compensatory for a gap); odynophonia to granuloma or MTD. Hoarseness that appears over seconds to minutes should raise concern for vocal fold hemorrhage (or a psychogenic cause). (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 2, p 11)
canonical_layers.localize: **Physiology**: normal vibration depends on pliable epithelium/superficial lamina propria over the vocal ligament/muscle. **Key point**: lesion depth predicts the stroboscopic effect. Superficial nodules/polyps may preserve some wave, whereas a cyst tethering the cover often creates focal stiffness and reduced/absent wave over the lesion. **Key trap**: a contralateral reactive lesion can develop opposite a unilateral primary lesion and should not automatically be excised as a second primary pathology.
canonical_layers.workup: **Initial step**: use flexible laryngoscopy with videostroboscopy when available to assess lesion morphology, symmetry, mucosal wave, closure pattern, and surrounding inflammation. **History**: ask about occupational voice demands, acute phonotrauma, smoking, anticoagulation, reflux/rhinitis symptoms, and prior surgery. **Red flag**: persistent unilateral irregular, leukoplakic, ulcerative, or vascular lesions require a neoplasm/dysplasia pathway rather than being labeled a benign polyp by appearance alone.
canonical_layers.manage: **First-line**: voice therapy, vocal-behavior modification, and treatment of relevant irritants are foundational, especially for nodules and many polyps. Observation is reasonable when symptoms are mild and the lesion is improving. **Surgical indication**: persistent symptomatic polyps/cysts, professional-voice limitations, or lesions with diagnostic uncertainty may require microlaryngoscopic excision. **Key trap**: steroids/antibiotics are not routine substitutes for treating phonotrauma or a structural lesion. **Capillary ectasia**: these dilated capillary arcades are seen mostly in female vocal overdoers, which suggests an estrogen effect. They lower vocal endurance and predispose to hemorrhage and hemorrhagic polyp. Stop NSAIDs and aspirin if possible; they do not raise hemorrhage incidence but worsen bruising. Control reflux and split practice into short sessions (e.g., three 20-minute sessions rather than one hour). If symptoms remain unacceptable, spot-coagulate the vessels every few millimeters; leftover dilations usually involute within weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 876–877) **Who decides and when**: elective phonosurgery should be patient-driven, with the surgeon as educator. Give one or two voice therapy sessions, reassess, and finish therapy if progress appears. The deciding question after maximum nonsurgical care is whether the patient can do what they need to do with their voice. Do not delay surgery for aspiration with dysphagia, impending airway compromise or concern for cancer. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 9, p 70)
canonical_layers.operate: **Goal**: phonomicrosurgery aims to remove the lesion while preserving as much normal cover and superficial lamina propria as possible. **Cysts**: careful microflap dissection reduces recurrence while minimizing scar. Rupture can make complete removal difficult. **Polyps**: remove only pathologic tissue and preserve adjacent epithelium. **Key trap**: excessive stripping creates scar/sulcus-like stiffness that may be more disabling than the original lesion, so postoperative voice outcome depends on tissue preservation, not just lesion disappearance.
canonical_layers.teach: Boards/chief framework: nodules = usually bilateral and therapy-responsive; polyp = usually unilateral phonotraumatic mass; cyst = subepithelial stiffness with reduced wave and often a surgical lesion when symptomatic. The operative goal is not 'take the bump off'—it is preserve the vibratory cover while eliminating pathology. **Pseudocyst and NSVFL**: a pseudocyst is a translucent, blister-like superficial lesion caused by glottic insufficiency (contralateral scar, paresis); treat by excision plus correction of the insufficiency. A nonspecific vocal fold lesion persists after therapy even though the voice has normalized; by definition it needs no surgery, only follow-up. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Pathological Conditions of the Vocal Fold", p 28) **Outcome counseling numbers**: well-done phonomicrosurgery for benign lamina propria lesions in a compliant patient improves voice more than 95% of the time. Improvement differs from return to premorbid ability, which is less likely. Resect conservatively and accept occasional repeat surgery rather than risk permanent scar. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 9, p 71)

candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. You are considering AOM / OME / Tympanostomy Decisions. Separate acute otitis media (AOM) from otitis media with effusion (OME). AOM requires acute symptoms plus middle-ear inflammation/effusion, classically a bulging tympanic membrane or new otorrhea not from OE; OME is fluid without the acute inflammatory syndrome. Recurrent AOM and chronic OME are different decision pathways. When is AOM / OME / Tympanostomy Decisions the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
candidates.answer_text: Diagnose AOM by pneumatic otoscopy/otoscopy rather than symptoms alone. For persistent OME, document duration, laterality, hearing status, tympanic-membrane structural change, speech/language/developmental risk and school/listening impact. Audiology is important when OME persists or hearing impact is suspected. Do not obtain routine CT for uncomplicated middle-ear effusion. Recurrent AOM candidacy for tubes depends importantly on whether middle-ear effusion is present at the time of assessment rather than episode count alone.
candidates.explanation: This check tests the workup layer of AOM / OME / Tympanostomy Decisions. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
candidates.board_pearl: Boards/chief framework: do not collapse AOM, recurrent AOM, and chronic OME into one disease. AOM is acute infection/inflammation; OME is fluid without acute infection. Tube decisions are driven by effusion persistence, hearing/developmental impact, and whether recurrent-AOM patients actually have effusion when assessed—not by a memorized episode count alone.

canonical_layers.recognize: **Step one**: name the middle-ear state correctly. **AOM** (acute otitis media) requires acute symptoms plus middle-ear effusion with inflammatory tympanic-membrane findings. **Classic findings**: moderate/severe bulging or new otorrhea not caused by otitis externa. A red TM alone is NOT AOM. **OME** (otitis media with effusion) is fluid behind the TM WITHOUT acute infection. **Key trap**: after AOM, an asymptomatic effusion can persist for weeks and should not be mislabeled treatment failure. **Recurrent AOM** is a longitudinal recurrence phenotype -- classically >=3 well-documented episodes in 6 months, or >=4 in 12 months with one in the preceding 6 months. Infection count alone does NOT determine tube candidacy. **Primary immunodeficiencies that present with otitis**: X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia is suggested by recurrent otitis with tiny or absent tonsils and cervical nodes. In CVID, recurrent otitis occurs in about two-thirds of children. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome has the triad of small-platelet thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent otitis, although only about 27% show all three. About three-quarters of hyper-IgE patients have ear infections, and some need mastoidectomy. X-linked hyper-IgM, polysaccharide-specific antibody deficiency (± IgG2 subclass deficiency), and neutrophil disorders also cause recurrent otitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergy and Immunology", p 128–129) **Pneumatic otoscopy details**: judge position, color, translucency and mobility. Effusion behind a translucent drum may show an air-fluid level or bubbles that shift with head position; a full, bulging drum obscures the malleus. Validated otoscopists achieve about 87% sensitivity and 74% specificity for effusion against myringotomy (target minimum 80%/70%). In the neonate the drum is nearly horizontal, the canal is filled with vernix for the first days and the soft inferior canal wall moves with pneumatic pressure, mimicking drum mobility; the drum takes an oblique position by about 1 month. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Methods of Clinical Examination: Ear and Related Structures", p 306-312) **Natural history of post-AOM effusion**: After treatment, 30-70% of children still have middle-ear effusion. The mean duration is about 23 days, and only 6-26% still have fluid 3 months after the acute episode. Do not retreat an asymptomatic child for persistent effusion, because this drives resistance. Most children still have fluid at a 10-14-day visit, so that visit is useful only if symptoms persist. A 2-3-month check identifies chronic OME. 'Relapse' (the same signs within 4 days of finishing therapy) counts as treatment failure. 'Recurrence' at 5-14 days is usually a new infection. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 695-696, 702-703) **Hearing loss with middle-ear effusion**: OME usually causes a mild to moderate conductive loss averaging 20-30 dB (range 0-60 dB, about 25 dB on average). About a third of children with effusion hear at 15 dB or better, and about a quarter have thresholds up to 30 dB. Thin and glue-like fluid impair hearing equally, while a partly filled ear (bubbles or an air-fluid level) loses less. The loss is smaller at 2000 Hz, so a 500/1000/2000 Hz pure-tone average understates it. OME is the most common reason a newborn fails hearing screening, but SNHL must still be excluded. Bullous myringitis carries a high rate of mixed or sensorineural loss and needs an early audiogram. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 761-763)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize the problem to ventilation/inflammation of the **middle ear**, then define the consequence. **Exam**: pneumatic otoscopy establishes effusion. Tympanometry is useful when the exam is uncertain. Audiology quantifies the conductive hearing effect. AOM is an acute inflammatory event; OME is a persistent ventilation/effusion state. **Look separately for structural sequelae**: progressive retraction, atelectasis, ossicular erosion, or cholesteatoma. **Also look for higher-risk Eustachian-tube contexts**: cleft palate/craniofacial disorders or other developmental vulnerabilities. These findings can change surveillance urgency even when the child is not acutely infected.
canonical_layers.workup: **Build a timeline**, not a diagnosis from one visit. For suspected recurrent AOM, verify that prior episodes actually met AOM criteria and document whether middle-ear effusion is present TODAY. For OME, establish onset/duration when possible. **3-month rule**: if effusion persists >=3 months, obtain age-appropriate hearing evaluation. Obtain hearing testing earlier when the child is becoming a surgical candidate or a developmental concern is present. **At-risk screen**: identify children at increased risk for speech, language, or learning problems because of baseline sensory, physical, cognitive, behavioral, craniofacial, or developmental factors. Routine imaging is NOT part of uncomplicated AOM/OME. Image when complications or another structural process are suspected. **When the otitis-prone child needs an immune workup**: suspect primary immunodeficiency when infections are frequent, suppurative, unresponsive to antibiotics, or caused by unusual organisms. Also suspect it with mastoiditis or other complications, or with other serious infections, severe eczema, or failure to thrive. First exclude common contributors (daycare, smoke exposure, allergy, anatomic problems). Initial screening is quantitative immunoglobulins, CBC with differential, and vaccine-specific antibody titers. Re-immunize children with low titers and remeasure after 3–4 weeks. Total protein and albumin identify secondary hypogammaglobulinemia from protein loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergy and Immunology", p 128–129) **Tympanocentesis and myringotomy indications**: Perform diagnostic tympanocentesis, followed by myringotomy for drainage, in these situations: a toxic or critically ill child; a suppurative complication (mastoiditis, facial palsy, labyrinthitis, meningitis), where a tube is also placed; failure of appropriate antibiotics with persistent pain or fever; AOM that develops while the child is already taking an effective antibiotic; neonatal AOM; and an immunocompromised host. Severe otalgia is also an indication for myringotomy. Randomized trials showed that routine myringotomy, alone or added to antibiotics, did not improve outcomes, and myringotomy with placebo did worse than antibiotics. The incision should span both inferior quadrants. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 694-695, 724-725)
canonical_layers.manage: Manage the **disease state** before jumping to tubes. Treat AOM pain. Choose observation versus antibiotics according to age, laterality, severity, follow-up reliability, recent antibiotic exposure, and allergy. Do NOT use chronic prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent AOM. **OME watchful waiting**: for uncomplicated OME in a child not at increased developmental risk, watchful waiting for about **3 months** is appropriate because most effusions resolve. Antibiotics, antihistamines/decongestants, and systemic or intranasal steroids are NOT routine treatments for isolated OME. **Chronic OME surveillance**: if chronic OME is observed without tubes, reassess every **3-6 months** until it resolves, significant hearing loss appears, or a structural TM/middle-ear abnormality is suspected. **AAP 2013 antibiotic-vs-observation rules**: give antibiotics for any AOM under 6 months, for severe AOM at any age (moderate or severe otalgia, otalgia 48 hours or more, or temperature 39°C or higher), and for nonsevere bilateral AOM at 6–23 months. Nonsevere unilateral AOM at 6–23 months, and nonsevere AOM at 2 years or older, may be observed with treatment if there is no improvement in 48–72 hours. First-line is high-dose amoxicillin (80–90 mg/kg/day). Use amoxicillin-clavulanate if amoxicillin was given in the past 30 days, with concurrent purulent conjunctivitis (nontypeable H. influenzae), or with a history of amoxicillin failure. For penicillin allergy use cefdinir, cefuroxime or cefpodoxime; ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg for 3 days is an alternative. After a second failure, consider clindamycin with or without a third-generation cephalosporin and tympanocentesis. (Pasha 6e, Ch 9, pp 590–591) **Allergy drugs do not treat OME**: controlled trials and Cochrane reviews find no benefit from antihistamines, decongestants, or steroids for OME, and guidelines make no recommendation for allergy management as a treatment for effusion. Children with proven hypogammaglobulinemia and poor specific-antibody responses need IV or subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement rather than repeated empiric antibiotics. Base antibiotic choice on myringotomy cultures. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Allergy and Immunology", p 128–129) **Tube otorrhea specifics**: a Gram stain with white cells suggests nasopharyngeal pathogens (pneumococcus, H influenzae, Moraxella), whereas absence of WBCs suggests canal flora (Pseudomonas, S aureus). Quinolone-steroid drops resolved tube otorrhea about 2 days faster than quinolone alone and cleared organisms better than oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (81% vs 59%). Fungi grow from only ~2% of tube otorrhea, and there is no proof quinolone drops cause fungal otitis. Otorrhea persisting beyond 7-10 days warrants drop-delivery check (tragal pumping), microscopic toilet and culture; beyond 10-21 days consider CT/biopsy for cholesteatoma, LCH, rhabdomyosarcoma or osteomyelitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otorrhea", p 432-440) **AOM antibiotic choices**: First line is high-dose amoxicillin, 80-90 mg/kg/day in two doses. It has the longest time above MIC against nonsusceptible pneumococci, and the high dose overcomes most intermediate resistance. The book also uses high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin with 6.4 mg/kg/day clavulanate) for severe disease (temperature of 39 C or more, or severe otalgia), which reflects the 2004 AAP approach. Under the current AAP 2013 guideline, amoxicillin-clavulanate is chosen for amoxicillin use in the past 30 days, concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, recurrent AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin, or failure at 48-72 hours, not for severity alone. About 35% of NTHi and about 90% of Moraxella produce beta-lactamase. For penicillin allergy use cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime or ceftriaxone. The book offers azithromycin or clarithromycin for type I allergy, but AAP 2013 notes that macrolides have limited efficacy against pneumococcus and H. influenzae. TMP-SMX is unreliable because of pneumococcal resistance. IM ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg) is given once, or as 3 daily doses for treatment failure. Clindamycin covers pneumococcus only. Give a 10-day course to children under 2 years and to those with severe or recurrent disease, and shorter courses to older children with mild illness. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 693-694, 703-705) **CONFLICT -- observation criteria**: The book's text (built on the 2004 AAP table) states that every child under 2 years with AOM should get antibiotics. The *current* AAP/AAFP 2013 guideline allows observation with assured 48-72-hour follow-up in two groups: children 6-23 months with *nonsevere unilateral* AOM, and children 24 months or older with nonsevere AOM (unilateral or bilateral). Nonsevere means mild otalgia for less than 48 hours and temperature below 39 C. Always treat infants under 6 months, anyone with otorrhea or severe symptoms, and children 6-23 months with bilateral AOM. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 693, 708-709) **CONFLICT -- antibiotic prophylaxis**: The site (in line with AAP 2013) says not to use prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent AOM, and that is the current guideline position. The book still presents low-dose amoxicillin prophylaxis as a shared-decision option for children with 3 or more episodes in 6 months or 4 in 12 months. In the Casselbrant trial of effusion-free children, prophylaxis cut new AOM episodes more than tubes did, but tubes gave the least total time with otitis media (6.6% vs 10% vs 15% with placebo). The book also notes that prolonged low-dose amoxicillin selects resistant pneumococci. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 696, 727-729) **CONFLICT -- antibiotics for OME**: The book recommends a 10-day amoxicillin trial as a shared-decision option before tubes for chronic OME, citing a modest benefit in a Pittsburgh trial. The current AAO-HNSF OME guideline (2016) recommends *against* antibiotics, steroids, antihistamines and decongestants for OME, which matches the site. Both sources agree that antihistamine/decongestant combinations fail (two trials in more than 1000 children), that systemic steroids clear fluid only briefly (benefit gone within 2 weeks), that intranasal steroids do not work, and that Politzer or Valsalva autoinflation was ineffective for chronic effusion in children. Antihistamines given with AOM treatment actually *prolonged* the effusion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 696-698) **Preventing AOM beyond antibiotics**: PCV7 cut overall AOM episodes by only about 6-7% but reduced tubes for recurrent disease by about 20%. Serotype replacement followed, and PCV13 (2010) added six serotypes, including 19A, and children now receive PCV15 or PCV20 under the current CDC schedule. AOM complicates up to 67% of influenza infections in young children, and both injected and live influenza vaccines lower seasonal AOM (AAP: vaccinate everyone 6 months and older). Breastfeeding for at least 6 months is protective. Xylitol gum or syrup works only if given five times a day for 2-3 months and is useless once a cold has started, so adherence limits it. Probiotics are unproven. No licensed vaccine yet targets nontypeable H. influenzae or M. catarrhalis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 199, pp 2963-2964) **OME adjuncts and limits of tubes**: Nasal balloon autoinflation used three times a day improved effusion clearance at 3 months in a UK primary-care trial of 320 school-age children, but the effect was modest and it has not been shown to reduce tube surgery. Hearing aids are an option for persistent bilateral OME when surgery is contraindicated or declined. Eustachian tube balloon dilation has no supporting evidence in children. The hearing benefit of tubes is modest and fades after about 6-9 months (the usual tube lifespan). Benefit is greatest in young children with heavy infection exposure (daycare) and older children with bilateral loss of 25 dB or worse for at least 3 months. Adding adenoidectomy helps most at age 4 and older and cuts tube reinsertion by about 10%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 199, p 2966) **AOM pathogens and beta-lactamase rates**: S. pneumoniae about 50%, nontypeable H. influenzae about 45% (a third to half produce beta-lactamase) and M. catarrhalis about 10% (over 90% beta-lactamase positive). Amoxicillin is first line; observation for 48 hours is an option for nonsevere unilateral AOM at 6-23 months and nonsevere AOM over 2 years; cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime or ceftriaxone for non-severe penicillin allergy; acute tube otorrhea gets topical fluoroquinolone drops alone. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 186) **Prevention for the otitis-prone child**: Offer the conjugate pneumococcal vaccine and annual influenza vaccine (both reduce AOM). Address modifiable risks: smoke exposure, pacifier use, and large-group daycare. For early-onset or severe recurrent disease, look for an underlying cause: submucous cleft palate, nasopharyngeal obstruction or tumor, allergy, sinusitis, and humoral or cellular immune defects. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 696-697)
canonical_layers.operate: **Operative handoff**: what phenotype + what current ear status + what consequence? **Guideline-supported pathway**: chronic bilateral OME >=**3 months** with documented hearing difficulty. Chronic OME with attributable vestibular, school/behavioral, ear-discomfort, or quality-of-life symptoms may also justify tubes. **Recurrent AOM rule**: it becomes a tube pathway only when unilateral or bilateral middle-ear effusion is present at the candidacy assessment. **Key trap**: a child with recurrent AOM but NO effusion at that assessment should NOT receive tubes solely because the historical episode count is high. At-risk children with OME likely to persist deserve a lower threshold for intervention. The separate Tympanostomy Tube Indications card owns the exact candidacy and perioperative rules.
canonical_layers.teach: **Chief/boards framework**: AOM = acute infection + effusion; OME = effusion without acute infection. After AOM, persistent fluid does NOT equal persistent bacterial infection. **For OME**, the **3-month clock** triggers hearing assessment and chronic-disease decisions. **For recurrent AOM**, the decisive surgical discriminator is not merely '3 in 6 or 4 in 12' -- it is whether **middle-ear effusion is present** when tube candidacy is assessed. This parent card follows disease over time; the tube card answers whether and how to ventilate surgically. **Otitis media and development evidence**: In Teele's Boston cohort, more days with effusion in the first 3 years (especially the first year) went with lower speech, language and cognitive scores at ages 3 and 7 (adjusted full-scale IQ about 113 with the least effusion vs about 105 with the most). Paradise's Pittsburgh RCT found that prompt tubes in otherwise healthy children under 3 with persistent effusion did not improve developmental outcomes at 3, 6 or 9-11 years. A benefit was seen in children already at risk for developmental delay. Unilateral hearing loss should not be considered benign. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 38, pp 764-768)

residual_candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Local Flap Reconstruction is being considered. Defect depth, subunit, exposed critical structures and tissue laxity determine reconstructive options. When is Local Flap Reconstruction indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
residual_candidates.answer_text: Design tissue movement and standing-cone management before incision; protect pedicle and avoid tension across free margins.
residual_candidates.explanation: This check tests the operate layer of Local Flap Reconstruction. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
residual_candidates.board_pearl: The reconstructive ladder is not a mandate to use the simplest technique when it gives a predictably poor functional result.

canonical_layers.recognize: For general facial local-flap decision-making, start with the defect: size, depth, vascular bed, exposed cartilage/bone/nerve, aesthetic subunit, free-margin involvement, skin laxity, scar orientation, and whether adjacent tissue can be recruited without distorting the eyelid, lip, nasal ala, brow, or hairline. **Key principle**: choose a local flap only when vascularized neighboring tissue can restore coverage with an acceptable donor deformity.
canonical_layers.localize: **Core principle**: name the movement before naming the flap. **Advancement** moves tissue primarily along one vector. **Rotation** pivots an arc of tissue into a defect. **Transposition** moves tissue over intervening intact skin. **Interpolation** crosses intact skin on a pedicle and therefore requires later pedicle division. Bilobed flaps are double-transposition flaps that redistribute closure tension and are commonly used for selected small distal-nasal defects. Rhombic and nasolabial/melolabial designs solve different geometry and tissue-match problems. The best flap recruits laxity from where the face can spare it.
canonical_layers.workup: **Sequence**: reconstruct from the inside out. Confirm oncologic clearance when applicable, assess depth and missing support, then mark relaxed skin-tension lines, aesthetic-unit boundaries, natural creases, and the intended tension vector before infiltration distorts landmarks. Ask whether primary closure, secondary intention, a skin graft, or a regional/interpolated flap would produce a better functional result. **Key trap**: a local flap is not automatically superior merely because it provides color-matched skin.
canonical_layers.manage: **Design principle**: blood supply plus tension. Preserve a broad viable base for random-pattern flaps, avoid unnecessary narrowing or torsion, undermine in the correct anatomic plane to gain mobility, and distribute tension away from free margins. Dog-ears, standing cones, and Burrow triangles are geometry problems. Pincushioning is favored by concentric scar contraction, thick subcutaneous tissue, and poor lymphatic drainage. On the nose, use bilobed or other local flaps selectively rather than allowing a convenient design to distort multiple subunits or retract the alar rim. **Delay phenomenon**: partially raising and replacing a flap increases total blood flow (not shunt fraction), reduces distal vasoconstriction, and develops collaterals through choke vessels. Benefit appears with as little as 24 hours, peaks around 4 days (no further gain to 14 days), lasts up to about 6 weeks, and still works in irradiated tissue. Nicotine impairs flap survival, an effect reversed experimentally by stopping 2 weeks before surgery. E-cigarettes appear similar. Hyperbaric oxygen helps compromised pedicled flaps only if started early (little benefit after 24 hours). A transcutaneous O2 rise of 50 mm Hg or more on a test dive predicts response. ICG angiography can show adequate perfusion for paramedian forehead flap division as early as about 2 weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 77, pp 1094–1098)
canonical_layers.operate: **Operate by vector**, not by memorized drawing. Size the flap after the true defect is known, incise cleanly, elevate without injuring the vascular base, mobilize enough that the flap reaches without excessive tension, obtain meticulous hemostasis, and inset the key functional edge first. Check eyelid closure/ectropion risk, oral competence, alar position, and nasal-valve shape before final sutures. **Key trap**: if the defect needs independent lining, cartilage/bone support, or substantially more surface area than adjacent tissue can safely provide, escalate reconstruction instead of stretching a local flap beyond its job. **Named geometric flaps**: the classic rhombic (Limberg) flap uses 60° and 120° angles with equal sides, placing maximal tension away from the defect. The Dufourmentel variant uses more acute angles for a broader base. Rotation flaps need a peripheral incision about 4–5 times the defect diameter and may use a back-cut or Burow's triangle. A-to-T (O-to-T) closure hides scars along the hairline, brow or upper lip. V–Y advancement lengthens tissue (lip, columella). Elliptical excisions need about 3–4:1 length:width with ~30° apices. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 447–450, 520) **Geometry numbers**: a rhombic flap suits defects with roughly 60/120-degree angles. Draw it from the 120-degree corner toward adjacent laxity. In a bilobed flap, the first lobe can be up to about 20% smaller than the defect and the second about 20% smaller than the first. On the cheek, base it inferiorly and orient scars in natural lines. A random transposition flap is classically limited to 3:1 length:width, but rich facial vascularity often allows more. Scalp rotation flaps must be large relative to the defect because scalp is inelastic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 21, p 313, 325-326) **Cheek and forehead repair**: an island subcutaneous-pedicle V-Y cheek advancement flap is designed with a surface area 1.5 to 2 times the defect. It can advance 2 to 3 cm, with 2 cm of undermining at the margins. Superiorly based melolabial transposition flaps recruit lower medial face laxity. For forehead defects, preserve brow symmetry and hairlines and prefer horizontal scars (except midline). Bilateral advancement (H-plasty) and O-T / A-T closures are standard. Large defects may need 6 to 12 weeks of tissue expansion before excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 21, p 327-329)
canonical_layers.teach: BOARDS/CHIEF FRAME: LOCAL FLAP = 'Where is the expendable adjacent laxity, what movement recruits it, what is the vascular basis, and where will the closure tension go?' Know advancement versus rotation versus transposition versus interpolation, and protect facial free margins from the secondary vector.

residual_candidates.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. A visible frenulum is not itself an indication for surgery; functional breastfeeding, tongue mobility/speech and dental issues must be demonstrated in context. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
residual_candidates.answer_text: Support feeding first and reserve frenotomy/frenuloplasty for selected functionally significant cases after shared decision-making.
residual_candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Ankyloglossia / Maxillary Frenulum. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
residual_candidates.board_pearl: Teach: treat function, not a photograph of a frenulum.
review_basis: Cummings 7e: Ankyloglossia and Tight Maxillary Frenula

canonical_layers.recognize: A visible frenulum is not itself an indication for surgery; functional breastfeeding, tongue mobility/speech and dental issues must be demonstrated in context. **Epidemiology**: only an estimated 15%–44% of infants with ankyloglossia actually develop breastfeeding problems, and the prevalence appears to fall with age as the frenulum stretches or tears, so the diagnosis alone does not predict dysfunction. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, pp 3069–3071)
canonical_layers.localize: Localize restriction to the lingual frenulum and distinguish true functional tethering from feeding mechanics, neuromuscular or craniofacial causes.
canonical_layers.workup:
Use feeding/lactation or speech assessment when relevant. **Key trap**: avoid anatomy-only scoring as the sole decision maker.

**Document** a functional feeding or articulation problem with direct observation and lactation/speech assessment rather than grading appearance alone. For breastfeeding, assess latch, maternal pain/trauma, milk transfer, weight gain, positioning, and alternative causes. **Key point**: an upper-lip frenulum is common anatomy and should NOT be released solely because it looks prominent. **Coryllos anatomic types**: type I inserts at the tongue tip, type II just behind the tip (both 'anterior' tongue-tie), type III at the mid-to-posterior undersurface, and type IV is a broad submucosal band restricting the tongue base ('posterior' tongue-tie). Because every infant has a frenulum, liberal use of this scheme can label nearly any newborn as tongue-tied, so it should not drive surgery on its own. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, p 3070) **Functional scoring tools**: the Hazelbaker tool (HATLFF) grades seven tongue movements (lateralization, lift, extension, spread, cupping, peristalsis, snap-back) and is thorough but cumbersome; the Bristol Tongue Assessment Tool (BTAT) is a quicker four-item, 0–2 point screen in which low scores mean worse function. In children over about 3 years, measure tongue-tip protrusion past the lower incisors and the interincisal distance with the tongue tip held on the upper teeth. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, p 3070)
canonical_layers.manage:
Support feeding first and reserve frenotomy/frenuloplasty for selected functionally significant cases after shared decision-making.

**Begin** with skilled feeding support. Consider lingual frenotomy when a restrictive lingual frenulum clearly contributes to persistent breastfeeding dysfunction despite conservative help. **Counsel** that evidence is strongest for short-term maternal nipple-pain improvement and less certain for long-term feeding or prophylactic speech benefit. **Key trap**: do NOT promise prevention of sleep, dental, or speech disorders without a demonstrated functional indication. **Maxillary frenulum and diastema**: a midline upper incisor gap normally narrows as the permanent canines erupt (around age 10); gaps under ~3 mm often close on their own (closure is 85%–99% likely at ≤1.5 mm and about 50% at ~1.85 mm). Labial frenectomy may be considered when the gap exceeds 2–3 mm after the lateral incisors erupt; timing relative to orthodontics is debated, and evidence for routine lip-tie release in infants is lacking. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, p 3075)
canonical_layers.operate: Procedure planning considers age, bleeding, salivary ducts, tongue musculature and need for simple release versus formal frenuloplasty. **Neonatal frenotomy safety**: performed without general anesthesia; minor bleeding is typical. Oral 24% sucrose is effective analgesia, whereas topical lidocaine or benzocaine should not be used in infants (FDA boxed warning for seizures and methemoglobinemia). Rare serious complications include hemorrhage with hypovolemic shock and submandibular swelling from injury to the Wharton ducts. Older children get a horizontal-to-vertical (diamond) frenuloplasty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, pp 3072–3073)
canonical_layers.teach:
Teach: treat function, not a photograph of a frenulum.

Treat function, not a photograph or score. Maxillary frenulum appearance alone is not an operative diagnosis.

residual_candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Prominent ear often reflects antihelical underfolding, conchal excess or both. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
residual_candidates.answer_text: Mustardé/Furnas-type concepts and cartilage modification are tailored to the deformity while avoiding overcorrection.
residual_candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Otoplasty. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
residual_candidates.board_pearl: Treat the anatomic cause of prominence, not every ear with the same suture pattern.

canonical_layers.recognize: Prominent ear (typically flagged by parents/patients as ears that 'stick out') most often results from one or both of two anatomic defects. The first is an underdeveloped or absent antihelical fold -- loss of the normal antihelical curve, so the helix sits more anterior and lateral. The second is excess conchal bowl depth/height pushing the ear away from the scalp. The two frequently coexist and produce different degrees of prominence at different points along the ear. **Other auricular deformities and thresholds**: a protruding ear has an auriculocephalic angle over 40° (normal 25–35°, rim 15–20 mm from mastoid, height ~6 cm adult, ~20° posterior tilt). Cryptotia buries the upper auricle under mastoid skin (Z-plasty/skin graft, or cartilage graft if severe). Cup/constricted ear has a tight helix and scapha needing helical-scaphoid release. Associated syndromes include Treacher Collins, hemifacial microsomia/Goldenhar, CHARGE and Down. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 491) **Epidemiology**: prominent ears occur in about 5% of white people. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance. The usual causes are an underfolded antihelix and a deep conchal bowl with a high conchal wall. The antihelix normally folds at about weeks 12 to 16 of gestation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, p 433)
canonical_layers.localize: **Reference points**: assess prominence at three levels -- superior helix, mid-ear, and lobule. Antihelical underdevelopment mainly affects the upper ear, while conchal excess affects the mid/lower ear. Measuring the conchoscaphal angle and helix-to-mastoid distance at each level localizes which component (or both) is driving the deformity in a given patient before choosing a technique.
canonical_layers.workup: Analyze deformity component and asymmetry before selecting sutures/cartilage techniques.
canonical_layers.manage: Mustardé/Furnas-type concepts and cartilage modification are tailored to the deformity while avoiding overcorrection. **Neonatal molding**: newborn cartilage is pliable, likely because of circulating maternal estrogen, so taping or splinting in the first weeks (ideally within about 6 weeks) can correct prominent, lop and Stahl ears without surgery. Treatment usually lasts 4 to 6 weeks, and as little as 2 weeks if started in the nursery. In one cohort, about 57% of newborns had an ear deformity at 1 week. Many deformities self-corrected, but protruding ears did not. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, p 435)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: functionally or psychosocially significant prominent ear, most commonly addressed in childhood but performed at any age. **Setup**: posterior approach with an elliptical skin excision. Examine and mark the deformity components (antihelical fold, conchal bowl) preoperatively. **Key steps**: for antihelical underdevelopment, recreate the fold with cartilage-scoring (**Stenström-type**) techniques and/or permanent mattress sutures (**Mustardé-type**) placed from the scapha to the concha. For conchal excess, reduce or set back the conchal bowl (**Furnas-type** conchomastoid sutures, or conchal cartilage excision) to decrease the helix-to-mastoid distance. **Danger structures**: the external auditory canal (avoid narrowing it with overly aggressive conchal setback) and the cartilage's blood supply, since over-thinning or scoring too deeply risks cartilage necrosis or visible sharp edges. **Failure mode**: applying the same suture pattern to every ear rather than matching the technique to the specific deformity component present, and overcorrection, which produces an unnatural 'pinned-back' or telephone-ear appearance and is difficult to reverse. **Postoperative plan**: a protective headband/dressing to prevent traumatic disruption of the new fold while it sets, and monitoring for hematoma (a surgical emergency for cartilage viability) or infection (chondritis). **Farrior technique and complications**: Farrior combines posterior cartilage wedge excision with mattress sutures. Reverse telephone deformity is undercorrection of the middle third or overcorrection of upper pole and lobule. Telephone ear is fixed by anchoring helical root to temporalis fascia and/or conchomastoid grafting. Best timing is age 5–6 when the ear is ~85% of adult size. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, p 492) **Technique details**: Mustardé antihelical sutures are permanent horizontal mattress sutures. Each takes a 4- to 6-mm bite through cartilage and anterior perichondrium, usually 1 to 3 sutures. Furnas sutures anchor the concha to mastoid periosteum. Place conchomastoid sutures before the Mustardé sutures, and rotate the bowl so it does not narrow the external canal. Partial-thickness scoring bends cartilage away from the scored side (Stenström principle). Incisionless percutaneous suture otoplasty is an option. Treat the lobule with a cauda helicis cut or skin excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, p 434-435)
canonical_layers.teach: Treat the anatomic cause of prominence, not every ear with the same suture pattern. **Otoplasty complications**: early complications are hematoma (which can progress to infection, chondritis or cauliflower ear), pain, infection and cartilage necrosis. Late complications are suture extrusion or granuloma, keloid, numbness (great auricular nerve) and cold sensitivity. Loss of correction is more common with suture-only techniques and usually occurs in the first 3 months. It can reach about 40%, so mild overcorrection is advised. Telephone ear comes from overcorrecting the middle third. Reverse telephone ear and vertical-post deformity come from technical errors. Asymmetry up to 2 to 3 mm is acceptable. Cutting techniques relapse less but cause more irregularities. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, pp 435-438)

residual_candidates.prompt: A patient is assessed in facial plastics/trauma clinic. Scar outcome reflects tension, orientation, inflammation, patient biology and time. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
residual_candidates.answer_text: Sun protection, silicone/pressure, steroid/5-FU, laser, revision or flap/Z-plasty based on scar phenotype.
residual_candidates.explanation: This check tests the manage layer of Scar Management. The reveal comes from the live canonical Deep Curriculum, so the question is testing the concept itself rather than a generic red-flag template.
residual_candidates.board_pearl: Do not revise an immature scar early unless function demands it.

canonical_layers.recognize: Recognize which scar phenotype you are treating before intervening. **Hypertrophic scars** stay within the original wound borders and often improve over time. **Keloids** extend beyond the original margins and can recur aggressively after excision. Widened, depressed, or contracted scars reflect tension, poor apposition, or free-margin traction rather than an inflammatory scar process.
canonical_layers.localize: Scar quality is driven by wound tension and orientation relative to relaxed skin tension lines, depth of injury, degree and duration of inflammation, and patient-specific biology (skin type, prior keloid history, anatomic location -- sternum, deltoid, and jawline are higher-risk sites for hypertrophic/keloid scarring than eyelid or upper lip).
canonical_layers.workup: Assess hypertrophic vs keloid vs widened/depressed/contracted scar and functional distortion.
canonical_layers.manage: Sun protection, silicone/pressure, steroid/5-FU, laser, revision or flap/Z-plasty based on scar phenotype. **Keloid protocol**: intralesional triamcinolone with massage every ~3 weeks. Excision only combined with steroid (excision alone recurs frequently). Pressure and silicone. Radiation for severe/refractory keloids. Pulsed-dye laser. Cryotherapy for small lesions. Risk factors are age under 30, darker skin (5–15% incidence in Black and Hispanic patients), and tension. Hypertrophic scars do not recur after excision. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 524–525) **Keloid regimen numbers**: excision alone recurs in 45-100% of keloids, so always add an adjuvant (steroid, 5-FU, radiation or pressure). Intralesional triamcinolone 10-40 mg/mL every 2-4 weeks, then monthly. Triamcinolone with 5-FU beats either alone. Silicone sheeting should be worn 8-12 hours a day for 6-12 months. Keloids are up to 15 times more common in darker skin. Imiquimod helps only ear keloids. (Cummings 7e, Ch 18, p 264-267) **Earlobe keloid after piercing**: The keloid usually sits on the medial (posterior) lobule with a core along the piercing tract to a small lateral opening. Excise the whole core sharply. Close the lateral defect simply and the medial defect in two layers, injecting triamcinolone into the subcutaneous tissue before closure. Follow with a few weekly triamcinolone injections to reduce recurrence. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 630)
canonical_layers.operate: **Indication**: a scar causing functional distortion (free-margin retraction, contracture limiting motion), or one that has failed nonsurgical measures and is mature enough to revise. **Setup/key steps**: nonsurgical management (silicone sheeting, pressure, sun protection, intralesional steroid or 5-fluorouracil, pulsed-dye or fractional laser) is first-line and should be given adequate time before considering revision. When revision is indicated, techniques are matched to the scar's geometry. Straight-line scars crossing tension lines benefit from Z-plasty or W-plasty to reorient them. Depressed/widened scars may need re-excision with layered closure and eversion. **Danger structures**: depend on location (facial nerve branches near cheek/temple scars, for example). The more general hazard is operating in the wrong phase of scar maturation. **Failure mode**: revising an immature scar -- typically before **12-18 months**, or before hypertrophic changes have had a chance to soften -- unless function specifically demands earlier intervention. Early revision on an actively remodeling scar has a higher recurrence/re-widening rate. **Postoperative plan**: continued sun protection and silicone/pressure therapy after revision, with reassessment of the revised scar over the following year before considering any further procedure. **Z-plasty geometry**: equal limbs and angles. Length gain is ~25% at 30°, ~50% at 45°, ~75% at 60° (classic), ~120% at 90°. Angles under ~20° risk tip necrosis, over ~75° create dog-ears. The new central limb lies along the line joining the free limb ends, and peripheral limbs should parallel RSTLs. W-plasty uses limbs under ~6 mm and is 'regularly irregular' (no length gain). Geometric broken-line closure (5–7 mm units, irregularly irregular) camouflages better. Use W-plasty/GBLC for long scars across RSTLs, along the mandible or hairline. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 521–523) **Revision timing**: Pasha allows revision either around 12 months (mature) or at 6–9 weeks (peak fibroblast activity), and earlier for an obviously misplaced scar. Other sources defer elective revision for 12–18 months. Teach both: elective cosmetic revision is usually deferred to maturity, but early revision is acceptable for clearly malpositioned or functionally distorting scars. (Pasha 6e, Ch 8, pp 519–520) **Revision technique and timing**: many unfavorable scars can be revised after the first 60-90 days, and early realignment may speed maturation. Scars otherwise keep improving for 12-36 months. Dermabrasion works best 6-8 weeks after injury or revision. Z-plasty lengthens by about 25%, 50% and 75% at 30, 45 and 60 degrees. W-plasty and geometric broken-line limbs should be 5-7 mm and do not lengthen the scar. Wait 6-12 months after isotretinoin before dermabrasion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 18, p 260-264) **Choosing a revision by scar orientation**: Simple fusiform excision suits scars within about 0-30 degrees of the RSTLs. Z-plasty suits about 30-60 degrees. W-plasty or geometric broken-line closure suits about 60-90 degrees, with GBLC preferred for long scars. Dermabrasion or laser can be added about 6 weeks after revision. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1051)
canonical_layers.teach: Do not revise an immature scar early unless function demands it.
